units.tr: Of birth, virtue and learning: to the noble man Rudolf Salice, senator of the Rhaetian order at Chur, my lord and long-cherished friend, whom I greatly esteem.

units.la: DE laudibus historiae Samuelis multi copiosè dixerunt & eleganter, ornatißime Salicae: ac vt nulli dixissent, omnium tamen sensibus & oculis expositum est, quantam illa rebus humanis vtilitatem afferat. Itaque in re satis per se commendata & aperta, non vtar pluribus verbis. Hoc verò non praeteriuerim, historiam Nabalis, quae vigesimo quinto capite prioris libri describitur, in hac non postremam esse. Habet enim complura animaduersione dignissima, & exulceratißimo hoc nostro seculo cumprimis accommoda. Nam (vt pauca tantum capita in transcursu attingam) primò ex illa colligimus, quod ad confirmandam fidem non parum facit: Pijs non semper ea, quæ cuperent, suppete- re: sed eos nunc his, nunc illis ærumnis ac ca- lamitatibus exerceri. Dauid certè, vir (etsi suos quoq; næuos habuerit) secundum cor Dei, Saulem habet hostem potentissimum: sed & in deserto summa annonæ inopia la- borat: Nabale interim, homine ebrioso, pla- neq; impio, omni rerum copia abundante. Videmus etiam, viros bonos, Deiq; amantes nonnunquam turpiter labi, grauibusq; flagitijs implicari. Dauid certè, ira commo- tus, non tantum inflammatur ad cædem, sed etiam excitat & incendit alios, quos ta- men antea ab omni insolentia satis repres- se rat. Nec dubium est, quin iusiurandum te- merarium & iniustum perfecturus fuisset, nisi Deus eum impediuisset, animumq; eius per Abigaelem auertisset. Elicimus etiam ex narratione ista ab Euclionibus, itemque ebriosis, qualis Nabal fuit, nihil recti, nihil honesti expectandum. Deniq; (vt multa alia prudens præterea) hinc cernimus, Deum interdum pios hac quoq; in vita sereniore vultu
units.tr: Many have written at length and elegantly in praise of the history of Samuel, most distinguished Salice. And even if no one had written about it, its value to human affairs lies open to everyone's senses and eyes. Since the matter is sufficiently commended and clear in itself, I will not use many words. I would not, however, pass over this: the story of Nabal, described in the twenty-fifth chapter of the first book, is no small part of that value. It contains many things most worthy of attention, and especially suited to this most festering age of ours. To touch on only a few points in passing, first we gather from it something that contributes not a little to strengthening faith: the godly do not always obtain what they desire, but are exercised now with one trouble and now with another. David, certainly, a man (though he had his own faults) after God's own heart, has Saul as his most powerful enemy, yet in the wilderness he also labours under the greatest shortage of food, while Nabal, a drunken man and utterly impious, abounds in every kind of wealth. We also see that good men who love God sometimes fall shamefully and become entangled in grave wrongdoing. David, certainly, moved by anger, is not only inflamed to slaughter but also stirs up and kindles others, whom he had previously restrained well enough from all insolence. Nor is there any doubt that he would have carried out a rash and unjust oath, had God not hindered him and turned his mind away through Abigail. From this narrative we also draw, concerning misers and likewise drunkards such as Nabal was, that nothing right and nothing honourable is to be expected of them. Finally (as the wise man notes among many other things), we see here that God sometimes looks upon the godly, even in this more serene life, with a kindly countenance,

units.la: Ruled out: none. vultu aspicere, ac præmijs cumulatissimè ornare: Dauid certè, exantlatis prope infinitis laboribus, tandem ad regni fastigium peruenit. Abigail, quæ diuturnam crucem, sub Nabale viro stulto, duro, & importuno pertulerat: cui tamen illa nunquam negauerat officium vxoris probæ: Dauidi matrimonio tandem iungitur. Quid multis? Quemadmodum lapilli quidam, etsi exigui sunt, insignes tamen habent virtutes: ita narratio ista referta est doctrinis salutaribus & consolationibus efficacissimis. Id quum videret Ludouicus Lauaterus, Tigurinæ ecclesiæ Antistes dignissimus, historiam istam peculiari commentario ante biennium illustrauit: in eo quoq; locos aliquot communes scitu dignissimos, vt de officio legatorum, coniugum, seruorum, iuramento, bello, homicidio, abijcienda vltionis libidine, ebrietate, polygamia, etc. breuiter quidem ac succinctè: sed perspicuè & solidè tractauit. Eum, quum nō sine magno, etiam doctiorum applausu viderem excipi, superioribus mensibus de voluntate ipsius auctoris ex Germanica in Latininam linguam transtuli. Nec tamen adstrin-xi me vlli seruituti, sed hoc vnum spectaui, vt quàm verissimè sententiam familiari, si non proprio semper, Latino sermone redde-rem. Alicubi exempla alia, quod in vtramq; partem vim habeant maximam, ex Græ-cis & Latinis Oratoribus ac Poetis adieci.
units.tr: and heaps them with the richest rewards. David, certainly, after enduring almost endless labours, at last reached the summit of the kingdom. Abigail, who had borne a long cross under Nabal, a foolish, harsh and troublesome husband, yet had never refused him the duty of a good wife, was at last joined to David in marriage. What more is there to say? Just as some small pebbles, though tiny, have remarkable virtues, so that story is full of salutary teachings and most effective consolations. Seeing this, Ludwig Lavater, most worthy Antistes of the Church of Zurich, explained that history a couple of years ago in a special commentary. In it he also treated, briefly and succinctly, yet clearly and soundly, several common topics most worth knowing: concerning the duty of envoys, spouses and servants, oaths, war, homicide, the abandoning of the lust for vengeance, drunkenness, polygamy and so on. When I saw that work received with great applause, not without the approval of the more learned, I translated it from German into Latin in recent months, with the author's own wish. Yet I did not bind myself to any servitude; I aimed only at this, to render his sense as truly as possible in a familiar Latin, if not always in his own words. In places I have added other examples, from Greek and Latin orators and poets, since they have the greatest force on either side.

units.la: Hanc autem qualemcunq; opellam nostram sub felici nominis tui auspicio ideò prodire volui: Primò, quod argumentum commen-tarij huius magnam partem tibi, præstan-tissime Salicae, cumpri-ùs conuenire, mihi visum est. Quid enim? Certè, quum is præ-cipuè contra fœdum quidem, sed nimium vulgare ebrietatis vitium dirigatur, tu ve-rò eam vitæ viam ingressus sis, vt iuuentus tua multorum senectuti exemplo esse possit,
units.tr: I wished to bring out this little work of ours, whatever its worth, under the happy auspices of your name, for this first reason: the subject of this commentary seemed to me to pertain largely to you, most excellent Salice, and especially so. For since it is directed chiefly against the foul yet all too common vice of drunkenness, and you have entered upon that path of life by which your youth can be an example to the old age of many,

units.la: ( Temulentiam profectò fœcundissimam plurimorum vitiorum matrem, si quis alius toto pectore detestaris: sobrietatem suauis-simam piarum cogitationum, ac in primis precum nutriculam, toto animo colis) nul-lus magis idoneus acquiri posse visus est, patronus. Deinde in scriptione ista nonnihil dignitatis ac splendoris versioni huic no-stræ accersere voli. Enimuerò, quùm non solum in urbe nostra, adeoq; tota Rhætia, propter amplam cumprimis & nobilem familiam, & ex qua ea Rhætica nationis lumina extiterunt, quorum claritatem nulla vn quam obscurabit oblivio, magno sis in precio: sed alibi quoq; permultis in locis ob singularem optimarum artium, principum item linguarum, Græcæ puta, Latinæ, Italicæ, Gallicæ, Germanicæ, cognitionem ac peritiam, sis notissimus: non dubito, quin, vel eo nomine, mea hæc translatio plurimis gratior & acceptior sit futura. Nolim tamen dissimulare huius nuncupationis quoq; cau sam non postremam fuisse, perpetuam dulcissimæ amicitiæ nostræ recordationem, quæ inter nos pueros in schola parentis mei, viri (absit invidia dicto) nunquam satis laudati, certè de iuuentute Rhætica optimè meriti coaluit: & in hunc vsque diem feliciter propagata: nuper mutuo compaternitatis, quam vocant, vinculo confirmata, in extremam vtriusque horam durabit.
units.tr: (you detest drunkenness, the most fruitful mother of many vices, with your whole heart, if anyone does, and you cherish sobriety, the sweetest nurse of pious thoughts and above all of prayers, with your whole soul), no one seemed to me a more fitting patron. Next, I wish in this writing to add some dignity and splendour to our translation. Indeed, you are held in high regard not only in our city and so throughout Raetia, on account of your ample and especially noble family, from which those Rhaetian lights arose whose brightness no oblivion will ever obscure, but also in many other places, for your singular knowledge and skill in the best arts and likewise in languages: Greek, Latin, Italian, French and German. I do not doubt that, for this reason alone, my translation will be more welcome and acceptable to very many. Yet I would not wish to hide that the cause of this dedication was not the least the lasting memory of our most sweet friendship, which grew up between us as boys in the school of my father, a man (let no one take offence at the word) never sufficiently praised, who certainly deserved best of the youth of Raetia. It has happily continued to this day, and recently it was confirmed by the mutual bond of compaternity, as they call it, and it will last until the final hour of each of us.

units.la: Tuum est, hanc meam προσφώνησιν non aliter, quàm abs me facta est, accipere. Me rebatur quidem tuorum in me meos q; collatorum beneficiorum magnitudo, luculentiorem aliquam memoris animi significationē. Sed, nosti illud Comicū; Vt quimus (aiunt) quando, ut volumus non licet. Maiora tamen fortasse alia subsequentur, si munusculum hoc, paruum quidem, at à magno animo profectum, tibi non ingratum fuisse cognouero. Quod superest, eum, qui voluntates hominum & cogitationes, quò vult, impellit, te ad ampliora diu ut seruet incolumem, etiam atq; etiam rogo. Curia Rhetorum. Calendis Maijs. Anno instaurata salutis CIↃ. IↃ. LXXXVI. Tui studiosissimus Ioan. Pontisella.
units.tr: It is for you to receive this my prosphonesin [προσφώνησιν] in no other way than as it was made by me. I thought indeed that the greatness of your benefits to me and mine would call for some more brilliant sign of a grateful spirit. But you know that saying of the comic poet: "We do what we can, since we may not do what we wish." Perhaps greater things will follow, if I learn that this little gift, small indeed but coming from a generous mind, has not been unwelcome to you. For the rest, I ask again and again that he who drives the wills and thoughts of men whither he pleases keep you safe for a long time, for still greater things. The Court of the Rhaetians, 1 May, in the year of restored salvation 1586. Your most devoted, Ioan. Pontisella.

units.la: PIETATE, PRVDENTIA, OMNIQVE VIRTVTVM GENERE PRAESTANTI VIRO, Matthiae Vualthero, amplissimae Reipublicae Bernensium senatori dignissimo, domino meo reuerenter colendo.
units.tr: To the man outstanding in piety, prudence and every kind of virtue, Matthias Vualther, most worthy senator of the most illustrious Republic of Bern, my lord, to be reverently honoured.

units.la: SALVERE te plurimum, vir clarissime, cupio, tibíque omnia mea officia & obsequia offero. Deinde te scire volo quòd posteaquam certis & mihi destinatis cõcionandi horis, libros sancti prophetæ Samuelis & Regum, pro mea tenuitate in templo maioris templi vrbis Tigurinæ sum interpretatus, & vsque ad historiam de vita & obitu Nabalis peruenissem, eam quandoquidem institutione & consolatione plena atque referta, nostrisque temporibus apprime accomodata videbatur, paulò fusius tractaui, & in decem conciones distribui. Postea quoq; meas obseruationes breuibus annotaui, & scripto comprehendi, vt eas in lucem edere omnibusq; familiares reddere possem.
units.tr: I wish you very many greetings, most distinguished sir, and I offer you all my duty and service. Next, I want you to know that, after I had expounded the books of the holy prophet Samuel and the Kings, to the best of my ability, in the great church of the city of Zurich at the hours set aside for my preaching, and had come to the history of the life and death of Nabal, I treated that history somewhat more fully, since it seemed full of instruction and comfort and especially suited to our own times, and I divided it into ten sermons. Afterwards I also set down my observations briefly and committed them to writing, so that I might publish them and make them available to all my friends.

units.la: Non quòd meos libellos hinc in de in bibliopolijs ostentandi gratia prostare velim, verùm vt Nabales temulenti, qui fortasis in lectionem huius historiæ incident, vel eam audituri sunt, in se ipsos descendant, & turpissimo ebrietatis & crapulæ vitio vitæq; impię valedicentes, pœnitentiam agant. Vt etiam honestæ & bonæ matres familiâs, quarum mariti dies noctesq; vino sunt obruti, & cum domum à poculis reuertuntur, ipsas cum tota familia miserè tractant, ex hoc præstantissimæ huius fœminæ Abigaelis exemplo, consolationem percipiant. Deinde etiam alia multa introduco, quæ à textu non aliena, & ad emendationem & institutionem vitæ nostræ valde sunt accomodata.
units.tr: I do not wish my little books to be put on display in the bookshops here and there merely to show them off. Rather, I hope that drunkards like Nabal, who may happen to read this history or hear it, will look into themselves, renounce the most shameful vice of drunkenness and carousing, and the wicked life that goes with it, and repent. I also hope that honest and good housewives, whose husbands are buried in wine day and night, and who, when they return home from their cups, treat themselves and their whole household miserably, may find consolation in the example of the outstanding woman Abigail. Furthermore, I bring in many other things which are not foreign to the text and are very well suited to the correction and instruction of our life.

units.la: Quamuis autem scribendi libros nullus est finis, ita vt illa copia librorum alicui haud imerito nausea parere posit, tamen semper quantum inter illos discrimen sit diligenter est considerandum. Quidam enim non ad defendendā veritatem diuinam & propagationem verae & purioris doctrinae, verùm ad ad oppressionem eius, ad disidia & contentiones alendas spectāt, qui merito sunt odio habendi. Alij ad explicationem sacrosanctae scripturę, & ędificationem fidelium pertinent, qui haud imerito legendi & magnificiendi sunt. Euangelium enim regni, sicuti Christus saluator noster apud Matth. prędixit, prędicabitur in universa terra, vt sit testimonio omnibus gentibus: & tūc veniet finis. At nō solū verbo verum etiā scripto prædicari oportet, in cuius rei gratiam procul dubio Deus pro sua immensa clementia, hisce nouis simis temporibus nobile illud chalcographiae beneficium nobis communicauit.
units.tr: Although there is no end to writing books, so that such a multitude of books may reasonably cause nausea in someone, nevertheless one must always consider carefully what difference lies between them. For some books aim not at defending divine truth and spreading true and purer doctrine, but at its suppression, at feeding quarrels and contentions; these rightly deserve to be hated. Others serve the explanation of holy Scripture and the edification of the faithful; these rightly deserve to be read and held in high regard. For the gospel of the kingdom, as Christ our Saviour foretold in Matthew, will be preached in the whole world, as a witness to all nations, and then the end will come. But it must be preached not only by word but also in writing, and for the sake of this, without doubt, God in his immense mercy has in these most recent times granted us that noble gift of printing.

units.la: Hasce autem meas conciones, ob feruandisfime atque charissime vir, pro more antiquo et laudabili in tuo honorifico nomine apparere volui. Primum vt veterem amicitiam & familiaritatem, quam ante quadraginta fere annos, in aedibus dilecti mei affinis Caroli ab Aegeri piae memoriae, cum quo tum temporis versaba ris, primùm contraximus, hac occasione renouarem.
units.tr: Now, most respected and dearest sir, I wished these sermons of mine to appear under your honoured name, according to the ancient and praiseworthy custom. First, I wished on this occasion to renew the old friendship and familiarity which we first formed about forty years ago in the house of my beloved brother-in-law, Karl von Aegeri, of blessed memory, with whom you were then living.

units.la: Deinde vt occasionem haberem, te sedulo exhortandi, vt quemadmodum dum hactenus ab ebrietate, in primis vero impia & impura vita, cui Nabal deditus fuit, alienissimus fuisti, ita illis vestigijs insistere pergas. Et quandoquidem te Deus ad tantam dignitatem euexit, illiusque beneficio magnam authoritatem es consequutus, quàm maximè tibi danda erit opera, vt nō solùm omnis intem perantia & ebrietas apud vos extir-petur,sed & aliæ bonæ leges quæ in amplissima Bernensium Republica, in reformatione ecclesiæ ad confer-uationẽ disciplinæ & bonorum mo-rum latæ sunt, sartæ tectæ conser-uentur.
units.tr: Next, I wished to have the opportunity of urging you earnestly to continue to walk in the same footsteps: just as until now you have been far removed from drunkenness, and especially from the wicked and impure life to which Nabal was given over, so you should keep on. And since God has raised you to such great dignity, and through his blessing you have gained great authority, you should take the greatest pains that not only all intemperance and drunkenness be rooted out among you, but also that the other good laws which were enacted in the most illustrious Republic of Bern, in the reformation of the Church, for the preservation of discipline and good morals, be kept safe and sound.

units.la: Accedit adhæc etiam alia huius dedicationis causa, cum enim præte-rito hoc mense Maio, trecenti quin-quaginta honesti Tigurinæ vrbis ci-ues Bernam, veteris amicitię & amo-ris renouandæ causa, equis iter fecif-sent, non solùm publicè ab ampissi-mo & prudentissimo senatu, & com-muni ciuium Bernensium frequen-tia, tam multa omnis generis hono-ris & amicitiæ officia illis fuerunt præstita, vt illa pro dignitate non sa-tis prædicare & laudibus celebrare posint, verùm etiam priuatim ab ho-nestis ciuibus, multi ex publicis ho-spitijs in priuatas domos inuitati &
units.tr: There is also another reason for this dedication. For when, in this past May, three hundred and fifty honest citizens of the city of Zurich travelled on horseback to Bern in order to renew their old friendship and affection, they were shown so many kinds of honour and friendly services, not only publicly by the most distinguished and most prudent senate and by the general crowd of the citizens of Bern, that I cannot sufficiently proclaim and celebrate them as they deserve, but also privately by honest citizens, many of whom invited them from the public inns into their private homes and bestowed many kindnesses upon them.

units.la: { } deducti multisq; beneficijs affecti su erunt. In quorum numero tu nō postremus fuisti, qui dilectis meis fratribus aliisq; nostris ciuibus idem præstitisti, & de me in primis diligenter es perconctatus, quam ob rem tibi ingentes ago gratias.
units.tr: { } and were led away. Among these you were not the least, for you showed the same kindness to my dear brothers and our other citizens, and above all you made careful enquiry about me. For this reason I give you my immense thanks.

units.la: Præterea confido has meas conciones apud vos, ijs quibus tua probitas & integritas, cui ab ineunte ætate studuisti, perspecta est & cognita, ob quam etiam ad magnos honores & senatorij ordinis dignitatem promotus es, lectu non iniucundas fore, propterea quod tibi dedicatæ sunt & sub nominis tui auspicio in lucem prodeunt.
units.tr: Moreover, I trust that these sermons of mine will not be unpleasant to read among those who know and recognise your uprightness and integrity, which you have pursued from your earliest years, and on account of which you have been raised to great honours and to the dignity of the senatorial order. They are dedicated to you and come forth into the light under the auspices of your name.

units.la: Quamobrē te etiam atq; etiam rogatū volo, vt hac qualemcunq; meæ erga te beneuolentiæ significatione æque boniq; cōsulere, vereremq; nostram amicitiam inuiolatam conseruare digneris. Cōmendo te cum tuis Deo Opt. Max. qui tuam senectutē diuino suo spiritu roborare, teque ad extremum vitæ spiritum pro sua singulari bonitate & immensa misericordia, tueri & protegere dignetur. Salutato meo nomine plurimũ amicos meos colendos, filium tuum charissimum Turingũ, & Io. Vuierman, meum olim conuictorem, vnà cum aliis qui de me percontantur. Datæ Tiguri mense Iulio, Anno incarnati filij Dei. 1584.
units.tr: Therefore I ask you again and again to take this token of my goodwill towards you, however small, in good part, and to deign to keep our friendship inviolate. I commend you and yours to God, the best and greatest, who may deign to strengthen your old age by his divine Spirit, and to keep and protect you to your last breath of life, by his singular goodness and immense mercy. Please greet in my name my dear friends, your most dear son Turingus, and Johann Vuierman, my former housemate, together with the others who ask after me. Given at Zurich in July, in the year 1584 of the incarnation of the Son of God.

units.la: 72. Facie 2. adde ad vltimam lineam in prophetaice denunciarit, quàm à Deo comprecata sit regnum stabile & certum. Sensus tamen vtrinque idem est. 85. vers. 22. pro obiectam lege deiectam. 98. v. 6. pro ac, lege vt. Homilia 10. addendum argumentum. Dauid ambit Abigaelem, quæ matrimonium ei promittit. 120. b. vers. antepenultimo. Hoc non, lege, hoc enim. Reliqua facile lector emendabit.
units.tr: 72. Page 2. Add at the last line, after "prophetically announced" [in prophetaice denunciarit], the words "rather than that he prayed to God for a stable and certain kingdom" [quàm à Deo comprecata sit regnum stabile & certum]. The sense, however, is the same on both sides. 85, verse 22: for "thrown in the way" [obiectam] read "cast down" [deiectam]. 98, verse 6: for "and" [ac] read "that" [vt]. Homily 10: an argument must be added. David courts Abigail, who promises him marriage. 120, column b, second-last verse: for "Hoc non" read "hoc enim" [for this]. The reader will easily correct the rest.

units.la: NARRATIO DE VITA ET OBITV EBRIOSI NABALIS, Descripta 1. Samuel. 25. HOMILIA I.

units.la: Quis & qualis Nabal fuerit.
units.tr: Who and what kind of man Nabal was.

units.la: ET vir in Maon, cuius opes erant in Charmel, eratq; vir ille magnus valde, qui habebat ouium tria millia, & mille capras: fuit autem vt tonderet oues suas in Charmel.
units.tr: There was a man in Maon whose possessions were in Carmel, and he was a very great man, who had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. And it happened that he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.

units.la: 2 Porrò nomen viri Nabal: nomen verò vxoris eius Abigail: eratq; mulier illa prudens & pulchra forma: vir autem ille erat durus & malis moribus, atque Chalebita.
units.tr: 2 Now the man's name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. She was a prudent woman and beautiful in form, but the man was harsh and of evil morals, and a Calebite.

units.la: HOC caput duabus potissimum partibus constat. Priore breuiter describitur, mortuû Samuelem, quem omnes Israelitæ deflerunt, honorificè sepeliuerint.
units.tr: This chapter consists chiefly of two parts. In the first, it is briefly described how Samuel, who had died, was mourned by all the Israelites and honourably buried.

units.la: Ex eo, quòd Samuel obijsse dicitur, venire nobis in mentem debet, Omnibus hominibus esse moriendum. In libro Geneseos cap. 6. Enumerantur Patriarchæ illi annosi, qui ante diluuium floruerunt: Tandem vero additur eos obijsse, aut ad patres suos colleCtos esse. Christus ipse, quia homo natus fuit, se huic legi vniuersæ carnis subiecit. Sed & quotidie experimur, neminem sua prudentia, robore, clientelis, mortem auertere. Id pijs non tantum incutit horrorem, quantum carnalibus hominibus, qui alteram vitam nësciunt: sed potius ad doctrinam & consolationem eorum facit. Quis enim non libenter se tot comitibus itineris cõiungat? Quis postulare ausit, vt Deus ipsum solum superstitem esse sinat? Sed & dolorem minuit, cum nostri etiam coniunctissimi, decedunt, si cogitemus, illos præmitti, nobis mox sequendum esse.
units.tr: From the fact that Samuel is said to have died, we ought to call to mind that all men must die. In the book of Genesis, chapter 6, the aged patriarchs who flourished before the Flood are enumerated, and at the end it is added that they died, or were gathered to their fathers. Christ himself, because he was born a man, submitted to this law of all flesh. We also experience every day that no one averts death by his wisdom, strength or connections. This does not strike terror into the godly as much as into carnal men, who know nothing of another life; rather it serves for their teaching and consolation. For who would not gladly join himself to so many companions on the journey? Who would dare to ask that God let him alone survive? Grief is also lessened when our own closest kin depart, if we consider that they are sent on ahead and that we shall soon follow.

units.la: Deinde cum audiamus, nobis omnino moriendum esse, parati esse debemus, secundum Domini exhortationem, ac vigilare, ne hora illa imparatos subito opprimat. Nescimus certè, quando aut quo morbi genere, Deus nos sublaturus sit. Quo paéto verò ad mortem nos apparare debeamus, Christus suo exemplo nos docuit, &c.
units.tr: Then, since we hear that we must certainly die, we ought to be ready, according to the Lord's exhortation, and to watch, lest that hour overtake us unprepared. We certainly do not know when, or by what kind of sickness, God is about to take us away. But how we ought to prepare ourselves for death, Christ taught us by his own example, etc.

units.la: Quod Israelitæ lugent propter mortem Samuelis prophetæ, hominum est à natura bene institutorum. Nec enim solum moris est, sed natura insitum, vt mortuos nostros, eos præsertim, qui promouebant honorem Dei, hominumq; salutem, publicè, luctu prosequamur. Iactant Stoici ἀπάθειαν seu indolentiam non tamen in eis fuisse reperias. Vitia sunt, immoderatè, hoc est, si nimium lugeas, quo pacto reprehensum legimus à Deo Samuelem, cum Saulem regem, iam è regno abiectum, nimium defleret. Deinde, si indigna ibi fiant, vt lacerationes, &c. Aut, si fictè: Demum is luctus maximè improbatur, qui proficiscitur è resurrectionis negatione. Recte Sapiens ille: (
units.tr: That the Israelites mourn for the death of the prophet Samuel is a matter of men well instructed by nature. For it is not only custom, but implanted by nature, that we should publicly follow our dead with mourning, especially those who promoted the honour of God and the salvation of men. The Stoics boast of indolence [ἀπάθεια], but you will not find it in them. Those things are vices when immoderate, that is, if you mourn too much; as we read that Samuel was rebuked by God when he mourned excessively for Saul, already cast down from the kingdom. Then, if unworthy things are done there, such as lacerations, etc., or if the grief is feigned. Finally, that mourning is most condemned which arises from the denial of the resurrection. That wise man rightly says:

units.la: Mors mea ne careat lachrymis linquamus a-Mærorem, vt celebrent funera cum gemitu.
units.tr: Let my death not lack tears; let us leave grief, so that they may celebrate funerals with lamentation.

units.la: Modum autem in luctu seruandum, non imitandos mores gentilium, docet Paulus 1. ad Thessalon. cap. 4.
units.tr: That moderation is to be kept in mourning, and that the customs of the Gentiles are not to be imitated, Paul teaches in 1 Thessalonians, chapter 4.

units.la: De sepultura, non est quod plura annotemus, cum ea, quæ maioris videntur esse momenti, ad vltimum caput libri Iosuæ attulerimus. Nunc hoc tantum dicam, peccari in illa bifariam. Primum, si prorsus contemnatur, vt Diogeniani quidam faciunt, qui sibi perinde esse dicunt, vbicunq; cóputrescant: iubent se in aquas, aut etiam in fterquiliniu proijci. Deinde, si qui nimium sepulturæ tri buant, vt illi fecerunt, qui loca sepulturæ mi ris cæremonijs consecrarunt, & officere di xerunt animę, nisi in loco consecrato, corpo ra fuerint sepulta. Media tenenda est via. Si posimus habere sepulturam honestam, ne contemnamus eam: Sin corpus alitibus et se ris proijciendū intelligamus, rem Deo com mittemus, cuius, vt Psaltes dicit, terra est & plenitudo eius. Superstitio plane fugienda. Hic certe nihil legimus de templis & altari-bus exstructis Samueli, de eius reliquijs ef-fosis & adoratis, de peregrinationibus ad eum factis. Posteris demum temporibus, dor-mientibus, aut potius bella gerentibus epi-scopis multi tetri errores in ecclesiam irre-pserunt: Consecrata sunt cœmiteria præsti-giosa & ioculari ratione ab episcopis: Credi-tum est animæ prodesse, si cadauer in loco consecrato, quin, si propè summū altare co-putresc at: Nisi iusta ritè peracta fuissent, di-xerunt & publicè docuerunt, animab. creari periculum: adduxerunt pro testimonio spe-ctra & spiritus illos, qui cum gemitu opem expetunt: Hinc missę celebratę pro mortuis, precesq; pro eorum salute effusæ. Cœperūt etiam superstitiosi homines progressu tem-poris,
units.tr: Concerning burial there is no need to note more, since we have brought forward the matters that seem of greater weight at the last chapter of the book of Joshua. Now I will say only this: a fault is committed in it in two ways. First, if it is utterly despised, as certain Diogenians do, who say it makes no difference to them where they rot; they order themselves to be thrown into the waters or even onto a dunghill. Second, if some attribute too much to burial, as those did who consecrated places of burial with strange ceremonies, and said that the soul would be harmed unless the bodies were buried in a consecrated place. The middle way is to be held. If we can have an honourable burial, let us not despise it. But if we understand that the body is to be cast to the birds and beasts, we shall commit the matter to God, whose, as the Psalmist says, is the earth and its fullness. Superstition is plainly to be fled. Here indeed we read nothing of temples and altars built to Samuel, of his relics dug up and adored, or of pilgrimages made to him. In later times, while the bishops slept, or rather waged wars, many foul errors crept into the Church. Cemeteries were consecrated by the bishops in a showy and jesting manner. It was believed that the soul would profit if the corpse rotted in a consecrated place, indeed if it rotted near the high altar. Unless the funeral rites had been duly performed, they said and publicly taught, souls were in danger of being created. They brought forward as witnesses ghosts and spirits which seek help with groaning. Hence masses were celebrated for the dead, and prayers poured out for their salvation. Superstitious men also began, as time went on,

units.la: Superstitio exequiarū. poris,mortuorum ossa effossa serie dispone- re,& in hunc vsum sacella exstruere. Pontifi- ces eos,qui papalem sedem exaltarunt,in nu- merum Deorum retulerunt, reliquos cre- marunt,aut cadauera eorum & ossa,ex sepul- chris effossa, in sterquilinium proiecerunt. Sed et sacrifici sepulturas, quę ecclesiæ toti- us fuerunt,priuatis hominibus vendiderūt, ac ex preculis incerto sono demurmuratis, ex cereis, ex incantata crustula,imo ex cam panarum sonitu, non modo aurum & argen- tum conflarunt, verūm etiam prædia, deci- mas,redditus annuos, adhæc principatus & regna constituerunt. Et poterat ferri stulta superstitio,si de pecunijs solis ageretur, sed cum animarum salus & Christi gloria simul in periculum veniat,nullo modo disimula- ri potest. Pugnat enim cum Christi verbis, qui credentium animas non in iudicium ve- nire , sed à morte in vitam transfire ait. Quæ cū ita sint, procul à funeribus arceri debet, quidquid superstitionis aliquam speciem ha bet,ne de defunctorum salute in Christo du bitare videamur. Sed hæc hactenus.
units.tr: superstition of funerals: to arrange the bones of the dead, dug up, in rows, and to build chapels for this purpose. The pontiffs enrolled among the gods those who had exalted the papal see; the rest they burned, or threw their corpses and bones, dug out of the sepulchres, onto a dunghill. But they also sold to private persons the burial places which belonged to the whole Church, and from murmured prayers of uncertain sound, from wax candles, from enchanted little cakes, indeed from the sound of bells, they not only melted down gold and silver, but also established estates, tithes, annual revenues and, moreover, principalities and kingdoms. And this foolish superstition could be borne if it concerned money alone. But since the salvation of souls and the glory of Christ are at the same time put in danger, it cannot in any way be overlooked. For it fights against the words of Christ, who says that the souls of believers do not come into judgment but pass from death into life. Since these things are so, whatever has any appearance of superstition ought to be kept far from funerals, lest we seem to doubt the salvation of the dead in Christ. But so much for these matters.

units.la: Posteriore historiæ huius parte, prolixè narratur, quid inter Dauidem, Nabalem & Abigailem sit gestum.Est autem historia ista multiplici & doctrina & consolatione refer-
units.tr: The latter part of this history narrates at length what took place between David, Nabal and Abigail. This story is filled with manifold teaching and consolation.

units.la: ta.Primò videmus (vt præcipua tantùm capita Ἡρικῶς attingam) pios non semper habere, quæ cupiunt: sed multis sæpius ærumnis à Deo exerceri. Dauid quidem vir, secundum cor Dei (quamuis suos quoque næuos habuerit) præterquam quod illi in singulis momentis expectandum erat, quando à Saule iugularetur, summa rerum penuria cum militibus suis, quorum 600. habebat, laborat. Præterea maxima verborum contumelia, nullo merito, etiam exul, à Nabale cognato, afficitur. Abigail, fœmina lectissima, Nabali homini stulto & insolenti cohabitari cogitur, à quo nec ope nec consilio sustentata, insuper etiam contemnitur. Nec dubium id illi fuisse grauissimum tormentum, quòd in talem maritum incidisset. Apparet etiam ex historia ista, dilectos Dei seruos non planè ἁμαρτωλοὺς esse: sed nonnunquam sibi turpiter ira, vindictæ cupiditate, alijsq; prauis & vitiosis affectibus subripi: Et tamen à Deo in tempore retrahi, quasiq; frenari, ne sibi & aliis noceant, periculumq; afferant. Præterea docemur, ebrios & auaros nihil recte agere: sed ineptè & iniquè omnia. Proponitur etiam nobis in isto commentariolo, exemplum dissoluti patrisfamilias, matronæ frugi, serui fidelis.
units.tr: First, we see (to touch only the principal heads, heroically [ἡρωϊκῶς]) that the godly do not always have what they desire, but are often exercised by God with many troubles. David, indeed, a man after God's own heart (although he too had his faults), besides having to expect every moment that he would be slain by Saul, labours in the utmost want with his soldiers, of whom he had six hundred. Moreover, though an exile and without any fault of his own, he is subjected to the greatest verbal insult from Nabal, his kinsman. Abigail, a most select woman, is compelled to live with Nabal, a foolish and insolent man, by whom she is neither sustained with help nor counsel, and is moreover despised. Nor is there doubt that this was a most grievous torment to her, that she had fallen upon such a husband. It appears also from this history that the beloved servants of God are not altogether sinless [ἁμαρτωλοὺς], but sometimes are shamefully carried away by anger, desire for vengeance and other depraved and vicious passions; yet in time they are drawn back by God, and as it were restrained, lest they harm themselves and others and bring danger. Moreover, we are taught that drunkards and misers do nothing rightly, but foolishly and unjustly everything. There is also set before us, in this little commentary, an example of a dissolute householder, a frugal matron and a faithful servant.

units.la: Summa ex capita historiæ Nabalis delis, &c. Ostenditur, Deum eos, qui patien ter opem ipsius expectant, hoc quoq; in se-culo oculis, vt ille inquit, æquis aspicere, & ipsorum fortunam in melius commutare, alia-q; id genus complura.
units.tr: The summary of the heads of the history of Nabal, etc. It is shown that God looks upon those who patiently await his help, even in this age, with, as he says, equal eyes, and changes their fortune for the better, and many other things of this kind.

units.la: Historia ista partes habet complures, in quas non incommodè secari potest. Nos sin-gulas ex ordine, Deo benè iuuante, inspicie-mus, & quæ in illis nobis vel ad instituen-dam vel emendandam vitam, vel ad alen-dam ac confirmandam fidem ac patientiam à spiritu sancto proponantur, τῶν βασιλέων, percurremus. 1. Primò accurata Nabalis περσωπο-ποιία à nomine, diuitijs, vxore, animo, genere, pingitur, quam diligentius inspexisse, non fuerit inutile. Quod ad no-men, constat, vocem Nabal, proprie stipi-tem, vel truncum exsuccu denotare. Transfertur deinde ad homines, qui tàm in fusci-piendis, quam in agendis rebus pensi nihil, nihil cogitati habent. Non dissimili ratione stipes & truncus pro homine stulto, insul-so & fatuo apud Latinos ponuntur.
units.tr: This history has several parts, into which it can conveniently be divided. With God's good help we shall examine them one by one in order, and run through in their proper order [τῶν βασιλέων] what the Holy Spirit sets forth in them, either to instruct or amend our life, or to nourish and strengthen faith and patience. 1. First, Nabal's characterisation [προσωποποιία] is portrayed from his name, riches, wife, mind and family, which it will not be unprofitable to have examined more carefully. As to the name, it is established that the word Nabal properly denotes a stump or a dried-up trunk. It is then transferred to men who have no weight and no thought either in undertaking or in carrying out affairs. By no dissimilar reasoning, stump and trunk are used among the Latins for a foolish, dull and silly man.

units.la: In me(inquit Mendemus apud Comicu) quiduis harum rerum conuenit, Quæ sunt dif-ta in stultu: caudex, stipes, asinus, plumbeus. Cicero 1. de natura Deorum: Qui potest esse in eiusmodi trunco sapientia? &c. Hoc nome Nabali recte conuenisse, postea testis est eius vxor: Vide, inquit, mi Dauid, ne hominem despicatissimum, Nabalem, dignum iudicęs, in quę iras vertas: qui, sicuti nomine, ita re ipsa stultus est. Sæpe fit, vt nomina moribus siue bonis siue malis respondeant, fatisq;, vt inquit ille, suis conueniant. Sacræ literę hoc nominis, impijs, etiam versutissimis ac consultissimis, tribuunt, neq; id iniuria. Quid enim stultius, adeoq; demétius est, quàm, si quis nulla animæ ratione habita, vitam ducat Cyclopicam, excussoq; omni pietatis sensu, omnem numinis memoriā, quantum in se est, ex animo suo deleat, nec credat esse Deum, qui bonos præmijs, malos supplicijs condignis afficiat?
units.tr: "In my case," says Menedemus in the comedy, "none of the things said of a fool fail to fit: blockhead, stump, donkey, lead." Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, book 1: "How can there be wisdom in such a trunk?" etc. That this name fitted Nabal well is attested afterwards by his wife: "See, my David," she says, "do not judge that most contemptible man Nabal worthy of the wrath you direct against him. He is foolish in deed just as he is in name." It often happens that names correspond to character, whether good or bad, and, as that writer says, fit the fates. Holy Scripture assigns this name to the impious, even the most crafty and cunning, and not without reason. For what is more foolish, and indeed more demented, than to live a Cyclops' life, to ignore all regard for the soul, to strip oneself of every sense of piety and, as far as one can, wipe from one's mind all memory of the divine, and not to believe that there is a God who rewards the good with fitting prizes and punishes the wicked?

units.la: 2. Hiç Maoni habitauit, vrbe in tribu Iuda sita, quemadmodum ex 15. cap. libri Iofuę colligitur. Vnde est videre, Dauidem & Nabalem ex eadé tribu originem duxisse. Quæ res animum eius emollire debebat, vt de cibarijs Dauidi, primùm optimè merito, & de ipso priuatim, & de tota Republica: deinde cognato: postremò inopi & exuli, liberaliter dandis cogitaret. Sed hæc omnia apud ipsum nihil possunt, vt se vel verbis facilem prębeat. Nulla igitur excusatione dignus est.
units.tr: 2. Nabal lived at Maon, a city situated in the tribe of Judah, as is gathered from chapter 15 of the book of Joshua. Hence it can be seen that David and Nabal were of the same tribe. This fact ought to have softened his heart, so that he would think of giving liberally to David, who had deserved very well first of him both personally and of the whole commonwealth, then to a kinsman, and finally to a needy exile. But all these considerations count for nothing with him, so that he will not show himself kind even in words. He is therefore worthy of no excuse.

units.la: 3 Opes ipsius in Carmelo erant, eaeque longe amplissimae. Habuit enim ouium tria millia & mille capras: de armentis nihil dicitur. Verisimile est, illum habuisse pascua, oliueta, vineta, latissima & feracissima. Vbi vero tanta pecoris copia est, necessario magnus seruorum & ancillarum numerus est alendus. Cum Dauid Abigailem ambiret, venit quinq; ancillis comitata. An vero famulitia ipsius fuerint, vel mancipia, non exprimitur. Veteres non minimam facultatem partem seruis & ancillis aestimabant. Cum oeconomus Abrahami Isaaco Rebeccam ambiret, Sum, inquit, Labani socero, seruus Abrahami, hominis, quem Deus ditauit mirum in modum, oue, capra, boue, argento, auro, seruis, ancillis, camelis atq; asinis, &c. Genes. 30. Iacobus singulari industria rem suam plurimum auget, & numerosum pecus ouillum & caprinum, seruitiaq; & camelos atq; asinos comparat. Deus Nabalem ditum maximis opibus adauxerat,
units.tr: 3. Nabal's wealth lay in Carmel, and it was very great indeed. For he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats; of his herds of cattle nothing is said. It is likely that he had pastures, olive groves and vineyards, very broad and very fertile. Where there is such an abundance of livestock, a large number of male and female servants must necessarily be kept. When David was courting Abigail, he came accompanied by five maidservants. Whether these were his household attendants or slaves is not stated. The ancients counted their slaves and maidservants as no small part of their wealth. When Abraham's steward was courting Rebekah for Isaac, he said: "I am the servant of Abraham. I am a kinsman of Laban, a man whom God has blessed wonderfully with sheep, goats, oxen, silver, gold, male and female servants, camels and asses," etc. (Gen. 24). Jacob by remarkable industry greatly increased his property and acquired a large flock of sheep and goats, as well as servants, camels and asses. God had enriched Nabal with very great wealth.

units.la: Res pecuaria non solum quaestuosa, sed etiam honesta est. Patriarchae in veteri Testamento plerunq; omnes pastores fuere ὥσπερ γεωργίαν ζῶσαν γεωργοῦντες, &c. Cum Iosephus fratres suos ad Pharaonem euocasset, atq; is eos rogasset, quae nam essent ipsorum operaʼid est, quam artem exercerent (fortasis enim nolebat otiosos homines alere)Serui, inquiunt, tui sunt agricolæ & pastores, exemplo patrum nostrorum. Non pudet illos profiteri se pastores esse, quantumuis à pastoribus Ægyptios abhorrere probè scirent. Apud Græcos celeberrimus quisque pastor erat; hinc alios ποιμένας, alios πολυμηλὰς, alios πολυβοτὰς appellant. Romani quoq; vetustiores nihil in bonis, præter pecudes habebant. Nostri homines, si qui alij norunt, quàm quæstuosa sit βοσκηματικὴ. Nam vt omittam, quod infinitam armenti pecorisq; vim alpinis pascuis, quæ hoc peculiare & proprium habent, quod sub ipsis niuibus crescant, alant, caro certè, lac, butyrum, caseus, serum, aliaq;, quæ in alias regiones, exportantur, maximo veneunt.
units.tr: Keeping livestock is not only profitable but also honourable. Almost all the patriarchs in the Old Testament were shepherds, as if tilling a living farm [ὥσπερ γεωργίαν ζῶσαν γεωργοῦντες], etc. When Joseph had summoned his brothers to Pharaoh, and Pharaoh asked them what their work was, that is, what craft they practised (for perhaps he did not want to support idle men), they replied: "Your servants are farmers and shepherds, as our fathers were." They were not ashamed to profess that they were shepherds, although they knew well that the Egyptians abhorred shepherds. Among the Greeks every shepherd was famous; hence they called some shepherds [ποιμένας], some rich in flocks [πολυμηλὰς], some rich in herds [πολυβοτὰς]. The older Romans too had no wealth except livestock. Let our own people, if any others know, how profitable pastoral farming [βοσκηματικὴ] is. For, to pass over the endless numbers of cattle and flocks that graze on alpine pastures, which have this peculiar and distinctive feature, that they grow beneath the very snows, the meat, milk, butter, cheese, whey and other products, which are exported to other regions, sell for a great price.

units.la: Carmelus mons fuit in tribu Isachar, in quo Elias propheta, operum incredibilium effector, conuocatis sacerdotibus Baaliticis, constituto certamine, de sacrificio, cum illi litare Baali non potuissent, ipse Iehouæ sacrificauit, veritatemque religionis suæ euidenti miraculo comprobauit. Sed Carmelus, de quo nunc loquimur, locus fuit
units.tr: Mount Carmel was in the tribe of Issachar, where the prophet Elijah, the performer of incredible works, summoned the priests of Baal, set up a contest about the sacrifice, and when they could not offer acceptable sacrifice to Baal, sacrificed himself to Jehovah and proved the truth of his religion by an evident miracle. But the Carmel of which we are now speaking was a place

units.la: Carmelus. 1. Reg. 18. fuit in tribu Iuda.In libro Iosue Maon, Carmelus, & Ziph coniunguntur, forte ideo, quod se contingerent.In genere, omnem locum cultum frumento, vineis & pascuis significat. Sic Tempe apud Latinos proprie loca sunt inter Olfam & Olympum interiecta longe amoenissima: communi autem & latiore appellatione, quaecunq; loca amoeniora, nemora praesertim atq; aquas habentia denotant.Isaiae 42. praedicitur, desertum esse commutandum in Carmelum, id est,agrum fertilissimum.Etsi Nabal Maoni habitaret: tamen possessiones suas & greges in regione ista habebat:quemadmodum hodie quoq; ciues ditiores in vrbibus agunt:extra vrbem praedia villasq; habent.
units.tr: Carmel (1 Kings 18) was in the tribe of Judah. In the book of Joshua, Maon, Carmel and Ziph are joined together, perhaps because they bordered on one another. In general, the name signifies any place rich in grain, vines and pastures. So among the Latins Tempe is properly a most pleasant valley lying between Ossa and Olympus, but in common and wider usage it denotes any pleasant places, especially groves and places with water. In Isaiah 42 it is foretold that the desert will be turned into Carmel, that is, a most fertile field. Although Nabal lived at Maon, he nonetheless had his estates and flocks in that region, just as today wealthier citizens live in cities yet have farms and country houses outside the city.

units.la: 4 Additur illum magnum fuisse:non quod corporis abundas &παχύσωρ fuerit(quanuis nec hoc a vero abhorreat, eoque magis quod quotidie laute viueret,ac tanquam abdomini natus esset, cuticulam curaret) sed quod magni nominis esset, summaeq; apud omnes auctoritatis. Solet enim mundus opulentiores in ore atq; oculis habere, ac, vt illorum gratiam & fauorem quoquo modo aucupetur,illos turpissime adulari,magnisque titulis ornatos,tantumnon in theatrum producere,& quiduis in eorum gratiam simulare & dissimulare. Eosdem rebus acci-fis & afflictis,fortunisq; vel consumptis atq; exhaustis, vel casu aliquo amissis atq; ereptis,contemnit, nec vnius quidem aisis æsti matos,tantumnon pedibus conculcat,idem que plane accidit, quod ab Horatio dictum est: Diffugiunt cadis
units.tr: 4. It is added that he was a great man, not because he was bloated in body or fat-necked (although this is not far from the truth, especially since he lived sumptuously every day and, as if born for his belly, took care of his skin), but because he had a great name and the highest authority among all. For the world is accustomed to keep the wealthier in its eyes and mouth, and to flatter them most shamefully in order to win their favour and goodwill by any means, to parade them, decorated with great titles, almost on the stage, and to feign or dissemble anything for their sake. The same world despises those who are reduced and afflicted, whose fortunes are used up and exhausted or lost and snatched away by some chance, and tramples them almost underfoot, not valuing them at a single penny. The same thing happens that Horace described: The friends scatter from the emptied casks

units.la: Cum sece siccatis amici,
units.tr: When the jars are drained, the friends

units.la: Ferre iugum pariter dolosi:
units.tr: Deceitfully refuse to bear the yoke together:

units.la: vt cum Ariftodemo Spartiate, qui diuitias simul & amicos amiserat,exclamare possint: χρήματα, χρήματα ἀνὴρ, πενιχρὸς ὁ ἰδεῖς πόλεις ἐσθλὸς ἀλλὰ τίμιος: id est,pecunia pe cunia vir: pauper nemo bonus aut honore dignus.
units.tr: So that they may exclaim with Aristodemus the Spartan, who had lost both his riches and his friends: [Money, money makes the man; the poor man, though seen, is not noble but despised] [χρήματα, χρήματα ἀνὴρ, πενιχρὸς ὁ ἰδεῖς πόλεις ἐσθλὸς ἀλλὰ τίμιος], that is, money makes the man: no poor man is good or worthy of honour.

units.la: Quidam simpliciter accipiunt,illum magnum fuisse,id est,locupletem , opibusq; abundantem.Sic Genef.26.de Ifaaco dicitur: illum fauente Domino,in dies magis magisque creuisse,ita vt perquam magnus effet,id est,opulentisimus factus fit.Quod per species probatur:Abundabat enim,inquit Moses de Ifaaco, ouium & caprarum,abundabat itemboum pecore & seruitio,&c. Quare inuidia commoti Palestini,&c.
units.tr: Some take it simply that he was great, that is, wealthy and abounding in riches. So in Genesis 26 it is said of Isaac that, the Lord favouring him, he grew more and more day by day, so that he became very great, that is, became exceedingly rich. This is proved by the particulars: for, as Moses says of Isaac, he abounded in flocks of sheep and goats, he also abounded in herds of cattle and in servants, etc. Therefore the Philistines, moved by envy, etc.

units.tr: 5. Abigail was the wife of this Nabal, a woman of notable prudence and elegant beauty. She received her name because she cheered her father at her birth

units.la: Nabalis coniux prudens et formosa. exhilarasseт. Talem fœminam nancisci, magnum est Dei donum. Recte Solomon: Mulier Chail, inquit, id est, sedula, & mente prædita corona est viri sui, mulier autem confusionis, hoc est segnis parumq; frugi, est quasi putredo in ossibus eius. Sensus est, Fœmina frugi, quæ rei familiaris administrandæ perita est, œconomiam sedulo curat & impigrè, viro non tam adiumento est quàm ornamento: E contra segnis & parum frugi, damnum viro affert irreparabile, & molestiam ineluctabilem. Ac vt morbus & vitium in ossibus curatur difficile: ita dolor ex tali muliere in intima penetrat. Non dubium est, quin multi satis frugi essent fuoq; fungerentur officio, si in commodas incidissent coniuges. Sed quod vxores sint, quæ suum officium ignorant, nec discere volunt: ac quamuis diligantur, ipsæ eos contemnant & tantumnon conculcent, domo pulsi tempestate illa ad bonos socios, tanquam in portum tutissimum se recipiunt, curasq; mero abluunt: paulatimq; dissolutæ vitæ in tantum afuescunt, vt exinde vix ac ne vix ad mentem meliorem redeant. Additur, vxorem Nabalis eleganti forma fuisse: quæ res fœminæ magnam beneuolentiam conciliat: præsertim si ad corporis speciem, morum concinnitas accedat. Cætera, sicuti inauris aurea in rostro suis: ita mulier formosa, eademque mente & iudicio carens. Hac de re pulchræ extant etiam apud Ethnicos sententiæ, quas hoc loco adducere, nimis longum foret.
units.tr: Nabal's wife was prudent and beautiful; she cheered him. To get such a woman is a great gift of God. Solomon rightly says: "A woman of worth [Chail], that is, diligent and endowed with understanding, is a crown to her husband, but a woman of shame, that is, slack and of little thrift, is like rottenness in his bones." The meaning is this: a thrifty woman, skilled in managing the household, carefully and tirelessly looks after the housekeeping, and is to her husband less a helper than an ornament. On the other hand, a slack and thriftless woman brings her husband irreparable loss and inescapable trouble. Just as a disease or defect lodged in the bones is hard to cure, so the grief caused by such a wife penetrates to the innermost parts. There is no doubt that many men would be thrifty enough and would do their duty if they had met with suitable wives. But there are wives who do not know their duty and are unwilling to learn it. Although they are loved, they despise their husbands and almost trample on them; and when driven from home by such a storm, the husbands take refuge with good companions, as in the safest harbour, and wash away their cares with wine. Gradually they become so accustomed to a dissolute life that afterwards they scarcely, if at all, return to a better mind. It is added that Nabal's wife was of elegant beauty. This quality wins a woman great goodwill, especially if fineness of character is joined to beauty of body. Otherwise, a beautiful woman who lacks sense and judgment is like a gold ring in a pig's snout. There are fine sayings on this matter even among the heathen, which it would take too long to cite here.

units.la: 6 Sed quibus moribus fuit Nabal iste? Primò dicitur: Illum durum fuisse & aspe-rum, qualis apud Terentium Demea describitur. Id quod vel inde est videre, quod etiam recte monente, audire quenquam vellet: unde postea seruus: Perditior, inquit est, quàm ut admonendus esse videatur, vel admonitionem, eo, quo fit, animo accipiat: Item, quod cum per legatos, homines honestos, exul Dauid commeatum humiliter peteret, non solum, bene merito, eum negat, verum etiam contumeliam verborum addit, & Dauidem tribulem suum, tanquam fugitiuum & perduellem vituperat: Item, quòd vxor eius, fœmina prudentia & forma insignis, tempus adeundi captare cogitur, quo illum de Dauidis iracundia iusta, & de suo periculo, cum fructu certiorem reddat.
units.tr: 6 But what was this Nabal's character? First, he is said to have been harsh and rough, like Demea as Terence describes him. This is evident from the fact that he would not listen to anyone, even when someone advised him rightly. Hence a servant later says: "He is too far gone to seem worth admonishing, or to take admonition in the spirit in which it is given." Likewise, when David, an exile, humbly asked for provisions through envoys who were honest men, Nabal not only refused him, though he deserved them, but also added insults and called David, his fellow tribesman, a runaway and a rebel. Again, his wife, a woman of wisdom and outstanding beauty, was forced to look for a moment to approach him, so that she could inform him, with some profit, of David's just anger and of his own danger.

units.la: Additur, illum malis & distortis moribus fuisse. Neq; id abs re. Enimuero neq; dicere neq; facere quidquam pensi habebat. Quidquid in mentem veniebat, id, fretus opibus & potentia, ad audendum erat proiectissimus, nec Deum metuens, nec homines revereritus: adhaec ebriosus erat: deniq; extreme auarus, qualis Euclio à Plauto describitur, & ingratus. Vbi vero scelera ista dominantur, necesse est ex vno inconuenienti absurda sequi infinita. Sunt enim scelera ista tanquam venae & scaturigines quaedam, ex quibus omnis generis mala perpetim emanant, quemadmodum quotidiana experientia docemur. Si quis fraeno mandatorum diuinorum se non patiatur retrahi, illum affectibus suis indulgere necesse est, à quibus abreptus ex alio in aliud praeceps scelus ruit. Nabal, id est stultus & vesanus in corde suo dicit: Non est Deus: corrupti sunt, abominabiles facti sunt studio, non est, qui bene agat. Consulatur Psalmus 53.
units.tr: It is added that he had bad and perverse morals, and this is not beside the point. Indeed, he had no scruples about what he said or did. Whatever came into his mind, relying on his wealth and power, he was utterly bold to dare, fearing neither God nor men. Besides, he was a drunkard, and in the end extremely miserly, like Euclio as Plautus describes him, and ungrateful. Where such vices hold sway, it is inevitable that countless absurdities follow from one wrong. For these vices are like veins and springs from which every kind of evil flows out continually, as daily experience teaches us. If anyone does not allow himself to be held back by the bridle of the divine commandments, he must indulge his passions, and carried away by them he rushes headlong from one crime into another. "Nabal, that is, the fool and madman, says in his heart: There is no God. They are corrupt, they have become abominable in their doings; there is none who does good." Let Psalm 53 be consulted.

units.la: 7 Nabal iste à Calebo ortus fuit. Calebus vir fuit egregius & praestans, de tribu Iuda. Amandatus in Chananaeam explorator, terram esse rerum abundantissimam refert: vincibilem quoq; contra socios incredulos tanta animositate affirmans, vt à populo seditioso tantum non lapidibus peteretur. Dei omnipotentis veritatem semper defendit, nec Dei auxilio vnquam destitutus fuit. Solus in terram promissam, quam vere laudat uerat,venit cum Iofua.In eadem terra præ‐mium,quod ipsi Moses pollicitus fuerat, o b tinuit:& vrbes Gigantum Hebrone habi‐tantium expugnatos possedit:Duces Gigan tum tres superauit & obtruncauit:sua fœli‐citate posteris demonstrans, quàm sit bo‐num sequi Dominum. Sed ab illo ita dege‐nerauit Nabal,vt ipse ex se natus esse vide‐retur:Quemadmodum hodie quoq; sæpe fit vt homines pij & egregij,tales liberos relin‐quant, vt magis ex vsu rerum humanarum fuerit,illos absq; liberis decedere.Quod for tè ideo fit, vt agnoscamus ἐυτεχνίαν fingu‐lare Dei donum esse, non rem naturalem. Certè si boni prudentesq; parentes, filios bonos prudentesq; semper procrearent, in eam sententiam veniremus, vt putaremus rem esse naturalem, ac per traducem quasi ad posteros deriuari: Iam cum videamus, præstantium virorum liberos plerunq; de‐generare, vnde tritum sermone prouerbiū, Heroum filij noxæ: manifestum est,hanc rem ab alio principio pendere,id est,vt cla‐rius dicam,ἐυτεχνίαν Dei munus esse,non à natura prouenire. Vidit hoc ex parte De‐mosthenes, qui quodam in loco dicit: ἀγαθῶν ἀνδρῶν ὥσπερ εἰμαρμένη ἐίη, φάυλος
units.tr: 7 This Nabal was descended from Caleb. Caleb was an outstanding and excellent man, of the tribe of Judah. Sent as a scout into Canaan, he reported that the land was most abundant in all things, and he declared with such courage that it could be conquered, against his unbelieving companions, that the seditious people almost stoned him. He always defended the truth of the almighty God, and was never abandoned by God's help. He alone, with Joshua, came into the promised land, which he had truly praised. In that same land he obtained the reward Moses had promised him, and he took possession of the cities of the giants who lived in Hebron. He overcame and slew the three chieftains of the giants, showing to posterity by his own good fortune how good it is to follow the Lord. But Nabal so degenerated from him that he seemed to have been born of himself alone. It happens today too that pious and excellent men often leave such children that it is better for them, in terms of human affairs, to die without children. This happens perhaps so that we may acknowledge that eutechnia [ἐυτεχνίαν], a good disposition of children, is a singular gift of God and not a natural thing. Certainly, if good and wise parents always produced good and wise children, we would come to the view that it is a natural thing, passed on by descent as it were to posterity. But since we see that the children of outstanding men mostly degenerate, whence the common proverb: the sons of heroes are a curse, it is clear that this matter depends on another source; to put it more plainly, eutechnia [ἐυτεχνίαν] is God's gift and does not arise from nature. Demosthenes partly saw this, who says in a certain place: it is as though by fate that the sons of good men turn out bad [ἀγαθῶν ἀνδρῶν ὥσπερ εἰμαρμένη ἐίη, φάυλος].

units.la: Heroum filij cur plerunq; noxæ.
units.tr: Why the sons of heroes are mostly a curse.

units.la: φαύλας ἀποβάνειν τὰς ὑὰς: id est, A viris egregijs, perinde quasi fato quodam accidat id, improbos proficisci filios. Quantam vero molestiam pariat liberos degeneres relinquere, quiuis facile potest intelligere. Sedulo igitur in id incumbent parentes, suo officio in illis educandis, castigandis, & in viam reuocandis ne desint. Viri vero principes, assentatores à liberis abarceto. Etenim si homines huiusmodi procul ab illis abesse contigerit, nec naturam facilè mutari, nec educationem irritam fieri, temere putandum est: quandoquidem potentes raro mali euadunt, vbi desunt cupiditatum ministri, vt recte èt est à Diodoro dictum.
units.tr: [φαύλας ἀποβάνειν τὰς ὑὰς]: that is, it happens, as if by some fate, that the sons of excellent men turn out wicked. How great a trouble it is to leave degenerate children, anyone can easily understand. Parents, therefore, must diligently apply themselves to their duty of bringing them up, correcting them and recalling them to the right path, and not fail in it. Magistrates and princes should keep flatterers away from their children. For if such men happen to be far from them, it is rashly supposed that neither their nature is easily changed nor their upbringing made useless, since the powerful seldom turn out bad where there are no servants of their desires, as Diodorus rightly said.

units.la: Illi vero qui pijs & illustribus parentibus prognati sunt, illorum virtutem sedulò imitantor: caueantque ne quid maioribus suis indignum committant. Id autem eos in primis obseruare oportebat, qui generis vetustate gloriantur, quæ hodie omnis nobilitatis fundamentum esse putatur. Enimuero inutilis prorsus est natalium splendor, nisi posteri maiorum virtutes imitentur, famíliasq; suas illustribus factis, & omni virtutum genere amplius nobilitare pergant. Nabali certè turpiter à maiorum virtute desciscenti, claritas generis dedecori potius
units.tr: Those who are born of pious and distinguished parents should carefully imitate their virtue and take care not to commit anything unworthy of their ancestors. This especially ought to be observed by those who boast of the antiquity of their family, which today is thought to be the foundation of all nobility. Indeed, the splendour of birth is quite useless unless descendants imitate the virtues of their ancestors and go on to ennoble their families by illustrious deeds and every kind of virtue. Certainly, for Nabal, who shamefully departed from the virtue of his forebears, the distinction of his family was a disgrace rather than an ornament.

units.la: B fuit quàm ornamento. Ita, si quis parenti-bus ortus sit illustribus, qui operam suam Principibus Rebusque publicis summa cum laude navarint, ipse vero dies noctef-que pergrœcetur, sanctissimo Dei nomine ad blasphemias & periuria identidem fœdè abutatur, ludar, lenonum omnium fores in-fringat, Dei verbum contemnat, nihil non sibi licere putat, et proiecta quiduis audendi licentia in omne scelus ruat, ostentatione dehonestatur potius quàm illu-stratur. Nam vt præclarè Satyricus:
units.tr: B So, if someone is born of illustrious parents, who have served princes and the commonwealth with the highest praise, but he himself spends days and nights in debauchery, repeatedly abuses the most holy name of God for blasphemies and perjuries, plays, breaks into the doors of all the brothels, despises God's word, thinks nothing is not permitted to him, and with his licence to dare anything rushes into every crime, he is disgraced by his display rather than illuminated. For, as the satirist brilliantly puts it:

units.la: Nobilitas sola est atq; vnica virtus.
units.tr: Nobility is one and only virtue.

units.la: Huc egregius ille apud Senecam locus: Ne-mo, inquit alteri nobilior, nisi cui rectius in-genium & artibus bonis aptius. Qui imagi-nes in atrio exponunt & nomina suæ familiæ longo ordine ac multis stemmatum illi-gata flexuris, in parte prima ædium collo-cant, noti magis quàm nobiles sunt, &c.
units.tr: To this belongs that excellent passage in Seneca: "No one is nobler than another, unless he has the better nature and is more fitted to good arts. Those who set out images in the hall and their family names in a long row, tied together by many twists of pedigree, and place them in the front part of the house, are better known than noble, etc."

units.la: Videmus ex prima historiæ huius par-te, Deum promiscue bonos & malos diui-tijs augere: eosque vicissim depauperare. Nabal circumfluebat omnibus copijs, atque in omni rerum abundantia viuebat: E, con-tra, Dauid cum suis summa rerum inopia la-borabat. Quod si quis inde voluisset conclu-dere (vt plerunque fit) Deus Nabalem dile-xit. Am. xit. Amplissimas enim illi opes conc efsit: Dauidem cum suis odio habuit: Summa enim illos in egestate esse passus est, perperā fecisset. Nec enim ex diuitijs aut pauperrate possumus statuere de beneuolentia aut odio Dei erga quenquam. Ista enim promisscuè contingunt & bonis & malis. Atqui, vt in eo hominis vita ac salus sita nō est, si facul tatibus abūdet, vel ipso Christo testetur nec ab alijs vel corporis, vel fortunæ bonis, puta bonitate generis, autoritate, vxore formosa & prudenti, eā pendere certū est. Nabal quidem ista habebat omnia: Sed quod timore Dei, vera fide & sapientia destitutus esset, ista omnia ipsi nec ornaméto, nec adiumēto fuere, quin ipsi, vt omnib⁹ infidelibus, ad pernī ciem fecerūt. Nō inscitè Salomon: Quid prō dest stultō, nqt, quod maximè abundet opi bus, cū sapiētiā pecunia cōparare nō possit.
units.tr: We see from the first part of this history that God enriches good and bad alike without distinction, and in turn impoverishes them. Nabal was surrounded by all kinds of wealth and lived in every abundance; on the contrary, David with his men laboured in the greatest want. If anyone wished to conclude from this (as usually happens) that God loved Nabal, he would be mistaken. For God heaped great riches on him, and God hated David and his men, whom he allowed to be in the greatest poverty. Nor can we determine from riches or poverty whether God's favour or hatred is toward anyone, for these things happen indiscriminately to good and bad. And yet, just as a man's life and safety do not lie in having plenty of goods, as Christ himself testifies, so it is certain that they do not depend on the goods of the body or of fortune, such as the goodness of his birth, his authority, or a beautiful and wise wife. Nabal indeed had all these things. But since he lacked the fear of God, true faith and wisdom, all these things were for him neither an ornament nor a help, but rather, as with all unbelievers, they worked his destruction. Not unwisely did Solomon say: "What good is it to a fool that he abounds most in wealth, since he cannot buy wisdom with money?"

units.la: Hæ & aliæ descriptiones tam piorum quàm impiorum hominum, diligenter con siderandæ sunt, vt cogitemus quorum veli mus esse similes aut dissimiles. Quod si vide mus alios lapsos (Est enim hoc malū nobis natura insitū, vt qui in nostris vitijs execuiti re & nobis mirificè blandiri solemus, in alie nis obseruādis quouisLynceo sim⁹ oculatio res) aliorū exéplis cautiores redditi sapere,
units.tr: These and other descriptions of pious and impious men must be considered carefully, so that we may think about whom we wish to be like or unlike. If we see others fallen (for it is a natural evil implanted in us that we usually are blind to our own vices and flatter ourselves wonderfully, while we are quicker than any Lynx at noticing faults in others), let us be made wiser by the examples of others and become more cautious.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV
units.tr: DE VITA ET OBITV

units.la: vitamq; nostram, Dei ope,sapientius insti-tuere discamus. At si alios præclarè & honestè se gessisse cernamus, illorum exempla nobis ad imitationem proponemus, Deum ardentissimè precati,vt nobis gratiam suam sanctumq; spiritum largiatur,quò ipsi secun-dum voluntatem suam sanctissimam, in ve-ra fide & vitæ integritate seruire,studiaq́ue nostra probare possimus.
units.tr: Thus, by God's help, we may learn to order our life more wisely. But if we see others having conducted themselves excellently and honourably, we shall set their examples before us for imitation, earnestly praying God that He would grant us His grace and His Holy Spirit, so that we ourselves may be able to serve Him according to His most holy will, in true faith and integrity of life, and to approve our endeavours.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi. HOMILIA II.
units.tr: ON THE LIFE AND DEATH OF NABAL THE DRUNKARD. HOMILY II.

units.la: Dauid legatos suos ad Nabalem mittit,vt se commeatu iuuet.
units.tr: David sends his envoys to Nabal, asking him for help with provisions.

units.la: 4 Andiuit itaq; Dauid in deserto, quod tonderet Nabal oues suas.
units.tr: 4 David therefore heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.

units.la: 5 Misit ergo Dauid decem pueros, dixitq; Dauid pueris: Ascendite in Char-mel, & ite ad Nabal,ipsumq; salutate no-mine meo pacifice.
units.tr: 5 So David sent ten young men, and said to them: "Go up to Carmel, go to Nabal, and greet him peaceably in my name."

units.la: 6 Et dicite: Sic viuenti, & tu sal-uus, & domus tua salua, & omne quod est tibi saluum.
units.tr: 6 "And say: 'Long life to you! Peace be to you, to your house, and to all that is yours.'"

units.la: 7 Nunc autem audiui,quod tonden-tes tibi testibi: Iam pastores, qui sunt tibi, fuerunt nobiscum, non affecimus eos ignominia, nec defuit eis quicquam omnibus diebus, quibus fuerunt in Charmel.
units.tr: 7 "Now I have heard that you have shearers. Your shepherds who were with us, we did not wrong them with insults, and nothing was missing for them all the days they were in Carmel."

units.la: 8 Interroga pueros tuos & renunciabunt tibi. Inuenient ergo pueri gratiam in oculis tuis: in die enim bono venimus: Da obsecro, quod inuenerit manus tua seruis tuis & filio tuo Dauidi.
units.tr: 8 "Ask your servants, and they will tell you. Let my young men find favour in your eyes, for we have come on a good day. Please give whatever your hand finds to your servants and to your son David."

units.la: SEcunda historiae huius parte commemoratur Dauidem legatos suos, viros honestos, ad Nabalem misisse, qui ab illo cibaria suo nomine peterent. Ordine autem hoc Spiritus sanctus vtitur.
units.tr: The second part of this story records that David sent his envoys, honourable men, to Nabal, to ask him for food in David's name. The Holy Spirit observes an order in this.

units.la: Primo dicitur, unde istos miserit. Ex deferto, nempe Pharan, quod in Arabia Petraea, non procul a tribu Iuda situm fuisse volunt: In deserto isto nulla commeatus copia erat. Quare necessitas, durum, quod aiunt, telum Dauidé impellit, ut a Nabale aliquid petat, qui vel mentione loci facta cogitare debuisset, illum necessitate eo compulsum. Nec enim hic obiectioni illi locus: Cur necessaria pecunijs non comparat? Nam vt illis fuisset instructissimus: tamen, isthic loci, quae comeret, non suppetebant.
units.tr: First, we are told where he sent them from. They want it to be from the wilderness, namely Paran, which lay in Arabia Petraea, not far from the tribe of Judah: In that wilderness there was no supply of provisions. Hence necessity, as they say, a hard weapon, drove David to ask something of Nabal, who, by the very mention of the place, ought to have reflected that David had been compelled there by necessity. Nor does the objection apply here: "Why did he not buy what he needed with money?" For even if he had been very well supplied with money, still there was nothing there to buy.

units.la: Secundo tempus annotatur. Quum, audiffet,inquit auctor noster, quod tonderet Nabal oues suas,misit Dauid decem pueros &c.Multum in eo situ est,vt suo rem quam que aggrediaris tepore, praesertim, si quid ab alio velis impetratum.Nam ,vt vulgo dicunt, vna hora dat, quod centum aliae non ferunt.Non inscitè Salomon,Omnia,inquit suam tempestiuitatem habent.Huius praece pti non ignarus poeta de Anna Didonis fo rore sic canit:
units.tr: Second, the time is noted. When he had heard, our author says, that Nabal was shearing his sheep, David sent ten young men, and so on. There is much in choosing the right moment for whatever you undertake, especially if you wish to obtain something from another. For, as people commonly say, one hour brings what a hundred others cannot. Solomon wisely said: "Everything has its proper time." A poet who was not unaware of this precept sings of Dido's sister Anna:

units.la: Sola viri molles aditus & tempora noras.
units.tr: You alone knew the soft approaches and the times of men.

units.la: Horatius mittens Augusto librum, monet nuncium, vt in tempore illum adeat; nempe:
units.tr: Horace, sending his book to Augustus, advises the messenger to approach him at the right time, namely:

units.la: Si validus, si laetus erit; si dens, poscet.
units.tr: If he is well, if he is cheerful, if he is at leisure, he will ask.

units.la: Historici tradunt Vespasianum id temporis fuisse facillimum & indulgentissimum, quo in balneum triclinium què transfibat: eaque momenta atque occasionem domesticos ad aliquid petendum magnopere captasse. Nempe melfem, messis tempore, et vindemiam,vindemiae,faciendam censebant. Recte ergo facere Dauid quoque sibi visus est,si legatos suos eo tempore ad Nabalem mitteret,quo illum tonsuram ouium facere inaudiuerat. Quemadmodum enim nos in fine messis & vindemiae epulum lautum operarijs exhibemus.(Den schmeckt oder frey banen Sanctum/dentrunten ita olim diuites solebant in tonsura ouium magna conuiuia agitare, in quibus amicos laute & prolixe accipiebant. Id ita esse, vel ex historia de Abfolone apparet, in qua narratur, ipsum tanto odio ab Ammone propter Thamarem sororem suam ab eo violatam, dissedisse, ut cum eo nunquam omnino neque amice loqueretur neque inimice. Venit tandem in mentem, ut tempus tonsurae ouium (quam luna decrescente a veteribus fieri fuisse solitam, Marcus Varro testatur) arriperet. Inuitat ergo, vrget & quodammodo cogit patrem regem: Qui se primo excusat, ne grauis ei sit, vincitur tamen & Amnonem cum aliis filiis mittit: Amnon, quod se non solum vocari videret, & longum tempus intercesisset a stuprata Thamare, eoq; consideret, iniuriam hanc obliuioni iam datam esse, ad conuiuium venit, in quo, cum vino meracius sumto, hilarior factus esset, a feruis Abfolonis incautus obtruncatur, &c. De conuiuijs tonsorijs vide Stuccium libro primo Antiquitatum conuiuialium, Capite vigesimo tertio.
units.tr: Historians relate that Vespasian at that time was most easy-going and indulgent, when he went to the bath and to dinner; and that his household had greatly sought those moments and opportunities for asking for something. Indeed they thought that the harvest should be made at harvest time, and the vintage at vintage time. So David also thought he was acting rightly if he sent his envoys to Nabal at the time when he had heard that he was shearing his sheep. For just as we at the end of harvest and vintage give a rich feast to the workers (German marginal note: that tastes good, or: drink freely and toast the health), so in former times the rich were accustomed to hold great banquets at sheep-shearing, at which they received their friends richly and lavishly. That this was so appears even from the history of Absalom, in which it is related that he was so hostile to Amnon, on account of his sister Tamar whom Amnon had violated, that he would never speak with him, either friendly or unfriendly. At last it came into his mind to seize the time of sheep-shearing (which, as Marcus Varro testifies, the ancients were accustomed to do when the moon was waning). He therefore invites, urges and in a way compels the king his father. The king at first excuses himself, lest he be a burden to him, but he is overcome and sends Amnon with his other sons. Amnon, seeing that he was not only being invited, and that a long time had passed since he had ravished Tamar, and thinking that this wrong had now been given over to oblivion, came to the feast, where, having drunk wine rather freely and become merrier, he was cut down by Absalom's servants while off his guard, and so on. On banquets at sheep-shearing see Stuccius, book one of the Antiquities of Banquets, chapter twenty-three.

units.la: Tertiò, quot & quales miserit, indicatur. Misit ergo Dauid (inquit auctor) decem pueros, (infra seruos vocat) dixitq; Dauid illis: Ascendite,&c. Sed cur decem? Nimirum vt auctoritatem sibi legatione ista aliquam compararet. Saepe enim fit, vt cum a pluribus rogamur, illis quod petunt, demus: idem ipsum paucioribus non largituri. Sed cur iuuenes? Nempe quod in eorum gratiam plus nonnunquam faciamus, quàm decrepitorum, quos, quod prima quoque die decessuros, ideoq; nec fraudi nec emolumento nobis esse posse credamus, leuius aliquanto, quàm pro meritorum aetatisq; ratione par sit aestimamus. E contra iuniorum gratiam, quod & contumeliarum & beneficiorum diu memores fore putemus, tantum non emendicamus.
units.tr: Third, it is indicated how many and what sort he sent. So David (the author says) sent ten young men (below he calls them servants), and David said to them: Go up, etc. But why ten? Clearly so that he might gain some authority for himself by this embassy. For it often happens that when we are asked by several people we grant what they seek, though we would not grant the same thing to fewer. But why young men? Because we sometimes do more for the young than for the aged, whom we think will soon die, and so cannot be either a loss or a gain to us; we value them rather less than their merits and age would warrant. On the other hand, we almost beg for the favour of the young, because we think they will long remember both insults and benefits.

units.la: Quarto, oratio, quam Dauid legatis suis dictauit describitur. Est autem illa omnino artificiosa. Nihil enim in ea eorum praetermittit, quae hominem istum ad benignitatem adducere posset.
