Primo mandat illis, vt Nabalem suo nomine quàm officiosissimé salutent, dicantque: Sic viuenti & tu salus & domus tua salua, & omne, quod est tibi, saluum. Sensus est: Deus Optimus Maximus velit, vt ista, qua nunc vteris, felicitas sit perpetua: nec tantum tibi, sed etiam familiae: nec familiae tantum, sed etiam armentis & gregibus.
units.tr: Fourth, the speech which David dictated to his envoys is described. It is entirely skilful. For it omits nothing that could bring that man to kindness. First he orders them to greet Nabal as courteously as possible in his name, and to say: Long life to you, peace to you, to your house, and to all that is yours. The meaning is: may God, the Best and Greatest, will that this prosperity which you now enjoy be perpetual, not only for you but also for your household, and not only for your household but also for your herds and flocks.

units.la: Ex eo,quod pij alijs à Deo fausta precantur,colligimus,quæ habemus bona, ab vno Deo,tanquam ex fonte, fluere & manare omnia: qui si ille manum a nobis vel leuiter abstraheret, de nobis actum esset. Certè,si illa omnia ex nobis ipsis haberemus,non opus esset illa vel nobis vel alijs à Deo precario emendicare. At subinde pij alijs à Deo fausta ac felicia omnia precantur. Relinquitur ergo ab illo solo ea prouenire omnia, quemadmodum etiam D. Iacobus testatur, qui inter alia cap.1. eleganter & verè: Omne, inquit,munus bonum, & omne perfectum donum supernè est, descendens à Patre, id est,auctore luminum, apud quem non inest tranfmutatio, aut conuersionis obumbratio,&c.
units.tr: From the fact that the godly wish prosperous things for others from God, we gather that all the good things we have flow and issue from God alone, as from a fountain. If he withdrew his hand from us even slightly, it would be all over with us. Certainly, if we had all these things from ourselves, there would be no need to beg them from God, either for ourselves or for others. But the godly constantly wish prosperity and happiness for others from God. It remains, therefore, that all these things come from him alone, as St James also testifies, who elegantly and truly says in chapter 1 among other things: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning," and so on.

units.la: Deinde ex salutatione ista videmus, Dauidem,aliosq; fideles non rapi spiritu liuido & inuido, quorundam more,qui tantum non prospera aliorum fortuna dirumpuntur: Tam abest,vt alios, opibus vel honoribus auctos velint. Quin communem alijs solem & aerem esse ægrè ferunt.At quanto rectius,Deo gratias agerent pro beneficijs in alios quoq; collatis, toto pectore precati, vt illos longum saluos & incolumes præstare dignetur.
units.tr: Next, from this greeting we see that David and the other faithful are not carried away by a spirit of envy and jealousy, like some people who are almost torn apart by the prosperous fortune of others. So far from it, they do not wish others to be enriched with wealth or honours. Rather, they bear it with difficulty that others share the same sun and air. But how much more rightly would they thank God for the benefits bestowed on others too, praying with their whole heart that he would deign to keep them safe and unharmed for a long time!

units.la: Salutationi subiungit breuem & mode-
units.tr: To the greeting he adds a brief and modest ...

units.la: Commemoratio beneficiorum, quibus illum affecisset. Iam pastores, inquit, qui sunt tibi, fuerunt nobiscum, non affecimus eos ignominia: nec defuit eis quicquam omnibus diebus, quibus fuerunt in Charmel, &c. Sensus est, Se cum pastoribus Nabalis, non solum sine vllo maleficio, verum etiam cum magno beneficio esse versatos, ita vt eos ab omni iactura tutos praestiterint, quamdiu fuerint in Charmelo. Hebraea vox significat, pudore suffundere. Si pastores nunc oues, nunc capras aliquas amisissent, nec rationem potuissent reddere, quo nam fuissent abactae, non pulchrè stetissent. Enimuero cum creditorum rationem dare nō possumus, pudore suffundimur. Iacobus Genesis 31. exprobrat Labani socero suo, quod feris ereptum nihil ad ipsum retulerit: ipse semper praestiterit damnum: eum ipsi semper imputasse: si quid per furtum amissum sit, tam interdiu quam noctu, suo periculo amissum esse. Ex quo apparet, Dauidem cum suis custodem potius Nabalis, quàm militem fuisse.
units.tr: A reminder of the benefits with which he had favoured him. Now, he says, your shepherds who were with us, we did not wrong them with insults, and nothing was missing for them all the days they were in Carmel, etc. The meaning is that he and his men had been among Nabal's shepherds not only without any harm but with great kindness, so that they had kept them safe from every loss for as long as they were in Carmel. The Hebrew word means to suffuse with shame. If the shepherds had now lost some sheep or goats and could not give an account of where they had been driven, they would not have been in a good position. But when we cannot give an account to our creditors, we are suffused with shame. Jacob in Genesis 31 reproaches his father-in-law Laban that what was torn by wild beasts he never brought back to him; he himself always bore the loss, and Laban always charged it to him: whatever was lost by theft, whether by day or by night, was lost at his own risk. From this it appears that David and his men were rather guardians of Nabal's flocks than soldiers.

units.la: Id autem non tantùm dicere vult Dauid legatos suos, sed etiam probat à testibus. Testes verò citat non quosuis, sed Nabalis ipsius seruos, Interroga, inquit, pueros.
units.tr: David wants this not only to be said by his messengers but also to be proved by witnesses. He cites as witnesses not just anyone but Nabal's own servants: Ask the young men, he says.

units.la: Commemoratio beneficiorum, verf. 7.
units.tr: Recollection of the kindnesses, verse 7.

units.la: Testimonia verf. 8. rostuos, & renunciabunt tibi. Quasi diceret: Nisi huius nobis rei tui famuli testes esse possint, eia, male pereamus. Infra famulorum unus Abigaeli refert, Dauidem cum suis pro muro ipsis noctes diesq; aduersus abigeos & feras fuisse, donec versati cum eis sint, pascendo pecudes. Nec enim parvum in istis regionibus periculum erat a leonibus, vrsis, alijsque feris: Unde legimus, Dauidem, cum Isai parentis sui oues pascerent, cum leonibus & vrsis congressum: &c. Iacobus patriarcha non abs re verebatur, ne Iosephus, quem tantopere adamabat, à feris discerptus esset. Tunica, inquit, fili mei: Fera mala deuorauit eum: rapiendo raptus est Iosephus meus. Adhaec Syri, Arabes, Amalechitae, alijque, praedatores, cum viderent Dauidem ibi esse cum exercitu, non audebant accedere, vt nec fures ac abigei. Quod certè beneficium erat non vulgare. Oues enim, stolidum & simplex animalis genus, saepius deuiantes, feris vel abigeis praeda fiunt. Quàm ingens bonum sit, bonum habere vicinum nemo facilè dixerit. Certè, si ille fidus noftriqueque cupidus fuerit, ne bos quidem, vt prouerbio fertur, perierit. Unde Hesiodus: ῾Ο μέγιστος καλεῖν, ὅσις σὲ ἐγγύθι ναίει, id est, interprete Guldibeccio.
units.tr: Testimony, verse 8: "...and they will tell you." As if he were saying: unless your servants can be witnesses to this matter for us, let us perish miserably. Further on, one of the servants reports to Abigail that David and his men had been a wall to them night and day against cattle-thieves and wild beasts, until they had been living with them, pasturing the flocks. In those regions the danger from lions, bears and other wild beasts was not small. Hence we read that David, while pasturing his father Jesse's sheep, fought with lions and bears, etc. The patriarch Jacob had good reason to fear that Joseph, whom he loved so dearly, would be torn apart by wild beasts: "Your son's tunic," he said, "an evil beast has devoured him; Joseph my son is surely torn in pieces." Moreover, the Syrians, Arabs, Amalekites and other raiders, seeing David there with his army, did not dare to approach, nor did thieves and cattle-rustlers. This was certainly no small kindness. Sheep, a foolish and simple kind of animal, often wander off and become prey to wild beasts or thieves. How great a good it is to have a good neighbour, no one could easily say. Surely, if such a man is faithful and kind to us, not even an ox, as the proverb goes, will perish. Hence Hesiod: "The greatest... (he who dwells near you)," that is, in the translation of Guldibeccius: [Ὁ μέγιστος καλεῖν, ὅσις σὲ ἐγγύθι ναίει].

units.la: Eum autem in primis inuita, qui propè te habitat: Quid ita?
units.tr: Indeed you should especially invite him who lives near you. Why so?

units.la: εἰ γὰρ τό, inquit Poeta, ἠ ἀχνὴ ἐγχώριον ἄλλο γλύπτω, γεί ὄγνες ἀζωσι ἔκιον, ζώ σαν τὸ ὄ πηοί, id est, eodem interprete:
units.tr: For, as the poet says, "if some other thing falls upon the neighbours' ..., neighbours come up ungirt, but kinsmen come girded," that is, in the same translation: [εἰ γὰρ τό ... γεί ὄγνες ἀζωσι ἔκιον, ζώ σαν τὸ ὄ πηοί].

units.la: Si enim tibi & negotium domesticum ali quod contingat, Vicini discincti accedunt, cinguntur verò cognati. Id quod & cassitæ apologus apud A. Gellium indicat, vbi cognati multò minus faciūt,quàm vicini. Nec id Themistoclem fugit,qui, vt est apud Plutarchum,cum prædium venditurus esset, etiam hoc per preconem addendum censuit, quod haberet bonum vicinum.
units.tr: For if some domestic trouble befalls you, neighbours come running up ungirded, while relatives come girded. The fable of Cassita in Aulus Gellius shows this too, where kinsmen do far less than neighbours. Nor did Themistocles overlook this: as Plutarch relates, when he was about to sell an estate, he also had it proclaimed by the herald that the property had a good neighbour.

units.la: Querat tamen aliquis,vnde Dauid tot mi lites potuerit alere,si non prædabatur? Respondeo. Consentaneum est,quosque suis, pro parte, cibaria misisse. Deinde prædati quidem sunt,sed non ex populo Dei,verùm ex Palæstinis,Syris, Arabibus, Amalechitis & alijs, quos sciebant iamdudum hostes fuisse à Deo declaratos. Quid? quod nō omnes eo ingenio fuere, quo Nabal? Ac, credibile est, multos hinc inde viros bonos fuisse, qui liberaliberaliter,idq; sponte sua,manus clam por-rexerint: Quosdam vero ex metu, ne abiL-lis infestarentur. Quia vero constabat, Da-uidem cum suis custodem potius Nabalis quàm militem fuisse, omnino ipsius fuisset, cognatum, omnium rerum egenum, com-meatu aliquo iuuare. Nam & Ethnici, ijs à quibus beneficijs sunt affecti, naturâ duce, gratiam reponendam scribunt. Inter alios præclarè Cicero, Nullum, inquit, officium referenda gratia magis necessariu est. Quod si ea, quæ acceperis vtenda, maiore mensu-ra,si modò poísis, iubet reddere Hesiodus, quidnam beneficio prouocati facere debe-mus? Tantum ille. His præmissis, Dauid, quid petat,paucis exponit.Inueniant,inquit, pueri gratiam in oculis tuis,id est, Benignè fac nobis,ac, quod commodum tibi videbitur, contribue. In die enim bono, hoc est, fausto ac felici,venimus. Si quis nos occupet, cum esculentis abundamus, liberaliores habet. Difficiliores experturi, cum nihil est parati, vel etiam aliunde corrogandum, quod alijs impertiundum esset. Deinde, cum frontem exporreximus, plerumq; nos faciliores ro-gantibus præbemus. Dicimus: Eia, Sina-mus illum nobiscum gaudere. Hodie festus dies est,ac solennis, &c. Herodi non præter caussam vitio vertitur, quod natali suo, in quo aulicis suis conuiuium opiparum parauerat, Iohannem Baptistam, prophetam maximum, nuptias incestuosas damnantem, in custodia Macheruntina capite minui imperarit, nec illum festiuitate sua frui dignatus sit. Ad eundem modum Nabalis omnino fuisset, tam bono fauftoq; die, legatos istos minus iniuria afficere: eoque magis, quod ea esset Dauidis modestia, vt suos milites vocaret Nabalis seruos: seipsum vero eius filium: eo fortasis nomine, quod Dauid esset minor aetate. Solenne enim in sacris literis est, vt iuniores, aetate proiectos, patres, illi vicissim minores aetate, filios appellent.
units.tr: Someone may still ask: how could David feed so many soldiers if he did not plunder? I answer: it is likely that the men of Nabal's district sent them food in part. Moreover, they did plunder, but not from God's people; they plundered Philistines, Syrians, Arabs, Amalekites and others whom they knew had long since been declared enemies by God. And why not? Not all were of the same disposition as Nabal. It is credible that many good men here and there gave freely and of their own accord, secretly extending a hand, and some out of fear, lest they be harassed by David's men. But since it was clear that David and his men were a guard for Nabal rather than soldiers, it was altogether fitting that he should help his kinsman, who lacked everything, with some provisions. For the heathen too, by the guidance of nature, write that a kindness received must be repaid. Among others, Cicero clearly says: "No duty is more necessary than the repayment of a favour." And if Hesiod bids us to repay with a larger measure, if we can, what ought we to do to those who have been moved by a kindness? So much for him. With these things premised, David briefly sets out what he is asking. Let the young men, he says, find grace in your eyes, that is: be kind to us, and give whatever seems fitting to you. For we have come on a good day, that is, a fortunate and happy day. If someone catches us when we have plenty of food, we are more generous. Those who are tested when nothing is ready, or when something must be gathered from elsewhere to be given to others, are harder. Then, when we have cheered up, we generally show ourselves more easy to those who ask. We say: "Come on, let us allow him to rejoice with us. Today is a festive and solemn day," and so on. Herod is not unjustly blamed, because on his birthday, when he had prepared a sumptuous banquet for his courtiers, he ordered John the Baptist, the greatest prophet, who condemned his incestuous marriage, to be beheaded in the prison at Machaerus, and did not deign to let him share in his festivity. In the same way, it would have been altogether proper for Nabal, on so good and fortunate a day, to treat these messengers less unjustly; and all the more so because David was so modest that he called Nabal's servants his own soldiers, but called Nabal himself his son, perhaps for this reason, that David was younger in age. For it is customary in Holy Scripture for younger men to call older men fathers, and for them in turn to call younger men sons.

units.la: Denique petitionem repetunt, sed, Da obsecro, inquiunt, quod inuenerit manus tua servis tuis, & filio tuo Dauidi. Sensus est: Habes instructum conuiuium tonsoribus tuis: ex eo potes nobis commode partem aliquam decidere, ad ipsius Dauidis, tui propè dicemus filij, eiusque comitum famem propellendam. Nihil praescribunt, quantum debeat dare, sed, quantum, inquiunt, manus tua inuenerit: id est, quantum tibi videbitur. Adhaec ista non petunt verbis durris ac violentis: sed quàm mollissimis ac blanblandisimis. Si indignationis vel leuisimam significationem dedissent,eumq; coge re voluissent,non mirum fuisset, illos ab ipso, re infecta, ablegatos: Sed demittunt se, appellant seipsos, vti diximus, seruos ipsius: herum, filium. At nihil in seruos,prefertim fideles, ac cumprimis filios nimium censetur.Incredibile dictu, quantum apud cordatos viros possit, si te submiseris, verbisque placidis opem gratiamque petas. Vix ac ne vix quidem immuneratus ab illis discesseris. Sed quod Dauidi res esset cum homine stulto & temerario, nihil plane impetrat, quamuis æquissima esset ipsius postulatio. Quid enim? Non petebant, vt se suosque spoliaret, sed, quæ sibi commodum esset, largiretur. Adhæc nihil postulant, quod vel cum honestate pugnet, vel facultates ipsius excedat, vel etiam ipsi fraudi ac detrimento vllatenus fit. Est quidem amicis gratificandum, sed quousque patitur æquum & honestum. Resteque omnino Pericles, amico roganti, vt pro se falsum diceret testimonium, cui adiunctum erat iusiurandum, id est, periurium: respondit, se quidem amicum esse, sed vsq; ad aram:sentiens aliquoufq; gratificandum amicis,sed citra numinis religionisq; violatione.
units.tr: Finally they repeat the request: Give, I beg you, they say, whatever your hand finds to your servants and to your son David. The sense is: you have a banquet prepared for your shearers; from it you can conveniently set aside some part for us, to relieve the hunger of David himself, who, as we say, is almost your son, and of his companions. They do not prescribe how much he should give, but "whatever your hand finds," they say, that is, whatever seems good to you. Moreover, they do not ask in harsh and violent words, but in the most gentle and flattering terms. Had they shown even the slightest sign of indignation, or wished to compel him, it would not have been surprising if they had been sent away by him empty-handed. But they lower themselves: they call themselves his servants, as we said, and call him their master and father. Yet nothing is considered too much for servants, especially faithful ones, and above all for sons. It is hard to believe how much you can gain with wise men if you humble yourself and ask for help and favour in gentle words. You will scarcely, if at all, leave them without being enriched. But because David had to deal with a foolish and rash man, he obtains nothing at all, although his request was most just. For what did they ask? They did not ask him to strip himself and his people, but to give what was convenient for him. Furthermore, they ask for nothing that either conflicts with honesty, exceeds his means, or is in any way to his loss or harm. One must indeed oblige friends, but only so far as what is just and honourable allows. Pericles too, when a friend asked him to give false testimony, to which an oath was attached, that is, perjury, answered that he was indeed a friend, but only as far as the altar: he judged that friends must be obliged up to a point, but without violating divine majesty and religion.

units.la: Nabal, si non fuisset caput sine cerebro, etiam à nemine requisitus, tamen sponte sua, Dauid principi suo, honestum aliquod munus contribuisse debebat. Ita 2. Samuel 17. Dauidi eiusque comitibus, postquam Mahanaim ventum est, obtulerunt Sobis, Machir, & Barzilæus stragula, pelues, vasa fictilia, triticum, hordeum, farinam, polentam, fabas, lentes, fruges tostas, mel, butyrum, oues, caseos bubulos, ad commeatum. Suspicabantur enim (inquit autor) homines fame, lassitudine, sitiq; per deserta loca laborare, &c.
units.tr: Nabal, even if he had not been a head without a brain, ought of his own accord to have given some honourable gift to David his prince, even if no one had asked him. So in 2 Samuel 17: when they came to Mahanaim, Shobi, Machir and Barzillai brought David and his companions coverlets, bowls, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, parched corn, honey, butter, sheep and cows' cheese for provisions. "For they suspected," the author says, "that the people were suffering from hunger, weariness and thirst in the wilderness," and so on.

units.la: Sed quid ex ista postulatione colligimus? Primò videmus, Pios quoque, fame, aliisque calamitatibus à Deo exerceri. Dauid certè vir pius, ac, nullo suo merito, in exilium pulsus, cum suis fame colluctatur: inter quos, vt demus multos fuisse quibus res ad restim redierit: plures tamen viros bonos & honestos fuisse consentaneum est. Dicit quidem Dauid, Se puerum fuisse, & iam consenuisse: neque tamen vidisse virum bonum derelictum, aut eius progeniem vestum desiderasse. Sed & Salomon, Non committ Deus, inquit, animam iusti, hoc est, iustum famere. Sensus tamen vtrinque est, nisi Dei gloria, hominisq; salus aliud requirat.
units.tr: But what do we gather from this request? First, we see that the godly too are exercised by God with hunger and other calamities. David was certainly a godly man, and, though he had done nothing to deserve it, was driven into exile, and with his men struggled with hunger; and among them, even if we grant that some had their means reduced to nothing, it is nonetheless likely that many good and honest men were there. David indeed says that he had been a boy and had now grown old, yet he had not seen a righteous man forsaken, or his offspring begging for bread. But Solomon also says: "God will not let the soul of the righteous famish," that is, that the righteous man will not go hungry. Yet the sense on both points is the same, unless the glory of God and the salvation of man require otherwise.

units.la: Vult enim Deus aliquando exploratam pio rum hominum fidem, patientiam & obedientiam ad imitatione proponere,ac docere, famem potius extremam tolerandam,quàm à veritate vel latum vnguem discedendum, vel quiduis aliud, præter officium,designan dum.Item : Copiam rerum Dei donum esse, eoq; ardentioribus votis petendam. Dauid alias quoq; fame laborauit: vt cum ab Achimelecho Pont.Max. panes propositionis pe teret,quibus vesci non erat ipsi licitum neq; ijs qui cum eo erant, sed solis sacerdotibus. Apostoli præ fame spicas euulsas,fricant sab batho,& comedunt. D.Paulus de se ipso testatur,se famem,sitim,frigus & nuditate per tulisse. Ad Hebr.11.scribitur,ouillis & caprinis pellibus,hoc est, vilibus & asperis amicti bus sanctos ad extremam inopiam redactos, ferarum instar coactos in asperrimis locis vi uere. Quot Martyres in carcere,fame,siti,fri gore sunt enecti? Christus ipse plus semel esuriuit. Quamuis autem Deus non semper corpori necessaria suppeditat:tamé suis præ stantiora largitur: fidem puta, dilectionem, patientiam,&c. Quare non est,quod Diabo lum audiamus, qui nobis suspicionem inijcit: Deum nobis malè velle,qui nos fame affligat. Quin nos hisce alijsq; exemplis vete-
units.tr: For God sometimes wills to set before the godly, as an example for imitation, the tested faith, patience and obedience of pious men, and to teach that extreme hunger is to be endured rather than that one should depart from the truth even a hair's breadth, or do anything beyond one's duty. Likewise: that abundance of goods is a gift of God, and must be sought all the more eagerly by prayer. David also suffered hunger at other times, when he asked Ahimelech the high priest for the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him or his men to eat, but only for the priests. The apostles, from hunger, plucked ears of corn, rubbed them, and ate them on the Sabbath. St Paul testifies of himself that he endured hunger, thirst, cold and nakedness. In Hebrews 11 it is written that the saints, reduced to extreme poverty, clothed in sheepskins and goatskins, that is, in cheap and rough garments, were forced to live like wild beasts in the most desolate places. How many martyrs were starved to death in prison by hunger, thirst and cold? Christ himself hungered more than once. Although God does not always supply the body with what it needs, yet he bestows on his people better things: faith, love, patience, and so on. Therefore there is no reason for us to listen to the Devil, who puts into our minds the suspicion that God wishes us ill when he afflicts us with hunger. Rather, let us be raised up and sustained by these examples, old and new, and let us reflect, as is the truth, that David and others struggled with hunger, and yet were pleasing and acceptable to God.

units.la: C ribus ac nouis erigamus ac sustentemus, ac, quod res est, cogitemus, Dauidem aliosque cum fame colluctatos: & tamen Deo gratos & acceptos fuisse. Item: Hominem non consueto solùm & naturali victu (quem omnem panis vocabulo Hebraei comprehendunt) su ftentari, sed quauis alia re, quam Deus decreuerit, aut ad hoc destinarit, vt nobis alen dis atque feruandis seruiat. Quare nos neque de victu anxiè folicitos esse debere, neque propter penuriam à fide & obedientia, Deo debita, discedere: sed in huius prouidentiam & curam paternam respicere, qui & velit et possit nobis prospicere, licet omni bus naturalibus præsidijs destituamur. Sed nec sola hæc est vita hominis, qua hic viuitur, sed melior in cœlis habetur, quæ neq; pa ne neque alijs edulijs sustentatur, sed fide in Christum obtinetur, & æternum durat, &c.
units.tr: with these and other examples, old and new, raise ourselves up and sustain ourselves, and consider, as is the truth, that David and others struggled with hunger and yet were pleasing and acceptable to God. Likewise: a human being is sustained not only by his customary and natural food (which the Hebrews comprehend under the single word "bread"), but by any other thing that God has decreed or appointed to serve for nourishing and preserving us. Therefore we ought neither to be anxiously concerned about food, nor to fall away from the faith and obedience owed to God because of want, but to look to the fatherly providence and care of him who both wills and is able to provide for us, even though we are deprived of all natural aids. Moreover, this is not the only life that man lives here; a better life is kept in heaven, which is sustained neither by bread nor by other food, but is obtained by faith in Christ, and endures forever, etc.

units.la: Nec verò mirum est, Diabolum homines egestate atq; rerum omnium penuria ad desperationem folicitare. Christum ipsum occasione famis aggressus est: nimirum quòd speraret, hanc caussam fore, cur vel impatientius ferret famem, vel de Dei patris erga se voluntate dubitaret, & proinde sibijpsi vijs illicitis consuleret.
units.tr: Nor indeed is it strange that the devil stirs men up to despair through poverty and the lack of all things. He attacked Christ himself by means of hunger, no doubt because he hoped that this would be the reason why Christ would bear hunger more impatiently, or doubt the Father's will toward him, and so seek for himself by unlawful means.

units.la: Deinde exemplo Dauidis militumq; eius discidiscimus, quid illorum, qui commeatu aut publico aut priuato destituuntur, fit officij. Dauid, etiamsi laboret inopia rerum: mal-uult tamen mendicando quàm latrocinio vi ctum quærere. Videt Nabalem esse diuitem & cognatum suum. Non tamen ex eius pa-scuis prædas agit: sed precario aliquid ab il-lo petit. Non dicit: Itàne verò ille tot oues, & capras domi aleret, nos militiæ cum famè colluctaremur? Itàne verò ille dies noctesq; perpotaret, & in delitijs ageret: nos vix ac ne vix quidem vitam toleraremus? Age,par titionem instituamus. Hæc,inquá,aliaq; hu-ius generis nō intonat: sed,vt dixi, etiam mi les,quantum potest,à rapina cauet,ne suo ex-emplo latrones & sicarios ad nequitiam fa-ceret audaciores. Ac quidem præclarè. Iu-stitia enim virtus est, quæ suum cuiquè tri-buit. Sed & Paulus: Qui furabatur,inquit, nè furetur amplius, sed potius manuum la-bore bona comparet,vt habeat, quod egen-tibus, impertiat. Hodie tamen furtis tàm publicis quàm priuatis,nihil pro pudor, est communius,adeò vt multi, etsi aperte ma-nus in res alienas inijciant, tamen se fame excusatos autument. Verè quidem Menan-der:
units.tr: Next, from the example of David and his soldiers we learn what the duty is of those who are deprived of supplies, whether public or private. David, although he suffers want of things, nevertheless prefers to seek food by begging rather than by plunder. He sees that Nabal is rich and his kinsman. Yet he does not carry off booty from Nabal's pastures, but asks something from him as a favour. He does not say: "Does he then feed so many sheep and goats at home, while we are struggling with hunger in the army? Does he then drink all day and night and live in luxury, while we can scarcely, if at all, endure life? Come, let us make an exchange." He does not thunder such things, nor others of this kind; but, as I said, the soldier also, as far as he can, guards against robbery, lest by his example he make robbers and assassins bolder in wickedness. And rightly so. For justice is the virtue that gives each his due. But Paul also says: "Let him who stole steal no more, but rather work with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to share with those in need." Yet today, to our shame, nothing is more common than thefts, both public and private, so that many, even when they openly lay hands on the property of others, think themselves excused by hunger. Truly, Menander says:

units.la: λιμὸς, inquit, μέγιστον ἀλγῶ ἀνθρώποις (ἐφυ) fames ... de ...
units.tr: "Hunger," he says, "is the greatest pain for men ... (by nature) ... hunger ... of ..."

units.la: λιμὸς γὰρ δὴ ἐδ᾽ οἱ ἔςιν αὐτεπάγγελτον ἐπῶ, id est: Fames maximus dolor hominibus est, Fami enim nullum est contradicere verbum. Nec praeter rem Malesuada à Virgilio dicitur. Vnde sapiens ille: Duo, inquit, postulo à te, ne prohibeas à me, hoc est, ne mihi deneges, priusquam moriar. Vel, quo ad vixero. Vnum: Vanitatem & verbum mendax remoue à me: Alterum: Paupertatem & diuitias ne dederis mihi: tribue mihi mediocre fortunâ, mox explicat, Ale me panę demensi mei, qui satis mihi fit vnde alar, qui mihi conuenit: postea rationem vtriusq; subdit: Ne forte (si scilicet diuitias mihi concesseris) satier & negem Dominum (vt declarat) & dicam, Quis est Iehoua? (Huc enim saepe satietas adducit ad securitatem, qua in Dei obliuionem venitur) & ne forte ad inopiam redigar, ac furer, & praehendam, id est, asfumam nomen Dei mei, scilicet in vanum, peierans: vt pauperibus moris est, quo rem faciant. Nec tamen est, quod Christianus malesuado isti consultori aures praebeat. Quin cogitet, Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris: benedictionemq; Dei expectans patienter paupertatis onus ferat: non furetur, alijsq; medijs illicitis famem propulset. Quamuis enim egestas aliquantulum eleuet crimen,
units.tr: For hunger has no need of words to urge it on, that is: Hunger is the greatest pain for men, for there is no word that can contradict hunger. Nor is Malesuada (the goddess of ill counsel) named by Virgil without reason. Hence that wise man says: "Two things I ask of you: do not refuse me them before I die, or, as long as I live. The first: remove from me vanity and a lying word. The second: give me neither poverty nor riches; give me a moderate lot," and then he explains: "Feed me with the bread that is my due, so that I may be fed with what is suitable for me." Afterwards he adds the reason for each. "Lest perhaps (if you should grant me riches) I become satiated and deny the Lord (as he declares) and say, 'Who is the LORD?'" (for satiety often leads to security, by which one comes to forget God), "and lest perhaps I be reduced to poverty and steal, and take hold of, that is, take up the name of my God, namely in vain, by perjury, as is the custom of the poor, who do so to get something done." Yet a Christian ought not to lend his ears to that counsellor of evil. Rather let him consider: "What you do not want done to you, do not do to another," and, waiting patiently for the blessing of God, let him bear the burden of poverty; let him not steal, nor drive off hunger by other unlawful means. For although want somewhat lessens the crime,

units.la: Prouer. 30. erimen,non tamen prorsus tollit. Scriptu- ra autem (vt hoc obiter addam) per furtum non intelligit tantùm furtum vulgo sic di- ctum, sed quidquid est malarum artium,& aucupiorum,quibus aliena captamus, & ad nos vi, aut specie recti transferre molimur.
units.tr: Prouer. 30. it does not wholly remove it. Scripture (to add this in passing) understands by theft not only what is commonly called theft, but whatever wicked arts and snares there are, by which we seek to catch what belongs to others and to transfer it to ourselves by force or by the appearance of right.

units.la: Apparet etiam hoc loco,quantum discri- minis sit inter milites Dauidis & Cares no- stri seculi.Dauid,etsi non haberet stipendia, quibus aleret milites:tamen non patitur eos concutere quenquam,aut cuiusquam Iudæi fortunis manus afferre. At nostri hodie milites, non ita modestè se gerunt.Oportet,in quiunt,hoc dare. Et, si quis, quamuis verecunde,neget,putant iniuriam sibi ingentem fieri. Apud veteres Romanos,castrensis disci plina seuerissimè colebatur. Postremò tamen eo ventum est infolentię,vt Cicero scribat,milites Romanos socijs ciuitatibus multo graviores esse quàm hostes.Ita hodie passim imponuntur ciuitatibus huiusmodi præ-sidia,vt ciuibus multò potius sit ab hostibus oppugnari,quàm ab illis defendi.Quocunq; eunt,nó gallinas tantùm,anseres,anates præ-dantur,sed & oues, porcos, boues abigunt. Quid multis? vt Ziganis, ita illis venientibus omnes portæ occludendę, omnes ferę obsiguandæ.
units.tr: It also appears here how great a difference there is between the soldiers of David and the soldiers of our own age. David, although he had no pay with which to feed his soldiers, nevertheless does not allow them to shake down anyone, or to lay hands on the property of any Jew. But our soldiers today do not conduct themselves so modestly. "We must be given this," they say; and if anyone, however respectfully, refuses, they think a great wrong is done to them. Among the ancient Romans, military discipline was cultivated most strictly. Yet at last it came to such insolence that Cicero writes that Roman soldiers were far more burdensome to allied cities than enemies were. So today such garrisons are imposed on cities everywhere, so that it is far more likely for the citizens to be attacked by these than defended by them. Wherever they go, they plunder not only hens, geese and ducks, but also drive off sheep, pigs and oxen. What more need be said? As when the Gypsies come, so at their coming all gates must be shut and all wild beasts locked up.

units.la: Sed quid de militibus dicimus, cum constet, illos, qui stipe ostiatim corrogant, non-nunquam fœminis, villarum curam absenti-bus maritis agentibus, incendium minari, nili, quæ petunt, euestigio largiantur. Quin & liberos haud paucos inuenias, qui res pa-rentum nostu furtim exportant, easq; in cœ-nopolijs ac ganeis abliguriunt et dilapidant. Hi, non possunt cum Dauide dicere: Rem nullam amisisti, Enimuerò iam hæc, iam illa amittunt. Dicunt quidem, se veros ac naturales paternorum bonorum hæredes esse: At iudicio Dei non carent peccato. Quod si parentes pauperes sint, & filij nihilominus hoc faciant, aggrauatur crimen: Parentes enim suos reuereri ac alere debent, non iniuria afficere ac spoliare. Hoc Ethnici quoque viderunt: Plautus in Pseud. Egóne patri surripere possim quicquam cauto scroni? Atque adeò si facere possem, pietas pro-hibet, &c. Clarius est Solomonis nostri il-lud: Qui patrem inquit, & matrem diripit, & negat esse scelus (quod post mortem in eorum bona sit successurus) is socius est vi-ri exterminationis, id est, sicarij. Inde enim facilè adducetur, vt, sicarijs adiunctus, alios quoq; diripiat. Recte Comicus:
units.tr: But why do we speak of soldiers, when it is well known that those who collect alms from door to door sometimes threaten women, who manage the farms while their husbands are away, with fire, unless they immediately grant what they ask? Indeed you may find not a few children who secretly carry off their parents' goods at night and squander and waste them in taverns and brothels. These cannot say with David: "You have lost nothing"; for now this thing, now that, is lost. They say indeed that they are the true and natural heirs of their parents' goods; but in the judgment of God they are not free from sin. And if the parents are poor, and the children nonetheless do this, the crime is made worse; for children ought to revere and feed their parents, not wrong and despoil them. The heathen too saw this: Plautus in the Pseudolus: "Could I steal anything from my father, who is careful of his property? And even if I could, piety forbids it," etc. Clearer still is that saying of our Solomon: "He who robs his father and mother, and says it is no crime (since after their death he will succeed to their goods), is a companion of a destroyer, that is, of an assassin." For from there he will easily be led, joined with assassins, to plunder others also. Rightly the comic poet says:

units.la: Qui mentiri, aut fallere infeuit patrem, aut Audebit, tantò magis audebit cæteros.
units.tr: He who has learned to lie to his father, or to deceive him, will dare, and will dare all the more to do the same to others.

units.la: Postremò, exemplum in Dauide modesti ac demissi animi habemus. Etenim cum mul tis argumentis autoritatem sibi ipsi astruere potuisset: vt quod sæpius in prælijs & vrbium obsidionibus vitam suam præsentissimę morti obiectasset, Nabale interim cum suis epulis & potationibus inseruiente: Quod non tantùm tribui Iudæ (ex qua Nabal quoque ortum trahebat) sed toti regno hacte-nus ornamento fuisset: Quod Saulis gener esset, quo licet minus vteretur propitio, tamen primo quoq; die in gratiam redire posset: quod iam nunc in Regem à propheta vn ctus, suo tempore ipsi vel commodo vel detrimento esse posset: alijsq; eius generis: tamen ea tantum obiter commemorat, quæ ad rem cumprimis faciebant, Milites suos, vt aliquoties dixi, appellat seruos Nabalis, & ipsum eius filium. Si Dauid fuisset animo ela to, non se in tantum demisisset, vt Nabalem, hominem tenacem, crudelem & fordidū, alterū parentem agnoscere: sed se iniuria infi gni eo nomine affici clamasset. Coegisset illū cibaria promere: dixisset: Age periculū facia m⁹, vter fit fortior. Sed quod didicisset, in alienas res nō inuolādū, verecūda in petēdo, vti diximus, vtitur oratione, ne id quod petit, exigere magis quàm rogare, & in mercedis potius, quàm beneficij loco numerare videa-tur. Ad eundem modum nos quoq;, omissa Thrasonica iactatione, nos ipsos nostraque gloriosius nō ostétabimus: sed humilitati stu-dentes, omnia, Pauli more, omnibus siemus. In primis vero potenti Dei manu nos sub-mittemus, idq; eo magis, quod licet plerisq; superbia iter esse ad huius vitæ splendorem videatur: scriptura tamen ex aduerso teste-tur, ignominiam quidem esse superbiæ mer-cedem, modestiæ vero gloriam. Quod cum multis testimonijs probare possemus, vnico Petri dicto contenti erimus. Is peculiares multas virtutes Christianorum commen-dans, modestiam in primis vrget. Modestia, inquit, estote intus ornati. Nã Deus super-bis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Quod si alios beneficijs ornauerimus, ea nō semper inculcabimus, odiosiúsue ob oculos ponemus, sed, vel taciti præteribimus, vel si omnino in memoriam reuocare visum fue-rit, vt: vbi quid ab eo, quem beneficio nobis obstrinximus, petere impetrareq; cupimus, in transcursu quasi, mollissimis verbis signi-ficabimus potius, quàm cômemorabimus.
units.tr: Lastly, we have in David an example of a modest and humble spirit. For although he could have asserted his authority by many arguments, such as that he had so often exposed his life to present death in battles and sieges of cities, while Nabal in the meantime was feasting and drinking with his men; and that this had hitherto been a credit not only to Judah (from which Nabal also drew his origin) but to the whole kingdom; that he was Saul's son-in-law, and although he might be less favoured by Saul, yet could return into favour on any day; that he had already been anointed king by the prophet and in due time could be of advantage or harm to Nabal; and other things of this kind: nevertheless he mentions only those things in passing which especially bore on the matter. He calls his soldiers, as I have said several times, the servants of Nabal, and Nabal's son himself. If David had been of a proud spirit, he would not have humbled himself so far as to acknowledge Nabal, a stingy, cruel and filthy man, as a second father; he would have cried out that he was being wronged in that name. He would have forced him to bring out provisions and said: "Come, let us test which of us is the stronger." But because he had learned not to seize what belongs to others, he uses a modest manner of asking, as we have said, so that what he seeks might appear to be asked rather than demanded, and reckoned as a favour rather than a benefit owed. In the same way we too, setting aside Thrasonic boasting, will not display ourselves and our own things too boastfully; but, aiming at humility, we will become all things to all men, after the manner of Paul. Above all, we will submit ourselves under the mighty hand of God, and all the more so because, although pride seems to many to be the way to the splendour of this life, Scripture on the contrary bears witness that shame is the reward of pride, but glory the reward of modesty. Since we could prove this by many testimonies, we will be content with one saying of Peter. Commending the particular many virtues of Christians, he especially urges modesty: "Be clothed with humility within, for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." And if we have conferred benefits on others, we will not always keep harping on them, nor set them before their eyes in an offensive way; but either pass them over in silence, or, if it seems right to bring them to mind at all, we will mention them in passing, as it were, and in the gentlest words signify them rather than recount them; especially when we wish to ask for and obtain something from the one whom we have bound to us by a benefit.

units.la: Nam vt scite Sosia apud Comicum:
units.tr: For, as Sosia says cleverly in the comic poet:

units.la: isthæc commemoratio.
units.tr: This is a recounting of favours.

units.la: Quasi exprobratio si immemoris beneficii.
units.tr: It is like a reproach to one who forgets a kindness.

units.la: Rectèq; omnino Orator: Odiosum sanè genus hominum, inquit, officia exprobrantium, quæ meminisse debet is in quem collata sunt, non commemorare qui cötulit. Cui simile Senecæ illud: Lacerat animum & premit, frequens meritorum commemoratio. Nec male Cato:
units.tr: And the orator is quite right: "Odious indeed is the class of men who throw their services in people's faces. The one on whom the favour was conferred ought to remember it; the one who conferred it should not mention it." Similar is Seneca's saying: "Frequent recounting of one's merits lacerates and oppresses the mind." Cato also says well:

units.la: Officium alterius multis narrare memento: Atq; alijs cum tu benefeceris, ipse fileto, &c.
units.tr: Remember to tell many of another's kindness, but when you have done good to others, be silent yourself, etc.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi HOMILIA III.
units.tr: THE LIFE AND DEATH OF NABAL THE DRUNKARD. SERMON III.

units.la: Missi ad Nabalem famuli Dauidis ad petenda cibaria, repudiantur ab eo.
units.tr: The servants sent by David to ask for food are rejected by Nabal.

units.la: 9 Venerunt ergo pueri Dauidis & alloquuti sunt Nabal iuxta omnia verba hæc, nomine Dauidis & quieuerunt.
units.tr: 9 So the young men of David came and spoke to Nabal according to all these words, in David's name, and they waited.

units.la: 10 Respondit autem Nabal seruus Dauidis & dixit: Quis est Dauid? & quis filius Isai? hodie multi sunt serui, qui separant se singuli à facie dominorum suorum.
units.tr: 10 But Nabal answered the servants of David and said: Who is David? And who is the son of Jesse? Today there are many servants who each break away from the face of their masters.

units.la: 11 Et tollam panem meum & aquam meam & victimam meam quam occidi tonsoribus meis, ut dem viris, quos non no ui, unde nam sint?
units.tr: 11 Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat that I have killed for my shearers, and give it to men whom I do not know, where they come from?

units.la: 12 Itaq; conuerterunt se pueri Dauidis in viam suam, & reuersi sunt. Quum venissent autem, annunciauerunt ei secundum omnia verba hæc.
units.tr: 12 So the young men of David turned back on their way and returned. When they came, they reported to him according to all these words.

units.la: SVperiori sermone audiuimus, Dauidem legatos suos ad Nabalem misisse, qui aliquid per humanitatem ab eo auferrent, idque eo magis, quod & fausto die venissent, &, quum greges eius essent in vicinia, tamen nihil ex eis rapuissent. Porro quomodo excepti sint à Nabale, quid item responsi tulerint, cognoscemus. Præmittitur tamen, legatos Dauidis ad Nabalem venisse, & alloquutos esse Nabalem iuxta omnia verba hæc, nomine Dauidis: & quieuisse id est, sine dicendi facto conticuisse, responsum q; expectasse.
units.tr: We heard in the previous sermon that David sent his envoys to Nabal to take something from him by way of courtesy, all the more so since they had come on a festive day and, although his flocks were nearby, had taken nothing from them. We shall now learn how they were received by Nabal and what answer they brought back. It is stated first, however, that David's envoys came to Nabal and spoke to him in David's name according to all these words, and that they were silent, that is, they stopped speaking and waited for an answer.

units.la: Quo loco nobis exemplum legatorum fidelium proponitur. Nihil enim eorum præ termittunt, quæ iniuncta erant. Quantam voluptatem nuncij fideles mittentibus eos afferant, Salomon eleganti similitudine ostendit. Quod est frigus niuis mesis tempore, inquit, messoribus æstu fatiscentibus (eorum enim vires fatiscentes recreat, &c.) Hoc
units.tr: Here the example of faithful envoys is set before us. For they omit nothing of what they were commanded. Solomon shows with an elegant comparison how great a pleasure faithful messengers bring to those who send them: "As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, to reapers faint with heat" (for it refreshes their failing strength, etc.). This

units.la: Exodus.
units.tr: Exodus.

units.la: Verf. 9.
units.tr: Verse 9.

units.la: Legati fideliter in legatione versentur.
units.tr: Messengers should conduct themselves faithfully in their embassy.

units.la: Prou. 25. verf. 13. Hoc ipsum est fidelis legatus mittentibus eum. Domini nanq; sui animum reficit & refocillat. Reuersus enim referт, quod feliciter in sua legatione & fideliter gesit. Capiter 3. Nuncius impius ait, qui scilicet legationem fideliter non exequitur (vt ex αὐτῇ θέσει licet deprehendere) cadet in malum: Legatus autem verax, vel fidelis, sanitas. Hoc est salubris sibi primum ipsi est: item & ijs à quibus mittitur, dum videlicet legationem suam obiens, malo occurrit, ob quod mitte-batur. Decem illi exploratores, quos in terram hostilem Moses miserat, animos populi deijciunt: duo autem, Calebus nempe & Iosua, augent & confirmant.
units.tr: Prov. 25, verse 13. This is just what a faithful messenger is to those who send him: he refreshes and revives the spirit of his master. For on returning he reports what he has carried out successfully and faithfully in his embassy. Chapter 13: an impious messenger, that is, one who does not carry out his embassy faithfully (as may be gathered from the antithesis [ἀντιθέσεως]), falls into evil; but a true or faithful messenger is health. This is wholesome first for himself; likewise for those by whom he is sent, since in carrying out his embassy he meets the evil for which he was sent. Those ten spies whom Moses sent into the hostile land dismayed the people's minds; but the two, Caleb and Joshua, encouraged and strengthened them.

units.la: His subijcitur responsum Nabalis, quod certè durum ac valdè inhumanum fuit. Nam acerbissimè in iuuenes Dauidis inuectus: Quis est, inquit, Dauid? Non fuit Dauid ita obscurus, vt de illo nefando quidem quidquam acceperit. Pueris etiam in triuijs notus erat. Nam quum in bello Palestino certamen cum Goliatho gigante, qui exercitum Israeliticum præ suo robore & mole contemnebat, & ex eo provocabat clamore fortissimum quenque, singulare fusce-pisset, eumq; armis pastoralibus & in spe-ciem contemnendis deiecisset, mulieres & puellæ quæ solitæ sunt triumphos principum ornare tripudijs & canticis, Dauidem in choreis collaudarunt, & eum Saulo tantum prætulerunt, quantum mille hominibus præferuntur decem millia. Deinde in vulgus notum erat, eum iam vnctum esse à Samuele. Ionathas enim & Saulus ipse palàm, audiente populo dixerat, eum esse regnaturum. Sed & Abigael eum postea salutat regem. Quot prælia ab eo tempore confecit decantatissima? Non dubium mihi est, quin Nabal prius sæpius gloriatus sit tribulem suum, tot & tam præclara facinora edidisse. Hoc enim plerunq; solent illi, qui à virtutibus maiorum solent degenerare. Vnde prouerbium: Laudant parentes infelices liberi. Quis igitur non videat Nabalem ex contemptu quæsisse: Quis iste sit Dauid? Sic Pharao, cum Moses & Aaron diuinum diuino iussu populum auocarent, Quis iste est Iehoua, inquit, ad cuius ego iussum Israelitas dimittam? Ego verò neq; Iehouam noui, neq; Israelitas dimittam, &c. Nostra tempestate, cum ex sacris literis, & præsertim ex epistolis Paulinis, falsa doctrina de meritis, alijsque capitibus salutem concernentibus oppugnaretur, multi impudenter rogarunt: Quis est iste Paulus? Non quod illis ignotus est. tus essET: (nam diuinos etiam honores illi haberi voluerunt)sed quod eum contemne rent,hacq; in parte non audiendum iudica-rent.Quid igitur? Nos (aiebant)loquendo quiduis obtinebimus:nobis dicere ac facere,quidquid libet, licet. Quis nobis dominabitur?
units.tr: To this follows Nabal's answer, which was certainly harsh and very inhospitable. For he railed most bitterly against David's young men: "Who is David?" he says. David was not so obscure that he had heard nothing of that notorious man. He was even known to boys in the streets. For when, in the Philistine war, he took up single combat with Goliath the giant, who despised the Israelite army for its strength and bulk and challenged every bravest man with his shouting, and when he had struck him down with his shepherd's weapons, which were considered contemptible, the women and girls, who were accustomed to adorn the triumphs of princes with dances and songs, praised David in their choruses and set him above Saul by as much as ten thousand is set above a thousand. Then it was widely known that he had already been anointed by Samuel. For Jonathan and Saul himself had openly said, in the hearing of the people, that he would reign. And afterwards Abigail greets him as king. How many battles, most celebrated, did he fight from that time on? I have no doubt that Nabal had often boasted that his fellow countryman had performed so many and such splendid deeds. For this is usually what those do who degenerate from the virtues of their ancestors. Hence the proverb: "Unhappy children praise their parents." Who therefore does not see that Nabal asked out of contempt: "Who is this David?" So Pharaoh, when Moses and Aaron were calling the people away at the command of God, said: "Who is this Jehovah, at whose command I should let Israel go? I neither know Jehovah, nor will I let Israel go," etc. In our own time, when false doctrine concerning merits and other matters that concern salvation was being attacked from the sacred letters, and especially from the Epistles of Paul, many shamelessly asked: "Who is this Paul?" Not because he was unknown to them (for they even wanted divine honours paid to him), but because they despised him and judged that he should not be heard in this matter. What then? "We," they said, "will prevail by talking; we may say and do whatever we please. Who will rule over us?"

units.la: Addit:Quis filius Isai?Saul vt & Seba,alijque, qui in Dauidem hostili animo erant, per contemtum Dauidem filium Isaij vocabat:forte quod Isaius, quem Iesse dicunt Euangelistæ,homo obscurus, neq; maioribus suis par esset, & cum filiorum octo pater esset,diuitijs non affluerat: ideoq; pompas facere non posset. Quod tamen ipsi ignominiæ non cesit. Sed & Solomonis filio Roboamo Israelitæ proauum Iesse expro- brarunt,cum ipsorum postulationi non annuisset.Si de generis dignitate disputandum sit,Dauid præstantioribus parentibus ortus fuit quàm Saulus : caq; re non erat,quod adeò contemtim de Dauide loqueretur.Non ita pridem Saulus clitellarius fuerat,asinasque patris perditas quærierat: Sed nec Nabal prosapiam Dauidi exprobrare debuisset. Quanuis enim ex vna eademq; tribu orum ducerent:tamen, vt tribus in familias certas erant diuisæ, Dauidis prosapia longè Erat illustrior, ceu ex qua Mesias secundum carne prodire debuit. Hodie quoq; multos inuenias, qui genere suo glorientur, & praesse eos quoq; contemnant, & tanquam ex alto despiciant, qui illos genere & virtute lon gè antecellunt.
units.tr: He adds: Who is the son of Jesse? Saul, as well as Seba and others who were hostile to David, used to call David "the son of Jesse" out of contempt, perhaps because Jesse, whom the evangelists call Isai, was an obscure man, not equal to his ancestors, and since he was the father of eight sons he was not rich and so could not make a display. Yet this did not bring disgrace on David. Indeed, the Israelites also reproached Rehoboam, son of Solomon, with his grandfather Jesse, when he had not granted their request. If the question is one of the dignity of birth, David was born of more distinguished parents than Saul; there was therefore no reason for him to speak so contemptuously of David. Not long before, Saul had been a carter who had searched for his father's lost asses. But Nabal ought not to have reproached David with his family either. For although they came from one and the same tribe, nevertheless, since the tribes were divided into certain families, the family of David was far more illustrious, since from it the Messiah was to come according to the flesh. Even today you will find many who boast of their birth, and despise those who far surpass them in birth and virtue, and look down on them as if from a height.

units.la: Sed non tantum in Dauidem contumeliosus est Nabal, verum etiam in eius commilitones. Eos enim accusat perfidiae aequè ac Dauidem, cum ille semper fidelissimus extiterit & Saulo ipsi & Reipublicae. Hodie multi sunt serui, inquit, qui separant se singuli à facie dominorum suorum. Quasi dicat: Augetur quotidie numerus seruorum, qui turpiter à dominis suis deficiunt, obedientiamq; debitam illis negant. Vulgo rebelles vocantur.
units.tr: But Nabal is insulting not only to David but also to his fellow soldiers. For he accuses them of treachery just as much as David, although David has always been most faithful both to Saul himself and to the commonwealth. Today there are many servants, he says, who each break away from the face of their masters. As if he said: the number of servants who shamefully desert their masters and deny them the obedience they owe is increasing every day. They are commonly called rebels.

units.la: Non leuiter peccant subditi, qui debitam obedientiam Magistraribus non praestant in rebus licitis. Sacrae enim literae passim inculcant: Subditorum esse, vt propensis in magistratuum obseruationem animis, suam illis obedientiam approbent, siue edictis parendum, siue tributa soluenda, siue subeunda publica munera atque onera, quae ad communem defensionem spectent, siue qua alia iussa capessenda. Loca quae huc faciunt, adducere superuacaneum est. Maximè illustria sunt Rom. 13. Tit. 3. 1. Petri 2.
units.tr: Subjects who do not render the obedience they owe to magistrates in lawful matters sin not lightly. For the sacred letters everywhere impress that it is the duty of subjects, with minds inclined to observe the magistrates, to show their obedience to them, whether by obeying edicts, or paying taxes, or undertaking public offices and burdens that pertain to the common defence, or by undertaking any other commands. It is superfluous to adduce the passages that bear on this. The most illustrious are Romans 13, Titus 3, and 1 Peter 2.

units.la: Sed & serui heris suis pareant, non ab illis ad alios transfugiant, & se vi in libertate vin dicent. Quod si domini illos manu mittant, possunt beneficium illud amplecti. 1. Cor. 7. Cætera non caret peccato, colla iugo velle subtrahere. Ex quo apparet, Nabalem non leue crimen Dauidi, eiusq; militibus impingere, dum illos perfidiæ accusat, ac rebelles vocat. Nec enim ignorabat, Dauidem immerentem à Saulo socero suo infestari: nemi-nem Saulo fideliorem extitisse Dauide: Ad-hæc probè norat, multos, qui ad Dauidem transierant, id eo tantum nomine fecisse, vt vel saluti suæ consulerent, vel quod illum sanguinis proximitate attingerent, vel quod illi omnia cuperent, vel quod effrænè Saulî libidinem impotentemq; tyrannidem vltrà ferre non possent. Quod si ista ignora-bat, tamen omnino prius quæsisse, & rem diligentius inuestigasse oportuit, quà cõuitia ista tanquà ex plaustro in homines nihil minus cõmeritos, iacere. Esto fuerint inter Dauidis milites, qui neuis suis nõ caruerint: tamen insontes fontiu supplicio inuoluere pleнũ iniustitiq; erat. Nõ solũ, sine vllo maleficio aut iniuriâ, verũ etiâ cũ magno beneficio cũ ipsius pastorib. erant versati. Debebat ergo eos aliqua mercede munerari. Nostri dicũt: Etiâ in latrone, posse latrocinium cõmitti.
units.tr: Servants too should obey their masters, not flee from them to others, and by force claim their liberty for themselves. But if their masters should manumit them, they may embrace that kindness. 1 Cor. 7. Otherwise it is not free from sin to wish to withdraw the neck from the yoke. From this it appears that Nabal did not lay a light charge on David and his soldiers when he accused them of treachery and called them rebels. For he did not fail to know that David, being guiltless, was harassed by Saul his father-in-law, and that no one had been more faithful to Saul than David. Moreover, he knew well that many who went over to David did so only for this reason: either to look to their own safety, or because they were related to him by blood, or because they desired all things from him, or because they could no longer endure Saul's unbridled lust and impotent tyranny. But even if he was ignorant of these things, he ought at least to have inquired first and investigated the matter more carefully, before hurling such insults, as if from a cart, at men who deserved them no less. Granted that there were among David's soldiers some who were not free of faults, it was nonetheless wrong and unjust to involve all the innocent in the punishment of the guilty. They had been with his shepherds not only without any wrongdoing or injury, but even with great benefit. He ought therefore to have rewarded them with some payment. Our people say: even against a robber a robbery can be committed.

units.la: Quod si nos quoq; aliquando minori pau perum studio ducamur, & in conferendis eleemosynis tardiores fimus,illico Nabalem istum in memoriam reuocabimus, ne nos eodem,in quo ille,scelere alligemus.Nabal, auctus,inquit,hodie numerus est feruorum qui à suis dominis turpiter deficiunt. Nos conquerendi causas longè grauiores habe-mus.Numerus enim validorum, quos vo-cant mendicantium, indies augetur. Olim pudebat homines viritim stipem aut ostia-tim panem emendicare. Hodie neminem hominum mendicitatis pudet: Quin noui quotidie Mendicantiũ ordines exsurgunt. Nonnulli fe artifices manuarios facientes, queruntur, fe nullas in operas incidere. Quod fi illos velis conducere, nufpiam ap-parent, ac tantum non ἀφαντοι fiunt. Pars fe amanuenses fingunt.Alij studiosos,cui rei vt fidem faciant, quemadmodum psittaci suum χαῖρε: ita isti formulam aliquam me-moriæ mandant, qua doctos Latinis verbis de viatico compellent. Si longiorem cum illis sermonem instituas, elingues ac fi fyde-re tacti effent, reddideris. Alij alijs dolis ac fraudibus vtuntur. Sed, vt in specie isti à fe discrepent:tamen hoc in genere habent o-mnes mnes: μισόπονοί sunt, & cum corporis atque ingenij viribus nonnunquam valeant, nihil tamen operis honesti faciunt, ac, quod mali caput est, plerunque ea, quae mendicando conficiunt omnia, in gaueas, popinas, scorta consumunt. Indigni ergo sunt, qui in Rebuspublicis bene constitutis, nedum in Ecclesijs ferantur. Viderunt hoc sapientissimi quique inter gentes, quos grauis & prudens Reipublicae administratio commendat. Apud Athenienses enim Areo pagitae singulos cives obseruabant, qua quisque arte vixeret: & in ius trahi curabant omnes, qui se turpi & inerti otio addixissent. Apud Romanos autem, ne qui mendicarent duodecim tabularum lege cautum fuit. Ete nim quotidiano vsu edocti erant, mendicationem bonis moribus inimicam, & omnium scelerum quasi seminarium atq; fomentum esse. Quod si ignauos istos fucos & ἀργούς homines Magistratus non coerceat & in ordinem redigat, ne vere pauperibus fraudi sint: praestat decem eiusmodi nebulonibus eleemosynam quantulamcunque, saltem ob ita turae societatem, conferre, quam vnum, in quem recte beneficium collocatur, inanem dimittere. Agnouerunt hoc gentium philosophi, quorum princeps Aristoteles, cum ho-
units.tr: If we too are sometimes moved by a lesser zeal for the poor, and are slower in giving alms, let us at once call this Nabal to mind, lest we bind ourselves in the same crime in which he was caught. Nabal says: "Today the number of servants who shamefully desert their masters has grown." We have far graver grounds for complaint. The number of able-bodied people whom they call beggars increases daily. In former times men were ashamed to beg alms from person to person, or bread from door to door. Today no one is ashamed of begging. Indeed, I see new orders of beggars rising up every day. Some pretend to be manual craftsmen and complain that they cannot find any work. If you want to hire them, they are nowhere to be seen, and they practically vanish [ἄφαντοι]. Others pose as clerks. Others, to make people believe them, learn some formula by heart, as parrots learn their [χαῖρε], and with it they address learned people in Latin about their travel money. If you begin a longer conversation with them, you will find them tongue-tied, as if they had been struck dumb. Others use various tricks and frauds. But although they differ in their kinds, all of them share this trait: they are averse to work [μισόπονοί], and although they sometimes have the strength of body and mind, they do no honest work at all. And, what is the worst of it, they usually spend everything they get by begging on cages, taverns and whores. They are therefore unworthy of being tolerated in well-ordered commonwealths, let alone in churches. The wisest men among the nations have seen this, those whom the serious and prudent administration of a commonwealth commends. For among the Athenians the Areopagites watched over each citizen, to see by what trade he lived, and took care to bring before the court all who had given themselves to shameful and idle leisure. Among the Romans, moreover, it was provided by the law of the Twelve Tables that no one should beg. For they had learned from daily experience that begging is hostile to good morals and is, as it were, a seedbed and fuel of all crimes. But if the magistrate does not restrain these lazy drones and idlers [ἀργούς] and bring them into order, so that they do not truly become a disgrace to the poor, it is better to give ten such scoundrels some alms, however small, at least for the sake of human fellowship, than to send away empty one person to whom a benefit is rightly given. The philosophers of the nations recognised this too, the chief of whom was Aristotle. When he had given money to a man who was wicked and unworthy, yet needy, and was reproved for it by his friends, he is said to have replied: "I did not pity him, but nature did."

units.la: mines mini improbo & indigno, egeno tamen nu- mum dedisset, & eo nomine ab amicis repre- henderetur, respondisse fertur: Non sum il- lius misertus, sed naturae.
units.tr: When he had given a coin to a worthless and unworthy man, though one in need, and was rebuked for it by his friends, he is said to have replied: "I did not take pity on him; I took pity on nature."

units.la: Adhaec, Tollam ne, inquit, Nabal, panem meum, & aquam meam, & victimam meam, quam occidi tonsoribus meis, vt dem viris, quos non noui, vndenam sint? &c. Quibus verbis Dauidem etiam iniustitiae arguit, & eum tonsoribus postponit: ac si quis messo- rem pluris faciat, quam eum qui coluerit & ararit terram. Isti enim tondent tantum greges: Dauid autem eos in tuto seruauerat. Et tamen: Scilicet ego panem, inquit, aquam q; meam, & quae mactaui ad alendos meos ton- sores, dem hominibus mihi prorsus ignotis. Panem primo nominat: deinde aquam, sub qua vinum, zythum, poscam, &c. intelligit. Interim non praeteriuerim, magna illis in locis aqua- rum penuriam fuisse. Habet quidem Palestina suos fluuios, riuos, lacus, fontes: sed tamen multis locis fontes arescunt, in summis illis ardoribus, id quod in nostra quoq; Heluetia quae aquis saluberrimis abundat, anno 1540. multis locis accidit. Beneficium ergo fuit, si quis alteri potum frigidae aquae porrexit. Ruthae 2. Boazus Ruthae hortatur, vt si sitiat, po- tat potum, ex ipsa vasis, quibus ipsi seruī hau- riunt. Victimę nomine, non carne tantum, sed
units.tr: Moreover, Nabal says: "Shall I take my bread, and my water, and my meat which I have killed for my shearers, and give it to men whom I do not know, where they come from?" etc. In these words he accuses David of injustice too, and places him below the shearers, as if someone should value a reaper more than the man who has tilled and ploughed the land. For the shearers only shear the flocks, but David had kept them safe. And yet, Nabal says: "Of course I shall give my bread and my water too, and what I have slaughtered to feed my shearers, to men who are wholly unknown to me." He names bread first, then water, by which he understands wine, cider, vinegar, and so on. Meanwhile I must not pass over the fact that in those regions there was a great shortage of water. Palestine indeed has its rivers, streams, lakes and springs, but in many places the springs dry up in the great heats, which in our own Helvetia, though it abounds in very wholesome waters, happened in many places in the year 1540. It was therefore a kindness if anyone offered another a drink of cold water. In Ruth 2, Boaz urges Ruth that when she is thirsty she should drink from the vessels from which his servants draw. By the name of victuals he means not only meat, but all kinds of food, apart from bread, which he had mentioned specifically. Notice, however, that he confidently calls his bread, water, and meat all his own. Yet it is clear that we have nothing of our own, but must receive all things to use from God as a loan, and that only at his pleasure. I wish we would sometimes weigh this well. Certainly this consideration would humble the crest of pride and would warn us not to despise so arrogantly the poor and needy who ask us for their food. For soon it would occur to us that the same may perhaps be our situation before God, and that we need to be fed by his alms no less than those who beg for bread at the door of our house.

units.la: {a} Nabal Dauidem accusat inimicitias & tonsoribus postponit. Vers. 11.
units.tr: {a} Nabal accuses David of hostility and places him below the shearers. Vers. 11.

units.la: {b} Aquarum penuria magna in Palestina. omnis generis cibos intelligit, praeter panè, cuius peculiaré mentione fecerat. Aduerte aút,illú confidenter panè,aquam, carné,sua omnia vocare.At constat, nos propriú nihil habere:sed vtenda omnia à Deo mutuo acci pére,idq; precario.Quod vtiná feri aliquan tò expenderemus. Certe ista cófideratio & superbiæ cristas deprimeret,& moneret,ne pauperes & egenos fastidiremus tam info-lenter,qui victú suum à nobis flagitát. Nam mox succurreret, eandé nostrá forte esse à-pud Deú,cui9 eleemosyna nō minus nos ali oportet,quàm eos, qui ad noftrę domus o-stium panem mendicant.
units.tr: {b} Great shortage of water in Palestine. He means every kind of food, except bread, of which he had made special mention. Notice, however, that he boldly calls his bread, water, and meat all his own. Yet it is certain that we have nothing of our own, but must receive all things to use from God as a loan, and that only at his pleasure. I wish we would sometimes consider this. Certainly such reflection would bring down the crest of pride and would warn us not to despise so insolently the poor and needy who ask us for their food. For soon it would come to mind that our own situation before God may perhaps be the same, and that we must be fed by his alms no less than those who beg for bread at the door of our house.

units.la: Cogitasse debebat Nabal:Nisi homines i-sti custodes potius quá milites fuissent, iam nunc tonsuram ouium fecissem:Sed greges meos defenderunt:Æquum igitur est, vt eo rum nō minus ratione habeam quàm tonso-rum. Iam nō cōtenderant,vt quæ suis tonso ribus parasset , in milites distribueret, sed quę sibi cōmodū esset, decideret:Sed & diê festum studio expectarant ,quo conuiuium pro more lautissimum fecerat, vt illum ha-berent obsequentiorem.Diues erat, & habe-bat,quod & seruis & alijs posset esse satis.Po-stea enim,quum Abigail,clam illo,munus ad Dauidem deferт satis amplum , tamen satis reliquit & illi & operis. Nam fe præ alijs vino adobruerat, & conuiuium tantum non regium instruxerat.
units.tr: Nabal should have considered this: "If these men had been guardians rather than soldiers, I would already have sheared my sheep. But they defended my flocks. It is fair, therefore, that I take account of them no less than of the shearers." They had not been striving that he should distribute to his soldiers what he had prepared for his shearers, but that he should cut off what was convenient for himself. They had also eagerly awaited the festal day on which he had made, as usual, a most lavish feast, so that they might find him more compliant. He was rich, and he had what would be enough both for his servants and for others. Afterwards, when Abigail brought a fairly generous gift to David without his knowledge, he still had enough left both for himself and for his workers. For he had drowned himself in wine more than others, and had prepared a feast hardly less than royal.

units.la: Interim non abs re miretur aliquis, hominem istum, alioquin durum & tenacem, operis suis conuiuium opiparum apparasse. Inuenias enim qui seruis suis ac mercenarijs ne bucellam quidem optent. Carnes putre-scere, panem mucescere, poma marcescere malunt, quàm in tempore promere. Qualifcunq; fuerit Nabal: tamen operis suis conuiuium largum fecit. Ethnici quoq; docuerunt benignè esse contrahendum cum ijs quorum opera vti volumus, aut quorum operam conduximus: ijsq; cibum liberaliter subministrandum. Inter quos præclarè Hesiodus: μισθὸς ϑῆτ, αἰνὸς εἰ φίλω εἰρηνεύω ἀρ-χῶ ἐσω. Id est interprete Vlpio Frisio, Dicta prius merces famulo detur, idq; benignè. Idem docet Cicero: Meminerimus, in-quit, etiam aduersus infimos iustitiam esse seruandam. Est autem infima conditio & fortuna seruorum, quibus non malè præci-piunt, qui ita iubent vti, vt mercenarijs, operam exigendam, iusta præbenda, id est, vt la-borem imperemus, & pro eo iusta, id est, vi-stum & amistum rependamus, faciamusq;, quod Simon Terentianus ait, vt iusta & clemens mens seruitus fit.Clarius est Dei illud:Boui inquit trituranti os ne obligabis. Nec absi- mile Syracidæ illud,qui vt asino onus,pabu lum & virgam,ita seruo deberi panem,dicit capite 33.disciplinam & laborem,ne scilicet sui officij oblitus,imperium in heriles filios vsurpare incipiat.Quod mutuatus Aristote les,Iam tribus,inquit,propositis,opere,ani- maduersione,& cibo:Si cibus suppetat sine opere,& animaduersione ,petulantia innas- citur:inter opera vero & animaduersione cibum non habere & iniustum atq; violen- tum est,& elidit frangitq; vires.D. Iacobus epistolæ suæ capite 5.de diuitibus inter alia Ecce,inquit,merces operariorum,qui mes- fuerunt regiones vestras ,à vobis intercep- ta,clamat:id est,vindictam quasi alto clamo reexposcit:& clamores eorum, qui metsue- runt,in aures Domini Sabaoth introierunt, hoc est, exauditi sunt à Domino multo po- tentiore quàm ipsi sitis,&c.
units.tr: Meanwhile someone may not unreasonably wonder that this man, otherwise harsh and stingy, prepared a sumptuous banquet for his workers. For you will find people who do not wish even a crumb for their servants and hired men. They would rather let meat rot, bread grow mouldy and fruit wither than bring out anything in time. Whatever Nabal was like, he nevertheless gave a generous feast for his workers. The heathen too have taught that one should deal kindly with those whose labour we wish to use or whose labour we have hired, and that food should be given to them generously. Among them Hesiod says it admirably: "Let the wage be paid first, and paid kindly" [μισθὸς ... αἰνὸς ... ἀρχῶ ... ἔστω]. That is, in the rendering of Ulpius Frisius: "Let the wage be given to the servant first, and given kindly." Cicero teaches the same: "Let us remember," he says, "that justice must be observed even towards the lowest." The condition and fortune of slaves is the lowest, and those who command them to be used as hired labourers do not command badly, namely that we require work and give what is just in return, that is, that we repay them with food and clothing, and make it, as Simon Terentianus says, a just and merciful servitude. Still clearer is that saying of God: "You shall not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn." Not unlike it is the saying of the Syracide, who says that as an ass is owed burden, fodder and whip, so a servant is owed bread, discipline and work, chapter 33, lest, forgetting his duty, he begin to usurp command over the household sons. Aristotle borrowed this, saying: "There are three things set before us: work, correction, and food. If food is supplied without work and correction, wantonness is born; but to have no food between work and correction is unjust and violent, and it breaks and destroys strength." St James, in chapter 5 of his epistle, speaking among other things about the rich, says: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped your fields, which by you is kept back, crieth; that is, they demand vengeance as with a loud shout, and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth, that is, they have been heard by the Lord, who is far more powerful than you are," etc.

units.la: Sed quæ hæc excusatio, quod inquit,se non nosse vndenam sint?At interrogare po- terat,cuiates essent.Non ignorabat,plerosq; ex illis suos tribules esse. Sed fac ex India a- lijsq; remotissimis regionibus fuisse. Num ideo se adeo inhumanum erga illos præbere debuisset?Nihil minus:Sed illos, vel eo nomine,quod homines essent,adhæc fameret quàm cōmendatissimos habere. Nō dubito quin sæpius audiuerit, Deum suis peregrinos aliosq; afflictos & oppressos homines, de meliori nota commendasse.
units.tr: But what kind of excuse is this, that he says he does not know where they come from? He could have asked where they were from. He was not ignorant that most of them were his own tribesmen. But suppose they had come from India or other most distant regions. Ought he therefore to have shown himself so inhumane towards them? Far from it. He should rather have counted them among the most commended for this very reason, that they were men, and besides, that they were strangers. I do not doubt that he had often heard that God commended strangers and other afflicted and oppressed men, of a better sort.

units.la: Sed quid? Non tantum inanes dimittied insuper contumeliâ verborū addit: quá generosos animos acerbius multò accipe, quàm verbera, infra latius persequemur. Hæc paulùm consideremus circumstantias. Quis ista maledicta iacit? Nabal homo vilissimus, si cum Dauide conferatur, & ditissimus nihil, etiam ex amplissimo munere in Dauid dem collato, decessisset.
units.tr: But what? He not only sends them away empty-handed; he adds insult to injury with words, which generous minds take far more bitterly than blows, as we shall pursue more fully below. Let us consider the circumstances for a moment. Who hurls these insults? Nabal, a most base man when compared with David, and rich in nothing, even if he had departed after receiving some most generous gift that had been given to David.

units.la: In quem? Primò in Dauidem, tribulem, imò principem suum, generumq; regis, optimè de se meritum, ideoq; nihil minus expectantem. Deinde in legatos Dauidis, quos cum iure gentium sacros & inuiolabiles esse ignorare non posset, honestè haberi eos, nō contumelijs obrui oportuit. Multa grauissima bella propter violatos legatos suscepta esse leguntur. Denique in milites famelicos rerumque omnium egenos: qui nobis non tam lege Dei, quàm natura commendantur.
units.tr: Against whom? First against David, his fellow tribesman, indeed his own prince and the king's son-in-law, who had deserved very well of him and therefore expected nothing less. Next against David's envoys, whom he could not fail to know were sacred and inviolable under the law of nations, and he ought to have treated them honourably, not overwhelmed them with abuse. We read that many very grave wars have been undertaken on account of violated envoys. Finally, against hungry soldiers, destitute of everything, who are commended to us not so much by the law of God as by nature itself.

units.la: Quando? Cùm minimè oporteret: cum lautum cōuiuium tonsoribus parasset: cum
units.tr: When? When it was least fitting: when he had prepared a lavish feast for his shearers,

units.la: Dauid eiusq; milites ab omnibus rebus es- sent imparatissimi, eoq; ope illius cumpri- mis indigerent.
units.tr: when David and his soldiers were utterly unprepared for everything and most of all in need of his help.

units.la: At qualia tandem sunt ista maledicta? Ma- xima, vt audiuimus, & grauissima. Cur au- tem? Nimirum quod nec Deum nec homi- nes vereretur : quod impudens adeoque χυνοκέφαλος esset, summoq; peregrinorū odio laboraret.
units.tr: But what kind of insults were these, in the end? The very greatest and gravest, as we have heard. And why? Clearly because he feared neither God nor men; because he was shameless and, as the Greeks say, a dog-head [κυνοκέφαλος], and suffered from the greatest hatred of strangers.

units.la: Si vel aliquid cerebri habuisset, sponte sua, etiam nonrogatus, hoc tam fausto die aliquam saltem de conuiuio isto partem de cidere debuisset (nam vt recte Mimus, Beni gnus etiā dandi causam excogitat) ac, quod res erat cogitare: Non tantum sine vlla in- iuria, sed maximo cum beneficio apud tuos sunt versati, sed & porrò tibi tuisque beni- gne possunt facere. Fac ergo tu quoq; vt illos tibi cōmendatos esse videant. Habes instru- ctum cōuiuiū tonsorib. tuis: Ex eo potes il- lis partē aliquā decidere. Quod si ieiunos & inanes ablegare velis, vide ne per vim aliqd auferant. Fames certè & mora, vt est apud Plaut. bilē in nasum cōciunt. Quid nō audét famelici? Item: Dauid primo quoq; die regi in gratiam denuò venit: vel rex declara- tur: Quantum tibi incommodares ipsi, si
units.tr: If he had had even a little sense, he should, of his own accord, without being asked, on such a happy day, at least have cut off some part of that feast for them. For, as the mime rightly says, the generous man even thinks up a reason for giving. And he ought to have considered what was the case: these men had lived among your people not only without any injury but with the greatest benefit, and they can still do you and yours good turns. So you too should make them see that they are commended to you. You have a feast prepared for your shearers; from it you could set aside some portion for them. But if you wish to send away hungry and empty-handed men, take care that they do not seize something by force. Hunger and delay, as in Plautus, stir up bile into the nose. What will the hungry not dare? Likewise: David came back into the king's favour again on the very first day, or was proclaimed king.
