How much would you be harming yourself if you allowed his soldier to leave you without being honoured with any office or gift?

units.la: {*} Ampli tryone. militem ipsius nullo vel honore vel munere ornatum à te discedere patereris? Omitto, quod Deus homines egenos, cum siti fame- que colluctantes, vehementissime nobis commendat, amplissimas q; illis, qui proxi- mis manus auxiliares porrigunt, promissio nes psalsim facit, &c.
units.tr: {*} Amphitryon. I pass over the fact that God most earnestly commends to us the needy, who struggle with thirst and hunger, and openly makes the most generous promises to those who stretch out helping hands to their neighbours, and so on.

units.la: Quod si illis nihil plane contribuere vo- luisset: tamen se excusare potuisset, ac molli- bus verbis dimissos, dicere: Se quidem illis omnia cupere, verum, quod illum imparatu offenderint, paucaq; in plures non sufficiat, sibi ipsi hoc tempore satisfacere non posse; Sed porro voluntatem suam reipsa liberali- ter declaraturum: aliaq; id genus. Certè, vt praeclarè Mimus, Pars beneficij est, quod pe titur, si belle neges. Verum ille nihil huius: Sed illos indignissimis conuitijs lacerat: nul li parcens. Habemus hoc plerunq; omnes, vt, vbi in mendicum aliquem inuecti fumus, vt plurimum aliquid stipis illi demus: vel, si plane nihil in illum conferamus opis, tamen Deo illum comendemus, qui eum bene iu- uet, fuaq; benedictione adaugeat. Nabal ve- ro nihil horum praestat: sed omnes mode- stiae terminos praetergressus, maledictis, vt saepius dictum est, immerenter vexatos, la- crante etiamnum stomacho dimittit.
units.tr: But even if he had wished to contribute nothing at all to them, he could still have excused himself, sending them away with gentle words and saying: that he indeed desired everything for them, but that since they had caught him unprepared, and since what little he had would not suffice for so many, he could not satisfy himself at this time; but that he would afterwards declare his will by deeds, generously, and other things of that sort. Certainly, as the mime nobly says: part of a kindness is what is asked for, if one refuses it politely. But he did none of this; instead he tears them apart with the most unworthy abuse, sparing no one. We all commonly have this habit: when we have come upon some beggar, we usually give him some alms; or, if we contribute no help to him at all, we at least commend him to God, that God may help him well and increase him with his blessing. But Nabal does none of these things; he goes beyond all the limits of moderation, and dismisses men undeservedly harassed with insults, as is often said, with his anger still raging.

units.la: Sed quid ex istis omnibus colligimus? Primò videmus,non esse quod spe nostra falsi,commotiores reddamur.Dauidem quo que aliofq; fideles,illi ipsi,quibus fe fuaq; omnia concredíderant,& à quibus omnia expectabant, turpissimè plus semel fefelle-runt:Deo nimirum ita volente,qui nobis hu-manam fiduciam semel omnem subtrahit,vt àse vno pendere tantos quantos doceat.Sa-maritani Christum ne recipere quidem in-tra vicum suum voluerunt, quod habitum proficiscentis Hierosolymam præferret. At ijdem (vt hoc obiter inferam) non multò post Simoni Mago locum dederunt, qui to-tam illam gentem horrendis erroribus fasci-nauit,& ab illis factum est belli initium, quo tàm ipsi quàm Iudæi à Romanis sunt deleti & extincti. Semper ergo animis nostris ob-uersetur Christi dictum : Peregrinus fui & collegistis me : neque graue sit eum excipe-re,qui,vt nemini grauis aut onerosus est: ita omnis boni thesauros in seipso reconditos habet,& solus suo merito nobis Patrem con-ciliat. Et cum hospitalitas per se laude di-gna sit,& sæpe multis salutem attulerit, non potest non laudatissima, & quouis præmio digna esse , qua ipse Dei Filius in membris suis excipitur.Sed hæc,vt dixi,obiter.
units.tr: But what do we gather from all these things? First, we see that we should not be made more anxious because our hope has been disappointed. David, and other faithful men too, were shamefully deceived more than once by those very people to whom they had entrusted themselves and all their goods, and from whom they expected everything. God, of course, was willing it so, for he takes away from us all human confidence, so that he may teach us that so many depend on himself alone. The Samaritans did not even want to receive Christ within their village, because he had set his face towards Jerusalem. But the same people (I will add this in passing) not long afterwards gave a place to Simon the Magician, who bewitched that whole nation with dreadful errors; and from them came the beginning of the war by which both they and the Jews were destroyed and wiped out by the Romans. Therefore let the saying of Christ always be before our minds: "I was a stranger and you took me in" [Matt. 25.]. Nor should it be burdensome to receive him who, as he is burdensome or onerous to no one, so he holds all the treasures of good things stored up in himself, and he alone reconciles us to the Father by his merit. And since hospitality in itself is worthy of praise, and has often brought salvation to many, it cannot but be most praiseworthy, and worthy of any reward, when the Son of God himself is received in his members. But these things, as I said, are in passing.

units.la: Deinde in Nabale exemplum eorum habemus, quos, si roges, verbis quidem delinire ac demulcere cogites, magis magisque irrites, difficilioresque ac morosiores reddas. Nabal, mollissima etiam oratione a Dauide rogatus, fit durior & asperior, & Cainicè legatis ipsius respondet: Quis est Dauid? quis Isai filius? quasi diceret, nihil mihi cum illo est comercij. Ita multi hodie etiam atque etiam rogati, mirabiliter morosi sunt, nec quicquam ad aliorum vtilitatē referunt. Nēpe vt nitri mordacitas affusione aceti adaugetur: sic arrogantiam in Nabalibus istis crescere videas, quoties molli brachio tractantur. Atq; hoc illud est, quod Basilius in quadam epistola dicit: Ἀρεγαπόμενα τὰ ἐπὶ ... τῶν ἀσπονδιώτεραν γίνεσθαι πέφυκε, id est, Mores hominis superbi quo magis demulcentur, eò insolentiores fieri solent. Cui Germanorum illud prouerbiū respondet: Wenn man den Guren Bittet / so grosset ... Scenæ tantisper seruiendum est, dum melior fortuna affulgeat. Erit illud profecto tempus, & illucescet aliquando ille dies, cum Demeæ isti tibi quoq; supplices fient. Ferè quidem fit in hoc mundo, vt pij ab impijs contemnantur, propter pietatem & iustitiam: sed è diuerso etiam contingit, vt impij piorum
units.tr: Next, in Nabal we have an example of those whom, if you ask them, you may think to soothe and mollify with words, but you only irritate them more and more, and make them more difficult and more peevish. Nabal, though asked by David in the gentlest speech, becomes harder and rougher, and answers David's envoys like Cain: "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?" as if he meant: I have no dealings with him. So many today, asked again and again, are wonderfully peevish and contribute nothing to the advantage of others. Indeed, just as the bite of nitre is increased by the pouring on of vinegar, so you may see arrogance grow in such Nabals whenever they are handled with a soft arm. And this is what Basil says in a certain letter: "The [behaviour] of the proud ... becomes more shameless [ἀσπονδιώτεραν γίνεσθαι πέφυκε]; that is, the manners of a proud man are wont to become more insolent the more they are soothed." To this the German proverb answers: "If one asks the proud man [Guren], he swells up [grosset]..." One must serve the stage for a while, until better fortune shines on us. That time will surely come, and one day will dawn when these Demeas will also become suppliants to you. Indeed it usually happens in this world that the pious are despised by the impious for their piety and justice; but on the other side it also happens that the impious

units.la: Impij aliquando supplices sunt pijs. piorum ope & consilio indigeant, eosq; ho- nore,velint nolint,afficere coguntur.Exem plis rem ad Solomonis illud : Incuruent fe mali ante bonos, & iniusti ad portas iusti, &c.illustrauimus.
units.tr: are sometimes suppliants to the pious, and need the help and counsel of the pious, and are compelled, whether they will or no, to show them honour. We illustrated this matter with examples, from the saying of Solomon: "The evil bow down before the good, and the unjust at the gates of the just," and so on.

units.la: Tertio nobis ingeniù auarorum & ebrio forum,tanquâ in tabella descriptum, ob ocu los hoc loco ponitur.Auarorû partes eflent, vt fe erga quosuis munificos declararent, in primis vero pauperû inopiam subleuarent: eoq; magis,quod à Deo difpefatores potius opum,quàm domini sint constituti.Sed ne- mo facilè rationes enumerauerit,quib.prę- posteram parsimoniâ & Cyclopicû erga e- genos rigorẽ exeufant. Cur, inquiunt,in ex- teros conferrẽ,quibus mei liberi ac nepotes opus habebunt?Cur senectuti,quę fumtuo- fa est,ac multorû indiga, necessaria alimenta subtraherẽ?Cur ea,quę labore &studio meo acquisiui,alijs datẽ, qui vel sua cócoxerunt, vel adhuc vitâ otiosam atq; inerte viuût,nec vlli bonâ gratiâ referunt? Aliquando in eos, quos ne de nomine quidé norunt,probra ac maledicta conferunt omnia. Cur non domi tuę,aiunt,agis?Cur nô laborasti,ne oftiatim victum emendicare cogereris?Nempe exil- lorû numero eris,qui Mendicitatẽ quęstum faciunt, ac, cum per vires corporis possint, nihil tamẽ operis honesti faciût, sed incertis sedibus vagando verè egenis eleemosynam sacrilegè præcidunt. Nonnunquam fe Iros & Codros faciunt, cum Croesi sint & Crasi. Quæ licet grauia sint & atrocia, tamen in illis magis ferenda sunt, qui humanitus loquendo, propria posident: quàm in officiis illis, qui donationes ab aliis pie factas, vt ex his ecclesiæ, scholæ, eleemosynæ publicæ aut priuatæ instituantur, & conseruentur, intercipiunt, vel sibi ipsis vendicant, tar diu suę numerant. Nec tamen est, quod isti vindices Dei oculos & manus, effugere posse sibi persuadeant. Qui enim Giezum, Ananiam & Sapphiram, in primis autem Iudam proditorem condignis poenis affecit: illeidè infidos istos alienarum rerum dispensatores, ne in hoc quidem sæculo inultos abire sinet.
units.tr: Thirdly, the nature of misers and drunkards, as if drawn on a tablet, is placed before our eyes in this place. It would be the part of misers to show themselves generous towards any men at all, and above all to relieve the poverty of the poor; and all the more so because they have been appointed by God to be stewards of wealth rather than its masters. But hardly anyone would easily list the reasons with which they excuse their perverse thrift and their Cyclopean harshness towards the needy. "Why," they say, "should I give to strangers, whom my own children and grandchildren will need? Why should I withdraw necessary food from old age, which is costly and needy of many things? Why should I give to others what I have gained by my own labour and effort, to those who have either squandered their own goods, or still live an idle and inactive life, and make no good return to anyone? Sometimes they heap all kinds of reproaches and curses upon those whose very names they do not even know. 'Why,' they say, 'do you not work at home? Why have you not laboured, so that you would not be forced to beg your food from door to door?' Surely you will be one of that number who make a trade of begging, and though they could, by the strength of their bodies, do nothing honest, yet by wandering from one unsettled place to another, they sacrilegiously cut off alms from those who are truly needy." Sometimes they make themselves Iruses and Codruses, when they are Croesuses and Crassuses. Although these faults are serious and atrocious, they are to be borne more easily in those who, speaking humanly, possess their own goods, than in those officials who intercept the gifts piously made by others, so that churches, schools, and public or private alms might be established and maintained from them, or who claim them for themselves and long count them as their own. Nor should these avengers of God persuade themselves that they can escape the eyes and hands of God. For he who has punished Gehazi, Ananias and Sapphira, and above all Judas the traitor, with fitting penalties, will not allow those faithless stewards of other people's goods to go unpunished even in this age.

units.la: Ebriosi etiamsi & ipsi sint ad rem attentiores: tamen in combibones quos ad facienda paria nonnunquam cogunt, profusè sunt liberales: quin, si tota dolia vnà cum vino in illos ingerere possent, non parcerent. Ebrij multa dicunt & faciunt, quę postea aliquando per iugulum redeunt. Vinum enim, sapientissimo mortalium teste, derisorem effi-cit: non quod vinum per se, si illo rectè vtamur, nos reddat ineptos, sed, si immodicè bibamus, in caussa est, vt consilia omnia & præcepta contemnamus, Dei iudicia non metuamus,flagitia,etiam turpissima,pro ludo habeamus. Vna hæc ebriorum cura est, vbi in bonos socios incidant:vbi generosum vinum infundatur Quo largius sumto, citra vllam Dei hominúmue reuerentiá metúmue,quicquid in buccam & mentem venerit, dicunt ac faciunt. Quod si adhæc opibus affluant,vt hoc loco Nabal, mirum quàm sibi placeant, velintque, quæ eblaterant ac designant omnia,etiam flagitiosissima,pro oraculis haberi, omniumque calculis ac suffragijs approbari. Tàm abest,vt eo nomine vel leuiter perstringi velint ac notari. Discamus ergo ex hoc exemplo,cauere ebrietatem,ex qua hæc & alia innumera mala consequuntur. Fugiamus Nabales, qui etiam non sitien tes ab bibendum cogunt. Curabimus item: ne alij ebrietati indulgeant: De quo vt omnes desperent:tamè si concionatores & magistratus,cæteris ad imitationem vitæ exem pla propositi,ab ebrietate sibi cauerent,vna eademq; opera & sibi consulerent,&ì popu lo eandem sobrietate impetrarent facilius.
units.tr: Even though drunkards are themselves more attentive to business, they are lavish with their drinking companions, whom they sometimes force into matching bouts of drinking. Indeed, if they could pour whole casks of wine into them, they would not hold back. Drunkards say and do many things which afterwards sometimes come back to bite them. For wine, as the wisest of mortals testifies, makes a man a mocker. The fault is not in wine itself, which does not make us foolish if we use it rightly, but in immoderate drinking, which makes us despise all counsel and precept, fear neither God's judgments, and treat even the most shameful disgraces as a game. The only care of drunkards is when they fall in with good companions, where fine wine is poured out. The more freely they drink, the more they say and do whatever comes into their mouth and mind, with no reverence for God or man and no fear of either. If they also abound in wealth, as Nabal did here, it is remarkable how pleased with themselves they are, and how they want everything they babble and plan, even the most shameful, to be treated as oracles and approved by the votes and suffrages of all. So far is Nabal from wanting to be lightly rebuked or branded for this. Let us therefore learn from this example to beware of drunkenness, from which these and countless other evils follow. Let us flee from Nabals, who compel even those who are not thirsty to drink. We shall likewise take care that others do not indulge in drunkenness, though we should not despair of this for everyone. Preachers and magistrates, who set examples of life for others to imitate, should guard themselves against drunkenness; by one and the same work they would both look after themselves and more easily win sobriety for the people.

units.la: Quartò:notorium insignis ingratitudinis hoc loco exemplum proponitur. Nemo est, qui, vel natura duce,nõ intelligat, se magnas illi gratias, adeoque se totum debere, à quo ipse vel sui multis magnisq; beneficijs sint ornati. Quod si referendi vires non suppetant, saltem verbis commemorare ea aliis ac praedicare non desinet. Nihil enim (ut prę clarè Cicero) tàm inhumanum, tàm immane, tàm ferum, quàm committere, ut beneficio non dicam indigni sed victi esse videamur. Atqui Dauid noster, de Nabale, ut supra diximus, optimè erat meritus, vel eo nomine, quod greges eius defendisset. Magna solet esse licentia militaris, vel quod viribus valeant, vel quod facilè latere possint, vel, si capiantur, quòd excusare possint inopiā & famem. Dauid tamen suos milites continuit in officio, eosq; ad eam disciplinam assuefecit, de qua Baptista apud Lucam concionatur: Neminem concusseritis, neq; calumniemini. Omitto, quod non ita pridem Palestinos, qui, eruptione facta, Ceilam obsidione cinxerant, exercitu suo, nihil minus expectantes, adortus fortissimè represit. Nihil iam dicam de aliis bellis, quæ Dauid pro salute patriæ suscepta, non sine summo capitis periculo plus semel felicissimè cofecit. Quæ omnia grato animo recolere, & vel aliqua mercede milites munerari: saltè verbis praedicasse debebat. Cui enim gratia tanta referri non rinon potest, quanta debetur: habenda tamen tanta est,quam maximam animus cape re potest. Sed quid? Pro beneficijs reponit contumelias: ac ne verbo quidem vllam gra ti memorisque animi significationem decla- rat. Quid ita? Non tàm quòd stultus eífet & vecors: sed quòd diuitijs infinitis circum- flueret. Opes enim inflant sæpe homines, & feroces atq; insolentes reddunt. Nec hodie desunt, qui beneficia pro maleficijs habent: quiq; de illis quæ agnoscunt beneficia, dum in eos conferuntur, postea nunquam cogitant: Item qui pro beneficijs maleficia repo nant, bestijs multis peiores,quæ illis,qui eis benè faciunt, plærunque gratiam referunt. Verè in ferrea fæcula incidimus. Agnosci- mus quidem omnes, Nabalem negato Dauidi commeatu grauiter peccaffe,ideoq; iustè ingrati cuculi nomine notari: & tamen idem in nobis vitium non animaduertimus,ne dicam emendamus: Quin nonnunquà os nostrum impudens in illos etiam, quorum in nos infinita exstant beneficia,plufquam Nabalicè stringimus. Ariftoteles, τοῖς φιλοσο- φίας κοινωνήσασι inquit, τιμὴ ἰσόῤῥυπῶ- ἂν αὐ ψυχοῖς. ἀλλ᾽ ἴσως ἱκανόν ὥσπερ τοῖς θεοῖς καὶ τοῖς γονεῦς τὸ ςιδλεχόμενον, Hoc est,Præceptoribus,qui veram sapientiam nobis impertiunt, non potest par honor & pretium à nobis referri. Sed fortassis,vt erga Deum & erga parentes satis est referre gratiam,quantam quisq; potest. At quot sunt hodie, proh dolor, malè grati discipuli, qui præceptores suos iamdudū piè hac vita defunctos & in Domino quiescentes, non minus crudeliter quàm indignè trastant, cum intus probè norint, se, nisi ipsi eos loqui docuissent, non habere quod dicerent. At quàto satius erat vel Plauti illud cogitare:Improbus est homo, Qui beneficium scit sumere & reddere nescit. Sed experientur illi quoque Solomonem veré dixisse,Ab eius domo,qui bonum malo penset, non facefcere malum.
units.tr: Fourth, a notable example of extreme ingratitude is set before us here. There is no one who, even by the guidance of nature alone, does not understand that he owes great thanks, and indeed his whole self, to the one by whose many great benefits he himself or his family have been honoured. If he lacks the power to repay, he will at least never cease to recall them to others and to proclaim them in words. For nothing, as Cicero says very clearly, is so inhuman, so monstrous, so savage, as to appear unworthy of a kindness, or rather, to appear beaten by one. Yet our David, as we said above, had deserved well of Nabal, if only for this reason, that he had defended his flocks. Soldiers usually have great licence, either because they are strong or because they can easily hide, or, if they are caught, because they can excuse their poverty and hunger. Yet David kept his soldiers in line and trained them to that discipline which the Baptist preaches in Luke: "Do violence to no one, nor accuse anyone falsely." I pass over how, not long ago, when the Philistines had made a sortie and surrounded Keilah, he attacked them with his army, which expected nothing less, and routed them most bravely. I say nothing now of other wars, which David undertook for the safety of his country and carried through most successfully more than once, not without great peril to his life. Nabal ought to have recalled all these things with a grateful mind, and at least rewarded the soldiers with some payment, or at least praised them in words. For a gratitude as great as is owed cannot be repaid, yet still it must be shown as great as the mind can grasp. But what happens? Instead of benefits he returns insults, and he does not declare by even a word any sign of a grateful and mindful heart. Why so? Not so much because he was foolish and mad, but because he was overflowing with infinite riches. For riches often puff men up and make them fierce and insolent. Nor are there lacking today those who regard benefits as wrongs, and who, while benefits are being conferred on them, acknowledge them, but afterwards never think of them again; likewise those who repay wrongs for benefits, who are worse than many beasts, which for the most part return gratitude to those who do them good. Truly we have fallen into an iron age. All of us acknowledge that Nabal grievously sinned in refusing David provisions, and therefore was rightly branded with the name of an ungrateful cuckoo. Yet we do not notice the same vice in ourselves, let alone correct it. Indeed, we sometimes shoot our shameless mouths against those very people to whom we owe infinite benefits, more than Nabal did. Aristotle says of those who have shared in philosophy: "honour cannot be paid to them equal to their deserts [τοῖς φιλοσοφίας κοινωνήσασι τιμὴ ἰσόρροπος], but perhaps it is enough, as with the gods and parents, to render what one can." That is to say, a fitting honour and recompense cannot be rendered by us to teachers who impart true wisdom to us. But perhaps, as with God and parents, it is enough to render as much gratitude as each one can. Yet how many disciples today, alas, are badly grateful, who treat their teachers, long since piously departed from this life and resting in the Lord, no less cruelly than unworthily, although they know full well that, unless the teachers had taught them to speak, they would have had nothing to say! How much better it would have been to think of that line of Plautus: "He is a wicked man who knows how to receive a benefit but does not know how to return it." But those people too will find out that Solomon spoke truly: "Evil shall not depart from the house of him who repays good with evil."

units.la: Quinto,videmus quantæ sint exilij miseriæ. Sunt quidem omnis generis aduersa carni nostræ per quam grauia:tamen vix vlla exilio molestius accidit: eò quod in illo concurrere videantur, quæcunque homini dura & intolerabilia videntur: qualia sunt, natalis soli amissio,opum iactura,viuendi in commoditas & labores difficillimi,ferè cum infamiæ nota coiuncti. Nam,vt verè Tyrtæus: Omnibus inuisus (inquit) quoscunque accesserit exul, Semper erit, semper spretus egensq; iacet. Nullus
units.tr: Fifth, we see how great the miseries of exile are. There are indeed all kinds of adversities very hard for our flesh; yet hardly any befalls a man more painfully than exile, because in it seem to meet all those things which seem harsh and intolerable to a man: such as the loss of one's native soil, the loss of wealth, a very hard life of want and toil, and generally coupled with the stain of disgrace. For, as Tyrtaeus truly says: "Hated by all, wherever the exile comes, he will always be, always despised and needy, he lies.

units.la: Exilij miseriæ summa.
units.tr: The sum of the miseries of exile.

units.la: Nullus honos generi est, & perdita gratia formæ est,
units.tr: No honour is left to his family, and the grace of his form is lost,

units.la: Cunctaque tabescunt membra dolore graui.
units.tr: And all his limbs waste away with heavy grief.

units.la: Curat nemo vagos & lædere nemo veretur,
units.tr: No one cares for the wanderer, and no one fears to harm him,

units.la: Non exul curæ dicitur esse Deo.
units.tr: The exile is said to be no concern of God.

units.la: Quod si vero quis ad homines non modo sibi antea ignotos, verum etiam barbaros & natura infidos atque crudeles, deniq; à religione sua alienos, vel etiam huius hostes, profugere cogatur, id demum omnia, quæ homini incommoda accidere possunt, longè superat. Has ærumnas tolerauit in exilio suo decennali Dauid, omnium iniurijs expositus, eaq; in re fuit typus Christi, qui, etiam infans, in Ægyptum fugere coactus fuit. Cur igitur nobis graue aut molestum sit, quod verus Dauid, æternus Dei filius, prior pro nobis passus est, quando ne in ea quidem terra tutas certasq; sedes habere potuit, quam sibi Deus præ aliis consecrarat, quæq; eius hæreditas in scripturis dici consueuit?
units.tr: But if someone is compelled to flee to men who are not only unknown to him before, but also barbarous and by nature untrustworthy and cruel, and finally alien to his religion, or even enemies of it, this surpasses all the misfortunes that can befall a man. David endured these hardships in his ten years of exile, exposed to the wrongs of all, and in this respect he was a type of Christ, who, even as an infant, was forced to flee into Egypt. Why, then, should it be hard or grievous for us that the true David, the eternal Son of God, has suffered before us, since he could not even in that land, which God had consecrated above others and which is customarily called his inheritance in the Scriptures, have a safe and secure dwelling?

units.la: Exul erat Christus, comites nos exulis huius
units.tr: Christ was an exile; we ought to be companions of this exile,

units.la: Esse decet, cuius nos quoq; membra sumus.
units.tr: Since we too are members of him whose exile it was.

units.la: Non est enim seruus maior hero suo, neque discipulus suo magistro præstantior. Ioan. 13. Interim illi, quibus Deus halcyonia concedit, exules non auersabuntur, omnique iniuriarum genere prosequuntur: sed
units.tr: For the servant is not greater than his lord, nor the disciple above his teacher. John 13. Meanwhile, those to whom God grants a halcyon peace will not turn away from exiles, but will pursue them with every kind of wrong; but

units.la: & hospitio exceptos benigne ac comiter habebunt. Multas ob causas homines exulant: non possumus semper, ut maxime velemus, in patria nostra manere: ne ergo hac in parte nos ethnicis inclementiores prębeamus. Cogitandum semper, nostros quoque non αυτοχθονας, sed advenas & peregrinos fuisse, item miras esse rerum conversiones & quotidianas imperiorum mutationes: gravia bella facile oriri, quibus multi ex sedibus suis & possessionibus auitis exturbentur: Memores igitur vicissitudinis rerum humanarum, recte nos erga alios geramus. Si qui sint inter exules, qui sub religionis veręprę textu alia agant, id bonis & innocentibus viris, qui tanquam ex incendio profugiunt, non debet esse fraudi. Patribus certe, qui Sardicæ convenerunt, adeo curæ fuere exules, ut proprio canone sanxerint, largam illis benevolentiam & humanitatem habendam: Canonis verba, si quis requirat, hæc sunt: οκληγόν δἱ καὶ βαρύτατον ἐλασίαν αδίκον υπομνηστία μὶ υποδὶχεσθαι ὐφ' ὐμών. πλείστην δέ καλουαγαθία ηέ φιλοφρονήσει οφεὓλει ὓποδὶχεσθαι ο τοιῖτωί, id est, duram est, admodumč graue, eum, qui persecutionem immerenter sustinet, non recipiat. pi à vobis. Enimuerò larga ei beneuolentia & humanitas est exhibenda, &c.
units.tr: they will receive them as guests and treat them kindly and courteously. Men go into exile for many reasons: we cannot always remain in our own country as much as we would most like; let us therefore not show ourselves harsher in this respect than the heathens. We must always reflect that our own ancestors too were not [αὐτόχθονες] natives of the soil, but strangers and sojourners; likewise that the turns of affairs are wonderful and the changes of empires daily; that grievous wars arise easily, by which many are driven from their homes and ancestral possessions. Mindful, then, of the changes of human affairs, let us behave rightly towards others. If there are among the exiles any who, under the pretext of true religion, act otherwise, this should not be held against good and innocent men, who flee as if from a fire. Certainly the Fathers who gathered at Sardica cared so much for exiles that they sanctioned by their own canon that a generous goodwill and humanity should be shown to them. If anyone asks for the words of the canon, they are these: "It is a hard and very grievous thing to refuse one who suffers unjust persecution without fault [ὀκνηρὸν δὲ καὶ βαρύτατον ... μὴ ὑποδέχεσθαι ὑφ᾽ ὑμῶν]; but such a man ought to be received by you with the greatest kindness and courtesy [πλείστην δὲ καλοκἀγαθίᾳ ἢ φιλοφροσύνῃ ὀφείλει ὑποδέχεσθαι]." That is, it is harsh and very grievous to refuse one who undeservedly bears persecution. Generous goodwill and humanity must be shown to him, and so on.

units.la: Postremò colligimus, quid hominės pij hodie etiam à Nabalibus expectare possint. Quemadmodum legati isti Dauidis, à Nabal ignominiosè habentur, ac pręter meritum conuitijs proscinduntur: ita etiamnum sunt, semperq; erunt, qui fideles veritatis culto-res, ac praesertim administros verbi, ipsisi-mos Dei legatos contumeliosè habitos, vio-labunt. Hæc enim semper fuit conditio pio-rum. Achabus Ahtri filius, regum omnium impijsimus, Heliam Thesbiten prophetarum maximum, seditionis concitatæ accu-sat: Sed ille se grauiter excusat, culpamq; om-nem in ipsum regem & Iezabele vxorem gentilem & maleficam confert. Non ego, inquit, Israelitas perturbo: sed tu, tuaq; paterna familia: qui, omisis Iehouæ præceptis, Baales sequimini: quæ causa fuit, vt Iehoua vobis istos ardores immiserit. Sed & Apostoli, quin & ipse Christus, rebelles audiunt. Hodie, qui Euangelium ex densissima caligine su periorum temporum restituerunt, appellantur schismatici, hæretici, apostatę. Quid ita? Nempe quod à sede, quam vocant, Apostolica decesserint. Interim tacitè præterenint, quod relicto cultu illicito à falsa doctrina non à vera fide,diuinoq; verbo desciuerint,itemq; quod à sanguinolenta purpuratæ meretricis synagoga, ad veram Ecclesiam transierint:ac quod eius rei caussas longè grauisimas habuerint. Deus enim passim iubet, vt nobis caueamus à pseudoprophetis, exeamus ex Babylone,& fugiamus idola.At quia eandem Dauidis,adeoque ipsius Christi sortem fuisse scimus, conuitia ista æquo & patienti animo ferre conuenit. Certè,nisi magnum esset,patienter audire conuitia,Christus ea ferenti non tanta proposuisset præmia. Dicent, inquit, omne malum contra vos: gaudete tamen & exultate: Ecce enim merces vestra multa est in cœlis. Demonstrandi particula vtitur, vt promissionis certitudinem faciat, & præmium quasi præsens ob oculos statuat. Hoc autem non definit, vt auari solent, sed multum & vberrimum fore pollicetur. Etenim, vt Apostolus ait, quæ in hoc tempore perpetimur, minimè paria sunt futuræ gloriæ, quæ olim reuelabitur: &, vt Isaias clamat,neque visu, neque auditu,imò ne cogitatione quidem comprehendi possunt, quæ Deus iis parauit, qui ipsum diligunt.In cœlis verò gloriam hanc nobis commonstrat, vt futuram expectemus, & eandem sciamus per mortem non amitti, sed
units.tr: Lastly, we gather what godly people may even today expect from Nabals. Just as David's envoys were treated with contempt by Nabal and torn apart with insults though they had done nothing to deserve it, so even now there are, and always will be, people who abuse the faithful defenders of the truth, and above all the ministers of the Word, God's own envoys. For this has always been the condition of the godly. Ahab son of Omri, the most wicked of all kings, accuses Elijah the Tishbite, the greatest of the prophets, of stirring up sedition. But Elijah answers him gravely and lays all the blame on the king himself and on his pagan and sorceress wife Jezebel. "I do not trouble Israel," he says, "but you and your father's house, who, having abandoned the commands of Jehovah, follow the Baals; this is why Jehovah has sent these troubles upon you." The Apostles, and Christ himself, also hear that they are rebels. Today, those who have restored the Gospel out of the very dense darkness of earlier times are called schismatics, heretics and apostates. Why so? Clearly because they have departed from what they call the Apostolic See. Meanwhile they quietly pass over the fact that they have turned away from illicit worship and false doctrine, not from the true faith and the divine Word; that they have passed from the bloody synagogue of the purple-clad harlot to the true Church; and that they had very weighty reasons for doing so. For God everywhere commands us to beware of false prophets, to come out of Babylon, and to flee idols. But since we know that David's lot, and indeed Christ's own, was the same, it is fitting to bear these insults with an even and patient mind. Certainly, unless it were a great thing to hear insults patiently, Christ would not have set such great rewards before those who bear them. "They will say every kind of evil against you," he says, "yet rejoice and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven." He uses the demonstrative particle to make the promise certain and to set the reward before our eyes as if it were present. He does not, however, limit it, as misers usually do, but promises that it will be large and most abundant. For, as the Apostle says, the sufferings of this present time are in no way comparable to the glory that will one day be revealed; and, as Isaiah cries out, what God has prepared for those who love him can be grasped neither by sight, nor by hearing, nor even by thought. He shows us this glory in heaven so that we may await it as something to come, and know that it is not lost by death, but

units.la: Matth.5. Luc.6. Rom.8. Isa.64. sed potius inueniri atque obtineri. In cœlis enim patria nostra est, & illic nobis locum parauit Christus, quem non aliter, quam in fide moriendo ingrediemur. Mercedis autem vocabulo vtitur, non vt meritis nostris aliquid deberi testetur, sed, vt doceat com‑pensationem fore laborum & afflictionum, quas hic sustinemus. Breuiter, patres imitatur, qui, cum filijs nihil debeant, præmij promissione, eos ad obedientiæ studium pelliciunt ac inuitant. Nam, si proprie loqui libeat, gratuitum est, quidquid nobis Deus promittit aut largitur: neque vllus apud eum merito locus est, cum imperfecta, mutila & centonum instar, polluta sint, quæcunque à nobis proficiscuntur. Sed dices: Ita nomen Dei perpetuò afficietur contumelia. Certè, nisi nos ei malo medeamur. Mederi autem oportet ea moderatione, quā vsus est Christus. Ego, inquit, dæmonium non habeo: Ego multa bona feci. Propter quod illorum vultis me lapidare? Paulus proscindebatur à Iudæis & pseudoapostolis. Ille modestissimè purgauit se & doctrinam suam epistolis, quas ad Ecclesias dedit. Sed de his postea.
units.tr: Matth. 5. Luc. 6. Rom. 8. Isa. 64. but rather found and obtained. For our homeland is in heaven, and Christ has prepared a place for us there, which we shall enter only by dying in faith. He uses the word reward not to testify that anything is owed to our merits, but to teach that there will be a recompense for the labours and afflictions we endure here. In short, he imitates fathers who, though they owe their sons nothing, win them over and invite them to zeal for obedience by promising rewards. For, to speak properly, whatever God promises or bestows upon us is a free gift; nor does any merit have a place before him, since whatever proceeds from us is imperfect, maimed and, like a patchwork, polluted. But you will say: in this way the name of God will be constantly insulted. Certainly, unless we remedy that evil. But we must remedy it with the moderation Christ used. "I do not have a demon," he says; "I have done many good works. For which of them do you wish to stone me?" Paul was torn apart by Jews and false apostles. He cleared himself and his teaching very modestly in the letters he sent to the churches. But of these things later.

units.la: In fine dicitur, Legatos Dauidis, cum nihil planè impetrassent, se conuertisse in viam.
units.tr: At the end it is said that David's envoys, having achieved absolutely nothing, turned back on their way.

units.la: Legati Dauid reuidi reuersi ... secta red. Ad. 2 Reg. 10. 1. Chron. 19. 2. Sam. 10. suam & reuersos esse, ac cum venissent, annunciasse ei, secundū omnia verba hæc, &c. Quo loco denuò nobis exemplum legatorum ac seruorū fidelium proponitur, Quem admodum enim bona fide, quæ in mandatis habebant, Nabali exposuerunt: ita non minori diligentia Dauidi referunt, quomodo à Nabale sint excepti: quid item ab illo tulerint responsi. Interim nemo negauerit, eos, qui à priuatis personis mittuntur, non semper teneri, vt ea, quæ vltro citroq; gesta sint mittentibus ad verbū omnia referant. Quid enim? Vt multæ simultates, quæ forte cædibus finirentur, inde oriuntur, si syllabatim referre velis, quæ imprudentius forte excederint, vel etiā vehementius ab alijs dicta sint: ita multæ tolluntur, si ea tantum, quæ ad mutuam pacem ac concordiam ineundam ac confirmandā faciunt, modesteq; ac prudenter responsa sunt, identidem inculcaris.
units.tr: Ad. 2 Reg. 10. 1. Chron. 19. 2. Sam. 10. David's envoys returned and came back to their own people, and when they arrived they reported to him all these words, and so on. At this point we are again offered the example of envoys and faithful servants. For just as they set out in good faith what they had been commissioned to say to Nabal, so with no less care they report to David how they were received by Nabal, and what answer they brought back from him. Meanwhile, no one would deny that those who are sent by private persons are not always bound to report to the senders everything that was said and done on both sides. For just as many quarrels, which might perhaps have ended in bloodshed, arise from this, if you wish to repeat word for word what some have said rather rashly or even more violently by others, so many quarrels are settled if one only repeats, again and again, those things which help to bring about and confirm mutual peace and harmony, and which were answered modestly and wisely.

units.la: Atque hęc ad tertiam historiæ huius partem annotasse sufficiat. Summa huc redit, vt exemplo Nabalis moniti, caueamus auariciam, ae ingratitudinem: conuitia nec in Deum nec in homines iaciamus. Condoleamus miseris & afflictis, illosq; omni ope & auxilio iuuemus.
units.tr: Let it suffice to have noted these things for the third part of this history. The sum of it comes to this: warned by Nabal's example, let us beware of greed and ingratitude; let us cast no insults either at God or at men. Let us grieve with the wretched and afflicted, and help them with every resource and aid.

units.la: DE
units.tr: Concerning

units.la: HOMILIA IIII.
units.tr: Homily 4

units.la: Dauid, audita Nabalis contumelia, non potest se tenere, quia de Nabale vltionem capiat.
units.tr: David, having heard Nabal's insult, cannot contain himself, because he wants to take revenge on Nabal.

units.la: 13 Et ait Dauid viris suis: Accingat se quisque gladio suo: Et accinxerunt se singuli gladio suo: ascenderunt post Dauidem fermè quadringenti viri: ducenti autem remanserunt apud supellectilem.
units.tr: 13 And David said to his men: Let each of you gird on his sword. And each of them girded on his sword, and about four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred remained with the baggage.

units.la: SVpra dictum est, Nabalem legatos Dauidis, qui commeatum à se petierant, non tantùm inanes dimisisse, verùm etiam graui verborum contumelia addita, Dauidem, tribulem suum, tanquam fugitiuum & perduellem vituperasse. Porrò, quo animo Dauid petulantiam istam acceperit, audiemus.
units.tr: It was said above that Nabal, when David's envoys asked him for provisions, not only sent them away empty-handed but also added a bitter verbal insult, reviling David, his fellow tribesman, as a runaway and a rebel. Next we shall hear how David received this insolence.

units.la: Primò imperat suis, vt se gladijs accingant. Quod postquâ & illi, qui necem hominis istius ἀςόρῳ proculdubio anhelabant, & ipse fecit, profecti sunt circiter quadringenti viri, Dauidé sequentes, ducentis apud impedimenta remanentibus, nempe ne illa amitteret. In alijs enim rebus male instituta posterioribus consilijs corrigere possumus; at in bellis idem facere nõ licet. Ideo Scipio Africanus dicere solebat, Turpe verbū esse Imperatoris: Non putarã. Prudenter itaq; in castris omnia esse agenda, ne hoc dictĕrium, locū nimis sero inueniret. Post aliquot versus dicit, se pœnitere, quod greges Nabalis, à quo nihil minus exspectasset, quàm vt bonû, malo pensaret, incolumes contra abigeos, & bestias, itemq; hostes, qui subinde in prædā effundebantur, conferuasset, ita vt nihil omnino de suo deperdiderit. Næ ego frustra, inquit, coseruaui omnia, quę habet iste in de sertis, ita vt nihil omnino de suo deperdiderit: & reddidit mihi malū pro bono. Nomen Nabalis non exprimit, quod irati solent, vt qui hostes ne nomine dignos censeant. Ad hęc: Sic faciat, ait, Deus inimicis Dauidis, & sic addat, si reliquero ex omnibus, quę habet vsq; mane, mingentem ad parietem. Iurisiurandi formula, qua hic vtitur, non plenè est expressa. Sensus tamen est: Ita perdat Deus hostes meos mihiq; subijciat, vt ei ante crastinū ex omnibus quę habet nihil prorsus reliqui faciam. Per mingentem ad parietē non nulli sexum virile intelligunt, quod soleant mares vrinā ad parietem reddere: dicuntq; Dauidem constituisse solis mulieribus parcere. Quod in expugnationibus vrbium & castrorum fieri videmus,vbi viris occisione deletis, mulieribus tantum parcitur. Sed quia postea Abigaeli dicit, Deus prohibuit me,ne te perderem, apparet hoc non posse exponi tantum de virili sexu. Nam ita nihil periculi fuisset Abigaeli. Sensus ergo est:Sed ne canem quidem Nabali reliquum facturū. Solent enim canes proximam quenque parietem, sublato altero pede,commingere. Phrasis ista in libris Regum sæpiùs vsurpatur,eaq; extrema pernities vel internecio indicatur.1.Regum.14. Achias propheta Silonites Ieroboami vxori,de filij morbo se consulenti,prædicit & pueri mortem & mariti cum omne eius posteritate interitum,adeò vt nec canis sit euasurus.2. Regum 9. Deus ad prophetam Elisæi discipulum, qui Iehu regem vngebat, vt vniuersam Achabi domum perderet,&eius memoriam genusq; stirpitus ex Israelitis tolleret:De Achabo,in quit,ne commistorem parietis reliquum faciam,&c.Hostes irati nonnunquam nec canibus nec felibus parcunt. Flauius Vopiscus refert Aurelianum imperatorem cum Thyanam venisset, eamq; sibi clausisse portas comperisset, iratum iurasse, se tantam {a}stragem editurum, vt ne canem vnum in ea viuum relicturus esset. Militibus spe praedae acrius incumbentibus, Heraclemon quidã, ne cum caeteris occideretur, vrbe prodidit, in quam introducto exercitu, visione quadã territus, vitam omnibus ciuibus Aurelianus concesisit, praeterquã proditori, dicens ei fi-dem seruare non potuisse, qui patrię non percerit. Rogat, de ciuibus sententiam cur mutasset, Ne canem vnum, inquit, me relicturum dixi, hominibus igitur praeteritis, canes omnes trucidate.
units.tr: First, he orders his men to gird on their swords. After this they did so, and so did he, and about four hundred men set out following David, while two hundred stayed with the baggage, namely so that he would not lose it. For in other matters, when something has been badly arranged, we can correct it with later decisions, but in war it is not allowed to do the same. Hence Scipio Africanus used to say that the phrase "I shall not think it" was a disgraceful one for a commander. Therefore everything must be done prudently in the camp, lest that word find the place too late. A few verses later he says that he regrets having preserved the flocks of Nabal, from whom he had expected nothing less than good in return for evil, safe against thieves and wild beasts, and likewise enemies, who from time to time made raids on them, so that he had lost nothing at all of his own. "In vain, then," he says, "have I kept safe all that this fellow has in the desert, so that nothing of his was lost; and he has repaid me evil for good." He does not express Nabal's name, as angry men usually do, as if they judged enemies unworthy of a name. Moreover: "May God do so to David's enemies, and so add to them, if I leave of all that he has until morning anyone who pisses against the wall." The form of oath he uses here is not fully expressed. The sense, however, is: may God so destroy my enemies and subject them to me that I shall leave nothing at all of everything he has before tomorrow. Some understand "one who pisses against the wall" as the male sex, since males are accustomed to urinate against a wall, and they say that David had resolved to spare only women. This we see happen in the storming of cities and camps, where, when the men have been slain, only the women are spared. But because he afterwards says to Abigail, "God has prevented me from harming you," it appears that this cannot be explained as referring only to the male sex; for in that case Abigail would have been in no danger at all. The sense, therefore, is: he would leave not even a dog to Nabal. For dogs are accustomed to urinate against whatever wall is nearest, lifting one leg. This phrase is used quite often in the books of Kings, and it signifies utter destruction or extermination. (1 Kings 14.) Ahijah the Shilonite, when consulted by Jeroboam's wife about her son's illness, foretells both the death of the boy and the ruin of the husband together with his whole posterity, so that not even a dog will escape. (2 Kings 9.) God, speaking through the prophet's disciple who was anointing Jehu king, says that he is to destroy the whole house of Ahab and remove his memory and lineage from Israel root and branch: "Of Ahab," he says, "I will leave no one who pisses against the wall," etc. Enraged enemies sometimes spare neither dogs nor cats. Flavius Vopiscus reports that the emperor Aurelian, when he came to Thyana and found that its gates had been shut against him, swore in anger that he would make such a slaughter that he would leave not even one living dog in it. As the soldiers pressed on eagerly in hope of plunder, a certain Heraclemon, so as not to be killed with the rest, betrayed the city; and when the army had been led in, Aurelian, struck by some vision, granted life to all the citizens except the traitor, saying that he could not keep faith with him, since he had spared neither his own country. When he was asked by the citizens why he had changed his sentence, he replied: "I said I would leave not one dog; therefore, having passed over the men, kill all the dogs."

units.la: Nec vero dubium est, quin iurata perfecisset Dauid, nisi Deus illū retraxisset, animūq; eius Abigaelis opera auertisset, ne cogitata praestaret. Enimueroira exceccatus, sibi plane persuaserat, se in homine istū ingratū rectè omnino exemplū statuere. Nec audis suos illū ab incoepto reuocasse, vel irā emollisse. Etenim cū cotumeliā istā cū Dauide cōmune habērent, pculdubio nihil illis gratius, nihil optati vltione de illo capieda accidisset.
units.tr: Nor is there any doubt that David would have carried out what he had sworn, unless God had restrained him and turned his mind away by Abigail's efforts, so that he would not perform what he had planned. Indeed, blinded by anger, he had fully persuaded himself that he was rightly setting an example against this ungrateful man. Nor do you hear that his men called him back from his undertaking or softened his anger. For since they shared the insult with David, undoubtedly nothing could have been more welcome to them, nothing more desired, than to take vengeance on him.

units.la: Ac quidē negari non potest. Nabalem eis causam ipsum subministrasse. Quid enim? Si cibaria illis praebert noluisset, tamen contumelia eos onerari non oportuit. Qui animo excelso sunt & generosa, multo acerbius accipiūt cōuitia quàm verbera. Eius rei Chrysostomus foftomus hanc ratione affert, quod pulsatio quę affertur corpori, distribuitur quodam inter corpus & animā: Conuitiū aut animum solū verberat. Et tamen omnino Dauidis fuisset, seipsum reprimere, iraq;, vt duce, non vt milite, vti. Quid enim? An ea causa, quod reddantur nobis mala pro bonis, nos vicisim mala reponemus? Ita mala crescerent in infinitum.
units.tr: And indeed this cannot be denied: Nabal himself had supplied them with the cause. For what? Even if he had refused them food, they ought not to have been burdened by the insult. Those of lofty and noble spirit take insults far more bitterly than blows. Chrysostom gives this reason for it: that a blow inflicted on the body is shared in some measure between body and soul, but an insult strikes the soul alone. Nevertheless, it was altogether David's duty to restrain himself and to use anger as a commander, not as a soldier. For what? Shall we, because evils are returned to us in place of good, in turn repay evil? In that way evils would grow without limit.

units.la: Sunt quidā, qui factū hoc Danidis excusent: sed illū grauiter peccasse, multis argumentis euinci potest. Primo enim nimis praeceps est ac credulus. Oportuit rem cōsidera tius expendere, & alterā quoq; partē audire. Quid enim, si nuncij illi mētiti essent? aut qd si vehementiores fuissent? aut, quid si vera Nabalis supra veritatē exaggerassent? Incredibile dictu, quātū noceat, si iudex vnā tantū partē audiat, aut liçet altera quoq; cognoscat, illi fidem adhibeat, quæ aures prius impleuit, aliasq; rationes nihili pendat. De Alexandro Magno legitur, quod, cum quidam aduersarium suum accusaret, altera aurem manu concluserit: Rogatus, cur non attente audiret, alteram aurem, respondit, se reo integram seruare. Demosthenes scribit, Iudices Athenis iurare coactos, quod vtram que partem audire vellent. Plato eius rei
units.tr: There are some who excuse David's deed, but that he sinned gravely can be proved by many arguments. First, he was far too hasty and credulous. He ought to have weighed the matter more carefully and also heard the other side. For what if those messengers had been lying? Or what if they had been more violent? Or what if they had exaggerated Nabal's words beyond the truth? It is incredible how greatly it harms when a judge hears only one side, or even when he hears the other side too, gives credence to the party whose words first filled his ears, and cares nothing for the other reasons. It is read of Alexander the Great that when a certain man was accusing his opponent, he shut one of his own ears with his hand. Asked why he was not listening attentively, he replied that he was keeping the other ear unbiased for the defendant. Demosthenes writes that the judges at Athens were compelled to swear that they would hear both parties. Plato illustrates this matter with an elegant comparison.

units.la: Dauid mis credulus. Altera pars audienda. vsum eleganti cóparatione illustrat.Quem-admodum,inquit, purpura si cum purpura & aurum cum auro conferatur, melius po-testiudicari : Ita si iudices vtramq; partem audiant. Nostro tempore multi principes non male erga viros bonos & religionis pu rioris amantes, suapte natura essent affecti: Sed quod consiliarijs vtantur, familiarisi-mè,qui ipsis rem mala fide referunt,praeci-puè si quid religionem concernat, fideles praepostero zelo persequuntur, eosq; ne co gnoscere quidem dignantur, ac, vt eos au-diant,tamen quod iam praeiudicijs sint occu pati ac sinistris suspicionibus imbuti, de in-stituto vix ac ne vix qdé discedút. Cogitare debebat Dauid:Quid si legati tui ęquo suis-sent vehementiores ? Certè consentaneum non est,ignorasse Nabalem,legatos iure gen tium ἀσπλὰς esse.
units.tr: David was too credulous; the other side must be heard. "Just as," he says, "when purple is compared with purple and gold with gold, a better judgement can be made, so judges should hear both sides." In our own time many princes, who by their nature are not ill disposed toward good men and lovers of purer religion, are nonetheless led astray because they make use of counsellors, very intimate with them, who report matters in bad faith, especially if anything touches religion; these counsellors pursue the faithful with a perverse zeal and do not even deign to hear them. And even when they are made to listen, because they are already preoccupied with prejudgments and steeped in sinister suspicions, they scarcely, if at all, depart from what they have begun. David ought to have considered: what if your envoys were more violent than they should have been? Surely it is not likely that Nabal did not know that the envoys were protected by the law of nations [ἄσπονδοι], that is, inviolable.

units.la: Sed quanuis constitisset,Nabalem verba ista euomuisse,imò Dauid ipse hæc suis au-ribus audiuisset,tamen feruente ira,arma ca pere non oportuit.Ira enim pessimus con-sultor est:Ira bulliente, neq; dicere neq; fa-cere pensi quidquam habemus. Irati inson-tes cum sontibus puniunt,nullumq; modú feruant.Cuius rei exemplum in Theodosio Imperatore (cæterà egregio principe) ha-bemus. bemus. Is enim accepto nuncio, magistratus aliquot in seditione quadam Thessaloni cæ orta, saxis obrutos, & contumeliosè tractatos fuisse, victus magnitudine iræ, neque ratione illius impetu refrenato, septem millia hominum iugulauit, innocentium cum reorum cæde confusa. Cuius tamen rei eum vehementer pœnituit. Quare legem, Ambrosio suggerente, tulit, quæ etiam in Codice de pœnis habetur (incipit, Si vindicari) qua præcipit, vt si princeps in causa sua iudicarit, iracundius, exequutio ad diem trigesimum differatur, quo corrigi possit sententia. Nec malè ille apud Comicum:
units.tr: But even if it had been established that Nabal had uttered those words, or even if David himself had heard them with his own ears, still he ought not to have taken up arms in a fit of seething anger. For anger is the worst counsellor: when anger boils, we have no thought either for speaking or for acting rightly. Angry men punish the innocent along with the guilty, and keep no measure. We have an example of this in the emperor Theodosius, otherwise an excellent prince. For when he received word that some magistrates had been stoned and roughly handled in a sedition that had arisen at Thessalonica, overcome by the greatness of his anger, and not restraining that impulse by reason, he had seven thousand people slaughtered, the innocent being killed in confusion along with the guilty. Yet he bitterly repented of this deed. Therefore, at Ambrose's urging, he enacted a law, which is also found in the Code under "On punishments" (it begins "If a matter is to be avenged"), which directs that if a prince has judged in his own cause, with too much anger, the execution is to be postponed to the thirtieth day, so that the sentence may be corrected. Nor did that comic poet speak badly: [the passage breaks off here.]

units.la: Omnia prius experiri, inquit, quàm armis sa pientem decet. Ira vinculum rationis est. Irati belluarum instar sæuiunt, & temerè in quos uis grassantur.
units.tr: "Before taking up arms, a wise man should try everything else," he says. Anger is a fetter on reason. Angry people rage like wild beasts and rush headlong upon whomever they wish to harm.

units.la: Neq; hic pedem sistit Dauid, sed seruis suis imperat, vt se quàm primum accingant. Hactenus illos ab omni insolentia represse- rat: nunc ipsos excitat & incendit. Quasi nō sufficeret, se ira commotum, ad cædem in- flammatum, nisi alios quoq; instigaret. Pec- catum alienum committitur, cum quidem scelus per nos non designamus, interim a- lios instigamus eosq; consilio atque opeiu namus. Sic hoc loco Dauid: Sic omnes ij,
units.tr: David does not stop here. He orders his servants to gird themselves as quickly as possible. Until now he had restrained them from every act of recklessness; now he rouses and inflames them. As if it were not enough that he himself was moved by anger and fired for slaughter, he also goads others on. We commit another's sin when we do not ourselves carry out the crime but still urge others on and assist them with counsel and help. So David does here, and so do all those

units.la: { } qui non se tantum, sed alios quoq; vino one-rant: nec finem faciunt, nisi se & alios in bestias tanquam Circeis poculis transformarint. Ecquis igitur illis, quę ab istis peccantur, non ascripserit?
units.tr: who burden not only themselves but others with wine, and do not stop until they have turned both themselves and others into beasts, as with the cups of Circe. Who, then, would not impute to such men the sins that others commit at their instigation?

units.la: Præterea Dauid satis declarat, se pœnite-re re recte facti. Certe frustra, inquit, conserua-ui, quæ iste habet omnia, &c. In Hebraico est, in mendacium, hoc est, vt ipse me deci-perem, Ac si diceret: Ego eum beneficio meo prouocaui ad mentiendum. Debuit ille quidem humanitatem meam aliquo of-ficio compensare: Nunc autem immemor omnis iustitiæ, afficit me intolerabili contu-melia. Atq; hoc illud est, quod Græcus red-didit εἰς ᾅδ′ιxov. Sed enim neminem recte factì pœnitere debet, etiamsi, vt exclamat Poeta
units.tr: Moreover, David makes it plain enough that he repented of doing right. "Surely in vain," he says, "have I kept all that this man has, etc." In the Hebrew it reads "into a lie," that is, so that I might deceive myself. It is as if he said: "I have provoked him by my kindness to lie. He ought indeed to have repaid my courtesy with some service; but now, forgetful of all justice, he heaps an intolerable insult upon me." This is what the Greek renders [εἰς ἄδικον], "unjustly." But surely no one ought to repent of doing right, even if, as the poet cries out,

units.la: Omnia sint ingrata, nihil, fecisse benignè, est. Quanto rectius cogitasset, Etsi tibi Nabal de est, tamen Deus non deerit. Si Nabal suum officium non fecit, an iccirco tu non facies tuum? Aut, si ille iniustus est, an ea causa tu non eris iustus? Si ne illi quidem, qui alieni sunt à Deo, frustra recte faciūt, quanto minus putare debeo ego, me ista incassum fecisse.
units.tr: "All things are ungrateful; to have done a kindness is to have done nothing." How much more rightly might David have thought: "Even if Nabal is ungrateful to you, God will not fail you. If Nabal has not done his duty, will you therefore neglect yours? Or if he is unjust, will you therefore not be just?" If even those who are estranged from God do not do good in vain, how much less should I think that I have done these things to no purpose?

units.la: Deniq; temerè ac inconsideratè ad iuran-dum fertur. Legitimum enim iusiurandum ornari oportet tribus hisce,(vt ab Hieronymo vocantur)quasi comitibus: Veritate nimirum, iustitia & iudicio:hoc est, vt clarius dicam,In omni iuramento videndum est in primis,vt verum sit,quod iuramus: deinde vt rectum sit & bonum. (Recte enim veteres dixere, Iuramentum non esse vinculum iniquitatis.) Postremo adhibendum est iudicium, ne temere, aut pasim, aut apud quosuis,aut,quacunque de causa, iuremus. Verum quidem erat, quod iurauit Dauid. Omnino enim decreuerat,iurata perficere. Iustitia autem & iudicium aberant. Nam quae haec iustitia, ob vnius peccatum,velle vniuersam fontis familiam euertere,& in ea ne cane quidè relinquere? Quod hoc iudicium insonte eadé cum fonte poena plectere? Quid enim seruitia,quae totos dies laborè distinebantur, quid infantes innocentes, si qui in illa domo fuerunt,quid mulier, cui mores mariti displicebant summopere,tanta animaduersione dignum commiserat? Quasi vero tormentum hoc non satis fuerit graue, quod in maritum istum incidisset, a quo nec ope nec consilio iuuabatur? Non ista iusti hominis verba sunt, sed furentis. At ita Dauid, prorsus oblitus sui, rapitur transuersus. Nec legem illam in memoriam reuocat, qua præcipit Deus, ne pater pro filio plectatur,vel filius pro patre:sed quisque suorum scelerū pœnas luat. In libris Regum & Paralipomen. laudatur rex Amasias,quòd sicarios,à quibus Ioas pater ipsius fuerat occisus,interfecisset : filijs autem illorum pepercisset. Atq; in eo loco citatur lex illa Deuteronom. Alia ratio Dei est.Is enim pro suo arbitratu quiduis facere, sontesq; ac insontes eodem reatu inuoluere potest.Quamuis,si rem recte velimus putare,coram Deo nemo insons est. Ac vt rectè Augustinus,potest Deus filium punire pro patre:quia,etsi enim eum affligit in hoc seculo,potest eundem in altero seruare,&c. Adhæc Deus videt peccata,vbi nos nulla vidimus.Nobis autem proposita est lex communis & ordinaria,quam sequamur.
units.tr: Finally, he rushes into an oath rashly and thoughtlessly. For a lawful oath ought to be attended by three companions, as Jerome calls them: truth, righteousness and judgment. That is, to put it more plainly: in every oath we must first see to it that what we swear is true; then that it is right and good. (The ancients rightly said that an oath is not a bond of iniquity.) Lastly, judgment must be applied, so that we do not swear rashly, or at random, or before just anyone, or for any cause whatever. What David swore was indeed true, for he had firmly resolved to carry out what he had sworn. But righteousness and judgment were absent. For what righteousness is it, on account of the sin of one man, to wish to overthrow the whole household of the fountain, not leaving so much as a dog alive in it? What judgment is it to punish the innocent along with the guilty, the fountain and the source alike? For what had the servants done, who were occupied all day with toil? What had the innocent infants done, if any were in that house? What had the wife done, who disliked her husband's manners so greatly, to deserve so severe a punishment? As if the torment were not grievous enough, that she had fallen to a husband from whom she received neither help nor counsel! These are not the words of a just man but of a raging one. Yet David, quite forgetful of himself, is carried headlong this way. Nor does he call to mind that law by which God commands that a father not be punished for his son, nor a son for his father, but that each should pay the penalty for his own crimes. In the Books of Kings and Chronicles King Amaziah is praised because he slew the murderers who had killed his father Joash, but spared their sons. And in that passage the law of Deuteronomy is cited. God's way is different. For he can do whatever he pleases at his own discretion, and involve the guilty and the innocent in the same charge. Yet, if we wish to judge the matter rightly, before God no one is innocent. And as Augustine rightly observes, God can punish a son for his father, because, although he afflicts him in this age, he can preserve him in the next, and so on. Moreover, God sees sins where we see none. For us, however, a common and ordinary law is set forth, which we should follow.

units.la: Ex his,quæ hactenus adduximus,abundè sonstare arbitror, Dauidem grauiter peccasse,vtut quidam velint,eum ista fecisse impulsu Dei. Nempe spiritum sanctum, qui eum antea retraxerat à cæde Saulis, nunc eum impulisse ad expetendam vindictam de Nabale dicunt. Sed quid opus est ista comminisci,præsertim quum videamus, Dauidem ea de re iustè ab Abigaele reprehendi, maximè verò cum videamus,Dauidé ipsum Deo gratias agere, quod se à nefario incepto reuocasset? Quid oportet Dauidem excusare plus quàm ipse velit?
units.tr: From what I have adduced so far, I think it sufficiently clear that David sinned grievously, even though some wish that he did these things at the prompting of God. Indeed, they say that the Holy Spirit, who had earlier restrained him from slaying Saul, now impelled him to seek vengeance upon Nabal. But why is there any need to invent such things, especially since we see that David was justly rebuked by Abigail for this very matter, and above all since we see David himself giving thanks to God that he had called him back from his wicked undertaking? Why should one excuse David more than he himself wished?

units.la: Sed enim, quid Dauidem hic facere oportuit? quaerat aliquis. Certè, ira feruente, non oramus. Respondeo. Primò mandatum illud Dei, Deuteronom. 32. cap. Mihi vindicta & ego retribuam: quod totidem verbis ab Apostolo Roman. 12. repetitur, in mentem reuocare debuisset. Deinde cum multas hactenus à Saule iniurias eleganter tulerit, ne fractus videatur, omnino suum esse, hanc quoque in se contumeliam patienter ferre. Adhaec exempla Patriarcharum aliorumq; fidelium sibi ad imitandum proponere debebat, qui & ipsi insignes quas ab ingratis hominibus acceperant iniurias, nō minus aequo quàm constanti animo illis remiserunt atq; condonarunt. Praeterea ignorare non poterat, nullam cum ea victoriam comparandam, quae de superatis affectibus reportatur. Adde, quod qui se vincit, id faciat, ita ut sibi quàm plurimum prosit, noceat nemini: quum is, qui, feruente ira, alios vincit, & urbes expugnat, fere non sine cruore & aliorum discrimine id faciat. Quod si in illum animadvertere, omnino decreuisset, quà rex iam tum designatus erat;
units.tr: But, someone will ask, what ought David to have done here? Certainly not pray, while his anger was blazing. I answer: first, he ought to have called to mind that command of God in Deuteronomy 32, "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay," which the Apostle repeats in almost the same words in Romans 12. Next, since he had hitherto borne so many injuries from Saul with admirable patience, lest he seem to have been broken, it was altogether fitting for him to bear patiently this insult too. Moreover, he ought to have set before himself as examples to imitate the patriarchs and the other faithful, who also, having received remarkable injuries from ungrateful men, forgave and pardoned them with a mind no less equitable than steadfast. Besides, he could not be ignorant that no victory is to be won over others comparable to that which is gained over one's own passions. Add that he who conquers himself does so in such a way that he benefits himself as much as possible and harms no one; whereas he who, while his anger is boiling, conquers others and storms cities, does so scarcely without bloodshed and danger to others. And if he had quite decided to take vengeance upon him, he had already been designated king,

units.la: {*} Fet. tamen cum ira nondum deferbuisset, de illo poenas sumi non oportuit, praesertim indicta causa. Enimuero, ut praeclare ille apud Tragicum:
units.tr: yet while his anger had not yet cooled, it was not right that punishment be exacted from him, especially with the cause unheard. Indeed, as that famous poet among the tragedians says so well:

units.la: Qui statuit aliquid parte inaudita altera,Aequum licet statuerit, haud aequus est.
units.tr: "He who decides upon something with the other party unheard, though he may decide fairly, is not fair."

units.la: Nec inscite orator ille Ethnicus, Prohibenda, inquit, maxime est ira in puniendo: nunquam enim iratus, qui accedat ad poenam, mediocritatem illam tenebit, quae est inter nimium & parum. Iam qua aequitate, quaiusti tia insontes eodem cum fontibus supplicio inuolueret, diligentius cogitandum erat. Norat, si quis alius optime Saulem eo nomine pesime apud cordatos omnes audire, quod Doegum in sacerdotes immisisset, eiq; imperasset, ut illos ad unum omnes hostili ferro vna cum uxoribus & liberis, nullo ipsorum merito, tolleret.
units.tr: Nor was that Gentile orator unwise when he said: "Anger must above all be restrained in punishing; for an angry man who comes to punishment will never keep that mean which lies between too much and too little." Now, with what equity and justice he could involve the innocent in the same punishment as the guilty, ought to have been considered more carefully. He knew, as well as anyone, how badly Saul was regarded by all sensible men for this very reason, that he had set Doeg upon the priests and ordered him to put them all to the sword, together with their wives and children, none of whom deserved it.

units.la: Quae de Dauide hactenus dicta sunt, non male ad nos transtuleris. Omnes enim natura impatientes irae sumus. Vbi primum nobis no assurgitur, excadescimus, statim q; ad vindicta philimus, quae ut Satyricus ille inquit, Bonum est vita iucundius ipsa, & rem ferro agere volumus. Inuenias qui gloriosum sibi esse existimet, si, Termini Rom. instar, nemini cedat. At multa sunt, quae suadet, iniurias, quae nobis illatae sunt condonandas esse om nemq; vindicta Deo comittenda. Primum Deus multis in locis hoc postulat. Ne dicas inquit Solomo, reddā malū: sed expecta Ie-hova & saluū faciet te: vel liberabit te. Sefus est: Ne cogitandū quidē, quomodo malū acceptum vel iniuriā vlciscare: vindicta Deo relinquenda, qui potens est vt vlciscatur: In eo sperandū, nec orandum eum, vt te vlciscatur, & de inimico poenas sumat, sed tantū vt te tueatur. Quod si feceris, pstabit. Quod si vel cogitatio, aut etiā sermo de vlciscenda iniuria phibetur, quanto magis factū? Etiā cogitationes apud Dominum peccati loco sunt. Huic nō absimile eiusde: Ne dicas, inquit, id est, ne cogites aut statuas, quemadmodū fecit mihi, sic facia ei: reddā ei secundū factū suū, id est, par pari reserā: illa mesura metiar alijs, qua mihi mensi sunt, &c. Matt. 5. 6. & 18. Christus idem pulchra similitudine docet. Doctrinæ respondet eius exemplum. Deus etiam inimicis suis beneficia confert, Solem suum exoriri facit super bonos & malos. Quid, quod filium suum dilectissimum, pro nobis etiā inimicis suis, in mortem tradidit? Roman. 6. cap. Sed & Christus, quum ne minima quidem peccati suspicio in eum cadere posset, virgis caesus, spinis coronatus, & cruci denique affixus. eam habuit orationem plenissimam pietatis:Pater,remitte illis : nesciunt enim quid faciant.Cuius aspersionem sanguinis, testatur apostolus,melius loquentem,quàm Abel.Hoc imitatus est postea Stephanus, Actor.7.Cogitandum est,Deum excitare nobis aduersarios,qui nos exerceant,exemplo Iosephi & Dauidis, qui Semei conuitiatori ignoscebat. Norat enim vterq;, hominem quamquam potest male aliquem odisse, pesfimeq; illi cupere,tamen, nisi permissu Dei, nocere nullo modo posse. Cogitandum etiam venit, nos commeritos esse:Si non in hoc,tamè in alijs casibus:Si nō quoad hunc, tamen quo ad alios homines,aut certè quoad Deum,idq; mille modis.Cogitandū item proximū noftrū illum,quæ eum dixisse aut fecisse contra nos putamus,fortasis nec dixisse vel fecisse,aut certè non malo animo dixisse vel fecisse:aut eum illius,quod fecit, dixit,iam pœnitere.Si non hoc tempore:fortè alio:si nunquam,Deum vindicaturū. Quid quod nemo,nisi à seipso læditur? Nam,qui se iniuriosè tractatos esse opinantur, si rem recta secum via reputent,comperient profecto,nullam se ab alijs iniuriā aut damnum accepisse.Etsi enim,quibus ipsi læduntur,ea extrinsecus eueniunt:tamen se maximè ipsi offenoffendunt,cum animum odio,cupiditate,in uidia,cótaminant.Adhæc si cedamus aduer sarijs,eorum impetus frangemus:at si refista mus,magis illorum furor exardescet.Ita tor menta bellica(bombardas à sono, quem e- dunt, vocant) muros,turres, aliasque res duras & obsistentes magno fragore ac ruina comminuunt: at si fimum,bombycem, alia- que mollia ac cedentia occurrant, quoda- modo delassantur, ac franguntur. Accedit etiam hoc,quod dum inimici sanguinem si- timus, illius vlciscendi spe pleni, dies no- ctesque in perenni quadam mala mentis a- gitatione ita versamur, vt nos potius læda- mus,quàm illos quos odio habemus. Ac sæ- pe fit,vt ex vno peccato multa peccata exi- stant. Nec iniuria dicitur,vlciscendi cupidi- tatem peccatum esse diaboli : quandoqui- dem ipse ab initio homicida fuit.Ioannis o- ctauo capite. Quamobrem Dei Filius Do- minus noster Iesus Christus, cum sibi mor- tem Pharisæi afferre cuperent, illos à patre diabolo genitos esse dixit.Denique illud sæ- pe etiam atq; etiam expendendum,breui fo re, vt mortem obeamus : Proinde quia tali tempore nobis optatissimum erit & maxi- mè necessarium,summam Dei misericordiâ impetrare, eam nobis ob oculos iam nunc, perpetuoq; proponamus,necesse est. Ita enim fiet,vt immanis illa vlciscendi cupiditas nobis exhauriatur,cum ad misericordiā im plorandā,nullū apti® maiūsue remediū inue nias,quàm obliuione iniuriarū, & amore in eos,qui nos aut nostros reaut orationevio larint.Certè nihil iniustius esse aut fingi potest,quàis qui cū hominibus durus fit,vt ne mini se det ad lenitatem ,idem postulet,vt in se fit mitis & benignus Deus.Sed ad con-textum.
units.tr: What has been said so far about David may be applied to ourselves without difficulty. For we are all by nature impatient of anger. As soon as we are not shown the respect we think due, we flare up at once and rush to revenge, which, as that satirist says, is "dearer than life itself," and we want to settle the matter with the sword. You will find people who think it glorious to yield to no one, like the Terminus of Rome. Yet there are many considerations that persuade us that the wrongs done to us should be forgiven and that vengeance should be committed to God. First, God demands this in many places. "Do not say," says Solomon, "I will repay evil; but wait for the LORD and he will save you, or deliver you." The sense is this: we must not even think about how to avenge an evil or an injury we have received. Vengeance is to be left to God, who is able to avenge. In him we must hope, and we must pray not that he avenge us and exact punishment from our enemy, but only that he protect us. If you do this, it will profit you. But if even the thought, or even the speech, about avenging an injury is forbidden, how much more the deed? Even thoughts are counted as sin before the Lord. Not unlike this is the saying of the same writer: "Do not say," he says, that is, do not think or resolve, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay him according to his deed," that is, tit for tat: "with the measure with which they have measured to me, I will measure to others," etc. (Matt. 5, 6 and 18). Christ teaches the same thing by a beautiful comparison. His example answers to his teaching. God also bestows benefits on his enemies, making his sun rise on the good and the evil. What of the fact that he handed over his most beloved Son to death for us, even though we were his enemies? (Rom. 6.) But Christ too, when not even the slightest suspicion of sin could fall upon him, was scourged, crowned with thorns, and finally fastened to the cross, yet he uttered that most full of piety: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." The apostle testifies that his sprinkled blood "speaks better than Abel." Stephen afterwards imitated this (Acts 7). We must consider that God raises up adversaries against us to test us, as in the example of Joseph and David, who forgave Shimei, the reviler. For both knew that, although a man may hate someone and wish him the worst, yet he can in no way harm him unless God permits it. We must also consider that we have deserved it, if not in this matter then in other cases, if not in regard to this man then in regard to other men, or at least in regard to God, and that in a thousand ways. Likewise, we should consider that this neighbour of ours perhaps did not say or do what we think he said or did against us, or at least did not say or do it with a bad intention, or that he now regrets what he said or did. If not at this time, perhaps at another; if never, God will avenge. What of the fact that no one is injured except by himself? For those who think they have been treated unjustly, if they reckon the matter rightly, will certainly find that they have received no injury or loss from others. For although the things by which they are harmed come to them from outside, yet they offend themselves most of all when they defile their minds with hatred, lust and envy. Besides, if we yield to our adversaries, we shall break their assault; but if we resist, their fury will blaze up all the more. So war engines (which they call bombards from the sound they make) shatter walls, towers, and other hard, resisting things with great crash and ruin; but if they meet dung, silk, or other soft and yielding things, they somehow lose their force and are broken. This also adds weight: while we thirst for our enemy's blood, full of hope of avenging ourselves, we spend days and nights in a constant restless agitation of mind, so that we harm ourselves rather than those whom we hate. And it often happens that from one sin many sins arise. Nor is it wrongly said that the desire for vengeance is the sin of the devil, since he was a murderer from the beginning (John 8). Therefore, when the Pharisees wished to bring about his death, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, said that they were begotten of their father the devil. Finally, this too must be weighed again and again: we shall soon die. Therefore, since at such a time the greatest and most necessary thing for us will be to obtain the great mercy of God, we must necessarily keep it before our eyes now, and always hold it out before us. For in this way that savage desire for vengeance will be drained out of us, since you will find no more suitable or greater remedy for imploring mercy than forgetting injuries and loving those who have wronged us or ours in word or deed. Certainly nothing can be more unjust, or even imagined, than that a man who is hard with other men, so that he gives himself to gentleness with no one, should demand that God be gentle and kind to him. But let us return to the context.

units.la: Quemadmodū verò hoc loco ditur,Dauidem,quod à Nabale cōtumeliose habitus est,in tantū nō dubitasse:quin Nabalé fortu nis omnibus euertere rectè statuerit,vt etiā sacramento ad eā rem obligarit:& tamé post paulò ipse fatetur,se modum omnę excessis se:Ita sæpe fit,vt alij quoq; viri boni,ira alijs-que affectibus sibi ipsis subrepti arbitren-tur,se rectè agere bonoq; omnino zelo du-ci:postea verò intelligant,se turpiter aluci-natos esse.Etiamsi in aliēnis vitijs obseruan-dis quoquis Lynceo oculatiores sim°,plerun-que tamen ad nostra vitia, talparum instar, cæcutimus & nobis mirificè blandiri sole-mus,perpetuoq; illud Poetæ verum est:
units.tr: But as is said in this passage, that David, because he had been insultingly treated by Nabal, did not hesitate so much that he rightly resolved to overthrow Nabal with all his property, and even bound himself to it by an oath; and yet a little later he himself confesses that he had exceeded every measure. So it often happens that other good men too, carried away by anger and other passions, think they act rightly and are led by a wholly good zeal; but afterwards they understand that they have been shamefully deceived. Although we may be sharper-sighted than any Lynceus in observing the faults of others, yet for the most part we are blind to our own faults, like moles, and we are wont to flatter ourselves wonderfully; and that line of the poet is always true:

units.la: Sed non videmus manticæ ,quod a tergo est.
units.tr: "But we do not see the wallet that hangs on our back."

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, tamen si nobis ipsis per-suaterį
units.tr: Since these things are so, yet if we have persuaded

units.la: suaserimus, nos bona conscientia aliquid agere, tamen nobis ipsis non facile fidem habebimus: multo minus affectibus frenos laxabimus: sed actiones nostras suspectas habebimus, Deum subinde ardentibus votis interpellantes, ut spiritu suo sancto nos regat, actiones nostras gubernet, ac salutaria consilia, praesertim in causis religionem concernentibus, subministret.
units.tr: ourselves that we are doing something with a good conscience, we shall not readily trust ourselves; much less shall we loosen the reins on our passions.
