Rather we shall hold our actions under suspicion, and from time to time we shall beseech God with burning prayers to rule us by his Holy Spirit, to govern our actions, and to supply us with salutary counsels, especially in matters concerning religion.

units.la: Quaerat autem aliquis, cur sacrae literae grauia sanctorum peccata tacite non praeterirent, sed illa quam diligentissime annotent? velut hoc loco, Davidis iuramentum leviter ac inconsiderate conceptum: alibi adulterium & iniustam caedem: Mosis impatientiam: Ionae rebellionem: Apostolorum ambitionem: Petri abnegationem: Thomae ὀλιγοπιστίαν, aliaque eius generis permulta. Respondeo: Ista non ideo recitari, ut ea imitemur: (virtutes enim ipsorum, non vitia imitanda sunt, recteque dicitur, Viuendum esse legib. non exemplis.) Sed 1. ut videamus illos, non sua sanctitate coram Deo iustificatos esse, sed fide in Messiâ: Caeterum natura sua homines fuere: Quod autem tot singularibus virtutibus excellue-runt, id Dei bonitate fuit factum, qui illos nonnunquam labi voluit, ut & ipsi & alii viderent, eos homines fuisse, humanisque affectibus obnoxios, adeoque suam miseriam & corruptionem agnoscerent. Deinde vt infirmitate eorum admoniti, cautiores reddamur atque ardentius Deum precemur, ne nos in tentationem inducat, sed a malo clementer liberet. Nam illi, qui tatis donis ornati fuerunt in gravia scelera prolapsi sunt, quid nobis, qui cum illis nullo modo comferendi sumus, accidere poterit? D. Paulus nos non temere admonet, vt qui sibi stare videtur, videat ne cadat. Tanto autem diligentiores esse nos conuenit, quanto plura nobis in hoc perditissimo omni vitiorum genere seculo, offendicula obijciuntur. Tertio vt si aliquando in atrocia peccata lapsi fuerimus, discamus etiam illorum exemplo, poenitentia agere, & a peccatis resurgere, vt Deus nobis peccata & poenas peccatis debitas remittat. Satanas enim iubet nos pergere in peccato; praecidens nobis spe veniae. At illorum exemplo discimus peccata nobis ex immensa Dei misericordia propter Christum remitti: & deinceps nobis diligentius a peccatis cauendum. Peccare humanum est: at in peccato pfeuerare, diabolicum. Denique colligimus, lapsos non reiiciendos, sed erigendos potius, ac si veram poenitentiam agant, benigne recipiendos esse. Vulgo dicitur, Eum, qui nunquam lapsus est, nunquam surrexisse. Si quis Dauidem, Petrum & alios propter lapsus reijcere voluisset, perperam fecisset. Luc.15.dicitur, angelos lætari ob vnum peccatorem, qui pœnitentiam agat & ad frugem redeat. Vera autem pœnitentia agnoscit peccati atrocitatem, fide misericordiam Dei in Filio suo propositam amplectitur, & à sceleribus sibi in posterum cauet.
units.tr: But someone may ask why the Holy Scriptures do not silently pass over the grave sins of the saints, but note them most carefully: as here, David's oath rashly and inconsiderately made; elsewhere his adultery and unjust killing; Moses' impatience; Jonah's rebellion; the ambition of the apostles; Peter's denial; Thomas's little faith [ὀλιγοπιστία]; and very many other things of that kind. I answer: these things are not recounted so that we may imitate them (for it is their virtues, not their vices, that are to be imitated; and it is rightly said that we must live by laws, not by examples). But (1) so that we may see that they were justified before God not by their own holiness but by faith in the Messiah; for they were men by nature. That they excelled in so many singular virtues was the work of God's goodness, who wished them now and then to stumble, so that both they themselves and others might see that they were men, subject to human passions, and so might recognize their own misery and corruption. (2) Then, that being admonished by their weakness, we may become more cautious and pray more earnestly to God that he not lead us into temptation but mercifully deliver us from evil. For if those who were adorned with such gifts fell into grave crimes, what can happen to us, who are in no way to be compared with them? St Paul does not carelessly warn us, "let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." And we ought to be the more careful, as more stumbling-blocks are placed before us in this most depraved age, abounding in every kind of vice. (3) Then, if at any time we have fallen into atrocious sins, we may learn from their example to repent and rise up from our sins, so that God may remit our sins and the punishments due to them. For Satan bids us go on in sin, cutting off from us all hope of pardon. But from their example we learn that our sins are remitted through Christ, from the immense mercy of God, and that from then on we must take more diligent care to guard against sin. To sin is human; but to persist in sin is diabolical. Finally we gather that the fallen are not to be cast off but rather raised up, and that if they repent truly they are to be received kindly. It is commonly said that he who has never fallen has never risen. If anyone had wished to reject David, Peter and the others because of their falls, he would have acted wrongly. In Luke 15 it is said that the angels rejoice over one sinner who repents and returns to a better life. True repentance acknowledges the enormity of sin, embraces by faith the mercy of God set forth in his Son, and guards itself from wickedness for the future.

units.la: Discamus ergo exemplo Dauidis ad institutionem simul & consolationem vt, id est, vt clarius dicam: Etiamsi non omnia sperata etiam à coniunctissimis, cui nos nostraque commisimus omnia, assequamur, idque præter meritum: imò vel contumelia afficiamur, vel malam gratiam reportemus: tamen non est, quod de vlciscenda iniuria aut ἀχαριστίας vitio cogitemus: Quin nos ipsos reprimamus, bonumque malo reddentes, causam nostram Deo, iustissimo iudici, de manu, quod dicitur, in manum tradamus.
units.tr: Let us therefore learn from David's example both instruction and consolation, that is, to put it more plainly: even if we do not obtain all that we hoped for, even from those closest to us, to whom we have committed ourselves and all that is ours, and that undeservedly; indeed, even if we are insulted or get an ungrateful return, yet we should not think of avenging the wrong or of the vice of ingratitude. Rather, let us restrain ourselves, repaying evil with good, and hand over our cause to God, the most just judge, out of our hand, as the saying goes, and into his hand.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi HOMILIA V.
units.tr: ON THE LIFE AND DEATH OF NABAL THE DRUNKARD: HOMILY V.

units.la: Famulorum vnus Abigaelem de insigni mariti contumelia edoctam, monet, vt sibi in tempore caueat.
units.tr: One of the servants warns Abigail, who has been informed of her husband's insulting conduct, to take care in good time.

units.la: 14 Abigail autem vxori Nabal retulit puer vnus e pueris, dicendo: En misit Dauid nuntios e deserto ad salutandû dominum nostrum: qui imuectus est in eos.
units.tr: 14 Now one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, saying: Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master, and he railed on them.

units.la: 15 Et viri boni fuerunt erga nos mirum in modum, neq; fuimus ignominia affecti, nec defuit nobis quidquam cunctis diebus, quibus ambulauimus cum eis, dum essemus in agro.
units.tr: 15 But the men were very good to us, and we were not abused, nor did we lack anything all the days we went with them, while we were in the field.

units.la: 16 Muri fuerunt nobis tum nocte tum interdiu, cunctis diebus, quibus cum eis pauimus pecora.
units.tr: 16 They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the days we kept the sheep with them.

units.la: 17 Nunc igitur scito, & vide quid facturâ: nam completum est malum contra dominum nostrum, & contra vniuersam domum eius: Ipse enim improbior est, quam vt possit quisquam cum alloqui.
units.tr: 17 Now therefore know and see what you will do; for evil is determined against our master and against all his house. For he is too wicked for anyone to speak to him.

units.la: A Nna sanctissima mulier, & magni illius Samuelis mater, in diuinissimo cantico suo inter alia testatur, Deum pedes eorum, quos beneuolentia sua dignatur, regere, vt incolumes perstent, & a lapsu exitiali tueri. Posset quidem Deus, si vellet, tantum gratiae suis conferre, vt omnino non peccarent: verum id non facit, sed certas ob causas finit ipsos interdum in grauia & atrocia peccata ruere. Primo, vt videant, quàm sint infirmi, & quàm facilè cadant, Deo subtrahente gratiam: Deinde, vt ardétiores sint in precibus, ac cum Dauide orét: Ne proijcias me à facie tua: & Spiritum S. tuum, ne auferas à me: ac lapsis ignoscant: nec temerè de quoquâ desperent. Permittit item hęc Deus, vt alij, eorum exemplo, cautiores fiant. Interim gratiâ suâ illis impertitur, ne in peccatis perfistant; sed seipsos erigant, nec peccata peccatis accumulent: ac vt illos indormire ij, nonnunquam patiatur: tamen à lapsu, qui ad æternâ mortem impellit, clementissimè tuetur, ac, vt serias de pœnitentia cogitationes suscipiunt, exsuscitat. Eius rei memorabile in Dauide exemplum habemus. Is enim impotenti suâ illa & inconsiderata vindictæ capiendę libidine, non leuiter peccat, atrocius impacturus, nisi Deus illum, opera Abigaelis, quàm vnus è seruis de certo periculo edocuerat, à cæde iniusta reuocatū, tantùm non retraxisset. Quomodo verò edocta sit, porrò, Deo bene iuuante, audiemus.
units.tr: The most holy woman, Hannah, mother of the great Samuel, testifies in her most divine song, among other things, that God guides the feet of those whom he deigns to favour, so that they stand unharmed and guards them from a deadly fall. God could indeed, if he wished, bestow so much grace on his own that they would not sin at all; but he does not do so, and for certain reasons he allows them sometimes to fall into grave and atrocious sins. First, so that they may see how weak they are and how easily they fall when God withdraws his grace. Next, so that they may be more fervent in prayer and pray with David: "Cast me not away from thy presence, and take not thy Holy Spirit from me"; and so that they may forgive the fallen and not despair of anyone rashly. God also permits this so that others, by their example, may become more cautious. Meanwhile he imparts his grace to them so that they do not persist in sin, but raise themselves up and do not heap sin upon sin; and although he sometimes allows them to fall asleep, he most mercifully guards them from a fall that drives to eternal death, and raises them up when they take up serious thoughts of repentance. We have a memorable example of this in David. For in that uncontrolled and thoughtless lust for vengeance he sins not lightly, and was about to commit a more atrocious deed, had God not, through the agency of Abigail, whom one of the servants had informed of the certain danger, almost completely withdrawn him from an unjust slaughter. How she was informed, with God's good help, we shall hear next.

units.la: Primò dicitur, Puerorum vnum (multos enim absq; dubio habuit) cum videret nihil spei esse ab hero suo ad Abigaelē accesisse, & quæ accidissent, ordine commemorasse: Nempe: Dauidem nuncios suos ex desertis ad Nabalem misisse, qui illum bene
units.tr: First, it is said that one of the young men (for he had undoubtedly many) saw that there was no hope from his master, and recounted in order to Abigail what had happened: namely, that David had sent his messengers from the wilderness to Nabal, to wish him well,

units.la: {Psal. 51} Psal. 51.
units.tr: Psal. 51.

units.la: dicerent, id est, perquam officiofisime su® nomine salutarent, illiq; prosperum rerum successum à Deo omnis boni fonte compre- carentur. (neque enim hic de magica bene- dictione loquitur) item, vt aliquid ab ipso commeatus, muneris loco per humanitate auferrent. Non caret emphasi,quod ex de- fertis, missos ait. Ita enim tacitè innuit, Da- uidem huc non libidine impulsum, sed ne- cefsitate,duro,iuxta prouerbium, telo ada- ctum: Nabalem verò acerbisime in eos inu® ctum esse.Hebraea vox, qua auctor hoc loco vtitur, significat inuolare in aliquem, more vulturum,accipitrum,miluorum, aquilaru, aliarumq; volucrium, quæ ex rapto viuunt. Sensus igitur est, illum, præteritis omnibus modestiæ finibus, impudentisimè eos alla- traffe. Cuius rei indignitatem vt often- dat,fecundo loco Dauidis beneficium mul- tis verbis amplificat. Et tamen illos,inquit, experti fumus viros plane bonos, nulla vn- quam contumelia aut damno affecti, quam- diu fumus inter eos rusticati.Quin pro mu- ro nobis noctes diesq; fuerunt, donec ver- fati cum eis fumus,pascendo pecudes. Sen- sus est:Illum non tantum non rapuisse quid- quam de rebus Nabalis, sed etiam feruaffe: fuiffeq; ipsis instar muri: nec tantum Daui- dem,
units.tr: that is, to greet him most courteously in his name, and to pray that God, the fount of every good, grant him prosperous success in his affairs (for he is not speaking here of magical blessing); likewise, that they might receive from him some provision as a gift of kindness. The phrase "from the wilderness" is not without emphasis, for it says the messengers were sent from the wilderness. For thus he tacitly intimates that David was driven here not by lust but by necessity, pressed by a hard weapon, as the proverb goes; and that Nabal had attacked them most bitterly. The Hebrew word the author uses here signifies to swoop down upon someone, in the manner of vultures, hawks, kites, eagles and other birds that live by rapine. The sense therefore is that he, passing all bounds of modesty, barked at them most shamelessly. To show the outrageousness of this, he next amplifies David's kindness with many words. And yet, he says, we have experienced those men as thoroughly good, never harmed by any insult or loss, for as long as we lived with them in the countryside. Indeed, by night and by day they were a wall to us, while we roamed with them tending the flocks. The sense is that he not only did not carry off anything of Nabal's goods, but actually protected them, and was a wall to them, protecting not only David but all his followers; and not once or twice only, but always, by day and by night.

units.la: Beneficio- rum Dauidis amplifi catio. verf.15. verf.16. uidem,sed etiam omnes eius satellites: idq; non semel tantum aut iterum, sed etiā semper,interdiu,noctuq;. Muri voce tuitionem significat acerrimam. Hoc sensu Salomon. Nomen, inquit, Domini turris roboris est: id est,tutissimum & validissimum præsidiū, Huc enim confugiet iustus tutusq; erit,ac si esset in arce fortissima adueniente hoste. Mox, Opes,ait,diuitis sunt, vt vrbs fortitudinis sui,& veluti murus eleuatus eius opinione ac cogitatione.Sensus est:Auari diuites confidunt opibus, ac si in munitissima vrbe essent,aut obiectu muri altissimi defenderentur. Zachariæ 2. Deus Hierosolymis spem facit, se porrò ipsi murum igneum fore.verf.5. Scimus autem,etiamsi alti ac densi sint muri, posse superari ab hostibus. Sed quis audeat se proijcere in ignem? Perinde est igitur,ac si Deus ita loquutus esset:Quaūis nulli sint excubitores, qui defendant Hierosolymam,nulli sint milites præsidiarij, nulli denique custodes, se tamen vnum sufficere: quia non modo murus sit futurus ad arcendos hostes,sed etiam ignis ad incutiendum terrorem. Sed & Latini muri propugnaculi & præsidij vocabula translatè ponunt. Sic Cicero in Pisonem, 6. Lex Helia, inquit,&Fufia cuersa est,propugnacula muriq; tranquillitatis & otij. Sic Horatius Mecoenatem praesidium & dulce decus suum vocat, itemq; Pollionem: Insigne moestis praesidium reis, vocat.
units.tr: Amplification of David's benefits. (v. 15, v. 16.) The word "wall" signifies the fiercest protection. In this sense Solomon says: "The name of the Lord is a strong tower": that is, the safest and strongest refuge, for the righteous flee there and are safe, as if in a strong citadel when an enemy approaches. Soon after he says: "The wealth of the rich is his strong city, and like a high wall in his own conceit." The sense is that rich misers trust in their riches as if they were in a most fortified city, or were defended by a high wall. In Zechariah 2 God promises Jerusalem that he will himself be a wall of fire round it (v. 5). We know, however, that even high and thick walls can be overcome by enemies; but who would dare to throw himself into fire? It is therefore just as if God had said: although there are no sentinels to defend Jerusalem, no garrison soldiers, no guards at all, he alone would suffice, because he would be not only a wall to keep off enemies but also a fire to strike terror. But Latin writers too use the words "bulwark" and "defence" figuratively for a wall. Thus Cicero, against Piso, book 6: "The Aelian and Fufian laws were overturned, the bulwarks and walls of tranquillity and leisure." Thus Horace calls Maecenas his protection and sweet glory, and calls Pollio "a distinguished protection for the sorrowing accused."

units.la: Tertiò, dispice, inquit, diligenter, quid agas: alioquin enim actum est de domino nostro & tota eius familia. Ac, ut magis illam moveat, Non differetur, ait, periculum: Iam iam paratum est malum. Iamdudum enim eius completa est malitia: In procliui est, ut Dauid veniat cū exercitu, & nos omnes ad vnum perdat. Vnde vero haec habebat? Noverat ventrem carere auribus: praeterea eos, qui indignè lacerantur contumelijs, se vix ac ne vix quidem cohibere: Prudenter ergo ex caussis suspicatur, contemtum istum Dauidi grauissimam accendisse iracundiam: ea vero inflammata hauddubiè erupturum in grauem vltionem. Certè contemtus cum quemuis mouere posset, multò planè illum grauius accendet, qui attulerit beneficium. Fieri quoque potest, illum à legatis Dauidis iam tum inaudisse, quid secū constituerint.
units.tr: Third, consider carefully, she says, what you are doing; otherwise it is all over with our master and his whole household. And to move her the more, she says: the danger will not be deferred; the evil is already prepared, now, now. For his wickedness has long since been brought to completion; it is likely that David will come with an army and destroy all of us to a man. But whence did he have this? He knew that the belly has no ears; besides, that those who are unworthily torn by insults can scarcely, or hardly at all, restrain themselves. Rightly, therefore, he conjectures from the circumstances that this contempt has kindled David's very grave anger, and that once inflamed, he will undoubtedly break out into severe vengeance. Certainly contempt could move anyone, but it will kindle far more fiercely in the man who has conferred the benefit. It is also possible that he had already heard from David's messengers what they had decided among themselves.

units.la: Deniq;, quod Abigael ipsi obijcere potuisset, cur ista non indicarit hero, tacitè occurrens. Vir, inquit, Belial est: Sensus est: Illum improbiorē & perditiorē esse, quam vt possit quisquam cum alloqui. Vir Belial, est, qui nullis vel diuinis vel ciuilibus,vel naturæ le gibus se astringi patitur, sed iugum excutit, nihil non æquum ac verum ducit, quod sibi facere collibuerit:fœdis affectibus indulges. Breuiter,qui nec sibi nec alijs prodest, &,vt Græci dicunt,γῆς βάεος,id est,telluris inu-tile pondus.
units.tr: Finally, Abigail, anticipating silently what could have been objected to her, asks why he did not report these things to the master. "He is a son of Belial," she says. The sense is that he is too wicked and abandoned for anyone to speak to. A man of Belial is one who allows himself to be bound by no laws, divine, civil or natural; he throws off the yoke, thinks nothing right or true that he has not chosen to do, and indulges foul desires. In short, he helps neither himself nor others; and, as the Greeks say, he is a burden of the earth [γῆς βάρος], that is, a useless weight upon the earth.

units.la: Quærat autem aliquis,an seruus iste pec-carit,herum suum appellando virum Belial? Respondeo, Quidquid huius dixit,nō eo di-xit, vt heri sui dignitatem vel minimo viola-ret:sed,vt heram suam excitaret magisq; mo-ueret,vt in tempore, quid actura esset, prouideret. Quod vel inde videre est, quod illu secundo herum suum appellet. Cætera,pec-cato non caret,alteri conuitium facere:Qua de re Christus,Matth.5. Qui fratri,inquit,di-xerit,fatue,tenebitur gehenna ignis. Sensus est,Eum,qui in conuitium eruperit, quo fra-tris existimatio læditur, absq; omni contra-dictione mereri, vt, ad inferos detrusus, æ-ternis cruciatibus puniatur. Infra Abigael, virum suum stultum & Belial appellat, &c.
units.tr: But someone may ask whether this servant sinned in calling his master "a man of Belial." I answer: whatever he said of this, he did not say it to violate his master's dignity in the least, but to rouse and move his mistress the more, so that she might foresee in time what she was going to do. This can be seen from the fact that the second time he calls him "his master." Otherwise, to revile another is not free from sin, and on this account Christ says in Matthew 5: "Whoever says to his brother, Thou fool, shall be in danger of the fire of hell." The sense is that whoever breaks out into insult, by which his brother's reputation is harmed, deserves without any dispute to be cast down to the lower regions and punished with eternal torments. Later Abigail too calls her husband a fool and a Belial, etc.

units.la: Hoc loco exemplum habemus serui fi-de, prudentia & iustitia præstantis. Fides ip-sius ex eo colligitur,quod heram,cum ab he-ro suo nihil spei esse cerneret, de pericu-lo impendente in tempore & maturè edocet,eique auctor est & suasor, vt huic malo conuenientia remedia in tempore adhibeat. Quamuis herus ipsum & alios inhumanius tractaret,& abfq; dubio subinde magna verborum contumelia oneraret: (Nam fi ita feeuijt in famulos alienos,quid fecifle illum putemus infuos?) tamen ipsi bene confultum cupit, ac,quantum in fe est,interitum ab illo auertere molitur.Fuissent, qui ab illo ad Da uidem defecissent,illumq; prodidissent.Cuius rei exempla apud veteres permulta exstant, ad quæ tamen minus obstupescemus, fi cogitemus, Omnes homines natura esse libertatis amantes & seruitutem,quantu pofunt,auersari. Quid ergo mirum,fi non faciè seruos inuenias, qui suos heros sincero amore prosequantur?Interim haud negaue rim,non paucos exstitisse, qui dominis suis in extremis quoque casibus fideles fe gratosq; præstiterint,& fe pro illis,morti etiam præfentifsimæ obiectarint.Quod fi dicas,fie ri posse, vt iste seruus commotus fuerit periculo suo: Facile enim videre potuisset fa-miliam illam non posse perire, nisi ad fe quoque pars eius periculi perueniret. Respondeo:Illu, fi hæc metuisset,potuisse fe in tempore,adornata fuga, in pedes conijcere, & surreptum aliquid fecu auferre,quo fe quocunque
units.tr: Here we have an example of a servant distinguished by faithfulness, prudence and justice. His faithfulness is shown by the fact that, seeing that he could expect nothing from his master, he warns his mistress in good time of the impending danger and advises and urges her to apply suitable remedies to this evil in time. Although the master treated him and others more harshly than was fair, and no doubt often loaded him with great verbal abuse (for if he behaved so towards other men's servants, what do we suppose he did to his own?), still the servant wishes him well and, so far as he can, strives to turn his ruin away from him. There would have been those who would have deserted him for David and betrayed him. There are very many examples of this among the ancients, and we shall be less astonished at them if we consider that all men by nature love liberty and shun slavery as far as they can. Why then is it surprising if you do not find servants who pursue their masters with sincere affection? Meanwhile I do not deny that there have been not a few who proved faithful and pleasing to their masters even in the most extreme circumstances, and who offered themselves to death itself, however imminent. But if you say that this servant may have been moved by fear for his own safety, since he could easily have seen that the household could not perish unless part of that danger reached him too, I answer: had he feared this, he could have taken to his heels in good time, once prepared for flight, and carried off something with him by stealth, by which he might have sustained himself, whatever the outcome of events.

units.la: Quot ferui, tot hostes.
units.tr: As many servants, so many enemies.

units.la: An hee fer uus dixerit fide aut me in motus. cunque rerum euentu,sustentaret.Plerunq; enim vt eleganter Plautus. Plagigera homi- num genera,quorum haud quidquá in men tem venit,vt rectè faciant. At cum est occa- fio data,tene, clepe, rape: hoc est eorum o- pus,vt mauelis lupos apud oues relinquere, quàm hos domi custodes.
units.tr: Whether this servant would have sustained himself by loyalty or by whatever outcome of events. For, as Plautus elegantly puts it, there are kinds of men who bear the marks of blows, none of whom ever thinks of doing right; but when an opportunity is given, it is: grab, steal, seize. That is their work, so that you would sooner leave wolves among the sheep than these men as guards at home.

units.la: Prudentiæ argumentum est,quòd ex cau fis colligit,quid fit futurum : Nempe Daui- dem contemtum legatorum suorum, quos natura ἀσπλὰς voluit,inultum abire nō per missurum:Item,quod ad dominam, fœminâ prudentia celebrem accedit, cum videret à hero suo nihil expectari posse, eamq; matu- rè commonet, vt diligenter,quid actura fit, dispiciat. Rem enim cunctationem non fer- re,nec paruum esse periculum,quod omni- no videatur impendere.
units.tr: It is a mark of prudence that he gathers from causes what is going to happen. Namely, he judged that David, who would not let the contempt shown to his envoys go unavenged (envoys whom nature has made [ἀσπλὰς] inviolable), would not let it pass unpunished. Likewise, he approaches the mistress, a woman famed for prudence, when he saw that nothing could be expected from his master, and warns her early that she should carefully examine what she is going to do. For the matter does not bear delay, and the danger, which seems wholly to be hanging over them, is not small.

units.la: Iustitia ex eo apparet, quòd integritatem Dauidis & militum eius côdignis laudibus exornat: quòd legatos Dauidis contumelio fè habitos indignè fert: quòd non frigidam suffundit,vt à hero gratiam ineat: dominum suum ab eo non commendat, cuius nomine rectius reprehendendus erat.
units.tr: Justice appears from the fact that he adorns the integrity of David and his soldiers with fitting praise; that he takes indignantly the shameful treatment of David's envoys; that he does not coldly fawn to win his master's favour; and that he does not commend his master to her, though it was rather for his master's conduct that he should have been rebuked.

units.la: Hinc ferui & ancillæ discant, quid fui fit officij.Nempe fidem suam heris probabunt, eorum salutem promotam cupient,quæ damno fore fraudiq; ipsis vident, pro virili, su- pertant, eosq; de periculis maturè edoceat, ne heros, ipsorum culpa, in corporis vel for- tunarum discrimen incurrisse, verè dici pos- sint. Quin, vt in duros, stultos ac deliros do- minos inciderint, vt non iniuria posint con- queri cum seruo illo Aristophanico:
units.tr: Hence let male and female servants learn what their duty is. Namely, they will prove their loyalty to their masters, they will wish their welfare to be advanced, and so far as they can they will ward off the losses and frauds that they see are coming upon them; and they will warn them of dangers in good time, so that the master cannot truly be said to have fallen into peril of body or fortune through the servant's fault. Indeed, even if they have fallen among harsh, foolish and mad masters, so that they may not unjustly complain with that servant of Aristophanes:

units.la: ὡς ἀργαλέον φεύγωμεν, ὦ Ζεῦ καὶ Θεοί, ἥλλον γλυκέως ὡς ἀφερδόπυτον διαπότας: Tamen officio suo nauiter fungentur : eoq; magis, vt diuinis præceptis morem gerant, qui in epistolis Pauli multis de illorum offi- cio agit. Ephes. 5. Coloss. 3. 1. Tim. 6. Tit. 2. D. Petrus hortatur seruos, vt cum metu heris non solum bonis & æquis, verùm etiam aspe- ris & iniquis pareant. Id enim & apud deum & homines gratiæ cedere. Suftentent se om- nes, qui tyrannis seruire coguntur, exem- plo serui huius, qui vt duro hero seruiat, ta- men ab illo ad Dauidé nó transit, sed se, obla- ta etiā occasione, fidelé præbet. Recté Eurip.
units.tr: "How grievous it is to flee, O Zeus and gods, rather than to live sweetly..." [ὡς ἀργαλέον φεύγωμεν, ὦ Ζεῦ καὶ Θεοί, ἥλλον γλυκέως ὡς ἀφερδόπυτον διαπότας]. Yet they will perform their duty vigorously, and all the more so in order to obey the divine precepts, of which Paul treats much in his epistles concerning the duty of such people: Ephes. 5; Coloss. 3; 1 Tim. 6; Tit. 2. St Peter exhorts servants to obey their masters with fear, not only the good and gentle but also the harsh and unjust. For this is pleasing both to God and to men. Let all who are compelled to serve tyrants sustain themselves by the example of this servant, who, though he serves a harsh master, does not pass over to David but, even when the opportunity is offered, shows himself faithful. Euripides rightly says:

units.la: Κακὸς γὰρ ὅσις μὴ τίβει τὰ διαπότων, καὶ ξυγγένηται καὶ ξυμφοιτᾷ κακοῖς. ἐγὼ μὲν εἴην καὶ πέφυχ' ὁμῶς λαβεῖς ἐν τοῖσι γεγωσοῖσιν ἡεἰθμικῶν ἡλλοισι, τάνομ' ἁ ἔχων, ἐλθ' ἄλλεγεν τὸν ὁ νᾶν, χρείασον γὰρ τόλ' ἢ ἄλλοιν κακοῖν ἐνδόντα.
units.tr: "For he is a wicked man who does not honour his master's fortunes, and who associates and consorts with the wicked. Let me be..." [Greek, garbled in the scan: Κακὸς γὰρ ὅσις μὴ τίβει τὰ διαπότων, καὶ ξυγγένηται καὶ ξυμφοιτᾷ κακοῖς…]

units.la: ἐνδὸν τὰ γενέσεις, τὰς φρένας ὅν τὰ τ πίλας, i.e. Malus est, quicunque dominiresnon colit, Et simul cum ipsis gaudet, vel propter incommoda dolet.
units.tr: [Greek, garbled in the scan] i.e. He is wicked who does not serve his master, and rejoices with him at his good fortune, or grieves at his misfortunes.

units.la: Ego sane licet natus sim serius: tamen Inter eximios numerandus sum Seruos. Nomen quidem non habeo liberum, Sed animum. Praestat enim hoc, quam duobus malis Vitium inuolui, ac tum improbae mentis esse, Tum aliis obedire, seruientem proximis.
units.tr: I indeed, though born later in time, shall be numbered among the distinguished servants. I have no free name, but I have a free mind. For it is better to be entangled in one evil, that of slavery, than in two: to have a base mind and at the same time to obey others, serving those who are nearest to us.

units.la: Nec male Seruus apud Comicum: — Hoc(inquit)tibi pro seruitio debeo. Conari manibus, pedibus, noctesq; & dies Capitis periculum adire, dum prosim tibi.
units.tr: Nor does the servant in the comedy speak amiss: "This," he says, "is what I owe you in return for my service: to strive with hands and feet, by night and day, and to face danger to my head, so long as I am of use to you."

units.la: Neq; vero mihi dubiu est, quin Abigael, adeoq; ipseDauid se gratos erga seruu istum declararint. Mirum enim, quam serui in herorum animos influant, vbi fidelitatem & integritatem ipsorum perspexerint. Veteres, cognita & explorata seruorum fide & diligentia, saepius illos libertate donatos manu miserunt. Nonnunquam eos adoptarunt, vel generos ascitos honore & opibus adauxerunt. Hinc Solomon Solers, inquit, aut cordatus seruus, imperabit filio familiaspa trem pudore afficienti, & inter fratres hereditatem diuidet, id est, partem cum filijs familiâs in hæreditate domini capiet, fortè quod herus propter fidem & integritatem eum vnà cum filijs hæredem scribat, volens vt in partem suarum facultatum veniat, vel quod tantę autoritatis fiat,vt hæreditatē diuidat,sed prior sensus melior videtur.Exem pla habemus in Iacobo,qui duxit filias Laba nis: & in Iofepho, qui ex seruili conditione in altissimum gradum euectus fuit.
units.tr: Nor is there any doubt in my mind that Abigail, and indeed David himself, showed their gratitude towards that servant. For it is remarkable how servants win the hearts of their masters when they have observed their loyalty and integrity. The ancients, once the faithfulness and diligence of servants had been known and tested, often gave them their freedom and sent them away. Sometimes they adopted them, or took them in as sons-in-law and enriched them with honours and wealth. Hence Solomon: "A wise servant," he says, "shall rule over a son who brings shame, and shall divide the inheritance among the brothers"; that is, he shall take a share of the inheritance along with the sons of the household, perhaps because the master, on account of his faithfulness and integrity, names him heir together with the sons, wishing him to receive a part of his property, or because he becomes of such authority that he divides the inheritance. But the former sense seems the better. We have examples in Jacob, who married the daughters of Laban, and in Joseph, who from servile condition was raised to the highest rank.

units.la: Quæ de feruis speciatim diximus,ea in ge nere ad omnes subditos trâsferre possumus, quorum est, Regibus,Principibus,Magistra tibus & reliquis, quorū potestati subijciun-tur,omne honoris, cultus, obseruantiæ ge-nus tribuere.Qua de re Paulus Ro.13.1.Tim. 2.Tit.3. Petrus secundo prioris Subiećti,in-quit,estote,cuiuis humanæ ordinationi pro pterDominū:siue regi,vt qui superemineat: Siue præsidibus, vt qui per eum mittantur, tum ad vltionem maleficorum, tum ad lau-dem recte agentium.Magistratus autem (vt hoc obiter indicem) humanam ordinatione vocat, non quod humanitus sit excogitata, (est enim hæc quoq; donum Dei præclarū, vt Demosthenes etiá ipse testatur)sed quod hominū sit propria: vt rectè obseruat doćtis simus Caluinus.Ac,quod per mirum fortas-se videatur, quamuis in nos sint inimico in-sensoq;
units.tr: What we have said particularly about servants we may apply generally to all subjects, that is, to all those who are subject to the power of kings, princes, magistrates and the rest, and to whom every kind of honour, worship and reverence is due. On this matter Paul speaks in Rom. 13; 1 Tim. 2; Tit. 3. Peter, in 1 Pet. 2, says: "Be subject to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake: whether to the king, as the one who excels, or to governors, as those sent by him, both for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of those who do well." Now (let me note this in passing) he calls the magistracy a human ordinance, not because it was devised by man (for this too is a noble gift of God, as Demosthenes himself also testifies), but because it belongs to men, as the learned Calvin rightly observes. And, what may perhaps seem strange, although they are hostile and ill-disposed towards us,

units.la: 1.Pet. 2. (note)
units.tr: 1 Pet. 2. (marginal note)

units.la: Magistratus Petrus cur ἀνθρωπίνων κτίσιν vocet. fensoq; animo, quamuis implacabiles: tamé non satis digna caussa est, cur eos non perof-ficiosé obseruemus. Nec enim hominum im probitatem aut nequitiam, si tales sunt Magistratus, sed diuinam autoritatē, quæ in illis est, reueremur. At verò si quid improbè, si quid iniquè imperent (cum id non ex potestate, sed ex iniustitia atq; animi peruersitate agant) omnino non sunt audiendi. Etenim, (vt recte Apostolus.) Obedire oportet Deo potius quàm hominibus, quod & Socrates ipse, vt pote à natura insitum, cognouit: Sic enim in Apologia, ἐγὼ μὲν ὦ ἀνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, inquit, ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς, καὶ φιλῶ, πείσομαι δὲ τῷ Θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ὑμῖν, id est, Ego quidem vos amplector & amo, viri Athenienses, sed Deo potius quàm vobis obtemperabo. Hæc Socrates: à quibus non abludit oratio Lycortæ ducis Achæorum apud Liuium: Veremur quidé vos Romani, inquit, &, si ita vultis, etiā timemus: sed plus & vere mur & timemus deos immortales, li.9. de.4.
units.tr: [Why Peter calls the magistracy a human creation (ἀνθρωπίνων κτίσιν).] …and ill-disposed in mind, though they be implacable, is not a sufficiently worthy reason why we should not dutifully observe them. For it is not the wickedness or depravity of men, even if such are the magistrates, that we revere, but the divine authority that is in them. But if they command anything wickedly or unjustly (since they act not from their power but from injustice and perversity of mind), they are by no means to be heard. For, as the Apostle rightly says, "We ought to obey God rather than men," which Socrates himself also recognised, as something implanted by nature. For in his Apology he says: "I indeed, men of Athens, greet and love you, but I will obey God rather than you." Socrates says this; and the speech of Lycortas, the leader of the Achaeans, in Livy does not differ from it: "We Romans, indeed, we fear and, if you wish, we even dread you; but we fear and revere the immortal gods more." Livy, book 9, decade 4.

units.la: Quemadmodũ verò seruus iste herā suam de periculo edocuit: Ita nos quoq; alij alios maturè admonebimus, & pericula, quantū in nobis est, ab inuicē propulsabimus. Si alios à via morum errare, si liberos vel etiā seruos ipsorū transuersos raptos omnia nefarie & libidinosè facere, si caput peti vel fortunas periclitari viderimus, maturè illos edocebimus, castigatosq; commodè non semel tantùm sed sæpius officij admonebimus, & vt in viam redeant, omni contentione elabo rabimus. Atqui id in primis Ministrorum verbi diuini fuerit. Quos cum dominus speculatores constituerit, qui diuinam iram ob pec catanostra accensam, signo buccinæ diuini verbi dato denunciẽt, diligenter auditores suos ad pietatẽ iustitiamq; cohortabuntur, quasiq̃ue accendent, ne, dum scelera sceleri-bus accumulare quodámodo pergunt, tem-porarijs & æternis supplicijs mastentur.
units.tr: Just as this servant informed his mistress of the danger, so too let us warn one another promptly and, as far as we can, turn dangers away from each other. If we see others straying from the path of right conduct, or their children or even their servants rushing headlong into wicked and lustful acts, or see their life or fortunes in peril, we should promptly instruct them, correct them fittingly, and remind them of their duty not once only but often, and labour with all our effort to bring them back to the right path. Yet this is above all the task of the ministers of the divine Word. The Lord has appointed them as watchmen, so that they may proclaim, once the trumpet of the divine Word has been sounded, the divine wrath kindled by our sins, and they should diligently exhort their hearers to piety and righteousness, and stir them up, lest, while they keep piling crime upon crime, they be punished with temporal and eternal penalties.

units.la: Neque verò satis est si alij alios diligenter cõmoneamus, sed obtemperandũ est sanis ā-liorũ cohortationib. Abigael nõ dicit, seruo: vide qd agas? Vnde tu hæc habes, mastigia? Nimirũ cum illis colludis, &c. sed, qua erat prudentia, rem istâ omnem secum in animo considerat, ac qua ratione malũ impendens auertat, diligenter dispicit. Noli similis esse Nabalis, qui nec sapiebat ipse per se, nec be-nè consulentem volebat audire. Qui eo sunt ingenio homines, malunt centies perire, quâ aliquê fidis admonitionibus locũ facere, pręfertim, si ab hominibus non adeò magnę auctoritatis cõmonitiones proficiscantur.
units.tr: Yet it is not enough for us to admonish one another diligently; we must also obey the sound exhortations of others. Abigail does not say to the servant, "See what you are doing? Where did you get this, you rascal? Surely you are in league with them," and so on. Rather, with her wisdom, she weighs the whole matter in her mind and carefully considers by what means she may avert the impending evil. Do not be like Nabal, who neither had wisdom himself nor wanted to listen to one who gave good counsel. People of that disposition prefer to perish a hundred times over rather than make room for some faithful admonition, especially when the warnings come from men of no great authority.

units.la: Recte Hesiodus:
units.tr: Hesiod rightly says:

units.la: ὕτῳ μὲν πανάεισ᾽, ὅς ἀυτὸ πάντα νοῆσαι, φεσασάμψ᾽ τάχ᾽ ἐπεὶ ξαῖ ἡς πλῶ ἦ- σιν ἀμείνω:
units.tr: Best of all is the man who understands everything for himself, considering what will turn out better both for the present and in the end. [ὧδε μὲν πανάριστος, ὃς αὐτὸς πάντα νοήσῃ, φρασσάμενος τά κ᾽ ἔπειτα καὶ ἐς τέλος ἔσσεται ἀμείνω·]

units.la: ἐσθλὸς δ᾽ ἀὐ καπεῖν᾽, ὅς δ᾽ εἰπόνθ᾽ πίθη᾽: ὅς ἢ κε μὴ θ᾽ αὐτὸς νοέῃ, μήτ᾽ ἄλλα ἀκέων ἐν θυμῷ ἔθλη᾽, ὅδ᾽ αὖτ᾽ ἀχρηΐος ἀνήρ.
units.tr: Good too is he who obeys one who advises well; but he who neither understands for himself nor, hearing another, takes the matter to heart, that man is useless. [ἐσθλὸς δ᾽ αὖ κἀκεῖνος, ὃς εὖ εἰπόντι πίθηται· ὃς δέ κε μήτ᾽ αὐτὸς νοέῃ μήτ᾽ ἄλλου ἀκούων ἐν θυμῷ βάλληται, ὅδ᾽ αὖτ᾽ ἀχρήιος ἀνήρ.]

units.la: Id est, interprete Melanchthone.
units.tr: That is, in the translation of Melanchthon:

units.la: Qui, nullo monitore, potest, facienda videre Quae decent, quaeque euentus in fine secundos Sunt tandem paritura, suisque obtemperat ipse Consiliis, mores vera ratione gubernans, Anteit hic alios virtute & laudibus omnes.
units.tr: He who, with no one to advise him, can see what is fitting to do, and what outcomes will at last prove favourable, and who himself obeys his own counsels, governing his conduct by true reason, surpasses all others in virtue and in praise.

units.la: Sunt alij minus ingenio plerique sagaces, Qui parere tamen curant meliora monenti, Laudandos inter recte numerantur & isti, Sed qui nec sapit ipse, nec audit recta monentes, Nec rapitur freno, nec legum vincula curat, Sed pronus sequitur, quò traxit caeca libido, Hic malus ac odio dignus ducatur, & idem Accerset poenas sibi tandem & tristia damna.
units.tr: There are others, fewer in number, though most of them shrewd in their wits, who nevertheless take care to obey one who advises better things; these too are rightly counted among those to be praised. But the man who neither has wisdom himself nor listens to those who advise him rightly, who is not checked by the bridle nor cares for the bonds of the laws, but rushes headlong wherever blind desire has drawn him, such a man should be regarded as wicked and worthy of hatred, and he will at last bring punishments and sad losses upon himself.

units.la: Non absimile est, quod prouerbio nostra te dicitur, Desperatum esse eum, extremique ingenij, qui nec ipse consulere nec alteri parere sciat. Welchem nit zraten ist/ Dem ist nit zhãlffen.
units.tr: Not unlike this is our own proverb, which says that a man is hopeless and of the lowest character who knows neither how to take counsel himself nor how to obey another. "Whoever will not take advice, to him no one can help."

units.la: Hoc vero deplorandum est,quod,etiamsi Deus non tantū verbo suo,sed & omni portentorum & prodigiorū genere,nos ad pœnitentiam inuitare non cesset,tamen securè illum contemnamus:ac,quod mali colophō est,illos quoque qui in hoc toti sunt, vt exci dium à nobis auertant, odio plūsquam Vatiniano prosequamur.
units.tr: This is truly to be lamented: even though God does not cease to invite us to repentance, not only by his Word but also by every kind of portent and prodigy, we nonetheless despise him with impunity. And, what is the crown of the evil, we pursue with a hatred more than Vatinian those very people who labour to turn away ruin from us.

units.la: Videmus etiam,neminem facilè contemnendum.Quoties enim homines,abiectisimæ etiam sortis,in bellis,seditionibus,incen dijs,aquarū eluuionibus, viris principibus opem tulerunt: Sæpe etiam est sub palliolo sordido sapientia. Hoc loco misellus seruulus Nabalem eum familia omni è manibus Dauidis & præsenti vitæ discrimine eripit.
units.tr: We see also that no one is to be lightly despised. How often have men of the humblest rank, in wars, seditions, fires and floods, brought help to princes! Wisdom often lies beneath a shabby cloak. In this place a poor little servant snatches Nabal and his whole household out of David's hands and from the present peril of life.

units.la: Nulli (vt præclarè Seneca) præclusa virtus est, omnibus patet, omnes admittit, omnes inuitat, ingenuos, libertinos,seruos,reges, exules.Non eligit domum nec censum : nudo homine contenta est.Quod si diligentius aliquanto animo cum nostro nobiscum cogitaremus,certè minus nos palparemus,minus alios contemtui,et ludibrio haberemus.
units.tr: Virtue, as Seneca says admirably, is shut out from no one; it is open to all, it admits all, it invites all: freeborn, freedmen, slaves, kings, exiles. It does not choose a house or a fortune; it is content with the bare man. If we considered this a little more carefully within ourselves, we would certainly flatter ourselves less, and would hold others in less contempt and mockery.

units.la: Nonnunquam Deus tenuiorum hominum opera,totis regnis ac imperijs bene facit : vt exempla Josephi, Danielis, & aliorum docent,&c.
units.tr: Sometimes God, through the labours of humbler men, brings great good to whole kingdoms and empires, as the examples of Joseph, Daniel and others teach, and so on.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi
units.tr: ON THE LIFE AND DEATH OF NABAL THE DRUNKARD

units.la: HOMILIA VI.
units.tr: HOMILY VI.

units.la: Abigael Dauidi muneribus accurrens, ad pedes accidit.
units.tr: Abigail hastens with gifts to David and falls at his feet.

units.la: 18 Festinauit itaque Abigael, & tulit ducentos panes & duos vtres vini, & quinq; oues paratas, & quinq; sata polentæ: & centum ligaturas vuarum siccarum, & ducentas massas caricarum, & imposuit asinis.
units.tr: 18 So Abigail hurried, and took two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five sheep already prepared, five measures of parched grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and loaded them on donkeys.

units.la: 19 Dixit q; pueris suis: Transite ante me: En ego post vos venio. At viro suo Nabal non indicauit.
units.tr: 19 She said to her servants: "Go on ahead of me; see, I am coming after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.

units.la: 20 Fuit vero illa equitante super asinum, & descendente per abditum montis, Ecce Dauid & viri eius descendebant in occursum eius, & occurrit eis.
units.tr: 20 She was riding on her donkey and coming down through a hidden part of the mountain, when behold, David and his men were coming down to meet her, and she met them.

units.la: 20 Porro Dauid dixerat: Certe frustra seruaui omnia, quæ iste habet in deserto, vt nihil defuerit ex omnibus, quæ habet: & reddidit mihi malum pro bono.
units.tr: 20 Now David had said: "Surely in vain have I guarded all that this man has in the wilderness, so that nothing of all that he owns was lost; and he has repaid me evil for good."

units.la: 21 Sic faciat Deus inimicis Dauidis & sic addat: si reliquero ex omnibus quæ habet vsque mane, mingentem ad parietem.
units.tr: 21 "May God do so to David's enemies, and more also, if I leave alive until morning any of all that he has, anyone who pisses against the wall."

units.la: 22 Quum autem vidisset Abigail Dauidem, festinauit & descendit de asino, & corruit coram Dauide, super faciem suam, & incuruauit se in terram. Corruit, inquam, ad pedes eius.
units.tr: 22 When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got down from the donkey, and fell on her face before David, and bowed herself to the ground. She fell, I say, at his feet.

units.la: SAlomon, Homo, ait, vel cor hominis cogitat viam suam: Dominus autem aptat vel dirigit gressum eius. Id ita esse, vel hinc apparet. Homines saepe deliberant apud se & proponunt, se hoc vel illud iter facturos: vel se hoc vel illud in opus educturos. Sed longè secus cadit. Deus enim, à quo nostra pendent omnia, longè aliud decreuit. Diuus Paulus multas ciuitates cum Timotheo spargendi euangelij causa, peragrauit: verum cum per Phrygiam & Galatiam iter haberet vetitus fuit, idque à spiritu Dei, ne in Asia verbum de Christo faceret. In Mysiam cum veniisset, Bithyniam erant profecturi: Sed Spiritus illos eo venire non passus est. Praeclarum quidem opus fuisset, si Euangelium in illis locis praedicassent: Sed Deus illo temporis articulo nolebat. Quid ita? Nempe traiecto mari, in Macedonia Verbum Dei annunciandum ipsis erat. E contra saepius pius facinus aliquod cum scelere coniunctum animo suscipimus: Sed à Deo clementissimè prohibemur. Eius rei hoc loco luculentissimum in Dauide exemplum habemus. Is enim omnino decreuerat, Nabalem fortunis omnibus euertere, ac quemadmodum saepe in peccatis nostris nobis ipsis blandimur, ita ipse sibi mirum in modum applaudebat, ac praeclarè agere, sibi persuadebat. Sed Deus, pro sua in suos benignitate, Abigaelis opera illum retrahit: Quae primò rerum omnium ignara, (alijs enim negotijs distrietaerat) mox vbi à seruo de periculo certo edocta fuit, vt praesenti malo occurrat, maturè & prudenter dispicit.
units.tr: Solomon says: "A man's heart devises his way, but the Lord directs his step." That this is so is clear even from this: men often deliberate with themselves and resolve that they will make this or that journey, or carry this or that work into effect. But things turn out far otherwise. For God, on whom all our affairs depend, has decided something quite different. Saint Paul travelled through many cities with Timothy for the sake of spreading the gospel; yet when he was passing through Phrygia and Galatia he was forbidden, and this by the Spirit of God, to speak the word of Christ in Asia. When he came into Mysia they were about to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them to go there. It would indeed have been a splendid work to preach the gospel in those places, but God did not want it at that moment. Why so? Clearly, the word of God was to be proclaimed to them in Macedonia, across the sea. On the contrary, we often take up some pious deed that is joined with wickedness in our minds, but we are most mercifully prevented by God. We have here a most striking example of this in David. For he had fully resolved to overthrow Nabal and all his fortunes; and just as we often flatter ourselves in our sins, so he applauded himself wonderfully and persuaded himself that he was acting well. But God, in his kindness toward his own, draws him back through Abigail's agency. She, at first ignorant of everything (for she had been occupied with other business), as soon as she was informed by the servant of the certain danger, quickly and prudently considers how to meet the present evil.

units.la: Nec enim fidelem seruuli istius admonitionem contemnit, ac, vtdenam ista habes? inquit: Ira id temporis bulliebat: Iam deferbuit paroxismus. Natura semper fuisti turbulentior: Quod si tibi metuis: loricam induas: aliaque id genus: Sed quod ingenium mariti perspectissimum haberet, probeque nosset, eum os suum ferreum in omnes γυμνὴ κεφαλὴν, laxare, vereri neminem, praesertim inter vina: adhaec, qua erat prudentia, non ignoraret, famem pessimum consultorem: famelicos nihil non audere: itemque generosos animos contemtu & ingratitudine quàm acutissimis telis vulnerari:deniq; legatos iure gentium sacros esse ac inuiolabiles: non secura est & in vtramque aurem dormit: Sed rem omnem alta mente reponit & maturè de αὐτοφαρμάκῳ cogitat. Ac recte quidem: Vtrinque enim hac in parte grauiter peccatur. Temerarium est,quiduis,quibusuis,abs- que delecta credere. Quantus enim illorum numerus est,quibus voluptas est, distrahere homines & inter se committere:discordias- que serere,vt summas coniunctiones ac societates fictis sermonibus dirimentes, amicissimos viros ad immortales inimicitias & ad arma compellant: Qui eo sunt ingenio, summopere sunt cauendi:nec temerè in fidem admittendi.Scitè Plautus in Capt.
units.tr: Nor does she scorn the faithful warning of this little servant, nor say, "What are you telling me? The anger was boiling at the time; now the fit has cooled. You have always been more turbulent by nature. If you fear for yourself, put on a breastplate, and so on." But since she knew her husband's temperament thoroughly, and knew that he let loose his iron mouth against everyone, bareheaded [γυμνὴ κεφαλὴν], fearing no one, especially over wine; and since, with her prudence, she was not unaware that hunger is the worst counsellor, that the hungry dare anything, and that noble spirits are wounded by contempt and ingratitude with the sharpest weapons; and finally that envoys are sacred and inviolable under the law of nations, she is not careless and does not sleep on both ears. Instead she lays up the whole matter in her deep mind and promptly considers a remedy against the poison [αὐτοφάρμακον]. And rightly so, for in this matter one sins gravely on either side. It is rash to believe anything from anyone without discrimination. For how many there are who take pleasure in pulling men apart and setting them against each other, sowing discord, so that by fabricated speeches they break the closest unions and alliances and drive the dearest men into endless enmity and to arms! Those of such a disposition must be guarded against with great care, and not readily admitted to trust. Plautus says aptly in the Captivi:

units.la: Qui cauet,inquit, ne decipiatur, vix cauet, cum etiam cauet:
units.tr: He who takes care lest he be deceived, scarcely takes care, since even when he takes care,

units.la: Etiam cum cauisse ratus, sæpe is cautor captus est.
units.tr: Even when he thinks he has been careful, the wary man is often caught.

units.la: E conuerso crudele est,fide semel omnes excludere,admonitiones omnes in vniuersum spernere,secureq; in vtramq;,quod dicitur, aurem dormire. Periculum enim contemnendo non vincitur ac propulsatur. Si Abigael fidelem istam pueri sui admonitionem in totum securè neglexisset, omnes vnà perijssent. Quot vrbes, quot munitiones captæ, quot gentes, quot populi cæsi ac deleti sunt, quod hostem contemserint, nullumq; admonitionibus locum reliquerint. Verum illud verbum est, vulgò quod dici solet: Mater timidi non flet. Enimuero vt recte Probus Æmilius, qui nihil nō metuit, neq; quid quam omnino contemnit, is tutioribus vsus consilijs, credens, quod videt, raro venit in periculum: ac, vt Mimus inquit:
units.tr: Conversely, it is cruel to shut everyone out by distrust, to spurn all warnings in general, and to sleep securely on both ears, as the saying goes. For danger is not overcome or repulsed by despising it. If Abigail had altogether securely neglected her servant's faithful warning, all would have perished together. How many cities, how many fortresses have been taken, how many nations and peoples slaughtered and destroyed, because they despised the enemy and left no room for warnings! But the common saying is true: "The mother of the timid does not weep." Indeed, as Probus Aemilius rightly says, he who fears nothing and despises everything, while he who uses safer counsels and trusts what he sees rarely comes into danger; and as the mime says:

units.la: Non cito perit ruina vir, ruinam qui timet. Qui verò securus est, nihilque metuendum ducit, incommodo ac periculo, quod vel ob seruare vel præcauere noluit, facilè vel ipse opprimitur, vel suis telam laboris ac infortunio rum plenam deducendam relinquit.
units.tr: "A man who fears his ruin does not perish quickly." But he who is careless, and thinks nothing to be feared, is easily overwhelmed himself by the trouble and danger which he would not prevent or guard against; or he leaves to his own people a web full of toil and misfortune to unravel.

units.la: Abigael nō discedit à marito, fugámue ad ornat. vt saluti suæ consulat, non instat cognatis aut affinibus, vt sibi vel in Dauidem, aut Saulé, qui fortasse remotior erat assint: Sed quemadmodum peritus medicus, ægrotum aliquem curaturus, primò causas morbi inuestigat: ac si ex calore nimio provenire comperiat, refrigerantia adhibet: si ex frigore, calefacientia. Ad eundem modum Abigael, cum videret maritum Dauidem duplici affecisse iniuria: primum, quod petenti nihil impertiffet:deinde, quod eum oneraf- set contumelijs:ad primum occurrit mune- ribus.Conuitia autem placat blanda & mol- li oratione,omnique honoris, cultus, & ob- feruantiæ genere.Viso enim Dauide,conse- ftim de asino desilit, & illum prona accidés, honorem eifupplicitcr præbet:vt partim in hoc,partim in sequenti sermone, Deo bene iuuante,audiemus.
units.tr: Abigail does not leave her husband, nor flee to save herself, nor press her kinsmen and relatives to stand with her, against David or Saul (who perhaps was more remote). Rather, like a skilled physician about to treat a sick man, she first investigates the causes of the illness; and if she finds it arises from excess heat, she applies cooling remedies; if from cold, warming ones. In the same way Abigail, seeing that her husband had wronged David in a double way, first, because he refused him anything when asked, and second, because he burdened him with insults, meets the first with gifts. She placates the insults with a soft and gentle speech, and with every kind of honour, courtesy and deference. For as soon as she sees David, she at once slides down from the donkey, and falling prone, humbly pays him honour, as we shall hear, God helping, partly in this speech and partly in the following one.

units.la: Non facit autem ista per seruos aut lite ras,sed,quod præsentiam suam multum pof fe crederet,ipsa fein viam dat. Vetus adagi- um est:Frontem occipitio priorem.Nec in- scitè dicitur : Præsentia hominis, præsentia leonis. Etiamsi seruum cumprimis fidelem misisset : verendum tamen erat,ne verbulo vnico,inconfideratius prolato,multum cau- fæ suæ obcesset.
units.tr: She does not do this through servants or letters, but, because she believed her own presence would carry great weight, she goes to meet him herself. There is an old proverb: "The forehead before the back of the head." And it is well said: "The presence of a man is the presence of a lion." Even if she had sent a most faithful servant, it had still to be feared that, by a single word spoken too rashly, he might greatly harm her cause.

units.la: Primò festinasse dicitur. Ac rectè qui- dem. Nam vt rectè ille apud Senecam, Ca- pienda rebus in malis præceps via est: in A- gamemn. Sæpe enim fit, vt dilationibus o- ptimæ causæ corrumpantur. Itaque dicere solebant: Occasionem à fronte tantum ca- pillatam esse,ab occipitio verò caluam, eo- que accipiendam:& semel arreptam non te- merè dimittendam. Nonnunquam tamen properato opus est : aliquando lentè festi-nandum n andum. Nam vt præclarè Hefiodus:
units.tr: First, she is said to have hastened. And rightly so. For, as the man in Seneca rightly says, "In troubles the way to take is headlong" (Agamemnon). For it often happens that the best causes are ruined by delays. Therefore they used to say that opportunity has hair only at the front, and is bald at the back, so it must be seized, and once grasped not carelessly let go. Nevertheless, sometimes haste is needed, and sometimes one must hasten slowly. For as Hesiod nobly says:

units.la: καιρὸς ὁ ὅτι ποσὶν ἀρίςῳ.
units.tr: Opportunity is best of all things when it comes on swift feet [καιρὸς ὁ ὅτι ποσὶν ἀρίςῳ].

units.la: Id est, interprete Erasmo:
units.tr: That is, in the translation of Erasmus:

units.la: rebus in omnibus illud Optimum erit, si quis tempus spectauerit aptū.
units.tr: In all matters that will be best, which is the one who has watched for a fitting time.

units.la: Deinde capit ducentos panes, duos vi-ni vtres, quinque oues apparatas, quinque sata polentæ, centum vuas passas, & ducen-tas palathas : asinisque imponit. Nos v-trium loco lagenis vtimur. Quemadmo-dum enim nos in nostris regionibus o-leum in vtribus vehimus : ita ipsi vinum, aquam, oleum, aliosque liquores mittere solebant: cuius rei complura in sacris literis exempla habemus. Rectè autem affert ea Abigael, quæ facere possent, ad curandum corpus, panem, vinum, carnes, polentam, & ad secundas mensas vuas & caricas. Hæc enim hominibus famelicis sciebat longè gratiora fore, quàm magna auri & argenti pondera. Muneribus non parua ac-cedit gratia, ex circumstantijs, puta, à quo, cui, quando, vbi, quem in finem offerantur. Rectè Poeta de munere exiguo quidem, sed opportuno: Odyf. ρ.
units.tr: Then she takes two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five sheep already prepared, five measures of parched grain, a hundred raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and loads them on the donkeys. We use flasks in place of skins. For just as we in our own regions carry oil in skins, so they used to send wine, water, oil and other liquids; we have many examples of this in Holy Writ. Abigail rightly brings things that could serve to sustain the body: bread, wine, meat, parched grain, and for dessert, raisins and figs. For she knew these would be far more welcome to hungry men than great weights of gold and silver. A gift gains no small favour from its circumstances, namely from whom, to whom, when, where, and for what purpose it is offered. The poet rightly speaks of a gift small indeed, but timely: Odyf. ρ.

units.la: ἀ ὄσις, inquit, ἀλίγῃ τε φίλῃ τε.
units.tr: "...though small, yet dear" [ἀ ὄσις, inquit, ἀλίγῃ τε φίλῃ τε.]

units.la: Id est, Exiguum munus, gratum tamen. Nec male Ouidius:
units.tr: That is: a gift is small, yet welcome. Ovid also writes well on this point:

units.la: acceptissima semper Munera sunt, auctor quae preciosa facit.
units.tr: Gifts are always most welcome, and it is the giver who makes them precious.

units.la: Ideo autem Abigael Dauidi hoc munus offert, vt illum mitiget. Munera enim flexanimam quandam vim & efficientiam habent.
units.tr: Abigail offers this gift to David so that she may soften him. Gifts have a certain power and force that bends the mind.

units.la: Lapis preciosus est munus in oculis domini fui: inquit Solomon, quoquo se verterit, prosperabitur, vel, prosperè eum faciet agere.
units.tr: "A precious stone is a gift in the eyes of its owner," says Solomon; "wherever he turns, he prospers," or, "it will make him act prosperously."

units.la: Capite 18. Munus hominis, ait, dilatare facit ei locum: id est, explicat eum & educit ab angustia in qua prius erat: & in conspectum magnatum adducit eum. Cap. 21. Donum, ait, in occulto datum, sedat furorem: & munus in sinum coniectum, indignationem vehementem. Docet autem vtrobiq; Salomon (vt hoc obiter addam) quid fieri soleat, non quidsit faciundum: Etsi est, vbi licitè dari possint munera, vt te è molestia explices, cùm alias non possis, si quid tibi apud magnos negotij fit. Sed interim, ne cuiquam simus iniurij, accurandum est. Munere saepe consequeris, quod alias non consequereris.
units.tr: In chapter 18 he says, "A man's gift makes room for him": that is, it opens him up and draws him out of the narrowness in which he was before, and brings him into the presence of great men. In chapter 21 he says, "A gift given in secret calms anger, and a bribe placed in the bosom calms great wrath." Solomon teaches both things, (to add this in passing) what usually happens, not what ought to be done. Yet there are cases where gifts may lawfully be given, so that you may extricate yourself from trouble when otherwise you could not, if some business of yours is at stake before great men. But meanwhile, lest we do wrong to anyone, care must be taken. By a gift you often obtain what you would not otherwise obtain.

units.la: Quod scripsit Ouidius:
units.tr: What Ovid wrote:

units.la: Munera, crede mihi, placant homines, Deosq;: Placatur donis Iuppiter ipse datis.
units.tr: Believe me, gifts placate men and gods: Jupiter himself is placated by gifts given.

units.la: Euripides in Medea vulgi sermone fai sse ce lebralebratum ostendit,cum ait:
units.tr: Euripides shows in the Medea that this saying was commonly celebrated, when he says:

units.la: πείθεν δ' ἀσέξ καὶ θεὸς λόγῳ· χρυσὸς ὁ χρειάσων μυρίων λόγων βροτοῖς, id est, interprete Erasmo:
units.tr: "Even gods are persuaded by gifts rather than words; gold, which is worth more to mortals than ten thousand words" [πείθεν δ' ἀσέξ καὶ θεὸς λόγῳ· χρυσὸς ὁ χρειάσων μυρίων λόγων βροτοῖς], in the translation of Erasmus:

units.la: Donis vel ipsos dicitant flecti Deos. Certe inter homines mille dictis luteum Præpollet aurum prorsus ac præponderat.
units.tr: "Even the gods themselves are said to be bent by gifts. Certainly among men gold far outweighs and surpasses a thousand words, as if they were mud."

units.la: Hodie quoq; dicitur, Nulla corda tam aspera esse, quæ auro rutilo non posint emolliri. Exempla eius rei duo de Iacobo patriarcha habemus: Genesis 32. & 33. vbi dicitur, Iacobum, cum audiret fratrem suum Esauum, cum quo iras gerebat, cum quadringentis hominibus ouiam venire, metuisse ne quid ab illo damni acciperet, eaq; re illi honestum munus amplumque adornat, videlicet oues & capras ducenas, capros & arietes viginti, camelos matrices cum suis pullis triginta, vaccas quadraginta, tauros decem, asinos viginti, asellos decem. Cogitabat enim secum (quemadmodum expresse Moses) Placabo faciem eius munere, quod ante cedit me, & postea videbo faciem eius, forte suscipiet faciem meam. Neq; eum spe sua sal sum esse, ex sequenti capite apparet, vbi dicitur, Esauum cucurrisse, & amplexatum esse Iacobum, fixisseq; oscula, quodq; pluris om
units.tr: Today too it is said that no hearts are so hard that they cannot be softened by shining gold. We have two examples of this concerning the patriarch Jacob, in Genesis 32 and 33. There it is said that Jacob, when he heard that his brother Esau, with whom he was at odds, was coming to meet him with four hundred men, feared that he would suffer some harm from him. For this reason he prepared a generous and large gift: namely two hundred ewes and goats, twenty rams and he-goats, thirty camels with their young, forty cows, ten bulls, twenty she-asses and ten foals. For he thought to himself (as Moses expressly says), "I will placate his face with the gift that goes before me, and afterwards I will see his face; perhaps he will accept my face." That his hope was not in vain appears from the following chapter, where it is said that Esau ran, embraced Jacob, fastened kisses on him, and, which must be done more than all else, wept with him.

units.la: Gen.33. nibus est faciundum, vnà fleuisse. Gen.43. cap.narratur Iacobum, vbi intellexisset præfectum Ægypti, à quo filij eius commeatum compararant (nesciebat enim eum Iosephum filium suum esse) in liberos suos acerbè inue ctum esse, itemq; Simeonem in custodiam coniecisse, iusssisse illis, secundò in Ægyptum descendentibus, ex eis quæ in illa ora habebantur rarissima, munus hero confici, honorisq; hero illi & gratitudinis ergo offerre. Nec enim ignorabat, eum qui munera offert quod & Salomon obseruauit, victoriam & honorem reportare. Plura autem donorum genera esse, neminé ambigere arbitror. Quædam enim honesta sunt ac laudabilia: quædá in honesta, & nulla cum laude coniuncta. Inter honesta id primum recensendum est, quod amicitiæ iam contractæ, aut contrahendæ gratia dari consueuit. Qualia extiterunt illa munera, quæ Abrahamus Abimelecho obtulit & è conuerso: fœderis nanq; & societatis inter ipsos initæ veluti pignus ac testimonium fuisse constat. Quibus addi possunt & illa, quæ Salomon & Hiramus Tyriorum rex sibi inuicem mittere solebant. Est & aliud donorum genus, quod ad placandos iratorum animos adhibetur: Cuiusmodi fuere, quorum modò mentionem fecimus, munera à Iacobo ad Esauum fratrem ad illius in se conceptam indignatione mitigandam missa: Et Abigaelis nostrae ad Dauidem, vt eius aduersus Nabalem maritum suum meri- to concitatam excandescentiam mitigaret. His adiungi possunt, quae honoris causa mit tuntur, munera: Cuius generis habentur illa quae Pharao rex Aegypti Abrahamo olim donauit: & postea Iosepho Israelis filio alter Pharao, quem etiam praefecit Aegyptijs. Salomon item quam plurima huiusmodi & ad alios misit munera, & ipse ab aliis recepit. Sed & Ezechias a Merodaco Babyloniae Rege data cum literis dona non respuit. Daniel insuper ab eiusdem Babyloniae re- gibus cohonestatus est maximis praemijs ac donationibus: Quas sane vir pius non accepisset, nisi se iusto titulo retinere illa posse existimasset. Qua in re illud obser- uandum est, munera in sacris literis haud in vniuersum prohiberi: Sed habendam esse rationem locorum, temporum, dan- tiumque ac recipientium personarum, nec non etiam causarum propter quas aut dantur aut recipiuntur ipsa munera. Sic enim fiet, vt percepturi facile simus, quae nam ad praescriptum diuini iuris siue dari, siue accipi, nulla reprehensione, dona posint. Iam & compertum est, multos Principes, multas item Respublicas hoc in confuetudi-ne habuisse, vt ciues suos ob egregium ali-quod facinus honestissime munerarint. Qualem seruasse morem Romanos, vt alios populos praetermittam, historici quàm plu-rimi contestantur: vt inde nimirum reliqui ad capessendam virtutem animosiores eo-rundem praemiorum spe fierent. Praeterea sunt quaedam dona publicè missa, publicéq; accepta, quibus principes principibus aut ob aliquam adeptam victoriam, aut ob ali-quem alium secundum euentum gratulan-tur. Huius extitisse generis videntur ea, quę Romanis ob victoriam de Samnitibus rela-tam à Carthaginensibus, atque ab Attalo re-ge aliam ob causam accesserunt. Postremò habet etiam Ecclesia sua munera: quae, quo-niam pietati tantum inseruiunt, non malè pia vocari possunt. Atque haec omnia, vti diximus, dari & accipi citra reprehensio-nem possunt. E contra dona sunt, quae quo-niam hominum mentes corrumpunt, dona corruptoria licuerit appellare. Nihil certè est tam iniustum, nihil tam difficile, quod per eiusmodi dona non impetretur, ac per-ficiatur, vt non sine causa Philippo Macedo-niae Regi consulenti, quibus potissimum rationibus vrbes expugnare, & hostium co-pias
units.tr: Genesis 43 tells how Jacob, when he learned that the governor of Egypt, from whom his sons had obtained provisions (for he did not know that this man was his son Joseph), had been harshly angered against his children, and had thrown Simeon into prison, ordered that on their second journey down into Egypt a gift be made for the lord, from the rarest things found in that land, and be offered to him as a mark of honour and gratitude. For he did not fail to see, as Solomon also observed, that the one who offers gifts wins victory and honour. I think no one doubts that there are many kinds of gifts. Some are honourable and praiseworthy; others are dishonourable and joined with no praise. Among the honourable gifts, the first to be counted is that which is customarily given for the sake of friendship already formed or to be formed. Such were those gifts which Abraham offered to Abimelech and in turn received from him; for it is established that they were a pledge and testimony of the covenant and alliance made between them. To these may be added those which Solomon and Hiram king of Tyre were accustomed to send one another. There is also another kind of gift, which is used to placate angry minds. Of this kind were those gifts sent by Jacob to his brother Esau to soften the anger conceived against him, and those of our Abigail to David, to soften his rage justly stirred against her husband Nabal. To these may be added gifts sent as marks of honour: of this kind are those which Pharaoh, king of Egypt, once gave to Abraham, and afterwards another Pharaoh to Joseph, son of Israel, whom he also set over the Egyptians. Solomon likewise sent very many such gifts to others, and himself received them from others. Hezekiah, too, did not refuse the gifts sent with letters by Merodach, king of Babylon. Moreover, Daniel was honoured by the kings of the same Babylon with the greatest rewards and largesses; which indeed a godly man would not have accepted unless he thought he could keep them on a just title. In this matter it must be observed that gifts are not forbidden in Holy Scripture in general; rather, account must be taken of places, times, givers and recipients, and also of the causes for which the gifts are either given or received. For in this way we shall easily perceive which gifts, given or received according to the prescription of divine law, may be without any blame. Now it is also well established that many princes and many commonwealths have had this custom: that they rewarded their citizens most honourably for some outstanding deed, so that others might be the more eager to pursue virtue by hope of the same rewards. The Romans kept this custom, as very many historians attest (to pass over other peoples), so that the rest might by that hope be made more zealous to seize virtue. Besides, there are certain gifts sent and received publicly, by which princes congratulate princes either for some victory won or for some other favourable outcome. Of this kind seem to be those which came to the Romans from the Carthaginians on account of a victory over the Samnites, and from King Attalus for another reason. Lastly, the Church also has its gifts, which, since they serve piety alone, may not badly be called pious. All these, as we have said, can be given and received without blame. On the other hand, there are gifts which, since they corrupt men's minds, may be called corrupting gifts.

units.la: Dona corruptoria. pias profligare posset, Apollo dixerit:
units.tr: Corrupting gifts.

units.la: ἀργυρέαις λόγχαισι μάχῃ κῆ πάντα νι- κήσεις. Id est, Argenteis hastis confligito, & omnia vinces. Sed & Marcus Tullius proœ mio action. Verrin. Verrem, qui suos iudi- ces corrumpere cogitabat, omnemque fa- lutis rationem in sola pecunia collocabat, ita disputantem inducit: Nihil esse tam fan- ctum, quod non violari, nihil tam munitum, quod nō expugnari pecunia posit. In hunc censum ea dona veniunt, quæ Daniel Anti- christum colentibus Deum suum Maijzim collaturū prædixit. Talia sunt, quæ Principes exteri, Rebufpublicis liberis offerūt, vt eos in fœdera pertrahant, quibus initis, eas ad quæuis bella paratas habeant. Talia sunt, quæ homines astuti & versipelles Iudicibus dant, vt sententias in fauorem suum ferant. Tale fuit quod Siba Dauidi ab impio filio pulso, obtulit: vt animum ipsius à Miphibo- fetho alienaret. 2. Samuel. 16. Cap. Talia sunt quæ adulteri matronis & virginibus osse- runt, vt illarum pudicitiam expugnent: Hęc atque alia id genus munera, vt nec danda sunt, ita nec ab alijs accipienda. Exodi 23. Ne donum, inquit Deus, accipite: Donum enim excæcat etiam perspicaces: bonorumq; virorum orationem peruertit.Deuteronom.16, ijsdem feré verbis idem repetit: Ne donum ait,accipito:nam donum & sapientum oculos excæcat,& iustorum orationem peruertit.Seuerius illud est eiusdé cap.27. vbi execrabilem illum pronunciat,qui donum accipit,vt homini per iniuriā vitam eripiat.Isaias,Vę,inquit,qui fontes absoluunt ob munera & insontibus suum ius eripiunt. Quam obrem vt lambens ignis stipulam consumit, vt festucam flamma conficit:sic illorū stirps tanquam putre quiddam erit:illorū frutex, quasi cinis abibit,qui domini repudiauerint legem & eius dicta contemserint. Dauid cū suis munus ab Abigaele oblatū,salua cōscien tia accipere potuit.Enimuerò non tam donum,quàm præmiū debitū ac cōdignū fuit.
units.tr: Nothing is so unjust, nothing so difficult, that it cannot be obtained and accomplished by such gifts; hence, not without reason, when Philip, king of Macedonia, asked by what means above all he could storm cities and rout the forces of his enemies, Apollo is said to have answered: "Fight with silver spears and you will conquer all" [ἀργυρέαις λόγχαισι μάχῃ κῆ πάντα νικήσεις]. Marcus Tullius also, in the proem of the action against Verres, introduces Verres, who meant to corrupt his judges and placed all his hope of safety in money alone, arguing thus: nothing is so holy that it cannot be violated, nothing so fortified that it cannot be taken by money. To this class belong those gifts which Daniel foretold that the god Maozim would bestow on those who worship Antichrist. Such are those which foreign princes offer to free commonwealths, to draw them into alliances, by which, once made, they have them ready for any wars. Such are those which crafty and shifty men give to judges, to pass sentences in their favour. Such was the offer Ziba made to David, when he was driven out by his impious son, to turn David's mind away from Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 16). Such are those which adulterers offer to matrons and virgins, to overcome their chastity. These and other gifts of this kind are neither to be given nor to be received from others. Exodus 23: "Take no gift," says God, "for a gift blinds even the keen-sighted and perverts the speech of good men." Deuteronomy 16 repeats the same thing in nearly the same words: "Take no gift, for a gift blinds even the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous." More severe is that in the same chapter 27, where he pronounces accursed the one who takes a gift to take a man's life unjustly. Isaiah: "Woe," he says, "to those who acquit the guilty for gifts, and take away the right of the innocent. Therefore, as a licking fire consumes the stubble, and as a flame consumes the chaff, so their root will be like something rotten, and their stem will go away like ash, because they have rejected the law of the Lord and despised his word." David, when he received the gift offered by Abigail, could accept it with a clear conscience; for it was less a gift than a due and deserved reward.

units.la: Abigael,vbi asinis munus,quod ad leuandum inopiam Dauidis cumprimis faciebat, imposuisset,iubet iuuenes suos præcedere: se mox insequuturam: Atque in eo sequuta est exemplum Iacobi Patriarchæ. Is enim cum rediret in terram suam & sciret, se Esauum fratrem vehementer habere offensum, præmisit ad illum seruos cum armentis & gregibus:inter quos distantiam esse voluit, nempe,vt pompa quadam ista distributa oculis aduenientis fratris magis arriderent, semperque initinere quodamodo detinerent & occuparent noua voluptate, vt spacium non daretur ad male cogitandum : & ita non vno sed multis arietibus ferox illius animus frangeretur. Non dubinm mihi est, quin Ahigael, quæ cauendum norat, ne esurienti occurramus, secum ipsa cogitarit: Dauidem, vtso amplissimo isto munere honorario, remissa ira, aliquanto placatiorem fore.
units.tr: When Abigail had loaded the donkeys with the gifts, which above all were meant to relieve David's want, she told her young men to go on ahead, and said she would follow shortly. In doing so she followed the example of the patriarch Jacob. When he was returning to his own land and knew that he had deeply offended his brother Esau, he sent servants ahead to him with herds and flocks, arranged in separate groups. He wanted this distribution, a kind of procession, to delight the eyes of his approaching brother and to keep him occupied with new pleasure all along the way, so that he would have no room to brood on evil. In this way his fierce spirit was broken not by one ram but by many. I have no doubt that Abigail, who knew she must take care not to meet a hungry man empty-handed, reasoned to herself that David, once this very generous honorary gift had been received, would lay aside his anger and be considerably more placated.

units.la: Non communicat ista cum viro suo, nimirum quod sciret eum nó esse passurum: Soli enim sibi viuere, benefacere neminisolebat: vel fortasse, quod videret eum esse in conuiuio, inter pocula, vbi nihil loci est consilio. Vino enim (vt veteri fertur prouerbio) sapientia obumbratur. Si quid recte fieri voluit, ipsam id facere oportuit. Nabal enim omnino ἀπρησόγοp& erat, ac quod de Polyphemo suo Poeta ait:
