units.tr: She did not consult her husband about this, no doubt because she knew he would not allow it. He was accustomed to living for himself alone and to doing good to no one. Or perhaps she saw that he was at a feast, among the cups, where there is no room for counsel. For wisdom, as the old proverb says, is overshadowed by wine. If she wished something to be done rightly, she had to do it herself. Nabal was altogether [ἀπροσήγορος] unapproachable, and what the poet says of his Polyphemus applied to him:

units.la: Nec dictu facilis nec visu affabilis vlli,
units.tr: Neither easy to speak to nor pleasant to look upon for anyone,

units.la: præsertim vino meracius hausto. Cæterà, non licet vxori inconsulto viro, donare, mutare, vendere, imò nec eleemosynas dare. Quod & Ethnici viderunt, inter quos Plautus eleganter: Peculi probă nihil habere addecet clá viro: Hoc viri censeo esse omne, quod tuū est, in Caff. Quanuis, si q bona habeat priuata,quæ ipsi cum marito non sint communia,alia ratio est:modò id honeste faciat: Communia autem bona largiri, iniussu viri, esset matrimonij iura violare. Iste autem casus alienus est,& extraordinarius. Nam si vir fatuus sit & delirus,vt opus illi sit curatore, vxor prospicere debet rebus communibus. Adhæc vxor redimere debet salutem viri, quibuscunq; potest honestis rationibus. Viri quidem est inferre: mulieris autem conseruare.Sed vt sapiens ait,est tempus seruandi,& est tempus dandi.Nec insci tè ille apud Comicum:
units.tr: especially when he has drunk his wine neat. Moreover, a wife may not give, exchange, or sell anything without her husband's consent, nor even give alms. The heathen also recognised this, and among them Plautus put it elegantly: "It does not become a wife to have any private savings. I hold that everything that is yours is your husband's," in the Casina. Yet if she has some goods of her own, which are not shared with her husband, the matter is different, provided she uses them honourably. But to give away common goods without her husband's order would be to violate the rights of marriage. This case, however, is exceptional and out of the ordinary. For if the husband is foolish and deranged, so that he needs a guardian, the wife ought to look after the common goods. Besides, a wife ought to redeem her husband's safety by whatever honourable means she can. It is the husband's part to bring in, but the wife's to keep. But, as the wise man says, there is a time to keep and a time to give. Nor was that saying of the comic poet unknown to her: "To neglect money in the right place is sometimes the greatest gain."

units.la: Pecuniam in loco negligere, maximum inter dum est lucrum.Sed & vulgo dicitur:Infelicé esse denarium illum planeq; ἄτοκον qui flo reno fraudi fit. Si Nabal dimidium tantum Dauidi volens dedisset, quantum postea vxor, proculdubio grato animo accepisset. Sed modum,quem omnes vno consensu in rebus omnibus dicunt esse optimum, nullû tenere doctus, profusè largus, qui hodie quoq; multorum mos est, vbi non esset opus erat:tenacissimus contrà, vbi cumprimis liberalitatem declarare oportuit.
units.tr: People also commonly say that a denarius is unlucky when it is given to a flatterer, and that it is utterly barren [ἄτοκον]. If Nabal had willingly given David only half of what his wife later gave, he would undoubtedly have received it with a grateful heart. But he did not keep the measure which everyone agrees is best in all things. He was lavish where it was not needed, a habit which many people still have today, and most stingy where generosity above all had to be shown.

units.la: Abigael, conscenso asino,descendit per occultam parte montis,vel vt per compendium facilius Dauidi occurreret.(viæ enim publicæ blicæ solent sæpe esse longiores) vel (quod mihi verisimilius videtur) ne cui obuiam fie ret, à quo posset impediri. Interea ipsa medi tabatur secum, apud Dauidem quam oratio nem esset habitura. Neque enim leue aut lu- dicrum erat, fœminam, cum viro ira concita to, præsente milite famelico, verba facere. Nam scitè Cato in proœmio orationis, qua dissuasit legem Agrariá, Arduum est ad ven- trem verba facere, qui careat auribus. Nam vbi de pastu agitur, non admittuntur hone- stæ rationes. Cicero ipse, celeberrimus ora- tor fatetur se non parum timuisse, nec pristi nam animi magnitudinem ad caussam Milo nis attulisse, cum videret noui iudicij nouâ formam: id est, vt ipse exponit, confessum Iu dicum corona non cinctum, vt solebat, seq; non vsitata frequentia stipatum esse. Nam il- la præsidia, inquit, quę pro templis omnibus cernitis, etsi contra vim collocata sunt, non afferunt tamen oratori aliquid, vt in foro & in iudicio, quanquam præsidijs salutaribus & necessarijs septi simus, tamen ne non ti- mere quidem sine aliquo timore posimus. Appareat ergo, Abigaelem fœminam magno & excelso animo præditam fuisse. Aliæ for- tasse mulieres in tanto periculo aut discef- sissent à viris, aut fugissent, aut à cognatis & affinibus auxilium atq; opem petijssent. Hęc verò nō dubitauit se furenti leoni obijcere.
units.tr: Abigail mounted her donkey and came down by a hidden path on the mountain, either to meet David more quickly by a shortcut (public roads are often longer), or, what seems to me more likely, so that she would not meet anyone who might hinder her. Meanwhile she considered within herself what speech she should make before David. For it was no light or playful matter for a woman, with her husband roused to anger and a hungry soldier present, to speak. Cato wisely said in the preface to his speech against the agrarian law: "It is hard to speak to the belly, which has no ears." For when the subject is food, honourable arguments are not admitted. Cicero himself, the most famous orator, confesses that he was not a little afraid and that he did not bring his former greatness of spirit to the defence of Milo, when he saw the new form of the trial: that is, as he himself explains, the court was not surrounded by its usual crowd and he was not attended by the customary throng. "Those guards," he says, "which you see placed before all the temples, though they are stationed against violence, nevertheless do not give the orator the same help as in the forum and in court. Though we are surrounded by protective and necessary guards, we cannot even be without some fear." It is clear, then, that Abigail was a woman endowed with a great and lofty spirit. Other women in such great danger would perhaps have separated from their husbands, or fled, or sought aid and help from their kinsfolk and relatives. But she did not hesitate to throw herself in the path of a raging lion.

units.la: Dauid, audito crudeli Nabalis responso, Næ ego, frustra, dixerat, conseruaui omnia, quę habet iste in saltibus, ita vt nihil omnino de suo perdiderit, & mihi bonum malo pensauit? At ita perdat Deus hostes Dauidis, vt ei ante lucem matutinam ex omnibus quæ habet, ne canem quidem reliquum faciam. Credibile autem est, verba ista hoc loco commemorari, non quod ea Abigael audiuerit, sed vt intelligatur, quàm opportunè ea occurrerit. Res enim ea cunctationem non ferebat: nec paruum erat periculum quod videbatur, impendere. Et tamen non adeo à vero est remotâ, Dauidé, cum Abigaele sibi aduersus eum descendenti, verba ista, iratorum more, qui vix ac ne vix iniurias illatas concoquunt, identidem ingeminasse.
units.tr: David, on hearing Nabal's cruel answer, had said: "Surely in vain have I kept safe everything that this man has in the wilds, so that he has lost nothing of his own, and he has repaid me evil for good! May God so destroy David's enemies that I leave him not so much as a dog of all that he has, before morning light." It is credible that these words are recalled here not because Abigail heard them, but so that it may be understood how opportunely she came. For the matter did not allow delay, and the danger that appeared was not small. And yet it is not far from the truth that David, as he came down against Nabal with Abigail, kept repeating these words again and again, in the manner of angry men who can scarcely digest the wrongs done to them.

units.la: Abigael, vbi primū vidit Dauidem ex aduerso cliuo descendentem, confestim de asino desilit, & illum prona accidens, honorem ei suppliciter præbet, eiq; ad pedes iacens, verba facere incipit: Vulgaris Orientalium hic mos fuit, vt se ad pedes Regum, Principum, & aliorum, quibus honorē deferre voluerunt, abijcerent, quemadmodū ad ȝ. Hest. exemplis adductis pluribus commonstrauimus. mus. Nos tantum genua inflectimus, nisi in conspectu magnorum Principum veniamus, coràm quibus in genua supplices procidimus. Nabal nullo Dauidi honore habito, fortè nec allocutione dignu iudicaffet. Nec enim ignorabat,illum Sauli in gratia non ef-fe. Ista verò, qua erat prudentia,animiq; demissione, in facie fe incuruat, & supplex ad pedes Dauidis proiecta, honorem illi condi gnum summisse habet.
units.tr: As soon as Abigail saw David coming down the slope opposite her, she immediately dismounted from the donkey, fell prostrate, and humbly paid him honour. Lying at his feet, she began to speak. This was the common custom of the Orientals: to throw themselves at the feet of kings, princes, and others to whom they wished to show honour, as I have shown in more detail with several examples drawn from Esther 3. We only bend the knee, unless we come into the presence of great princes, before whom we fall on our knees as suppliants. Nabal, giving David no honour, would perhaps have thought him unworthy even of a word. For he did not fail to know that David was not in favour with Saul. But she, with the prudence and humility of her spirit, bowed low before his face and, lying as a suppliant at David's feet, paid him the honour that was due to him, in a humble manner.

units.la: Iam verò in vulgus quoq; notum est, etiam feroces homines gestu isto ad commiseratiouem flecti. Exemplum afferam ex lib. 6.cap.2.Baptistæ Egnatij de rebus Veneto- rum.Franciscus Dandulus Venetus Orator missus in Galliam ad Clementem Pontificem Maximum,vt eum infestiorem Veneto nomini propter Ferrariam occupatam placaret, quum multa & varia secum agitasset consilia, neque à Pontifice ipso commotione quicquam impetraret, inusitati facinoris obeundi,(quod quidem neque antea neque in hanc ipsam ætatem auditu fit) consilium inijt. Nam quo tempore Clemens ipse cognitaret,quadrupes effectus, catenaque ferrea collo pressus ad Pontificis pedes canis in more sese substrauit. Quo nouo spectaculo Pontifex ipse attonitus, illum in gratiam recepit, Venetoq; nomini iniuriam dimisit, vt postea respublica Veneta gratissima & iucundissima illi fuerit, cui mortalium omnium congressum consuetudinemque interdixerat. Quę res adeò grata illi accidit, vt legatum istum non multò post Ducem crearint. Ipse cognométo Canis dictus est, quod canis more ad mensam Pontificis iacuisset, &c. Leo, quamuis animalium omnium sit ferocissimus: tamen vni illi ex feris clementia est in supplices. Prostratis parcit, vbi saevit, in viros prius quàm in foeminas fremit: infantes non nisi magna fame adortus. Qua de re Plinius lib. 8. natur. hist. cap. 16. multis. Nihil est magnum, quod non sit placidum, atq; vt eleganter Ouidius:
units.tr: Indeed, it is also well known among the common people that even fierce men can be moved to pity by such a gesture. I will give an example from book 6, chapter 2 of Battista Egnazio's history of the affairs of the Venetians. Francesco Dandolo, a Venetian orator sent into France to Pope Clement, the greatest of pontiffs, to appease him, since he was more hostile to the Venetian name because of the occupation of Ferrara, had considered many and various plans. Since he could obtain nothing by entreaty from the Pope himself, he resolved upon an unheard-of deed, one which was neither heard of before nor in our own age. At the time when Clement himself was in residence, he made himself a four-footed creature, and with an iron chain pressed on his neck, he threw himself down at the Pope's feet in the manner of a dog. The Pope, astonished at this new spectacle, received him back into favour and dropped the injury done to the Venetian name. Afterwards the Venetian state was most grateful and pleasing to him, to whom he had forbidden the company and association of all mortals. This matter turned out so well for him that not long afterwards they made him Doge. He himself was called by the nickname Canis, because like a dog he had lain at the Pope's table, and so on. The lion, though the fiercest of all animals, is alone among wild beasts in its clemency towards suppliants. It spares those who lie prostrate; where it rages, it rages against men before women; it attacks infants only under extreme hunger. Pliny discusses this in many places in book 8, chapter 16 of his Natural History. Nothing is so great that it is not also gentle; and, as Ovid elegantly says:

units.la: Quo quisq; est maior, magis est placabilis irae: Et faciles motus mens generosa capit. Corpora magnanimo satis est prostrasse leoni, Pugna suum finem, cum iacet hostis, habet. At lupus & turpes instant morientibus vrsi, Et quaecunq; minor nobilitate fera est, etc. Ite:
units.tr: "The greater a man is, the more easily he is appeased in anger, and a noble mind takes gentle impulses. It is enough for the magnanimous lion to have struck down a body; when the enemy lies down, the fight has its end. But wolves and foul bears press upon the dying, and whatever beast is less noble, etc." Go on:

units.la: Bonum ad virum cito moritur iracundia.
units.tr: "Anger quickly dies in a good man."

units.la: Qua verò oratione Abigael apud Dauidem sa fit, infra audiemus. Nunc ad ea, quę ex hoc sermone ad correctionem nostram elici possunt, descindimus.
units.tr: In what speech Abigail addressed David we shall hear below. Now let us turn to those things which can be drawn from this discourse for our correction.

units.la: Primò videmus, quanta sit nostrum omnium nium hoc exulceratissimo seculo cæcitas & stupiditas. Vnus seruulus ad Abigaelem venit, eamq; commouet, vt, quid agat, in tempore dispiciat. Dauidem contemtu & ingratitudine Nabalis inductû cum exercitu iam iam adesse. Verendum, ne temerè in omnes latus, insontes fontium supplicio indiscrimi natim inuoluat. Nec mora: memor sententiæ illius:
units.tr: First, we see how great is the blindness and stupidity of all of us in this most ulcerated age. A little servant came to Abigail and moved her to discern in time what she should do, since David, provoked by the contempt and ingratitude of Nabal, was now at hand with his army. There was reason to fear that he would rashly rage on every side and involve the innocent indiscriminately in the punishment of the guilty. Without delay, mindful of that saying: [5] "One must act at the right moment, and not hesitate," she applies fitting remedies in time, and considers with prompt and prudent care how to ward off the present danger.

units.la: Naue agere oportet, quod agas, non dubitarier: in tempore remedia congrua adhibet, & de præsenti periculo propulsando maturè ac prudenter cogitat. Ad nos veniunt serui Dei non semel atque iterum, sed quotidie: atque inter hos non pauci, viri vir tute, eloquentia ac doctrina solida quàm commendatissimi, qui, gallorum instar, pœnitentiam securis & dormientibus summo mane prædicant, & imminentes scelerū pœnas sancta dicendi libertate denunciant. Sed nec nos ipsos fugit, Deum iam inde à prima mundi origine in scelestos ac pœnitere nescios homines quàm grauissimè animaduer tisse. Accedunt infinita prodigia & ostenta, quibus similiter excitamur, vt de Dei ira, se de cœlo & in alijs mundi partibus nobis manifestante, cogitemus. Quin nos ipsi sententiam in nos peremtoriam stringimus, Res nostras non posse diutius consistere: Nos ita re à Deo ad quęuis supplicia rapi: Sed quid? Ne vnus quidem est, qui de pacando Deo, vel ad punctum temporis cogitationem, etiam leuissimam suscipiat. Ac cum nostrum omnium esset, illi donarijs: ac in primis pre cibus ardentibus occurrere: nescio qui fiat, vt in peccatis omnis loci ac ordinis homines sceleste pergant, aut ad creaturas potius quàm ad Deum conuertantur, aut quod verè ex raro contingentibus est, si aliquam, momentaneam & theatricam poenitentiam agant, qualem Israelitis Hoseas exprobrat, capite sexto. Non temere ergo Deus omnis generis plagas infert, quibus nos in viam reuocet. Agnoscamus nos manum ipsius, & ad ipsum conuertamur, & mox nobis sese propitium in Christo Iesu pace nostra dabit.
units.tr: The servants of God come to us not once or twice but every day, and among them not a few men most commended for virtue, eloquence and solid learning, who, like cocks, preach repentance to the careless and sleeping at the very early morning, and with holy freedom of speech announce the punishments of impending sins. Yet we are not unaware that God, from the very beginning of the world, has punished most severely wicked men who know not how to repent. Added to this are countless portents and omens by which we are similarly stirred, so that we may consider the anger of God, which He makes manifest to us from heaven and in other parts of the world. Indeed we ourselves pronounce a decisive sentence against ourselves: that our affairs cannot last much longer, and that we are thus being snatched by God to every kind of punishment. But what? There is not even one who takes up a thought, however slight, for a single moment about appeasing God. And although it was the duty of us all to meet Him with gifts, and above all with ardent prayers, I know not how it happens that men of every place and rank go on in sin wickedly, or turn to creatures rather than to God; or, which is truly rare, if they do perform some momentary and theatrical repentance, such as Hosea rebukes the Israelites for in chapter six. Therefore God does not without cause bring plagues of every kind upon us, by which He recalls us to the way. Let us acknowledge His hand, and turn to Him, and soon He will give Himself to us, propitious in Christ Jesus, and our peace.

units.la: Deinde, exemplo Abigaelis, discimus, ratione ac via absq; mora quaerendam, qua cū illis, quos vel à nobis ipsis vel nostris laesos nouimus, in gratiam quàm primum redeamus, ne videlicet ex ira, diutius seruata & fota, odium sequatur, cuius comes est inuidia: ex quibus coniunctis iniuriae iniurijs accumulantur, quae tandem pugnas & caedes pariunt. tiunt. Imô, quia odium consilia cruenta & cædes spirat, homicidij reos facit, apud Dei tribunal, omnes eos, qui illi indulgent. Ideo Ioannes Apostolus dicebat: Omnis, qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est. Sed quia de his infra pluribus agemus, hoc loco breviores fumus. Id tamen non præterierim, ad reconciliationem mutuam non parum in eo momenti esse, si animum nostrum muneribus in loco datis, alijsúe beneficijs declaremus. Munera enim, qualiacunque sint, signa sunt animi benè affecti erga eum, cui dantur. Non omnino malè Aristoteles: Munera, ait, placent & ambitiosis & avaris. Nam avarus quærit lucrum: ambitiosus gloriam. Itaque avaro paruum munus non potest esse satis. Ambitiosus autem nonspe ctat magnitudinem munerum. Satis esse putat, si vilum esse dignum, qui munere aliquo afficeretur. Ita Iacobus, ut & supra dixi-mus, cum secundo filios suos in Ægyptum mitteret, misit vnà munera ad Iosephum, qui præerat terræ. Nos etiam oportet, cum accedimus ad sacrum cœtum, ad Deum Regem regum, afferre nobiscum aliquid muneris, illudque dare pauperibus. Nam, quod pauperibus datur, id Deus sibi ipsi datum deputat. Fecit ille, ut hanc omnem rem recta putantes via, serias de poenitentia cogitationes suscipiamus, vt hoc vitae spacium emensi, coelesti aliquando beatitate fruamur, Amen.
units.tr: Then, from the example of Abigail, we learn that a method and way must be sought without delay by which we may return as soon as possible into favour with those whom we know to have been injured either by ourselves or by ours; lest, namely, from anger long kept and nursed, hatred should follow, of which envy is the companion, and from these combined, injuries are piled upon injuries, which at last produce fights and slaughter. Indeed, because hatred breathes bloody plans and murder, it makes all who indulge it guilty of homicide before the tribunal of God. Therefore the Apostle John said: "Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer." But since we shall treat these matters at more length below, we are briefer here. Yet I shall not pass over this: that for mutual reconciliation it is of no small weight if we show our mind by gifts given in the place, or by other benefits. For gifts, of whatever kind they be, are signs of a well-disposed mind toward the one to whom they are given. Aristotle says not altogether badly: "Gifts please both the ambitious and the avaricious." For the avaricious man seeks gain, the ambitious man glory; so for the avaricious a small gift cannot be enough, while the ambitious man does not look to the greatness of the gifts; he thinks it enough if the one who receives it is judged worthy of some honour. Thus Jacob, as I have said above also, when for the second time he sent his sons into Egypt, sent gifts along with them to Joseph, who presided over the land. We too must, when we come to the holy assembly, bring with us some gift to God, the King of kings, and give it to the poor; for what is given to the poor God counts as given to Himself. May He grant that, thinking this whole matter through by the right way, we take up serious thoughts about repentance, so that, having finished this span of life, we may at last enjoy heavenly blessedness. Amen.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi. HOMILIA VII.
units.tr: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi. HOMILIA VII.

units.la: Abigail Dauidi obuia facta, eius in Nabalem iram eleganti oratione pacat.
units.tr: Abigail meets David and, with an elegant speech, appeases his anger against Nabal.

units.la: 24 Corruit, inquam, [Abigail] adpedes eius & dixit: In me (ego domine mi) iniquitas: propterea loquatur obsecro ancilla tua in auribus tuis: et audi verba ancillae tuae.
units.tr: 24 She fell, I say, at his feet and said: Upon me, my lord, be the iniquity; therefore let your handmaid, I beg you, speak in your ears, and hear the words of your handmaid.

units.la: 25 Ne quaeso apponat dominus meus cor suum super virum Belial, super Nabal: quia secundum nomen suum sic est. Nabal nomen eius: & stultitia cum eo: Ego vero ancilla tua non videram pueros domini mei, quos miseras.
units.tr: 25 Let my lord, I pray, not set his heart upon that worthless man Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. But I, your handmaid, did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent.

units.la: 26 Nunc autem, domine mi, viuit Iehoua, & viuit anima tua, qui prohibuit te Iehoua, ne venires in sanguines, & seruaret manus tua te: nunc autem sint, sicut Nabal, Nabal, inimici tui, & qui quærunt domino meo malum.
units.tr: 26 Now then, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, the LORD has kept you from coming to bloodshed and from saving yourself by your own hand. Now then, let your enemies and those who seek evil against my lord be as Nabal.

units.la: 27 Nunc igitur benedictio hæc, quam attulit ancilla tua domino meo, detur pueris, qui ambulant ad pedes domini mei.
units.tr: 27 Now therefore let this blessing, which your handmaid has brought to my lord, be given to the young men who follow at my lord's feet.

units.la: 28 Parce obsecro præuaricationi ancillæ tuæ: Quia certò faciturus est Iehouah domino meo domum stabilem: quia prælia Iehouæ dominus meus præliatus est: & malitia non inuenta fuit in te à diebus tuis.
units.tr: 28 Pardon, I beg you, the trespass of your handmaid, for the LORD will surely make my lord a sure house, because my lord fights the battles of the LORD, and no evil has been found in you all your days.

units.la: 29 Et surrexit homo, ad persequendum te, & ad quærendum animam tuam: Sed erit anima domini mei ligata in fasciculo vitæ cum Iehoua Deo tuo: at animam inimicorum tuorum funda iaculabitur in medio sedis fundæ.
units.tr: 29 Though a man rise up to pursue you and to seek your life, yet the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the LORD your God; but the lives of your enemies he shall sling out, as from the hollow of a sling.

units.la: 30 Quum autem fecerit Iehoua domino meo bonum iuxta omnia, quæ loquutus est de te, & præceperit tibi, ut sis dux super Israelem:
units.tr: 30 And when the LORD shall have done for my lord all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and shall have appointed you ruler over Israel,

units.la: 31 Tunc non erit hoc tibi domino meo in offendiculum & offensionem cordis, & quod effuderit sanguinem sine causa, aut quod fecerit salutem dominus meus sibi: et benefecerit Iehoua domino meo, recordaberis ancillæ tuæ.
units.tr: 31 then this shall be no cause of grief or stumbling of heart to my lord, that he has shed blood without cause or that my lord has avenged himself. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, remember your handmaid.

units.la: ABigael,vt primum audiuit,Dauidem contemtu & ingratitudine Nabalis in ductu,ipsum fortunis omnibus funditus euertere statuisse,& iâ in ceruicibus esse, non diutius moras nectit, sed quòd nihil in ipso imminentis periculi limine perniciosius longa deliberatione posset, de propulsando illo maturè & prudenter cogitat. Enimuerò Dauidi ipsa occurrens non inanis accedit: sed amplissimum munus secum affert. In conspectum eius vt venit,confestim ex asino de silit,& ad ipsius pedes prouoluta, honorem illi summisse habet. Qua de re cum nuper di ctum sit,proximum est,vt,quali apud Dauidem vsa sit oratione,videamus.
units.tr: As soon as Abigail heard that David, provoked by Nabal's contempt and ingratitude, had resolved to overthrow utterly all his fortunes, and that the danger was already at their necks, she did not delay for long. Since nothing could be more destructive on the very threshold of imminent peril than a long deliberation, she quickly and prudently considered how to ward him off. Indeed, she did not go to meet David empty-handed but brought a most generous gift with her. As soon as she came into his sight, she immediately dismounted from her donkey and, falling prostrate at his feet, showed him humble honour. Since we have just spoken of this, it is next to see what manner of speech she used before David.

units.la: Elucet ex illa, eam non tàm prudentis, quam excelsi animi fœminam fuisse. Nec enim mirum fuisset,si præ metu obmutuisset, ac ne hiscere quidem potuisset. Orandum enim illi erat ad Dauidem, ira planè concitatum, atq; adeo ardente,præsente militefa melico. Iam verò nemo est,qui nesciat,Ventrem molestum esse interpellatorem. Agebatur deinde non tàm de sua, quàm totius familiæ capite & salute. Quot,etiam cordati homines,si quando vel ad senatum vel etiam plebeculam verba sint facienda, in tantum obstupescunt,vt etiamsi nec sua nec suorum res agatur, vbi nam locorum sint, aut quid dicant, planè ignorent? Sed & concionatores aliquando rem aliquam diligenter meditantur: postquam verò suggestum conscenderunt, & omnium oculos in se conuersos vident, trepidant: & quæ diligenter meditati sunt, quemadmodum optarent, proferre non possunt. Ista autem, animo plus quam virili, ad Dauidem orationem habet non mi nus grauem, quam fructuosam. Qua de re postea plura.
units.tr: It is clear from this that she was a woman not so much of prudence as of lofty spirit. For it would not have been surprising if, from fear, she had been struck dumb and could not even open her mouth. She had to plead before David, who was plainly stirred to anger and burning, with a soldier of his present. Now, who does not know that the belly is a troublesome intercessor? Moreover, the matter concerned not so much her own life as the head and safety of her whole household. How many even sensible men, when they must speak before the senate or even before the common people, are so struck with amazement that, although the matter concerns neither themselves nor their families, they completely forget where they are or what they are saying? Yet even preachers sometimes carefully prepare some subject; but once they have mounted the pulpit and see all eyes turned upon them, they tremble, and cannot bring out what they had carefully thought through as they would wish. But Abigail, with a spirit more than manly, makes a speech to David that is no less weighty than it is fruitful. More on this later.

units.la: Ac primò, quoniam factum Nabalis in Abigaelem confessio erat, adhæc inficiando, causæ suæ mensa obesse potuisset, id non negat, sed aperte se proviro fatetur. Incredibile enim dictu est, quantum opponit ingenua peccati confessio apud viros cordatos momenti habeat. Habemus, inquiunt, confitentem reum. Damno suo edoctus, posthac erit cautior. Quid igitur? Culpam condonabimus, eumque in gratiam recipiemus. Deinde, quod tale esset, quòd nullam plane admitteret excusationem, non defendit, sed culpam tantùm deprecatur. In me inquit, domine mi, iniquitas. Atq; ita prudenter se pro viro suo opponit, innocentem pro sonte, Mutatio enim personarum præcipitur à Rhetoribus: & multum prodest. Multa enim alijs,ac præsertim fœminis, facilè dan-tur, quæ iure ac merito negantur alij. Ita Christus se sp nobis interponit apud patrem, & peccata nostra perfert in suo corpore.
units.tr: First, since Nabal's act against Abigail was a confession of a fault, and since by denying it he might have harmed his own case, he does not deny it but openly admits it as a husband. For it is hard to say how much weight an open confession of sin carries with sensible men. "He confesses his guilt," they say; "having learned by his loss, he will be more careful hereafter. What then? We shall pardon the fault and receive him back into favour." Next, since the case was such that it admitted no excuse at all, she does not defend it but only begs pardon for the fault. Upon me, she says, my lord, be the iniquity. And so she prudently puts herself in her husband's place, the innocent for the guilty. For the change of persons is prescribed by the rhetoricians, and it helps greatly; many things are readily granted to others, and especially to women, which are rightly and justly refused to others. Thus Christ places himself between us and the Father, and bears our sins in his own body.

units.la: Mox, quoniam in mala caussa petenda est attentio,magniq; viri plærunq; hoc vitio laborent,vt vix à proposito discedant,nullasq; rationes admittant, orat eum, vt se attentè audiat.Loquatur,ait,ancilla tua in auribus tuis & audi verba ancillæ tuæ. Non hoc autem locotantùm, sed & postea,se appellat eius ancillam, illum autem dominū suum. Nempe, vt conuitia Nabalis ἀντιθέσει ista obducat. Nam ille, Quis, inquit,est Dauid,Isai filius? ac si ignobilis, ac obscurus esset. Hæc autem illum decies & quater salutat dominū suum, se sexies ancillam eius vocat.
units.tr: Next, since attention must be sought for a bad cause, and great men are commonly afflicted with this fault, that they scarcely depart from their purpose and admit no reasons, she begs him to listen to her attentively: let your handmaid speak in your ears, and hear the words of your handmaid. Not only here but also afterwards she calls herself his handmaid and him her lord, so as to set these terms over against Nabal's insults by antithesis [ἀντιθέσει]. For Nabal had said, "Who is David, the son of Jesse?" as though he were of no account and obscure. Yet she greets him as her lord fourteen times, and calls herself his handmaid six times.

units.la: Quo loco obiter discimus,honorem viris magnis, ac præsertim Principibus ac Magistratibus,condignum habendum. Quo Pauli illud:Cui timorem, timorem:cui honorē, honorem. Timorem enim,Hebrǝorum more,vocat obedientiam,eamq; ex animo proficiscentem:Honoris autem nomine intelligit, reuerentiam, quam Magistratui haberi par est,eamq; sinceram & voluntariam: Cuiusmodi fuit illa.Q. Fabij Maximi,filiü consulem reuerentis, vt refert Liuiu sDecad. 3. lib.4. Quanquam multò altius assurgere nos iubeat Paulus.
units.tr: Here we learn in passing that honour is to be shown to great men, and especially to princes and magistrates, as is fitting. To this belongs Paul's saying: "to whom fear, fear; to whom honour, honour." For in the Hebrew manner he calls obedience "fear," and that obedience which springs from the heart; but by the name of honour he understands the reverence that is fitting to be shown to the magistrate, and that sincere and voluntary. Such was the reverence of Quintus Fabius Maximus the younger, who, as Livy relates, rose before the consul, Decad. 3, book 4. Yet Paul bids us rise far higher than this.

units.la: Captata beneuolentia & attentione,mul-tis rationibus suadet Dauidi, ne suam iniu-riam velit vlcisci. Primum ab indignitate su-mens:Ne quæso apponat dominus meus,ait,cor suum super virum Belial hunc, super Nabal: Quia secundum nomen suum sic est. Nabal nomen eius: & stultitia cum eo. Sensus est: Stulti, si quem contemnunt, non faciunt id cum iu-dicio,nec eius,quem contemnunt, existima-tionem possunt lædere: Sed neque prudentes tanti faciunt,si aut à mulierculis,aut à pueris aut à morionibus contemnantur. Vident enim se nihilo minoris futuros apud homines cordatos, qui, etiamsi eos conuitijs peti videant, illis tamen non mouentur: Atqui nomen istius est Nabal, id est,stultus: & stultitia cum eo, id est, Egregie suo nomini respondet. Ecquid igitur, vir clarissime, quo non præstantior alter sapientia, iustitia & fortitudine in puniendo homine isto stolido atque futili heroicam iram exerceres? Certè de stultis ac vecordibus triumphi non aguntur. Non dissimili ratione Philo-ctetes apud Actium ingemiscit, in pennigero,non armigero in corpore sua tela exerceri. Nos, si quando videamus, virum prudentiæ nomine hactenus commendatum, cum stulto aliquo ac amenti contendere, sal se dicimus: Vter ex illis plus sapit, recteque: Famam ob stultum nō esse atterendam, monemus. Ἄν einem narren sol man sich nit verhönen.
units.tr: Having won goodwill and attention, she urges David with many reasons not to wish to avenge his injury. First, taking the argument from the unworthiness of the man: "Let my lord not set his heart," she says, "upon this worthless man Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him." The sense is this: fools, if they despise someone, do not do so with judgement, nor can they harm the esteem of the one they despise. But neither do the prudent make much of being despised by mere women, by boys, or by buffoons. For they see that they will be no less esteemed by sensible men, who, even when they see themselves attacked with insults, are not moved by them. And yet his name is Nabal, that is, fool; and folly is with him, that is, he answers well to his name. Then, most distinguished sir, who surpasses others in wisdom, justice and courage, what need is there for you to exercise heroic anger in punishing this stupid and frivolous man? Certainly no triumphs are won over fools and madmen. For a similar reason Philoctetes at Actium groans that his weapons are used against a feathered body, not an armed one. When we see a man, hitherto commended for prudence, contending with some fool or madman, we say that he is out of his senses, and rightly so: we advise that one should not waste one's reputation on a fool. "Ān einem narren sol man sich nit verhönen" (One should not mock oneself against a fool).

units.la: Quæret tamen aliquis, an Abigael officio probæ vxoris functa sit, cum viru suum appellat Belial & stultum? Christus enim aperte: Quisquis fratri suo dixerit, fatue, tene bitur gehenna ignis, Matth.5.versu 22. Respondeo. Ista vere erat Belial & stultus, Vnde illum nullo conuitio petit: sed suo nomine insignit. Qui illum familiariter norant, illum pro stulto habebant. Sed & Rabbini quidam aiunt, hoc illi cognomen à stultitia fuisse impositum. Deinde, quidquid huius dicit, non ex contemptu dicit, sed vt vitam illius caputque conseruet. Chirurgus enim partem aliquam carnis interdum amputat, vt totum corpus sit incolume: quod erat alioqui periturum. Cætera, nemo debet alium contumeliose conuitijs petere, nominibusque probrosis insignire. In primis verò vxorum est, vt omnem maritis suis reuerentiam deferant, non stultos, asinos, stipites, &c. &c. appelleat. Hæc enim ab illarum officio sunt aliena. Sed & parentes liberos suos diligenter commonebunt, ne alijs probrosa nomina indant. Nam, vt hodie crimen illud vulgare sit, constat tamen, ex procaci ista conuitiandi libidine multas turbas excitatas, litesq; grauissimas contractas.
units.tr: Yet someone will ask whether Abigail acted as a good wife should when she calls her husband Belial and a fool. For Christ plainly says: "Whoever says to his brother, 'You fool', shall be liable to the fire of hell," Matth. 5, verse 22. I answer: he truly was Belial and a fool, and so she attacks him with no insult, but marks him by his own name. Those who knew him intimately regarded him as a fool. Some of the rabbis also say that this surname was given him from his folly. Moreover, whatever she says of him, she says not out of contempt but so as to preserve his life and head. For the surgeon sometimes cuts away a part of the flesh so that the whole body may be kept sound, which otherwise would perish. As for the rest, no one ought to assail another with insulting abuse or brand him with disgraceful names. Above all, it is the duty of wives to show all reverence to their husbands and not to call them fools, asses, blockheads, and so on. For such things are foreign to their office. Parents too shall diligently admonish their children not to give other people shameful names. For although that crime is now common, it is certain that many disturbances have been stirred up and very grave lawsuits brought about by this shameless lust for abuse.

units.la: Sed, quoniam obijci poterat, Si vir tuus, fatuus erat, te tamen, cum valeres ingenio, oportuit ista curare: secundum ab ignorantia argumentum addens : Ego vero ancilla tua, inquit, non videram pueros domini mei, quos miseras, quasi diceret. Si ipsa de legatione tua aliquid audiuissem, omnino operam dedissem, ne adeo inhumaniter esses acceptus. Ac reuera consentaneum est, illam, quod conuiuio isto tonsorio occupata esset, harum rerum omnium ignaram fuisse. Duplex omnino ignorantia est, Vna affectata ac tantumnon voluntaria: cum ignorare volunt homines, quod scire & assequi poterant: adeoq; scientes prudentes, & tantumnō videtibus oculis cæcutiunt. Alia involuntaria, quando ea quæ scire nostra inter esset, tūm demū rescimus, vbi in omnibus tribus sunt decantata. Hæc, vt aliquā excusatio nē meretur : ita illa plane est ἀπαθεσφαλης. Interim obscurè perstringit illos nuncios, quod nihil sibi indicassent, quod tamen factum in primis oportuit. Scultitia enim Nabalis, insignisq; morositas in vulgus nota erat. Obiter etiam Dauidi indicat, quanto se scelere astringeret, si eos, qui nihil de legatio ne ista audiuissent, quibusq; ex animo contumelia ista dolebat, vindictam deliberatam in actu producens, hostili ferro temerè sustulisset. Insontes certè defendendi sunt ab injuria, non temerè trucidandi.
units.tr: But since it could be objected, "If your husband was a fool, you nevertheless, while you were well in your wits, ought to have taken care of these matters," she adds a second argument from ignorance: "But I, your handmaid, my lord, did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent," as if to say: if I had heard anything about your embassy, I would certainly have seen to it that you were not received so inhumanly. And indeed it is fitting that she, being busy with that shearing feast, was ignorant of all these things. There are altogether two kinds of ignorance. One is affected, and almost wilful: men wish to be ignorant of what they could know and understand, so that, though knowing and prudent, they grow blind while seeing with their eyes. The other is involuntary, when we learn only then of things that it was in our interest to know, when they have been noised abroad among all three parties. The first of these deserves some excuse; the second is entirely blameless. Meanwhile, she obliquely reproaches the messengers for having told her nothing, though this in particular ought to have been done. For Nabal's folly and notorious surliness were known to the public. Along the way, she also points out to David how great a crime he would be bound to commit if, by drawing his sword in deliberate revenge, he rashly slew those who had heard nothing of this embassy and who were sincerely grieved by the insult. Innocent people must certainly be defended from injury, not rashly slaughtered.

units.la: Tertium argumentum sumit ab auctoritate, adeoq; prouidentia diuina, ac quo magis illum moueat, interponit iusiurandum. Nunc autem domine mi, inquit, viuit Iehoua, & viuit anima tua, qui prohibuit te Iehoua, ne venires in sanguines, & seruaret manus tua te, &c. Vetuit quidem Deus, ne sanguinem innocentem temerè fundamus. Nam mox à diluuio, Noëo cum suis arcam egressō, Gen.9. hominem priuilegio donat, ne sanguis illius effundatur: legemq; dat, vt qui sanguinem hominis effuderit, per hominē sanguis eius effundatur: vbi persona ordinatur imperans & puniens homicidia: non cuilibet homicidam interficiendi potestas datur. Additur ratio: Nam ad imaginem Dei fecit hominem, scilicet eius conditor. Deuter.32. Mihi vin-
units.tr: She takes a third argument from authority, and so from divine providence, and to move him more, she adds an oath: "Now, my lord," she says, "as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, the LORD has kept you from coming to bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand, etc." God has indeed forbidden us to shed innocent blood rashly. For soon after the flood, when Noah came out of the ark with his family, God granted to man the privilege that his blood should not be shed, and gave the law that whoever sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed (Gen. 9). There a person is appointed to command and punish murders; the power of killing a murderer is not given to just anyone. The reason is added: for he made man in the image of God, namely of his Creator. Deut. 32: "To me belongeth vengeance"

units.la: {a} Non temerè sanguinem fundendum. vindicta, inquit Dominus, & ego retribuam. In decalogo, Ne occidas, ait, id quod de privata vicifcendi libidine debet intelligi, non de Magistratus auctoritate, quam confirmat, dum illum malum ex populo auferre fe uerè mandat. Sed hæc isto loco non attingit Abigael. Tantum vult dicere, Nō esse, quod existimet Dauid, mulierculam sibi ista dicere, Deum ipsum fe excitaffe, vt ipsum à scelere retraheret. Quapropter illi saltem fidem adhibendam. Ac certè, quos Deus curat, eos non tantum bonis cumulat, sed etiam impedit, ne, quæ male cogitarunt, maiori scelere in opus educant. Plures enim sunt gratiæ priuatiuæ, quàm positiuæ, vt præclarè Gerfon. Quæ cum ita sint, non et, quod in illos, qui nos ab auaritia, scortandi libidine, ebrietate, arrogantia, odio, ira, alijsque vitijs dehortatur, acerbius inuehamur, illosq; malis auibus pedem ad nos tulisse vociferemur: Quin, quod res est, cogitemus, illos à Deo missos ad nos, ac, quod nobis confultum cupiant, merito audiendos esse. Sed quid? Vbi ab alio, etiam bono animo castigamur, mox cum Menedemo Terentiano: Tantúmne est (exclamemus) ab re tua ocij tibi, aliena vt cures, eaq; nihil quæ ad te attinent? Multi illos ad χόρακας amandant.
units.tr: {a} Blood is not to be shed rashly. "Vengeance is mine, saith the Lord, and I will repay." In the Decalogue it says, "Thou shalt not kill," which must be understood of private lust for revenge, not of the authority of the magistrate, which God confirms when he commands that evil be removed from the people. But Abigail does not touch on this point here. She only wishes to say that David should not think that a mere woman is saying these things to him, but that God himself has stirred her up to restrain him from crime. Therefore she should at least be given credence. And certainly, those whom God cares for, he not only loads with good things, but also hinders from carrying out into deed, through greater wickedness, what they have wickedly thought. For there are more graces of withholding than of bestowing, as Gerson rightly says. Since this is so, let us not rail more bitterly against those who turn us from avarice, lust for whoring, drunkenness, arrogance, hatred, anger and other vices, and cry out that they have come to us with evil omens. Rather, let us consider what is the case: that they have been sent to us by God, and that, since they desire what is good for us, they deserve to be heard. But what? When we are rebuked by someone else, even with good intent, we soon say with Terence's Menedemus: "Is it so much (let us exclaim) that you have leisure to meddle with what is not yours, and with what does not concern you?" Many send such people off to the ravens.

units.la: Exod. 20.
units.tr: Exod. 20.

units.la: Quod Papistæ ex eo, quod Abigael Deü & animam Dauidis coniungit, inferunt: Quid igitur prohibet vel per sanctos iurare duntaxat, vel per Deum & per sanctos?Idq; eo magis, quod & Helias & Sunamitis, adde & Helisæ hac forma vsi sint. Respondemus: Asseuerationem fuisse arbitrariam, non solenne conceptumq; iuramentum. At licere in gratiam fratris veritatem attestari, alias dimus. Iurauit & apostolus per animā suam. Ac hic quoq; existimamus tacitè insinuari Deum. Quid enim aliud est, Viuit anima tua quàm ita te Deus viuum seruet, vt hoc verū est, quod nunc testor, vel hoc facturus sum, quod polliceor? Sed & extra controuersiam est, Vitam & salutem Pharaonis, quam Ioseph um attestatū legimus, Deum esse ipsum. Atq; ad hunc modum dissecuerunt hunc nodum, qui ante nos dissecuerunt. Monet.
units.tr: What the Papists infer from the fact that Abigail joins God and David's soul: "What then prevents us from swearing only by the saints, or by God and the saints? And all the more so since Elijah and the Shunammite, and Elisha too, used this form." We reply: that was an arbitrary asseveration, not a solemn and formal oath. But it is lawful to call the truth to witness for the sake of a brother; we have said so elsewhere. The apostle also swore by his soul. And here too we think God is tacitly hinted at. For what else does "as your soul lives" mean than "as God keeps you alive" (in the sense that what I now testify is true, or what I promise I will do)? Moreover, it is beyond dispute that the life and health of Pharaoh, by which we read that Joseph swore, is God himself. And in this way they have untied the knot which others untied before us.

units.la: Quartum argumentū à voto seu compre catione trahens. Nunc autem sint (ait) sicut Nabal inimici tui & qui quærunt domino meo malum. Sensus est: Conuitiatus quidem est tibi maritus meus; Sed non est illis viribus, vt te posisit lædere. Vtinam omnes hostes tui reddantur ita imbecilles & fatui. Atque ita tibi nullum à quoquam periculum metuendum. tuendum erit. Ac certè maius nobis ab illis est periculum, qui nos quidem assentatorie in os adulantur & palpant: interim clancu- lum id vnum agunt, vt existimationem no- stram criminatorie arrodant, vel etiam vi- tam eripiant. Quidam tamen putant, Abi- gaelem his verbis prophetice prædicere, quid marito suo effet euenturum: nempe Deum vlturum iram suam in illum, etiam si- ne ipsius opera. Ideoque non esse, quod ve- lit vindictam ab isto homine petere: sed Deo illam relinquere. Sed prior sensus est sim- plicior.
units.tr: The fourth argument, drawn from a wish or a prayer. "Now then," she says, "let those who are your enemies and who seek evil for my lord be as Nabal." The sense is this: my husband has indeed reviled you, but he has no strength by which he could harm you. Would that all your enemies were made so feeble and foolish. And so you need fear no danger from anyone. And certainly we have more to fear from those who flatter and fawn upon us to our faces while, in secret, they aim at one thing only: to gnaw away at our reputation by slander, or even to snatch away our life. Some, however, think that Abigail by these words prophetically foretold what would happen to her husband: namely, that God would avenge his anger upon him even without her own effort. And so she need not ask this man for vengeance, but leave it to God. But the former sense is simpler.

units.la: Quærat autem aliquis, an pij rectè, Dei nomine inuocato, diris deuoueant alijsq; sa tuitatem, virium imbecillitatem, extremam pernitiem, &c. imprecentur. Respondeo: Si tanquam in proprios inimicos à nobis fiant imprecationes, merito damnatur. Iubemur enim diligere inimicos & pro ijs precari. Matt. 5. Sin verò in eos, tanquam Dei ipsius hostes deploratos & omnino cõuictos fiant, non damnantur: modò tamen nec temerè nec falsò, quosq; tales esse præsumamus.
units.tr: Someone may ask whether the godly rightly call down curses with the name of God invoked, and pray for the destruction of their enemies, their feebleness of strength, their utter ruin, and so on. I answer: if such imprecations are made by us as against our own enemies, they are rightly condemned. For we are commanded to love our enemies and pray for them (Matt. 5). But if they are made against those who are, as it were, God's own enemies, deemed hopeless and utterly convicted, they are not condemned, provided that they are not made rashly or falsely, and that we presume such people to be such.

units.la: His præmissis, offert illi munera: eaq; in- ter pueros eius distribui mandat. Nunc igi- tur, benedictio hæc, inquit, quam attulit an- cilla vna domino meo, detur pueris, qui ambulat ad pedes domini mei. Quasi dicat: Haud negauerim dona ista à me allata virtu te tua non esse digna : distribue tamen illa seruis tuis, ac non tam rem,quàm animum voluntatemq; specta,si perfacultates licuis-set, longè promtissimam. Ac certè vt pro-uerbiali Græcorum hemistichio fertur:
units.tr: With these things premised, she offers him gifts, and orders them to be distributed among his young men. "Now then," she says, "let this blessing, which your handmaid has brought to my lord, be given to the young men who follow at my lord's feet." As if to say: I would not deny that these gifts brought by me are not worthy of your virtue; nevertheless distribute them to your servants, and look not so much at the thing as at the spirit and will, which, had means allowed, would have been by far the most eager. And indeed, as the proverbial Greek half-line runs:

units.la: ξενίων ꝟ θυμὸς ἄριςϾ,
units.tr: [ξενίων ἢ θυμὸς ἄριστος]

units.la: Id est,interprete Erasmo:
units.tr: That is, in the translation of Erasmus:

units.la: Verum in muneribus res præstantissima mens est. Exemplo fuerit Xerxes ille, qui a-quam manibus haustam, à rustico libenter accepit. Et Christus viduæ numulos,omni-bus diuitum muneribus prætulit. Recteq;
units.tr: Truly, in gifts the most excellent thing is the mind. Let Xerxes be an example, who gladly accepted water drawn in cupped hands from a country man. And Christ preferred the widow's farthings to all the gifts of the rich. And rightly so.

units.la: Ethnicus Poeta:
units.tr: The heathen poet:

units.la: Parua quidem fateor, pro magnis munera reddi.Cum pro concessa verba salute damus.Sed qui, quàm potuit, dat maxima, gratus abun-de est,Et finem pietas contigit illa suum.Nec quæ de parua pauper diis libat acerra,Thura minus grandi quà data lance valent.Agnaq; tam lactens, quà gramina pasta FaliscoVictima Tarpeios inficit ista focos.
units.tr: I admit that small things are returned for great, when we give words for a salvation granted. But he who gives the greatest gifts as best he can is abundantly thankful, and that piety has reached its end. Nor does the poor man's little incense, offered from a little censer, count for less than incense given on a great dish. And the lamb, as milky as the grass on which it fed at Falerii, that victim stains the altars of the Tarpeian rock.

units.la: Prudenter autem & valdè εὐτέχνως Abi-gael nunc demum munera ista Dauidi of-fert, postquam sibi viam rationibus aliquot grauissimis aperuisset, beneuolentiamque comparasset. Quem enim oderunt homines, eum solent reijcere cum muneribus. Quid tua, inquiunt, dona curo? Facesse hinc ex oculis, aliaq; id genus: Videant ergo sacrificuli Papistarum, quid faciant, qui sese plus quàm confidenter iactant quotidie oferre filium Dei. Nam ea in re (vt praeclarè Martyr ad hunc locum) bis peccant. Primum quod dicant, se offerre Christum Patri suo, quem offerre non possunt: deinde etiam, quod putent, quamuis ipsi sint nequissimi, tamen munus illud suum gratum fore Deo. Munera enim placere non possunt, nisi ille, qui dedit, prius placeat. Vt enim alter amore mouetur, vt det, ita alter amore mouetur, vt accipiat. Sed haec obiter.
units.tr: Abigail, prudently and very skilfully, now at last offers these gifts to David, after she had opened the way for herself by several very weighty reasons and won his goodwill. For men are wont to reject with their gifts those whom they hate. "What do I care for your gifts?" they say. "Get out of my sight," and other such things. Let the little priests of the Papists therefore see what they do, who boast more than confidently every day that they offer up the Son of God. For in this matter (as Martyr rightly says on this passage) they sin twice. First, because they say that they offer Christ to his Father, which they cannot do; then also, because they think that, however wicked they themselves may be, their gift will nonetheless be pleasing to God. For gifts cannot please unless he who gives them is first pleasing. For just as the one is moved by love to give, so the other is moved by love to receive. But these things in passing.

units.la: Donum, Hebraeorum consuetudine, berachach, id est, benedictionem nominat. Forte ideo munera benedictionis nomine appellarùt, quod agnosceret, ea quae haberent omnia, à Deo, qui est προφικι sci: Item quod persuasissimum haberent, se promtè dona in egenos conferendo, benedictos iri à Deo. 1. Samuel. 30. Dauid, vbi in Siclag venit, de praeda senioribus Iudae mittens, En vobis benedictio, inquit, de spolijs inimicorum Iehouae. Genef. 33. Iacobus donum fratri mittens,Suscipe quæso,ait, ben e dictionem meam,id est,munus,obseruantiæ ergò oblatum. i.Regum quinto capite simi- liter Naaman ait Elisæ:Suscipe quæso bene- dictionem à feruo tuo. Sed & Paulus in nouo Testamento collectam pro pauperi- bus factam ευλογίαν id est, benedictionem vocat.2.Corinth.9.Capite. Erafmus tamen (vt hoc in transcursu addam)bonam colle- ctionem vertit, hanc vocem deriuans ab εὐ & λέγω,id est,colligo, quod eiusmodi col- lationes Apostolus vocarit λογίας,1.Cor. 16.vers.1.&2. Apostolus enim proculdu- bio respexit ad Hebræorum consuetudinē, qui berachach, vti modò diximus, pro eo, quod benignè ac vltrò datur, accipiunt.
units.tr: The Hebrews customarily call a gift berachach [ברכה], that is, a blessing. Perhaps they named gifts blessings because they acknowledged that they had all they possessed from God, who is the provider (sc. of all things), and because they were thoroughly persuaded that those who readily bestow gifts on the needy will be blessed by God. In 1 Samuel 30, when David came to Ziklag and sent spoil to the elders of Judah, he said: "Here is a blessing for you from the spoils of the enemies of Jehovah." In Genesis 33 Jacob, sending a gift to his brother, said: "Accept, I pray, my blessing," that is, the gift offered as a token of respect. Likewise in 1 Kings chapter 5 Naaman says to Elisha: "Accept, I pray, a blessing from your servant." But Paul too, in the New Testament, calls the collection made for the poor eulogia [εὐλογίαν], that is, a blessing (2 Corinthians chapter 9). Erasmus, however (to add this in passing), translates it "good collection," deriving the word from eu [εὖ] and legō [λέγω], that is, I gather, because the Apostle called such collections logiai [λογίαι] (1 Corinthians 16, verses 1 and 2). For the Apostle surely had regard to the custom of the Hebrews, who, as we have just said, take berachach for what is given kindly and freely.

units.la: Oblatis donis,principalem propositio- nem repetens,Parce, inquit, præuaricationi ancillæ tuæ. Supra enim crimen mariti in se transtulerat, quintumque argumentum à possessione regni firma addens.Certò,ait,fa- sturus est Iehoua domino meo domum fidelem: id est,certam,stabilem, constantem, vt re- gnum perpetuò sit in tua familia.Antithesis est ad regnum Saulis. Nam in eius domo possessio regni infirma erat & caduca.Si sef- uaueris,inquit, domum nostram sartam te- stam
units.tr: Having offered the gifts, and repeating her main proposition, she says: "Pardon the transgression of your handmaid." For above she had taken the husband's crime upon herself, and now she adds a fifth argument drawn from the firm possession of the kingdom: "Surely," she says, "Jehovah will make for my lord a faithful house," that is, a certain, stable, constant one, so that the kingdom will be perpetually in your family. This is set in contrast to the kingdom of Saul, for in his house the possession of the kingdom was weak and fleeting. "If you shall have preserved," she says, "our house..."

units.la: {a} perpetui tate regni. vers.28. stam ab omni detrimento, etiam Deus seruabit tuam, tuorumque. Quod si caedem iniuste perpetraueris, proculdubio euertes res tuas, vt Saul euertit suas. Verè Prophe-ta: Vae, inquit, praedanti, cum tu non sis praeda factus: cum praedari desieris, tu quoque sies. Sed & Christus: Qua mensura, ait, metimini, vicissim metientur vobis. Exempla, quae ei fidem faciant, passim obuia sunt in sacris & profanis literis, tam publica quàm priuata. Quae vtinam aliquanto diligentius considerarent nostri, quibus quaestus vberrimus & honestissimus videtur, si vili pecunia conducti bella gerant mercenaria, exterorum tyrannorum iniusta facta & consilia iuuent, terras alienas depraedentur, & multa praeda onusti domum redeant. Sed surdis canitur fabula: non deerit autem suis partibus vniuersalis ille totius orbis iudex Iesus Christus, qui gloriosò aduentu tyrannidem omnem coercebit, & suos asseret, vt secum in coelis viuant & regnent. Sed & in hoc saeculo vt plurimum, qui in captiuitatem ducit, in captiuitatem abibit; Qui gladio occidit, eum oportet gladio occidi. Sed de his infra plura. Possumus etiam legere. Sic tibi Deus domum fidelem faciat: vt non tam illi propheticè
units.tr: [a] the perpetuity of the kingdom. Verse 28. "...safe from all harm; God will also keep yours and your people's safe. But if you commit unjust slaughter, you will undoubtedly overthrow your affairs, as Saul overthrew his." Truly the prophet says: "Woe to the plunderer, since you were not plundered; when you cease to plunder, you too will be plundered." And Christ too: "With what measure you measure, it will be measured to you in return." Examples that confirm this are everywhere to be found in sacred and profane letters, public and private alike. Would that our people considered these things a little more carefully, for whom gain seems most abundant and most honourable if, hired for cheap money, they wage mercenary wars, aid the unjust deeds and plans of foreign tyrants, plunder foreign lands, and return home laden with much booty. But the tale is sung to deaf ears. Yet that universal judge of the whole world, Jesus Christ, will not be lacking to his own side, who by his glorious coming will restrain all tyranny and claim his own, that they may live and reign with him in heaven. Yet even in this age, for the most part, whoever leads into captivity will go into captivity; whoever kills with the sword must be killed with the sword. But more on these things below. We may also read: "So may God make for you a faithful house," so that not so much in a prophetic manner...

units.la: Sextum argumentū ab officio pij & iusti bellatoris,bonaq;, qua haftenus commenda tisimus fuerit omnibus, fama & existima- tione trahens. Prælia, Iehouæ dominus meus prœliatus est: et malitia non inuenta fuit in te diebus tuis. Dauid haftenus strenuâ in bellis operâ nauarat,caputq; suum aduersus Pale- stinos aliosq; Dei hostes pro salute patriæ fortissimè obiectarat,eamq; à vi externa tu- tatus erat, rectè igitur Abigael eum prœlia- torem Domini vocat,tacitèq; illum,nec mi- nus in loco,muneris sui atque officij admo- net.Haftenus,inquit, te semper præclarè gè- rens:nulla vnquam sinistrafama laborastiū nulla grauiora scelera irruisti, quod viris e- tiam bonis, præsertim vernante sanguine e- uenit: Vide igitur sis,ne existimationem il- lam tuam illibatam deperdas, ac nunc demū innoxio sanguine te conspurces.Deus enim dedit tibi robur,vt prælieris prælia Domini. Ea tu non debes tanta turpitudine commaculare. Ne admisceas latrocinia tuis tantis victorijs. Deus enim te ad pugnandum vocauit,non ad latrocinandum.Quare non opprimes innocentes, sed parces supplicibus. Commune enim ius supplicum violare, tur pissimum esset heroico bellatori.
units.tr: The sixth argument, drawn from the duty of a pious and just warrior, and from the reputation and esteem that good deeds bring, which I have hitherto commended to all: "The battles of Jehovah my lord has fought, and no wickedness has been found in you in your days." Hitherto David had laboured vigorously in wars and had boldly exposed himself against the Philistines and other enemies of God for the safety of his country, and so he had been protected from external violence. Rightly, therefore, Abigail calls him the warrior of the Lord, and quietly, and no less aptly, reminds him of his office and duty. "Hitherto," she says, "you have always acted with distinction; no sinister rumour has ever troubled you, nor have you fallen into more serious crimes, which happens even to good men, especially when blood is hot. See to it, then, that you do not lose that good reputation unblemished, and do not now at last defile yourself with innocent blood. For God has given you strength so that you may fight the battles of the Lord. You ought not to stain these with such disgrace. Do not mingle robbery with your great victories. For God has called you to fight, not to plunder. Therefore do not oppress the innocent, but spare suppliants. For to violate the common right of suppliants would be most shameful for a heroic warrior."

units.la: Colligimus hinc, Militiam non omnem improbari, modò prælieris Domino: id est, vt clarius dicam, quod sentio, dummodo gloriam Dei spectemus, salutemque patriæ promotam cupiamus. Bellum, quod à belluis dici recte Festus ait, aliud iustum est, aliud iniustum. Quanquam, si verè agere volumus, bellum iniustum non est bellum. Est enim potius latrocinium. Bellum autem iustum ita potest non incomodè definiri. Est dissensio hostilis, qua edicto principis (principem homini priuato opponimus) vi & armis scelera reprimuntur, vt homines pacatè & tranquillè ex iustitia & pietate posint viuere. Hinc colliguntur tres illæ conditiones quæ vulgò feruntur de bello recte gerendo. Primò requiri auctoritatem publicam: deinde vt sit iusta causa, vt cum nostri hostes improbè facta non vindicant, & ablata non restituunt. Tertiò rectum propositum, ne sub prætextu bonæ causæ alia quæramus. Multum enim refert rem bonam per se, recto animo à nobis perfici. Quanuis autem bellum sit iustum, non tamen statim geri debet. Omnia tentanda potius quàm vt ad armma deueniatur. Imò, vt parcatur ciuili sanguini, sæpe recipiendæ sunt conditiones, quas videantur paulò iniquiores. Medici certè non vrunt aut secant, nisi cum totum corpus quodamodo videatur periclitari. Iam & hoc constat, præterquam quod multa in bel lo accidunt sæua & atrocia, ne finem qui- dem, vbi semel cœperis, imponere potes, vbi velis. Itaque Homerus rectè dixit: Omnium rerum facietatem esse aliquam, præterquam belli. Quod si res aliter componi non pos- sint, & possunt & debent Magistratus, ditio nes suas cum subditis armata manu tueri, in iuriasq; illatas propulsare. Nam si tradita il- lis est potestas, qua ditioni suæ quietem tue- antur, qua inquietorum hominum seditio- sos motus comprimant, qua vi oppressis o- pitulentur, qua in maleficia animaduertant: an maiore opportunitate proferre eam pos- sint, quàm ad capessendum eorum furorem, à quibus & priuatim singulorum ocium & communis omnium tranquillitas perturba- tur : qui seditiosè tumultuantur, à quibus violentæ oppresiones & indigna maleficia perpetrantur. Si legum custodes esse ipsos, & assertores conuenit, omnium conatus pa riter euertant oportet, quorum scelere le- gum disciplina corrumpitur. Imò si iure eos latrones plectunt, quorum iniuriæ in pau- cos tantum progressæ fuerint, an totam la- trocinijs regionem impunè affligi vastariq; sinent? Siquidem nihil interest, rex ne sit, an infima de plebe, qui in alienam regionem, in quam iuris nihil habet, irruit, eamq; hostiliter vexat: omnes aequè pro latronibus habendi sunt & puniendi. Sed & subditi eo rerum statu nullum vnquam principibus susis periculum denegabunt, quia corpora sua pro defensione illorum praesentissimae etiam morti obiectabunt, patriamq; pro virili parte defendere ac tueri conabuntur. Vt enim aures atq; oculos principum vocare vulgò solent eorum consiliarios: ita non insulte principum manus quis dicat, quos rebus agendis mandato suo praefecerint.
units.tr: From this we gather that not all military service is condemned, provided you fight for the Lord; that is, to speak more plainly what I think, provided we look to the glory of God and desire that the safety of our country be advanced. War, which Festus rightly says is named from beasts (bellua), is one thing just and another unjust. Yet if we wish to speak truly, an unjust war is not war at all; it is rather robbery. A just war, however, may not inconveniently be defined thus: it is a hostile contention by which crimes are repressed by force and arms, by the edict of a prince (we set the prince against a private person), so that men may live peacefully and quietly in justice and piety. From this are gathered the three conditions commonly laid down for waging war rightly. First, public authority is required. Second, there must be a just cause, so that our enemies do not avenge wrongs done and restore what they have taken away. Third, there must be a right purpose, lest under the pretext of a good cause we seek other things. For it matters greatly that a thing good in itself be carried out by us with a righteous mind. However, although a war be just, it must not be waged at once. Everything should be tried before we come to arms. Indeed, to spare civil blood, conditions often must be accepted which seem somewhat less fair. Doctors certainly do not burn or cut unless the whole body seems in some way endangered. Moreover, this too is established: apart from the fact that many savage and atrocious things happen in war, you cannot even impose an end on it when you wish, once you have begun. So Homer rightly said that there is some satiety of all things except war. But if matters cannot otherwise be settled, magistrates both can and ought to defend their dominions with armed hand, together with their subjects, and to repel the wrongs inflicted upon them. For if the power has been handed to them by which they protect the quiet of their dominion, by which they curb the seditious movements of restless men, by which they aid the oppressed with force, and by which they punish wrongdoers, could they bring that power to bear with greater justification than against those whose madness disturbs both the private leisure of individuals and the common tranquillity of all, who riot seditiously, and by whom violent oppressions and unworthy crimes are committed? If it is agreed that magistrates are the guardians and upholders of the laws, they ought equally to overthrow the attempts of all those by whose crime the discipline of the laws is corrupted. Indeed, if they rightly punish robbers whose injuries have extended to only a few, will they allow a whole region to be afflicted and laid waste by robbers with impunity? For it makes no difference whether a man is a king or the lowest of the common people, if he rushes into another's region, over which he has no right, and harasses it as an enemy: all alike are to be regarded and punished as robbers. Subjects too, in such a state of affairs, will never refuse any danger on behalf of their princes, since they will expose their bodies even to imminent death for their defence, and will strive to defend and protect their country to the best of their power. For just as princes are commonly accustomed to call their counsellors their ears and eyes, so, not without reason, one may call the hands of princes those whom they have set over affairs to be carried out at their command.

units.la: Ex his, quae hactenus de iusto bello diximus, facile colligere est, quid iniusti belli no mine intelligendum veniat. Nempe, si quis nulla accedente publica auctoritate, nulla lacesitus iniuria, cum quietè posset agere, nocendi cupiditate, vindicandi crudelitate, dominandi libidine, alioue prauo affectu arma sumat, aliorum libertatem oppugnet, sedibusque auitis exturbare moliatur: suosque ad res illicitas violenter cogat. Hinc non est, quod operam accomodent subditi. Neque enim debent esse subditi laniones, & immoderatorum Magistratus affectuū exe cutores & ministri. In Domino est parendum, Sednec ille præliari domino rectè dicipotest. qui de quaestu tantum sollicitus, quaeuis caustra sequitur, non curans an ille, cui operam suam accomodat, iustam ne habeat causam secusue. Quod tamen hodie nimis vulgare est. Quantus enim illorum numerus est, qui contra magistratuum suorum edicta, reclamante item conscientia, operam suam vilissimo precio conducti, illis locant, quos iam pridem ad extinguendam veritatem conspirasse noruntʼ Quae causa est, ut absque omni dicrimine pro hostibus habeat omnes ex quibus praeda sperari potest. Etsi aute nonnunquam magnam pecuniam colligant ex caedibus, tamen tandem cum ipsis, Deo ordinante, iure talionis agitur.
units.tr: From what we have said so far about just war, it is easy to gather what must be understood by the name of unjust war. Namely, if anyone, with no public authority intervening and provoked by no injury, when he could act quietly, takes up arms from a desire to harm, a cruel lust for revenge, a passion for domination, or some other perverse affection; if he attacks the liberty of others, strives to drive them from their ancestral seats, and violently forces his own people into unlawful acts, then that is unjust war. Hence subjects ought not to lend their help to such a man, for subjects ought not to be butchers, nor the executioners and ministers of immoderate magistrates' passions. "One must obey the Lord," but neither can he rightly be said to fight for the Lord who, anxious only about gain, follows any camp whatever, not caring whether the man to whom he lends his service has a just cause or not. Yet this is too common today. For how great is the number of those who, against the edicts of their own magistrates, and with their conscience protesting too, hire out their service at the cheapest price to those whom they know have long since conspired to extinguish the truth! The reason is that they regard as enemies, without any distinction, all from whom plunder can be hoped for. And although they sometimes gather large sums of money from slaughter, in the end, with God ordaining it, they are dealt with by the law of retaliation.

units.la: Videmus etiam, fame cumprimis consulendum. Nam vt vere Salomon, Lectius est nomen bonum, amplis diuitijs: & gratia bona, id est, fauor ac beneuolentia hominum, quae famae comes est, preciosior est quovis argento & auro. Ecclesiast. 7. voluptati, quae suauibus vnguentorum odoribus delectatur, opponit boni nominis σουὰα quam illis longe antecellere affirmat. Hanc igitur bonae famae voluptatem, quam bene, temperanter, iuste viuendo coparamus, omnibus diuitiarum, deliciarum, honorumque voluptatibus longe anteponere debemus: ac proinde hae de hac in re maximè elaborare, non vt diui-tijs,honoribus,delitijs cæteros mortales su peremus(quæ nos ipsos in extremo mortis discrimine derelinquunt)sed vt ita viuamus quò nos benè vixisse grata nobis superstitū hominū recordatio testetur, illorūq; fausta & amica cõmemoratio nos, quasi viuos hominū animis representet. Confultè Poeta: Omnia si perdas famam seruare memento,
units.tr: We see also that above all we must take thought for our reputation. As Solomon truly says, "A good name is better than great riches," and "good grace," that is, the favour and goodwill of men, which accompanies a good name, is more precious than any silver or gold (Eccles. 7). Setting pleasure, which delights in the sweet scents of ointments, against a good name, he says that the fragrance [εὐωδία] of a good name far surpasses it. Therefore we ought to set the pleasure of a good reputation, which we win by living well, temperately and justly, far above all the pleasures of riches, luxury and honours. Accordingly we should labour chiefly at this, not to outdo other mortals in wealth, honours and pleasures (which leave us in the extremity of death), but so to live that the grateful remembrance of the living testifies that we have lived well, and that their kindly and favourable commemoration of us represents us, as if alive, in the minds of men. The poet wisely says: "If you lose everything, remember to keep your good name, which once lost, you will be nobody."

units.la: Qua semel amissa,postea nullus eris.
units.tr: "Which once lost, you will be nobody."

units.la: Satanas vellet nos, semel lapsos, nunquam resurgere, sed in peccatis pergere. At con-tracta semel vitio macula,omnino feria resi-piscentia,quam quidam veterum non inele ganter secundam tabulam dixit, est eluen-da. Vt enim confracta naui,vnum vitæ seruandæ perfugium reliquum est, si forte tabulam aliquam de naufragio licet arripere: ita,post admissum crimen, nisi quis fide in Christum ad pœnitentiæ tabulam cöfugiat, sine dubio de eius salute desperandum est. Sed de his alibi quoq;.
units.tr: Satan would wish us, once we have fallen, never to rise again but to persist in sin. But once a stain has been contracted by vice, it must be washed away entirely by repentance, which some of the ancients not inaptly called the second plank. For when a ship is wrecked, the only refuge left for saving one's life is, if by chance, to grasp some plank from the wreck; so, after a crime has been committed, unless a person flees by faith in Christ to the plank of repentance, there is no doubt that his salvation must be despaired of. But of these things elsewhere also.

units.la: Sextò,Surrexit homo,inquit,ad persequen-dum te, & ad quærendum animam tuam: Sed illenon poterit tibi incommodare. Loqui-tur de Saule,qui Dauidem nunc ex insidijs, iam aperto Marte petens nulla iusta de cau sa,sublatum volebat.Sed & haud semel,tanquam in iuratum regni hostem, magnas in illum copias eduxerat. Verum spem illi faecit certissimam, fore, ut superior euadat David. Deum enim ipsum aduersus omnes hostium conatus defensurum. Homo quidam, inquit, te persequitur & te iam coegit in angustias: Verum si tu nobis perceris, erit anima Domini mei ligata in fasciculo vitae cum Iehova Deo tuo.Id est hostis ille tuus vitam nunquam tibi auferet. Suavissima phrasi dicit: Vitam Davidis colligatam fore cum Deo in fasciculo viventium. Res enim magni precij solemus diligenter colligere, ne nobis excidant. Pecunias bene colligatas, de collo suspendimus. Non dubium autem est, quin Deum Davidis Deum eo nomine vocet, quod illius opem & auxilium in rebus asperis saepius experitus esset.
units.tr: Sixthly: "A man has risen," it says, "to pursue you and to seek your soul." But he will not be able to harm you. This is said of Saul, who, now seeking David by ambush and now openly in war, wished him destroyed for no just cause. And more than once, as against a sworn enemy of the kingdom, he had led great forces against him. Yet the Lord gave David the most certain hope that he would prevail in the end, for God himself would defend him against all the attempts of his enemies. "A man," it says, "pursues you and has already driven you into straits. But if you are cut off by him, 'the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the LORD your God.'" That is, that enemy of yours will never take your life from you. She speaks in a most lovely figure: David's life will be bound up with God in the bundle of the living. For we are accustomed to gather carefully things of great value, lest they slip from us; we hang well-tied money from our necks. And there is no doubt that by the name God she means the God of David, because he had often experienced his help and aid in hard circumstances.

units.la: Quod de Dauide dicit Abigael, id ad pios omnes transferri potest. Enimuero Deus omnes in vniuersum pios συνδεδεμένους instar colligatos, sibi obstringit. Quod vel externo cum Abrahamo & femine eius pacto foedere elucet, Seminis enim nomine, non eos tantum intelligit, qui secundum carnem ab illo descendunt, sed quotquot in vnum Deum omnes spem suam ac fiduciam, Abrahami
units.tr: What Abigail says of David can be applied to all the godly. Indeed God in general binds all the godly to himself, as if they were bound together [συνδεδεμένους]. This is made clear even by the external covenant with Abraham and his seed; for by the name of seed he understands not only those who descend from him according to the flesh, but all who place their hope and trust in the one God, following the example of Abraham.

units.la: Quomodo anima Davidis in fasciculo viventium fuerit colligata. rahami exemplo collocant. Paulus enim fideles spirituales Abrahami filios vocat, Ex quibus omnibus efficitur, Deum se nobis quoque coniunxisse. Sed & arctissima illa necessitudo, quae nobis cum Deo intercedit, sanctissima maris & foeminae coniunctione, seu, ut uno verbo dicam, connubio declaratur. Quemadmodum enim ex humanis necessitatibus nulla inter se homines magis, quam matrimonij vinculum constringit: maximaque inter se vir & uxor charitate & beneuolentia deuincti sunt: ita Deus viscera pietatis effundit in pios, mutuumque amorem pollicitus parem experitur. De hoc vinculo Paulus ita scribit ad Romanos: Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? Id est, qua nos Deus in Christo vero animarum sponso dilexit? num oppressio num angustia, num persecutio, num fames, num nuditas, num periculum, num gladius? Imo in his omnibus plus quam victores sumus per eum qui dilexit nos. Nam mihi persuasum est neque morte neque vitam, neque angelos, neque principatus, neque potestates, neque instantia, neque futura, neque sublimitatem, neque profunditatem, neque vllam rem aliam creatam posse nos separare a charitate Dei, quae est in Christo Iesu, Domino nostro.
units.tr: How the soul of David was bound in the bundle of the living. For Paul calls the faithful the spiritual sons of Abraham. From all these things it follows that God has also joined himself to us. And that very close bond which exists between us and God is declared by the most holy union of man and woman, or, to say it in one word, by marriage. For just as no bond among human relationships binds people together more than the marriage bond, and husband and wife are bound to each other by the greatest love and goodwill, so God pours out the bowels of mercy upon the godly and, having promised mutual love, experiences an equal love in return. Paul writes about this bond to the Romans: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" That is, the love with which God loved us in Christ, the true bridegroom of souls: "Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?"
