Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.la: {a}Et Cbriftus de ea dem colligatione apud Ioannem, Oues meæ, inquit, vocem meam audiunt & sequuntur me: Et nemo eas poterit rapere de manu mea, &c.
units.tr: {a} Christ also, concerning this same binding, says in John: "My sheep hear my voice, and follow me. And no one shall snatch them out of my hand," etc.

units.la: Obseruandum autem est, Abigaelem non simpliciter dicere, Deus hostes tuos præcipites aget: sed anima aduersariorum tuorum, tanquam lapis ex funda excussus, rotabitur & in abyssum gehennæ præcipitabitur, vbi luctus est & stridor dentium. Quod Sauli aliisque hostibus Dauidis accidit, id omnibus fidelium hostibus certò eueniet, nisi mature resipiscant. Neque est, quod illorum iubilis & ouationibus moueamur. Quanuis enim nunc effusè cachinnentur, & sibi delitias faciant: tamen certo certius est, reseorum breui commutatas, risumque in eiulatum conuertendum iri. Lapis aliquandiu iacet in funda immotus: verum vbi primum ille vult, qui fundam manu tenet rotatur, & in aerem effunditur. Ita impij, plerunque nihil minus expectantes, à Deo disiecti in æternum supplicium rotantur. Id quod Salomon pulcherrima similitudine à turbine desumpta ostendit Prouerbiorum capite decimo. Vt transit turbo, ait, sic non erit impius: Iustus autem immotus manet.
units.tr: It must be observed that Abigail does not simply say, "God will cast down your enemies," but that the souls of your adversaries, like a stone hurled from a sling, will be whirled round and cast into the abyss of hell, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. What happened to Saul and David's other enemies will certainly happen to all the enemies of the faithful, unless they repent in time. Nor should we be moved by their rejoicing and exultation. For although they now laugh loudly and make merry for themselves, it is nonetheless more certain than certain that their pleasures will soon be changed, and their laughter turned into wailing. A stone lies for a while motionless in the sling; but as soon as he who holds the sling wishes, it is whirled and flung into the air. So the wicked, most often expecting nothing less, are cast down by God and whirled into eternal punishment. Solomon shows this by a most beautiful likeness drawn from a whirlwind in the tenth chapter of Proverbs: "As the whirlwind passes, so the wicked is no more, but the righteous remains immovable."

units.la: {a} Impij subito perient.
units.tr: {a} The wicked shall perish suddenly.

units.la: Vltimum
units.tr: The last point

units.la: Vltimum argumentum ex loco commu-ni de conscientia adducens: Quum autem fecerit Iehoua domino meo bonum, ait, iuxta omnia, quæ loquutus est de te & præceperit tibi, vt sis dux supra Israelem: Tunc non erit hoc domino meo in offendiculum & offensionem cordis et quod effuderit sanguinem sine causa, aut quod fecerit salutem dominus meus sibi, &c. Sensus est: Postquā Deus tibi benefecerit, & tu potitus fueris rerum, non erit tibi hoc offendiculum, ad quod cor tuum, tanquam pedes ad lapidem, impingat. Pollicetur ergo, quasi præmij loco, pacatam conscientiam: qua certe nihil est suauius & iucundius, vt è contra perturbata nihil est grauius & horribilius. Cuius rei exemplum in facinorosis euidentissimum habemus. Latrones plærunque omnes latrociniorum circumstantias referre possunt, Fures furtorum, etiam multiplicium, non facile obliuiscuntur. Quamuis autem nonnunquam præterire videatur flagitium, tamen perpetuò cubat in foribus, nec patitur authorem tranquilla esse conscientia: quæ, vt ad tempus dormire appareat, tamen suo tempore euigilat: & si non ante, saltem in agone mortis, mille testium instar, adstans, delictorum nostrorum (vt præclarè quodam loco Bernardus) ipsa testis est, ipsa iudex,ipsa tortor,ipsa accusat,ipsa iudi‐cat,ipsa punit,ipsa damnat. Multi, qui, flo‐rente ætate,quęstus caussa quæuis castra fe‐quuti sunt, aduentante senio à conscientia intus accusati, nonnunquam in agone mor‐tis desperant. Philippus posterior, post ne‐cem filij Demetrij animo magis quam cor‐pore æger,curisq; & vigilijs,cum identidem species & vmbrę insontis interemti filij eum diris agitarent,extin⁢ctus est cum execratio‐nibus Perfei.Hanc senserè Poetæ, cum de a‐quila Promethei fabulantur, quæ illius cor subinde enascens,rostro vellicet & contun‐dat. Sed & Cicero ait, non eas esse Furias, quæ finguntur à Poetis,sed eas, quæ perpe‐tuò verberant & cruciant animos sceleris a‐licuius malę sibi conscios. Quæ cum ita sint, à sceleribus sedulo cauendum erit ne conscientiam aggrauemus, magni faciamus hunc testem,& vbiq; præsentem metuamus. Dei sanè est vicarius longè oculatisimus,nec il‐lum latere quidquam possumus. Seuerus quoq; censor est,qui ad tribunalDei nihil de rigore iuris remittit. Pacatam autem studio innocentis vitæ & fiducia μεσίτυ nostri Christi,habituri sumus.
units.tr: Taking his final argument from the common topic of conscience, he adds: "When the LORD has dealt well with my lord, according to all that he has spoken concerning you and has appointed you to be prince over Israel, then this will not be a stumbling-block or a cause of grief of heart to my lord, that he shed blood without cause or that my lord avenged himself, etc." (1 Sam. 25.30–31). The sense is this: after God has dealt well with you and you have come into possession of affairs, this will not be a stumbling-block for you, against which your heart would strike as the feet strike a stone. He therefore promises a peaceful conscience as a kind of reward, and surely nothing is sweeter or more pleasant, just as, on the other hand, nothing is heavier or more dreadful than a disturbed conscience. We have a very clear example of this in wicked men. Almost all robbers can recall the circumstances of their robberies, and thieves do not easily forget their thefts, even when they are many. Although sometimes a crime seems to be forgotten, it nevertheless lies constantly at the door and does not allow its author a quiet conscience. Though it may appear to sleep for a time, it wakes at its appointed hour, and if not before, at least in the agony of death it stands by, like a thousand witnesses. As Bernard says excellently in one place, it is itself the witness, itself the judge, itself the torturer, itself the accuser, itself the one who passes sentence, itself the one who punishes and condemns our sins. Many who, in the flower of their age, pursued any camp at all for the sake of gain, when old age comes and they are accused within by their conscience, sometimes despair in the agony of death. Philip the younger, after the death of his son Demetrius, was sick in mind more than in body, and with cares and sleeplessness, since the images and shades of the innocent son he had killed kept tormenting him with dreadful visions, he died cursing, like Perseus. The poets understood this when they tell the fable of the eagle of Prometheus, which kept growing again in his heart and was continually plucked and battered by its beak. Cicero too says that the Furies are not those that poets invent, but those that constantly lash and torment the minds of those who are conscious of some wicked crime. Since these things are so, we must take careful care to avoid sins, lest we burden our conscience; let us hold this witness in high regard and fear him as present everywhere. He is indeed the most watchful deputy of God, and we cannot escape his notice. He is also a severe censor, who relaxes nothing of the strictness of the law at God's tribunal. But we shall have a conscience at peace through zeal for an innocent life and through trust in our mediator [μεσίτου], Christ.

units.la: In peroratione, Recordaberis, ait, ancillæ tuæ. Quidam putant,eam prophetico spiri‐tu præ‐ tu prædicere, sefore vxorem Dauidis. Potest tamen non incommodè exponi generaliter. Nam, si quid fausti alicui prædicimus, solemus addere:in tanta tua felicitate memineris mei.Ita Iofephus, cum prædixisset, pocillatorem Pharaonis rediturum ad gradum suum, subiecit, Vbi hæc euenerint, memor esto mei.Id quod ille post biennium demum præstitit. Forte quod non ausus es-set vllam Iosephi mentionem facere,ne quid inuidiæ subiret vel molestus esset ipsi regi. Hoc enim aulicis solenne est, perfidè infon-tes prodere & potius tradere iugulandos, quam vt offendant eos à quibus metuunt. Potest etiam hic esse sensus : Abigaelem, cum videret Nabalem esse moriturum & se fore viduam, prudenter considerasse, tum demum sibi opus fore alieno præsidio, &c.
units.tr: In the conclusion he says, "Remember your handmaid" (1 Sam. 25.31). Some think that she, by prophetic spirit, foretold that she would become the wife of David. It can nevertheless be explained without difficulty in a general way. For when we predict some happy outcome for someone, we are accustomed to add: "In your great good fortune, remember me." So Joseph, after he had foretold that Pharaoh's cupbearer would return to his position, added: "When these things come to pass, remember me" (Gen. 40.14), which he did only after two years. Perhaps Abigail did not dare to make any mention of Joseph, lest it bring some ill will upon her or be troublesome to the king himself. For it is customary for courtiers to betray the guilty treacherously, and to hand them over to be slaughtered rather than offend those whom they fear. There may also be this sense here: Abigail, seeing that Nabal was about to die and that she would be a widow, had wisely considered that she would then need the protection of another.

units.la: Elegans ista & suauis prudentis matronæ oratio multas, easque insignes doctri-nas complectitur: quarum partem recen-suimus: partem sequenter indicabimus. Ac primo quidem exemplum fidelis coniugis in Abigaele proponitur.Laudantur in histo-rijs Romanis Sabinæ, quæ precibus & inter-cursu suo prælium inter maritos & parentes diremerunt. Sed longè iustius laudatur Abi-gael, quæ illustri & ad omne posteritatis memoriam celebri facto, pietate suam erga maritum declarauit. Quamuis enim Nabal eam qua erat asperitate, indignius aliquanto tractaret: tamen illa nullum illi periculum denegat, sed pro salute illius, non fine capitis discrimine, apud Dauidem, ira tantum non ardentem, quàm diligentissimè intercedit. Fuissent, quæ eadem mariti non tantum exoptassent, sed & pro parte procurassent, dummodo ipsæ euasissent. Nō ita ista: Quin, vt maritum seruarent, quod aiunt, tectum ab omni detrimento conseruet, innocentem se pro fonte opponit, crimenque, vt diximus, in se ipsam transfert. Quod quid aliud est, quàm morte sua incolumitatem viri redimere velle?
units.tr: This elegant and pleasant speech of a prudent matron contains many and notable teachings, some of which we have listed and others we shall indicate in order. First of all, in Abigail the example of a faithful wife is set before us. The Sabine women are praised in Roman histories, who by their prayers and by their going between broke up the battle between their husbands and their fathers. But Abigail is praised far more justly, who by an illustrious deed, famous for all the memory of posterity, declared her devotion to her husband. For although Nabal treated her somewhat more unworthily, with the harshness that was in him, she nonetheless did not refuse him any danger, but on behalf of his safety, not without risk to her own life, most diligently interceded with David, who was almost on fire with anger. There have been women who not only wished for the same thing for their husbands, but even contributed their share towards it, provided that they themselves escaped. Not so this woman. Indeed, to keep her husband safe, to preserve him, as they say, untouched by any harm, she places herself before him as a guilty party, and, as we have said, transfers the crime onto herself. What else is this than wishing to redeem her husband's safety with her own death?

units.la: Huius exemplo mulieres, hodie quoque maritos, tametsi ipsis non in omnibus indulgeant, tamen non continuo deferant, vel etiam eadem clanculum moliantur, sed causam Deo committentes, ipsius opem patienter expectent, hac suffultæ spe, fore, vt à Deo non opprimantur, sed tempore cum primis opportuno liberentur. Nec enim is nos finit tentari supra id quod possumus: sed vnà cum tentatione etiam euasionem præstat, vt ferendo oneri pares simus. 1.Cor.10.
units.tr: Following her example, women today too, even though they do not indulge their husbands in everything, nevertheless do not at once abandon them, nor secretly plot the same things, but, committing their cause to God, patiently await his help, sustained by this hope: that they will not be crushed by God, but will be freed at the most opportune time. For he does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but together with the temptation he also provides the way of escape, so that we may be able to bear the burden (1 Cor. 10.13).

units.la: Secundo loco colligimus, quid nostri sit officij, si, Nabalis exemplo, vel nostri vel nos ipsi,alios verbo vel re priores læsimus. Nempe,vt Abigaelem factum mariti nec ne- gasse nec defendisse audiuimus, sed tantum culpam deprecatam esse: Ita nos quoq; non temere crimen admissum inficiabimur, ex- tenuabimus,sed ingenuè confitebimur, ve- niaq, petita spem faciemus, nos porrò pru- dentiores fore.Huc & Christi illud: Si mu- nus tuum,ait,attuleris ad altare, & illic me- mineris fratrem tuum habere aliquid con- tra te,omitte illic munus tuum coràm alta- ri,& abi:primùm reconciliator fratri tuo, & tùm veniens, offer munus tuum. Est autem obseruandum,vt hoc obiter annotem, Chri stum accommodare totam hanc commoni- tionem ad temporum suorum ratione.Itaq; inepti sunt, qui ex eo loco habenda nunc es- se altaria & vsurpandas eiusmodi oblationes colligunt.Cęterum hoc loco etiam atque e- tiam videndum erit,vt reconciliatio sit sin- cera,& ab omni dolo ac fraude aliena.Enim uero,vt inter homines nemini bono proba- tur,qui,vt prouerbio dicitur, vna manu pa- nem,altera lapidem ostentant,ita multò mi- nus Deo:qui cum sit ipsisima Veritas,nihil perinde vt mendacium & hypocrisin dete- statur,imprimis eam,quæ saluti aliorum infidias struit, & sub amicitiæ simulatione ad morem Iudæ nocere studet. Neque verò negauerim, esse, qui suæ non parum existimationi decedere putent, si veniam ab ijs petant, quos ipsi priores læserunt. Sed quicquid stultè isti ambitiosi metuant: certum tamen est, amplissimam hic sese offerre veræ & immortalis gloriæ materiam. Nam & nos ipsos vincimus, qua victoria nullam difficiliorem atq; gloriosiorem esse gentium quoque sapientes intellexerunt: & nobis amicos facimus ex inimicis: adhæc Dei exemplum imitati, nosipsos & alios seruamus: denique ex eo nouam animi fiduciam concipimus, qua confirmati in Dei conspectum prodire: huic nostra officia deferre & eundem inuocare audemus.
units.tr: Secondly, we gather what our duty is, if, following the example of Nabal, either we or others have wronged others, by word or deed, before us. Just as Abigail, when she heard of her husband's deed, neither denied it nor defended it, but only asked pardon for the fault, so we too shall not rashly deny a crime we have committed; we shall lessen it not, but openly confess it, and by seeking forgiveness we shall give hope that we will be wiser from then on. To this belongs also Christ's saying: "If you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift" (Matt. 5.23–24). It must be observed, as I note in passing, that Christ adapted this whole admonition to the circumstances of his own times. Therefore those are foolish who gather from this passage that altars and such offerings are now to be kept and used. Moreover, in this place we must also see to it that the reconciliation is sincere and free from all deceit and fraud. For indeed, just as among men no good man approves of one who, as the proverb says, shows bread in one hand and a stone in the other, so much less does God, who, being very Truth itself, abhors nothing so much as lying and hypocrisy, above all that which lays snares for the salvation of others and, under a pretence of friendship, strives to do harm after the manner of Judas. Nor would I deny that there are some who think they lose no little of their reputation if they ask pardon of those whom they themselves wronged first. But whatever these ambitious men foolishly fear, it is nonetheless certain that here is set before us a most ample matter for true and immortal glory. For we conquer ourselves, a victory which the wise men of the nations also understood to be none more difficult or more glorious; we make friends of enemies; moreover, imitating the example of God, we save both ourselves and others; finally, from this we conceive a new confidence of spirit, by which, strengthened, we dare to come into the sight of God, to offer him our duties, and to call upon him.

units.la: In primis verò Deo peccata confitenda sunt, idq; priuatim & publicè, cuius rei exempla multa leguntur in scripturis. Nihil enim minus consentaneum est, quam vt peccata ignoscat Deus, in quibus nobis ipsi blandimur: & ne in lucem proferat, prætegimus per hypocrisin. Quando tacui, inquit Dauid, vetustate collapsa sunt ossa mea, cum rugi- rem tota die: Quoniam interdiu & noctu in- graue scebat super me manus tua: versus est vigor meus in siccitates æstatis. Itaq; peccatum tum meum tibi notum feci, & iniquitatem meam non abscondi: Dixi enim, Confitebor aduersus me scelus meum Iehouæ: tu verò remisisti noxá peccati mei. Hæc ille, quibus consentiunt Ioannis illa: Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. At fi confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & iustus, vt remittat nobis peccata nostra, & purget nos ab omni iniquitate. Sed de his plura dedimus ad decimum tertium versiculum vigefimi octa ui capitis prouerbiorum Salomonis.
units.tr: Above all, sins must be confessed to God, both privately and publicly, of which many examples are read in the Scriptures. For nothing is less consistent than for God to forgive the sins in which we ourselves flatter ourselves, and, to keep them from coming to light, we cover them over through hypocrisy. "When I kept silent," says David, "my bones wasted away through my groaning all the day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as in the summer drought. Therefore I acknowledged my sin to you, and did not hide my iniquity; I said, I will confess my transgression to the LORD; and you forgave the guilt of my sin" (Ps. 32.3–5). So he speaks, and John's words agree with these: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1.8–9). But we have given more on these matters at the thirteenth verse of the twenty-eighth chapter of the Proverbs of Solomon.

units.la: Tertiò, exemplo Abigaelis discimus, iratos, per fe plus fatis insanientes, non esse in ftigandos, sed, quantum in nobis est, cohibebimus. Sed & alios, quos scelus aliquod deliberaffe scimus, ab incœpto reuocare satagemus. Sic & illos, quos fe ebrietati, auaritiæ, prauæ societati, fcortationi, chartis luso-rijs, &c. addixisse adeoque tantos quantos mancipaffe, cernimus, amicè castigatos dehortabimur. In primis verò operâ dabimus, vt, fi quos erroneas opiniones amplexos no uimus, eos in viam reuocare conemur. Nam fi iubemur bouem aut asinum, etiam inimici, educere, fi forte hæserit alicubi in fossa, aut errantem à via in viam reducere, quanto id magis præstare debemus. fratribus nostris? Neq; hic est, quod obijcia-mus, nos nulla apud eos authoritate ac gra-tia valere. Quasi Abigael de successu fuisset certa. Et tamen non dubitat, Dauidi, fameli-co milite stipato occurrere: tum quoq;, cum illum non marito tantum, sed vniuersæ fami-liæ excidium minatum esse certò cognouis-set. Quid igitur nostram apud alios interpo-nere autoritatem cunctamur? Quin, quan-tum potest quisq; proximum suum à scele-e prohibet. Sed quid fit? Dum alij in alios pro uinciam istam reijcimus, tandem iusto Dei iudicio promiscuè omnes perimus. Semper ergo nobis ob oculos Iacobi illud obuerse-tur: Fratres, Si quis inter vos aberrarit à ve-ritate, & conuerterit eum quispiam, id est, à via reuocarit: sciat eum, qui auerterit pecca-torem ab errore viæ suæ, seruaturum animâ à morte, id est, interitu æterno, & obtegturu multitudinem peccatorum, vel ipsius homi-nis errantis. Nam cum errore alia multa pec-cata deponet, vel suijpsius, hoc est, vnà cum piè instituto consequetur & ipse vitam æter-nam. Nam qui alios erudierint ad iustitiam, fulgebunt quasi stellæ ad perpetuas æterni-tates. Daniel. 12.
units.tr: Thirdly, from Abigail's example we learn that the angry, who already rage more than enough of their own accord, are not to be provoked further, but we shall restrain them as far as we can. We shall also labour to call back from their undertaking those whom we know to have planned some crime. So too, those whom we see have given themselves over to drunkenness, avarice, bad company, whoring, games of chance and the like, and have enslaved themselves so completely, we shall kindly rebuke and dissuade. Above all we shall take pains that, if we know anyone to have embraced erroneous opinions, we try to bring him back onto the right way. For if we are commanded to lead back an ox or ass, even an enemy's, should it perhaps have stuck somewhere in a ditch, or to lead a wanderer back from the wrong road onto the right one, how much more ought we to do this for our brothers? Nor is there cause for us to object that we have no authority or influence with them. As if Abigail had been certain of success! Yet she did not hesitate to meet David, surrounded by his hungry soldiers, even when she had clearly learned that he threatened the destruction not only of her husband but of her whole household. Why then do we hesitate to bring our authority to bear on others? Indeed, let each person keep his neighbour from crime as far as he is able. But what happens? While we throw this duty from one to another, at last, by the just judgment of God, we all perish together. Let that saying of James therefore always be before our eyes: "Brethren, if anyone among you wander from the truth, and someone convert him, that is, call him back from the way, let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death, that is, from eternal destruction, and will cover a multitude of sins, both of the sinner and of the erring man himself. For when he turns him from error, he will also put away many other sins, either his own, that is, together with a pious way of life he will himself obtain eternal life. For those who instruct others in righteousness shall shine like stars for ever and ever." Daniel 12.

units.la: Quartò argumenta quædam, quæ nos eò adducere debeant, vt iniurias, quas acce-pimus, pimus,æquo animo remittamus,atq; condo nemus,adducuntur. Nempe cum Abigaele penitius aliquanto considerabimus, à quo iniuria simus affecti. Quod si proueetioris fuerit ætatis,senectuti deliræ multùm dabi- mus:Si tenerioris,iuuentuti consilij inopię. Nam,vt Teutonico dicitur prouerbio. Ne-mo ante canos sapit. Semper aliqua in per-sona ipsius deprehendemus, quæ nos ab vl-cifcendi libidine reuocent, vt quod nostEr proximus,qui illo ipso,quo nos,amore com-plectendus veniat,quod frater,eodem, quo nos,sanguine redemtus. Cogitandum præ-terea est, qui nos simus : Christiani nempe, quorum sit iniurias condonare.Item nos ha-ctenus ab animi tranquillitate pacifq; & con cordiæ studio passim commendatos: Præ-terea : non temerè irrumpendum in partes Dei,qui, cum sibi vindictam attribuat, nos-tras hac in parte manus vult ligatas esse. Il-lum nostram iniuriam vindicaturum: Item: eos,qui affectibus suis indulgent, & in vlci-scendi cupiditate animo obstinato sint atq; obfirmato, raro à Deo fortunari: Denique, Conscientiam, cuius præcipua sit habenda ratio, quod ex tota vita omnia dicta & facta ad censuram reuocat,adeo vt in paruis sæpe graiter hæreat,hac ratione aggrauari.
units.tr: Fourthly, certain arguments are brought forward which ought to lead us to forgive the injuries we have received with an equable mind and to pardon them. Namely, together with Abigail we shall consider somewhat more closely by whom we have been wronged. If he is of more advanced age, we shall make much allowance for the foolishness of old age; if he is of younger years, for the lack of judgment of youth. For, as the German proverb says, no one is wise before grey hairs. We shall always find in his person something that calls us back from the lust for revenge: that he is our neighbour, to be embraced with the same love with which we ourselves are to be embraced; that he is our brother, redeemed with the same blood as we were. Next, we must think about who we ourselves are: Christians, whose calling it is to forgive injuries. Likewise, that we have hitherto been commended everywhere for tranquillity and peace of mind and for zeal for concord. Further, that one should not rashly break into God's province, who, since he claims vengeance for himself, wills our hands to be tied in this matter; that he himself will avenge our injury. Likewise, that those who indulge their passions, and are obstinate and hardened in mind in their desire for revenge, are seldom favoured by God. Finally, conscience, whose principal regard must be had, which calls all the words and deeds of the whole of life to judgment, so that it often sticks fast over small matters, is burdened by this reasoning.

units.la: L
units.tr: L

units.la: In primis vero colligimus, ex ista oratione, quàm nefarium sit peccatum, iniusta hominis cædes. Abigael non satis potest deliberatam Dauidis cædem exaggerare. Et tamen Nabal intolerabilia in Dauidem probra & conuitia iecerat. Adhæc homo planè ἀχρηςος, nulliusque frugis erat, præter faciem, hominis nihil habens. Quàm grauiter ergo illos in Deum peccare censendum est, qui, sola inuidia adducti, vili pecunia conduti, inuito Magistratu, quibusuis operam suam addicentes, quosuis abfq; deleftu, sed ante alios homines purioris religionis amantes, trucidant?
units.tr: Above all, from this discourse we gather how grievous a sin is the unjust killing of a man. Abigail could not sufficiently magnify the deliberate slaughter of David. And yet Nabal had uttered intolerable insults and reproaches against David. Besides, the man was plainly useless [ἄχρηστος], of no account, having nothing of a man but his face. How grievously, then, must those be judged to sin against God who, moved by envy alone and hired for paltry money, put to death, against the will of the magistrate, whomever they are set on, without distinction, and above all slaughter men who love a purer religion, offering their services to anyone at all?

units.la: Quia verò militia mercenaria hodie adeò vulgaris est, vt etiam in laude ponatur, amplius aliquid de homicidio dicendum est, vt, vel aliqui, atrocitate sceleris deterriti, in seipsos descendant. In primis verò memori mente reponendum est, quòd immensa illa vniuersæ terræ inundatione facta, hoc vnum in primis est, quod Deus homibus interdixit: Sanguinem, inquit, requiram animarum vestrarum de manu cunctarum bestiarum, & de manu hominis. In Euangelio etiam, quæ primum veteres leges à Domino explicatæ sunt, in ijs hæc prima est, de qua ex Exod.20. apud sanctum Matthæum
units.tr: Since mercenary soldiering today is so common that it is even held in praise, something more must be said about homicide, so that some, struck with fear at the atrocity of the crime, may come to themselves. First of all, it must be kept in mind that after that immense flooding of the whole earth, this is the chief thing God forbade to men: "I will require," he says, "the blood of your souls at the hand of every beast, and at the hand of man." In the Gospel too, where the old laws were explained by the Lord, this is the first of them, concerning which, from Exodus 20, it is written in the Gospel of St Matthew.

units.la: Gen.9. thæum ita scriptum est: Dictum est enim: Non occides, & reliqua, quæ hac de re eo ipso loco deinceps commemoratur. Exod. 21. ab altari auelli iubet illos, qui consulto & cogitatè cædem fecerunt, nullamque vt a-lijs, ἀσυλίᾳ concedit. Eodem capite, si quadrupes pauperiem fecerit, lapidatur & abijcitur, vnaquæ dominus lapidatur, si cornupetum fuisse bouem antea denunciatum sit, aut certè dominus pecunia redimitur: Si occiditur seruus, bouis lapidati dominus, occisi domino argenti siclos 30. expendit. Numeri 25. dicit Lex, sanguine humano pollui terram, nec ante eam expiari, quàm effundatur sanguis illius, qui alterius profudit. Neque aliam ob causam à sanguine hominem abhorrere voluit Deus, nisi vt omni ratione à nefaria hominis cæde & animum & manus abstineret. Sed & Prophetæ valdè in homicidas inuehuntur. Apud Isaiam capite primo negat Deus se preces populi sui exauditurum, eò quod manus ipsorum sanguine innocenti madeant. Apud Ezechielem, causas, propter quas populum suum deportari passus sit, enumerans, Iram, inquit, meam in illos effudi propter sanguine ab illis prodige in terrâ effusum, quâ stercoreis suis deastris polluerunt.
units.tr: Gen. 9. Matthew, it is written thus: "For it was said, You shall not kill," and the rest, which is recounted in that same place in what follows. In Exodus 21 he orders those who have killed deliberately and with forethought to be torn from the altar, and does not grant them asylum [ἀσυλία] as he does to others. In the same chapter, if an ox gores a man and he dies, the ox is stoned and cast out; and the owner too is stoned if it had previously been declared that the ox was a goring beast, or else the owner is released by payment of a sum of money. If a slave is killed, the owner of the stoned ox pays thirty shekels of silver to the master of the slain slave. Numbers 25: the Law says that the land is polluted by human blood and cannot be cleansed before the blood of him who shed it is poured out. God wished man to abhor blood for no other reason than that he might abstain in every way, both in mind and in hands, from the nefarious slaughter of a man. The Prophets too rail vehemently against murderers. In Isaiah chapter 1, God denies that he will hear the prayers of his people, because their hands drip with innocent blood. In Ezekiel, enumerating the causes for which he allowed his people to be carried away, he says: "I poured out my wrath upon them for the blood which they shed in the land, and which they polluted with their filthy idols."

units.la: Proverbiorum sexto inter sex vel potius septem illa, quæ Deus auersatur, numerantur manus, quæ sanguinem innocentem fundunt.
units.tr: In Proverbs 6, among the six, or rather seven, things that God abhors, are numbered the hands that shed innocent blood.

units.la: Sed, vt in toto isto negotio minus sit periculi, discernendum est inter cædes. Aliud enim fortuitum, & inuoluntarium, cædis genus est, vt cum alterum, præter voluntatem nostram, ignoranter, etiam amicum casu occidimus. Exemplum in lege ponitur, Deuteronomij 19. Vt si quis vadit cum proximo suo in syluam, vt secet ligna, & dum impellit manum suam, vt succidat arborem & securis excidat de manubrio, aliumque tangit, vt moriatur, id casu vel fortui to accidisse dicitur, non quidem Dei ratione, cuius prouidentia omnia eueniunt (& hoc ipsum Exodi 21. versu 13. explicatur) sed hominis tantum agentis respectu, cui præter propositum illud accidit. Quæ enim præter mentem & finem accidunt ijs, qui ratione agunt, casu fieri dicuntur, inquit Aristoteles lib. 2. Ac in hunc vsum Deus sex vrbes, ad quas isti se reciperent, tres vltra Iordanem & totidem in terra Chanaan, constituit, ne à propinquis occisi, ira adhuc bulliente, impetuosè obtruncarentur. Quod si quis ad aliquam vrbium illarum in porta (inquibus ad exer‑cenda iudicia seniores sedebant) caussam suam illis exponere debuit,& petere vt eum reciperent: Illi recipere eum debuerunt. Quod fi vindex sanguinis, hoc est, propin‑quior occisi cognatus, eum infequutus, ad poenas repetiffet, non debuerunt eum illi tradere. Sistere autem eum debuerunt iu‑dicio, coràm coetu vrbis illi us, in qua cae‑des facta erat, vt caussa cognosceretur & sta tuerent iudices, voluntaria ne, an fortui‑ta effet. Quod fi constabat,cædem per im‑prudentiam factam esse & homicidam nul‑las ante inimicitias cum interfecto exercu‑isse, iudicum sententijs absoluebatur : Sin vero rem aliter habere compertum fuisset, poenas dabat. Quamuis autem reus pro‑baret, fine voluntate & proposito cædem factam esse,& iudicum sententijs absoluere‑tur: tamen exulare ad mortem summi: Pon‑tificis vsque eum oportuit. Si vrbem pro‑fugij fuisset egressus, non defendebatur con‑tra vindicem sanguinis. Ex quo rursus ap‑paret, quanto odio Deus iniustas cædes prosequatur.
units.tr: But, so that in this whole matter there may be less danger, a distinction must be made among killings. For one kind of killing is accidental and involuntary, as when, against our will, we kill even a friend by chance without knowing it. The law gives an example in Deuteronomy 19: if someone goes with his neighbour into the forest to cut wood, and while he swings his hand to fell a tree the axe head flies off the handle and strikes the other so that he dies, this is said to have happened by chance or accident. Not indeed by God's reckoning, whose providence brings about all things (and this very point is explained in Exodus 21:13), but only with respect to the man acting, to whom it happened beyond his intention. For things that happen beyond the mind and purpose of those who act rationally are said to happen by chance, as Aristotle says in book 2. To this end God appointed six cities to which such persons might withdraw, three beyond the Jordan and as many in the land of Canaan, so that those who had been slain by their kinsmen, while anger was still seething, should not be violently cut down. If anyone had to set out his case before the elders sitting in the gate of one of those cities (where the elders sat to conduct judgments) and ask that they receive him, they ought to receive him. If the avenger of blood, that is, the nearest kinsman of the slain man, followed him and demanded punishment, they ought not to hand him over. They were to bring him to trial before the assembly of that city in which the slaying had occurred, so that the cause might be examined and the judges might decide whether it was voluntary or accidental. If it was established that the killing had been done through imprudence, and that the slayer had had no enmity with the slain man before, he was acquitted by the sentence of the judges. But if it was found otherwise, he paid the penalty. Although the accused might prove that the killing was done without will and purpose, and be acquitted by the sentence of the judges, nevertheless he had to go into exile until the death of the high priest. If he had gone out of the city of refuge, he was not defended against the avenger of blood. From this again it appears with how great hatred God pursues unjust killings.

units.la: Sed & in ijs homicidijs, quae non fpon‑te, neque meditato fiunt: sed fortuito ac praeter voluntatem,non parum interest,negligenter & incautè, secúsue hominem oc-ciderit. Exempli caussa: Si pharmacopæus pro mercurio alioue toxici genere, quo mures rattiue tolluntur, salutare pharma-cum porrigat: pharmacique loco venenum exhibeat, ex quo homicidium sequeretur: Fuisset quidem illud præter dantis volun-tatem, non tamen præter culpam: cum ma-iorem veneni curam habere deberet. Ita, si quis feram alitémue petiturus, per imprudentiam hominis obuij tempora feriat & mortis causam inferat, quamuis homicidij reus non sit, prorsus tamen insons esse non poterit, præsertim si tempestas nubila fuerit.
units.tr: But also in those homicides which occur not by design or deliberate intent, but by chance and against the will of the doer, it makes no small difference whether a man was killed carelessly and incautiously or not. For example, if a druggist, instead of mercury or some other poison with which mice and rats are destroyed, hands over a medicine meant to heal, and gives poison in place of the drug, from which a killing follows, the death would indeed have happened against the will of the giver, but not without his fault, since he ought to have taken greater care with the poison. Likewise, if someone, aiming at a wild beast or a bird, through the carelessness of a man who happens to be in the way strikes him at the time and causes his death, then although he is not guilty of homicide, he cannot be altogether free of blame, especially if the weather was cloudy.

units.la: Debebat enim cautior esse. Alius lapide per cliuum deuoluto obuio non quidē ὁ ἀπρὸς ἀ ΤΟΣ ... sciensq; quod dicitur, ac volens, sed casu quodam ac fortuito, mortem infert. Licet autem non sit eiusmodi casus homicidij reatu damnandus, haud tamen prorsus caret is culpa, cuius vano studio interijt proximus. Nam vt lapidem deuoluerret, nemo erat, qui cogeret. Sed in eo longè grauius peccatur, si quis iniusta & illicita re occupatus, hominem occidat: si quis ebrius gradi bus delapsus puerum oppresserit, vel, quem pro alio habebat, vel etiam bestiam rebatur, interemerit. Ebrietatis enim studium per se illicitū est & vitiosum. Unde Pittacus Mitylenæus, Si quis se per temulentiam aliquid commiisse dixisset, (Solet enim vulgus hominum ebrietatis obtentu crimen exTenuare:) duplici pœna afficiendum illum contendebat: primò quòd se nimio vino adobruisset: deinde quòd illo victus ac tantùmnon sepultus, nulla decori habita ratione, recti limites præter gressus esset. Huc philtra referri possunt: quæ, ut amantibus non porrigantur, necis inferendæ gratia, sed amoris conciliandi ac conglutinandi ergò: plærunque tamen fit, ut amoris loco, insaniam ac furorem afferant. Unde Ouidius illa fallentia vocat, (Sic enim videtur legendum, non pallentia) rectè addens,
units.tr: For he ought to have been more careful. Another man, when a stone rolling down a slope strikes a passer-by, does not intend or know it, but kills him by some chance and accident, [unforeseen ἀπροσδόκητος]. Although a casualty of this kind is not to be condemned as guilty of homicide, yet the one whose neighbour perished through his idle pursuit is not entirely free of fault. For there was no one who compelled him to roll the stone. But a much graver sin is committed when a man, busy with some unjust and unlawful affair, kills another: as when a drunkard, having fallen down the steps, crushes a boy, or kills someone whom he took for another or even thought was a beast. For the pursuit of drunkenness is in itself unlawful and vicious. Hence Pittacus of Mytilene contended that if someone said he had committed some act through drunkenness (for the common sort are wont to lessen a crime by pleading drink), he should be punished twice over: first, because he had drowned himself in too much wine; second, because, overcome by it and scarcely not buried, he had gone beyond the bounds of right, with no regard for decency. To this category belong love-potions, which are administered to lovers not for the purpose of inflicting death, but to win and bind their affection; yet for the most part it happens that, instead of love, they bring madness and frenzy. Hence Ovid rightly calls them deceiving (for so it seems to be read, not pale), adding:

units.la: Philtra nocent animis, vimq; furoris habent.
units.tr: Love-potions harm the mind, and have the force of madness.

units.la: Alterū permissum cædis genus est, quod ad eos Magistratus pertinet, quibus data est necis potestas, qua ex legū præscripto, iudicio; in facinorosos homines animadvertūt, et innocentes defendunt: Quo in munere dū iustè versantur, nō modo ij cædis nō sunt rei, sed huic diuinæ legi, qua cædes vetatur, maximè obediunt. Etenim legi huic finis is ppositus est, ut hominū vitę salutiq; cōsulatur. Magistratuū itè, qui legitimi sunt scelerū vindices, animadversiones eodē spectāt, ut audacia & iniuria supplicijs repressa, tuta sit hominū vita. Quare Dauid, In matutino, inquit, interficiebam omnes peccatores terrę, vt disperderem de ciuitate Domini omnes operantes iniquitatem.
units.tr: The second kind of permitted killing concerns those magistrates who have been given the power of death, by which, according to the prescription of the laws, after trial, they punish criminals and defend the innocent. In this office, while they act justly, they are not only not guilty of killing, but they especially obey that divine law by which killing is forbidden. For the purpose of this law is set before us, that the life and safety of men be cared for. Likewise, the punishments inflicted by magistrates who are lawful avengers of crimes aim at this same end, that boldness and wrong being checked by penalties, the life of men may be safe. Therefore David says: "In the morning I destroyed all the sinners of the land, that I might cut off from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity."

units.la: Qua ratione, ne illi quidem peccant, qui iusto bello, non cupiditate aut crudelitate impulsi, sed solo publicæ vtilitatis studio, vitam hostibus à Magistratibus armati adimunt.
units.tr: By the same reasoning, those also do not sin who, in a just war, not moved by greed or cruelty but solely by zeal for the public good, take the lives of enemies, being armed by the magistrates.

units.la: Illa ipsa, si quis salutis suæ defendendę causa, omni adhibita cautione, alterum interemerit, hac lege non teneri satis apparet. Enimuero vim vi repellere licere, naturæ vox est, communisq; omnium gentium lex, vt docet Tullius in orat. pro Milone. Sed Iurisconsulti distinguunt, qui ius humanū explicant: Vis ne repellatur cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ, an sine moderatione: adeò vt cum posis periculum effugere, nolis; sed aggressorem vimque tibi inferentem, interficere malis. Prima quidē ratione, nempe cum moderamine inculpatæ defensionis putant, concedunt́q; vim vi repellere. Vbi verò moderatio nō est adhibita, non putant licere. Theologi paulò aliter distinguunt. Putant enim spectandum esse eius, qui vim vi repellit, animum, & propositum, quia Deus, qui est χαρδιογνώστης, animum hominis in primis attendit, & ex nostro affectu nostras actiones dijudicat & distinguit, cum omnibus aliis in sceleribus & peccatis, tum maxime in homicidio, uti apparet Exod. capite 21. vers. 13. Leuit. 24. vers. 17. in verbis, Si non insidiatus fit. Ergo si quis vim reijcit à se, ut solam sui conseruandi & ab iniuria tuendi voluntatem intentionemq; habeat, non autem alterius offendendi, tunc non putant eum peccare. Sin autem vlciscendi vel laedendi animo id faciat, omnino damnandum censent, & merito: Est enim homicidium coram Deo.
units.tr: It is clear enough that the same law does not bind one who, for the defence of his own safety, with all caution applied, kills another. Indeed, that it is lawful to repel force by force is the voice of nature and the common law of all nations, as Tully teaches in his speech for Milo. But the jurists who expound human law make distinctions: whether force is to be repelled with the moderation of blameless defence, or without moderation; so that when you could escape the danger but would rather kill the aggressor who is offering you violence. On the first ground, namely with the moderation of blameless defence, they hold, and concede, that force may be repelled by force. Where moderation is not observed, they hold that it is not lawful. The theologians distinguish a little differently. For they hold that one must look to the mind and purpose of the one who repels force, because God, who is the heart-knower [καρδιογνώστης], above all attends to the mind of man and judges and distinguishes our actions by our affection, both in all other crimes and sins, and most of all in homicide, as appears in Exod. 21. vers. 13 and Lev. 24. vers. 17, in the words "if he did not lie in wait." Therefore, if someone repels force from himself with the sole will and intention of preserving himself and guarding against injury, and not of harming another, they do not think he sins. But if he does it with a mind to avenge or to hurt, they judge him wholly to be condemned, and rightly: for it is homicide before God.

units.la: Corollarij vice, historiam ex Theodorito attexam, ex qua appareat, quanta sit iniustae caedis atrocitas. Theodosius Imperator, ut est apud Theodoritum, assiduitate bellorum coactus, tributum ciuitatibus extraordinarium imperauit. Id quod Antiocheni graviter admodum ferentes, aeream Placillae laudatissimae Reginae statuam obiectam, per magnam vrbis partem traxerunt. Quare cognita Imperator, pro eo ac aequum erat, valde iratus, legatos Antiochiam misit, qui significarent, se de omnibus seditionis istius authoribus supplicium sumpturum. Ac cum iam aduenissent decreta minarum afferentes Elebachus,qui tum dux erat & Cæsarius regiæ magister , omnes in metu erant,minas exhorrentes. Macedonius autem,vir quidem literarum expers, cæterum in montiū verticibus agens,dieq; ac noctu sanctas Salvatori nostro preces offerens, præhensa in media vrbe vnius chlamyde,ambos de equis iubet descendere.At illi paruulum fenè, viles panniculos amictum,conspicati; primo risu excipere: Mox ductoribus quibusdam significantibus , qua vir ille esset virtute,de equis desiliunt,& contactis genibus eius veniam orant:Quibus ille,Referte, inquit,ô amici,Imperatori ,non Imperatorem esse sed lum,sed hominem quoq; : proinde non imperium tantum,verumetiam naturā illi considerandam esse.Quæ cum sit imago & similitudo diuina,ne tam crudeliter ac immaniter imaginem Dei iugulari præcipiat:irritaturum enim fabricatore illius imaginis supplicio:Multum item interesse inter inanimē & animalem viuentemq; & rationis compotem imaginem : Facile deniq; ipsis esse pro vna ærea imagine multas restituere. Ipsum verò facere non posse , vt vnum saltem pilū interemtorum fabricetur. Quæ cum illi ad Imperatorem detulissent , restincta iracundia,Antiochenos in gratiam recepit.
units.tr: By way of a corollary, I shall add a story from Theodoret, from which it may appear how great is the atrocity of unjust killing. The Emperor Theodosius, as is related by Theodoret, being compelled by the constant pressure of wars, imposed an extraordinary tribute on the cities. The Antiochenes, bearing this very grievously, dragged through a large part of the city a bronze statue of the most praised Empress Placilla, which had been thrown at them. When the Emperor learned of this, being very angry, as was only fitting, he sent envoys to Antioch to announce that he would take punishment from all the authors of this sedition. And when they had already arrived, bringing the decrees of threats, Elebachus, who was then commander and Caesarian master of the palace, all were in fear, dreading the threats. But Macedonius, a man indeed without learning, yet living on the peaks of the mountains, and day and night offering holy prayers to our Saviour, seizing the cloak of one man in the middle of the city, ordered both to dismount from their horses. They, seeing a man almost of little stature, dressed in mean rags, at first received him with laughter. Soon, when some of their guides indicated what kind of man he was in virtue, they leapt from their horses, and touching his knees begged his pardon. To them he said: "Tell the Emperor, my friends, that he is not only an emperor but also a man; therefore he must consider not only his power but also his nature. Since this is the image and likeness of God, let him not command that the image of God be slaughtered so cruelly and savagely; for the Maker of that image will be provoked by the punishment. Moreover, there is a great difference between an inanimate image, and an animate image that lives and has reason. Finally, it is easy for them to restore many images in place of one bronze image; but he himself cannot make even one hair of those who are killed." When they had reported these words to the Emperor, his anger was quenched and he received the Antiochenes back into favour.

units.la: Gentiles quoq; effusionem sanguinis humani valdè horruerunt,id quod abundè colligitur ex historia Ionæ, què nautæ, durum hominum genus,sceleris etiá fui forte conui ctum,vix tandé in mare proijciunt.Deù pro cati,ne ab ipsis sanguinis innocentis poenas repeteret.Cum Paulus ex naufragio enatas-set,& Barbari viperam à manu pendente viderent,mox suspicantur eum homicidam ef fe, & vindictam ab eo,cui mare & homines peperçerant poenas exigere.Pompilius Imperator,vt est apud Ciceronem, prouincià in bello Persico tenuit,in cuius exercitu Catonis filius tyro militauit.Cum autem ipsi vi deretur vnam dimittere legionem ,Catonis quoq; filium,qui in eadem legione militabat dimisit.Sed cùm amore pugnandi in exerci tu remansisset, Cato ad Pompilium scripsit, vt,si eum pateretur in exercitu remanere,se cundo eum obligaret militiæ sacramento, quia,priore amisso,iure pugnare cum hostibus non poterat.Adeo summa erat obseruatio in bello mouendo. Sed & ad filium literas dedit , in quibus scripsit,se audisse,eum missum factum esse à Consule, cum in Macedonia bello Persico miles esset. Monetigitur,vt caueat,ne prælium ineat.Negat enim ius esse qui miles non sit, pugnare cum hoste,&c.
units.tr: The Gentiles too greatly abhorred the shedding of human blood, which is abundantly gathered from the story of Jonah: the sailors, a hard kind of men, though convinced of their own crime by lot, scarcely at last cast him into the sea, praying that God would not exact from them the penalty for the blood of the innocent. When Paul had escaped from the shipwreck, and the barbarians saw a viper hanging from his hand, they at once suspected that he was a murderer and that Justice, which had not allowed him to perish at sea or among men, would exact punishment from him. The Emperor Pompilius, as is related by Cicero, held a province in the Persian war, in whose army the son of Cato served as a young soldier. When it seemed to him that he should discharge one legion, he also discharged the son of Cato, who was serving in that same legion. But when the son had remained in the army out of love of fighting, Cato wrote to Pompilius that, if he allowed him to remain in the army, he should bind him a second time by the oath of military service, since, having lost the first, he could not lawfully fight against the enemy. So great was the scrupulousness in beginning a war. He also gave a letter to his son, in which he wrote that he had heard that he had been discharged by the Consul, when he was a soldier in the Persian war in Macedonia. He therefore warns him to take care not to engage in battle; for he denies that it is lawful for one who is not a soldier to fight with the enemy, etc.

units.tr: The judgment of the Gentiles concerning homicide: Jonah 1.

units.la: Hæc vtinam diligentius aliquanto apud animum suum cogitarent illi, qui alijs subin de bella mouent, totosq; sanguinis riuos effundunt. Item illi, qui alios inter se committunt, magno pereq; ferendis discordijs & bellis delectantur: id quod iam multos annos eos fecisse costat, quos præ alijs paci & tranquillitari studere oportuisset. Nec vero ab horum hominum numero & culpa seiunguntur, qui exiguo precio conducti, quæuis castra sequuntur. Nam pleriq; illorum non legitimo magistratui, sed exteris principibus militant: imo ferè contra suorum principum edicta in militiam externam excurrunt. Deinde vocationem, quam à Deo habent, turpiter deserunt, & relictis artificijs manuarijs aut agricultura, hoc vitæ genus sequuntur, quo vix vllum hodie sceleratius excogitari potest. Finem vero non alium sibi propositum habent, quàm vt sit, quod ipsorum libidini sufficiat, & vt malè parta peius dilapident. Quæ causa est, vt abfq; omni discrimine pro hostibus habeant omnes, ex quibus præda sperari potest. Ita vero non sibi tantum, sed & regnis atq; gentibus suæ exitium accelerant. Persequitur enim illos maledictio Dei, qui iam pridem execratione & exitio dignos pronunciauit eos qui pro precio fundunt sanguinem innoxium. Et ex hi storijs constat, nulli regno aut genti impunè cesisse belligerandi libidinem. Sed meretur hoc quoq; flagellum incurabilis seculi no-stri impietas. Quod tunc demum à nobis auferetur, si à peccatis in viam iustitiæ & salutis redeuntes, pacem cum omnibus, quantum in nobis est, habeamus, concordiqueamicitia ac charitate etiam inimicos complectamur.
units.tr: Would that those who from time to time stir up wars against others and pour out whole streams of blood would consider these things a little more carefully in their own minds. Likewise, those who set others against one another and take great delight in enduring quarrels and wars: this, as is well known, they have been doing for many years, though they ought rather to have been devoted to peace and tranquillity above all others. Nor are those separated from the number and guilt of these men who, hired for a small price, follow any camp whatever. For most of them serve not a lawful magistrate but foreign princes; indeed they rush into foreign warfare almost against the edicts of their own princes. Then they shamefully desert the calling they have from God, and, leaving manual crafts or agriculture, follow a way of life than which hardly any more wicked can be devised today. Moreover, they have no other end in view than to have enough to satisfy their lust and to squander their ill-gotten gains all the more badly. This is why they regard everyone from whom plunder can be hoped for as an enemy, without any distinction. Thus they hasten their own destruction and that of kingdoms and peoples. For the curse of God pursues those whom he long ago declared worthy of execration and destruction, those who for a price shed innocent blood. And from histories it is clear that no kingdom or people has escaped unpunished the lust for waging war. But the impiety of our incurable age deserves this scourge too. It will be taken from us only when, returning from sins to the way of righteousness and salvation, we have peace with all, as far as lies in us, and embrace even our enemies with concord, friendship and charity.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi. HOMILIA VIII.
units.tr: On the life and death of Nabal the drunkard. Homily 8.

units.la: Dauid acceptis muneribus Deo gratias agit, qui sibi Abigaelis opera in tempore subuenisset.
units.tr: David, having received the gifts, gives thanks to God, who had come to his aid in time through Abigail's help.

units.la: 32 Et ait Dauid ad Abigail: Benedictus Iehovah Deus Israelis, qui misit te hodie in occursum mei.
units.tr: 32 And David said to Abigail: Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me.

units.la: 33 Et benedictum eloquium tuum, & benedicta tu, quæ prohibuisti me hodie, ne venirem in sanguines, & seruaret manus meas me.
units.tr: 33 And blessed be your speech, and blessed are you, who today kept me from coming to bloodshed and kept my hands from avenging myself.

units.la: 34 Et certè vinit Iehovah Deus Israelis raelis, qui pohibuit me, ne malefacerem tibi: quod nisi festinasses, veniisses, in occursum mihi, non remansisset ipsi Nabal, usque ad lucem matutinam, mingens ad parietem.
units.tr: 34 For truly, as the LORD God of Israel lives, who restrained me from doing you harm: unless you had hurried to come to meet me, Nabal himself would not have been left alive until morning light, pissing against the wall.

units.la: 35 Accepit ergo Dauid è manu eius quod illa attulerat ei, & dixit illi: Ascende in pace in domum tuam. Vide, audiui uocem tuam, & suscepi faciem tuam.
units.tr: 35 So David accepted from her hand what she had brought him, and said to her: Go up in peace to your house. See, I have heard your voice and granted your request.

units.la: {a}HOc loco cōmemorātur, quomodo se Dauid, acceptis ab Abigaele muneribus, gesserit. Ac primō quidē dicitur, illum Deo & Abigaeli gratias egisse, quod illorum opera à cǫde fuerit reuocatus. Deinde illum munera ab Abigaele oblata grato animo accepisse, eamq; saluam domum remisisse.
units.tr: {a}HERE it is recorded how David conducted himself after receiving the gifts from Abigail. First, it is said that he gave thanks to God and to Abigail, because he had been called back from slaughter through their help. Then, that he accepted with a grateful mind the gifts offered by Abigail, and sent her home unharmed.

units.la: Quod ad primum, Dauid Deo & Abigaeli gratias egisse narratur, quòd ab illis à cæde fuerit repressus. Deū secundò nominat Deum Israelis, non quod aliarum quoq; gentiū non sit Deus (Est enim tàm Gentilium quàm Iudæorum Deus) sed peculiariter illum hoc nomine insignit, quod se populo Israelitico multis vicibus multisq; modis manifestarit, eosq; ex omnibus gentibus in peculiū sibi delegerit, fœdus itē cū illis pepigerit, Mesiá promiserit, ac legē tradiderit, &c. Huic Deo gratias
units.tr: As to the first point, David is said to have given thanks to God and to Abigail, because he had been held back by them from bloodshed. He names God secondly as the God of Israel, not because he is not also the God of the other nations (for he is the God of Gentiles as much as of Jews), but because he marks him out peculiarly by this name, in that he revealed himself to the Israelite people many times and in many ways, chose them out of all nations as his own treasure, also made a covenant with them, promised the Messiah, and gave the law, and so on. To this God he gave thanks

units.la: {a} Deus Israelis, verf. 32. Heb. 1. Rom. 9. gratias egit, quod Abigaelem sibi miserit obuiam: Non clamat: Illam diaboli auspicijs pe dem huc tulisse. Nec enim in ea erat opinio-ne, illa forte fortuna ad se venisse.
units.tr: {a} God of Israel, verse 32. Heb. 1. Rom. 9. ...that he sent Abigail to meet him. He does not cry out that she had brought him here on foot under the auspices of the devil. Nor indeed was he of the opinion that she had come to him by some chance fortune.

units.la: Deinde mores Abigaelis depredicat: (He braea vox significat omne illud, ex quo quo-dammodo gustus de hominibus capitur) quae ipsum prohibuerit, ne veniret in sangui-nes, & se manu sua seruaret: id est, sua oratio ne a caede & vindicta iniuriae in se commisse a-uocarit. Sed & Deum immortalem testatur, qui ipsum illi male facere prohibuerit, nisi ipsa sibi occurrere properauisset, se Nabale ante diluculum fortunis omnibus euersu-rum fuisse.
units.tr: Then he extols Abigail's character (the Hebrew word signifies all that by which a kind of taste is caught from people): that her speech kept him from going to bloodshed and kept him from saving himself by his own hand; that is, that her words called him away from slaying and from avenging the wrong done to him. He also calls on the immortal God as witness, who restrained him from doing her harm, unless she had hastened to meet him, since he would have overturned Nabal and all his fortunes before dawn.

units.la: Dauid Abigaelem non superciliose repel-lit: vt solent ἀπεγόρπιοι, qui neminem ad col-loquium admittant: Non interpellat verba facientem, quod solent homines irati & prę-cipites, sed, vt oratione ad finem perducat pa-tienter expectat. Ad eundem modum nos quoq; alios pacato animo audiem9: vbi perorarint, respondebimus. Vidisti ne, quit Solomon, virum in rebus suis praecipitem? (alij angu-stius, in verbis suis) plus de stulto quam de illo sperandum. Ac hyperbolice loquitur. Alioquin stultum emendari non posse dixit Prou.17. verf.22. Sed, vt plane desperatum esse eum ostendat, qui temerè feratur ad quidlibet dicendum, vel agendum, ei ftultū præfert. Stultus certè tametsi aliquid dicat, non mox venit in periculum: πεϱιπιπτης autem & sibi & alijs pericula accersit. Deinde stultus libentius fe admoneri sustinet, quàm is qui non solum in verbis, sed & negotijs omnibus præceps fertur.
units.tr: David does not repel Abigail haughtily, as those do who are wont to admit no one to conversation [ἀπεγόρπιοι]. He does not interrupt her while she speaks, as angry and hasty men usually do, but patiently waits until she brings her speech to an end. In the same way we too should listen to others with a calm mind, and when they have finished, reply. "Have you seen a man hasty in his affairs?" says Solomon; "there is more hope of a fool than of him." (Others read more narrowly: in his words.) He speaks hyperbolically. Otherwise he would have said that a fool cannot be corrected, as in Prov. 17. verse 22. But to show that a man who is rashly carried off to say or do anything is quite beyond hope, he places him before a fool. A fool, though he says something, does not at once fall into danger; but the rash man [περιπίπτης] brings dangers upon himself and others. Further, a fool bears admonition more willingly than one who is carried headlong not only in words but in all his affairs.

units.la: Ac dum gratias Deo agit Dauid, qui sibi subuenisset in tempore, peccatum & temeritatem suam non inuitus agnoscit. Non illis est afimilis, qui etiamsi norint se peccare, tamen propositum pertinaciter vrgent. Qualis erat Amnon Dauidis ex Achinoe vxore filius. Enimuero, cum Thamarim ex alia matre sororem aggressam per vim stuprare vel let, Noli, frater mi, inquit illa, noli stuprare me: quasi diceret: Non debes esse corruptor sororis tuæ: Tu me potius tueri deberes, si qui me constuprare vellent. Esset contra naturam, si tu mihi vitium offerres. 2. Non ita, ait, in Israele fit. Noster populus, quem Deus sibi ex omnibus gentibus delegit, & ipsi se manifestauit, vt innocentia vitæ & sanctitate seruiat, alias habet leges: Externam opprimere non licet: multò minus sororem. Capitale scelus est: Exod.22. Leuit.20. Deuter.22. 3. Ne committas hanc iniquitatem vel stultitiam.
units.tr: And while David gives thanks to God, who had come to his aid in time, he acknowledges his own sin and rashness, and does so without reluctance. He is not like those who, even when they know they are sinning, stubbornly press on with their purpose. Such was Amnon, the son of David by his wife Ahinoam. For when he meant to force his sister Tamar, the daughter of another mother, she said: "Do not, my brother, do not force me," as if to say: you ought not to be the corrupter of your sister; you ought rather to protect me, if anyone wished to violate me. It would be against nature if you offered me this vice. (2) "It is not so," she says, "in Israel. Our people, whom God has chosen out of all nations and revealed himself to, to serve him in innocence of life and holiness, has other laws. It is not lawful to oppress a stranger, much less a sister. It is a capital crime: Exod. 22. Lev. 20. Deut. 22." (3) "Do not commit this iniquity or folly."

units.la: {a} 2.Sam.13. titiam.Cogita quàm graue peccatum fit,so-rori commisceri, nedum per vim stuprum offerre. 4. Nam & ego,quò me vertam cum meo probro?Fabula ero omnibus: Nemini matrimonio copulari potero. Nos dicere-mus: Nec Rhenus mihi hanc maculam elue ret.5. Tu verò velut vnus è stultis in Israele eris.Si feceris hanc stultitiam, si ita inconsi-derate egeris,timendum, ne existimatione tuam amittas,sultusq; ac insanus habearis: qui pro iure primogenituræ, primo quoq; tempore parenti succedere debebas.6. Quę so ergo regem alloquaris:neq; enim me tibi denegabit. Forte suspicabatur ipsum auctoritate sua quoquo modo aliquid de lege diui na relaxare posse:Quemadmodu hodie pon tifices,præter sacrarū literarū authoritatem dispensandi in prohibitis gradibus potesta-tem sibi arrogant.Vel,vt melius,meo quidé iudicio,Josephus scribit,hæc dicit, vt illum articulū temporis euaderet,quacunq; se ra-tione explicaret.Sed quid?Potuissent quidé argumenta ista apud sanos & cordatos ho-mines permultū:At Amnon istis non magis mouetur,quàm si dura silex stet,aut Marpe-sia cautes.Ac,sicut luscinia apud Hesiodum frustra accipitri concionatur. Ita Thamar surdo Amnoni fabulam narrat.Quippe pro
units.tr: {a} 2 Sam. 13. (4) "Think how grave a sin it is to lie with a sister, let alone to offer her a violated bond by force. (5) For where shall I turn with my shame? I shall be a fable to all. You will be counted as one of the fools in Israel. If you commit this folly, if you act so thoughtlessly, you must fear that you will lose your reputation and be thought foolish and mad, you who ought, by right of the firstborn, to succeed your father at the first opportunity. (6) Please, speak to the king; for he will not deny me to you." She perhaps supposed that he, by his own authority, could in some way relax the divine law, as today the popes arrogate to themselves the power to dispense in forbidden degrees, beyond the authority of the sacred letters. Or, as Josephus writes, which I judge better, she said this so that he might escape the difficulty of the moment by whatever means. But what then? These arguments could indeed have had great weight with sane and sensible men; yet Amnon is no more moved by them than if a hard flint stood or a cliff of Marpessus. And just as the nightingale in Hesiod preaches in vain to the hawk, so Tamar tells her tale to a deaf Amnon. Indeed,

units.la: M pria libidinū pœna est furor & cæcitas, quæ omnia moderata consilia spernit: vt Rom. i. Ephef. 4. scribitur.
units.tr: the proper punishment of lusts is madness and blindness, which spurn every moderate counsel, as is written in Rom. 1 and Eph. 4.

units.la: Quot sunt hodie, qui reclamante etiā conscientia contemto Dei & hominum iudicio, nefaria instituta pertinaciter persequūntur? Si mulierculam Dauidis exemplo deberent audire, & à proposito discedere, iam de existimatione suā plane actum vociferarentur.
units.tr: How many are there today who, even with conscience protesting, despising the judgment of God and of men, obstinately pursue wicked practices? If they ought to listen to a mere woman, as David did, and withdraw from their purpose, they would cry out that their reputation was utterly gone.

units.la: Etiamsi concionatores summa fide agant, ni hilq; relinquant intentatum, vt eos à sceleri bus & erroribus auocent: tam abest, vt eorū cohortationes, quo fiunt animo, accipiant, vt illos ne audire quidem dignentur. Imò vt aliorum monitis locum facerent aliquem, ta men in ministrorum gratiam nihil volunt fa cere. Inuenias, qui sibi nescio quam constan tiæ laudem arrogent, etiā cum in sceleribus pergant. At hæc non constantia est, sed per tinacia. In bonis causis nolle à sententia dis cedere, id demum laudi ducitur. Rectè Solo mon : Melior, inquit, id est, maiore laude dignus est, qui dominatur spiritui, id est, qui vitiosos affectus frænat, quàm qui vrbem ca pit. Quod Ethnicos ipsos vidisse illorū sen tentijs facilè docueris. Multi etiamsi graui ter errarint, nolūt tamē errores fateri. Quia illos extenuant: multi mordicus tuentur ac defendefendût. At quàto fati⁹ erat cogitare quod trito illo prouerbio fertur, Longè præsta‑re, recurrere, quàm malè currere. Gertè, qui sua scelera tegit, nunquâ aget prosperè: qui verò confitetur & derelinquit, misericordiâ consequetur. Prou. 28. verf. 13.
units.tr: Even when preachers act with the greatest faithfulness, leaving nothing untried to call them away from crimes and errors, they are so far from receiving their exhortations in the spirit in which they are given that they do not even deign to hear them. Indeed, though they might make some room for the warnings of others, they will do nothing at all to please the ministers. You will find men who claim for themselves I know not what praise of constancy, even while they persist in their crimes. But this is not constancy, it is obstinacy. To be unwilling to depart from an opinion in a good cause, that is indeed counted for praise. Solomon rightly says: "Better," that is, more worthy of praise, "is he who rules his spirit," that is, who restrains vicious passions, "than he who takes a city." That you could easily show from the opinions of the heathens themselves. Many, even when they have erred grievously, are unwilling to confess their errors, because they make light of them; many cling to them with teeth and nails and defend them. But how much better would it be to consider what the familiar proverb says: it is far better to run back than to run badly. Certainly, he who hides his crimes will never prosper; but he who confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy. Prov. 28, verse 13.

units.la: Quærát autem aliquis, quomodo Da‑uid iam lapsus Deo gratias agat, qui se à peccato repressērit? Enimuerò, an non cædem iam animo dēstinarat? Certè hoc satis est coram Deo, qui cor inspicit. Respondeo: Dicit quidē Ioannes, Eum, qui fratre suū odio habeat, homicidā esse, eoq; magis, si quis hoc nomine se det in viam, vt alteri necē inferat. Sed & Christus, Quicunq; ait, aspicit mulierem, vt eā concupiscat, iam adulterauit eam in corde suo. Interim magnum discrimen est inter peccata animo tantum concepta, & actu adimpleta. Pertinent quidem pecca‑ta recepta in corde ad idē genus, ad quod re ipsa & opere perpetrata: nō tamē æquè grauia sunt vel paria. Si quis mulierē concupi‑scat, peccatū quidē eius pertinet ad adulte‑rium: & tamē nō æquè grauiter peccat, ac, si illa literis, nuncijs, muneribus solicitata, ad‑ulterium reipsa cōmisisset. Eadē homicidij aliorumq; criminū ratio est: quæ cum intus in animo recluduntur, minus vehementia {*}unt & potentia,quàm cum ad facinus erum punt.Nisi enim ita esset,vt acutè Martyr,nul la essent impedimenta legum.Flumina enim vasta & tumentia perrumpunt aggeres,late que per campos vagantur : parui autem ri- uuli facile ripis suis continentur,&c.
units.tr: Someone may ask how David, already fallen, gives thanks to God for having restrained him from sin. For had he not already determined the slaughter in his mind? Surely this is enough before God, who looks into the heart. I answer: John says that he who hates his brother is a murderer, and all the more if someone sets out with that very purpose, to inflict death on another. And Christ says: whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Yet there is a great difference between sins merely conceived in the heart and sins carried into act. Sins received in the heart do indeed belong to the same kind as those committed in deed and work; yet they are not equally grave or equal. If someone lusts after a woman, his sin does indeed belong to adultery; and yet he does not sin as gravely as if he had been solicited by letters, messages and gifts and had actually committed adultery. The same reasoning applies to murder and other crimes: when they are shut up within the mind they are less vehement and less powerful than when they are carried out into deed. For if it were not so, as the sharp Martyr says, there would be no need of laws. Vast and swelling rivers burst through the dykes and wander widely over the fields, but small brooks are easily held within their banks, and so on.

units.la: Videmus hoc loco Deum,pro sua immen sa bonitate,non tantum mala poenæ,sed etiá mala culpæ à nobis clementer auertere.Sæ- pe enim mala consilia impedit,& vehemen- tes impetus frænat, ne nobis & aliis noceat. Vtitur autem ad hanc rem nonnunquam ex ternis medijs,vt hoc loco oratione fœminæ prudentis:aliquando alijs.Genesis 31. Laban Iacobum,qui ab eo plurimos annos de- spicatui habitus , partim cum sua familia se subduxerat,turmis armatis persequens, re- tracturus,vt mancipium, erat, nisi monitu Dei cohibita fuisset præceps insania.Eius v- nius beneficium est,in solidum, & quod faci mus bene & quod desistimus à malo.Cæte- rà actum esset de nobis.Nam ex proprijs vi- ribus non sumus idonei, qui vel cogitemus aliquid boni,nedum,tanquam ex nobis,per ficiamus. In tantum generali illa originalis peccati labe sumus infecti & corrupti. Nul- lum vitium adeò tetrum, adeò atrox est, ad quod non ferremur præcipites, nisi à Deo, qui
units.tr: We see here that God, in his immense goodness, graciously turns away from us not only the evils of punishment but also the evils of guilt. For often he hinders evil counsels and restrains violent impulses, so that they do not harm us or others. He uses for this purpose sometimes external means, as here by the speech of a prudent woman, and sometimes others. In Genesis 31, Laban, pursuing Jacob with armed troops, since Jacob had withdrawn from him with his family after serving him for many years despised and treated as a slave, would have dragged him back, had not his headlong madness been checked by God's warning. The benefit of this one God is complete, both that we do good and that we desist from evil. Otherwise it would have been all over with us. For by our own strength we are not fit even to think anything good, much less to accomplish it as if of ourselves. We are so infected and corrupted by that general stain of original sin that there is no vice so foul or atrocious to which we would not be hurled headlong, unless we were drawn back by God,

units.la: {*} qui in nobis & velle & perficere pro sua bona voluntate operatur, retraheremur. Dauid hoc loco aperte fatetur, Deũ obstitisse, quò minus cædé animo destinatâ patrarit. Quod si nos quoq; à nefarijs institutis auocemur, sciamus Dei hoc opus & beneficiũ esse, eoq; illi Dauidis exemplo, gratias agamus, eumq; comprecabimur, vt & nostram & aliorum famam illibatam tueri, & à malefactis clementissime cohibere velit.
units.tr: who works in us both to will and to perform, according to his good pleasure. David here plainly confesses that God prevented him from carrying out the slaughter he had intended. If we too are called away from wicked undertakings, let us know that this is God's work and benefit, and therefore let us give thanks to him, following David's example, and let us pray that he will be pleased most mercifully both to preserve our good name and that of others unblemished, and to restrain us from misdeeds.

units.la: Obseruandum autem, Dauidem non tantum Iehouæ Israelitarum Deo, qui Abigaelem sibi misisset obuiam: sed ipsi etiam Abigaeli gratias agere, quæ se suis rationibus à sanguine faciendo, & iniurijs per se ipsum persequendis cohibuerit. Neq; id iniuria. Ea enim huiusmodi vsa fuerat argumentis, & ἠθεσι & πάθεσι, quibus ipse vehementer commouebatur. Itaq; ea laudat, tanquam à Deo profecta. Idem nos quoq; faciemus, si quando Deus nos vel Magistratus, vel parentum, vel amicorum, vel vicinorum vel vxorum nostrarum opera à sceleribus retrahat, eisque eo nomine gratias singulares agemus.
units.tr: It is to be observed that David gave thanks not only to the LORD, the God of Israel, who had sent Abigail to meet him, but also to Abigail herself, who had restrained him by her reasons from shedding blood and from pursuing injuries with his own hand. Nor was this without reason. For she had used arguments of this kind, both ethical and pathetic, by which he himself was powerfully moved. Therefore he praises them as having come from God. We too will do likewise, if at any time God, through the agency of the magistrate, our parents, our friends, our neighbours, or our wives, holds us back from crimes, and we will give them special thanks on that account.

units.la: Videmus etiam, quantum posit apud viros prudentes mollis oratio. Iurauerat quidem Dauid, quo nihil alioqui erat lenius, se M 5
units.tr: We see also how much gentle speech can prevail with prudent men. David had indeed sworn, which was otherwise no mild oath, that he would destroy Nabal and all his household. He seemed to have a just cause for anger, both because he was the king and because Nabal had refused to protect his flocks.

units.la: Nabalem & omne eius familiam euersurum: & videbatur iustam iræ causam habere,cum quod rex esset,cum quod greges Nabalis desendisset:tamen cum rationes Abigaelis audisset,nō tantū ab instituto desistit,sed & Abigaelem magnificè prædicat,&se huic mulum debere testatur,quod ipsum ab incepto reuocasset,ne manus suas innocenti sanguine pollueret.Rectè Solomō:Mollis, inquit, responsio auertit iram: verbum autem doloris,id est,asperū,ascendere facit,id est,excitat furorem,quod ira in nares ascendat.Germani dicunt:Ein gut wort/sindt ein güte statt. Item: Zwen ruch stein/maletend nie rein. Cap.25. Lingua,ait,mollis frangit ossa:Sensus est:In candescentiam placata oratione frangi. Ferocisimi etiam homines oratione mansueta placantur. Cuius rei illustre habetur exemplum Iudic.8. vbi Gedeon Ephraimitas fecū expostulantes,quod ipsorū opera non vsus esset cōtra Midianitas,placida oratione cōpescit.Idē quoq; fecit Iephtes:In Actis Apostol.scriba quidā,aliis aliud clamantibus, (erat enim cōfusa concio,& pleriq;, qua de causa conueniessent,nesciebant)oratione placida tumultum Ephesinum sedat. Pronunciat enim simulachrū,quod colebant Ephesij delapsum è cœlo,& Paulum eiusq; comites nil
units.tr: Yet when he heard Abigail's reasons, he not only abandoned his purpose but also praised Abigail highly and declared that he owed her thanks for turning him from his undertaking, so that he would not stain his hands with innocent blood. Solomon rightly says: "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Prov. 15.1), that is, a bitter word makes fury rise, so that anger goes up into the nostrils. The Germans say: "A good word is worth a fine city." Likewise: "Two smooth stones never soil each other." Ch. 25: "A soft tongue breaks bones" (Prov. 25.15). The sense is that a fierce heat is broken when it is soothed by gentle speech. Even the most savage men are calmed by mild speech. A famous example of this is in Judges 8, where Gideon calms the Ephraimites, who were complaining with him that he had not used them against the Midianites, by a gentle speech. Jephthah did the same. In the Acts of the Apostles a certain scribe, while others shouted one thing and others another (for the assembly was confused, and most did not know why they had come together), calmed the tumult at Ephesus by a mild speech. He declared that the image which the Ephesians worshipped had fallen from heaven, and that Paul and his companions had said nothing offensive about their goddess.

units.la: Prou. 15. vers. 1. Actu. 19. tes nihil in ipsorum deam contumeliose locutos esse. Tandem concludit: Si quam priuatam litem habeat Demetrius, esse iudicia & magistratus. Publica vero negotia in concione legitima, no turbulenta: quae magistratum eidem conuenerit, non quæ vnius homi-nis impulsu & libidine temere occurrerit tractanda esse. Iniecto etiam metu, eos pa-cat: quia Proconsuli oblata erat occasio, vrbis mali e multandae, &c. Romae P. Seruilius populu oratione blanda sedat: Idé postea fa-cit Menenius Agrippa. Qua de re Liuius De cad. i. Quanuis, vt quod res est, dicam, optabile fit, vt inquit Euripides in Heraclidis, in hostem sapiente nec stolidum incidere, cum hic superior factus tantum sæuire soleat, apud illum verecundiæ, iustitiæ veniæq; locus fit. Nihil enim est magnum, quod non fit placidum. Unde Ouidius: vt supra quoq; citatû: Quo quisq; est maior, magis est placabilis ira, Et faciles motus mens generosa capit. Nec male veteri dicitur proverbio: Apud bonum virum cito moritur iracundia. E contra pusilli animi est indomitę irę frenos laxa re, eaq; pro duce, no p militie vti, & vindictæ cupidum esse. Proculdubio Dauid sic tacitus apud se cogitauit: Scio quam dulce fit inimicos, præsertim eos, quib. iuste irascaris,
units.tr: Prov. 15.1; Acts 19.
