(The scribe) finally concluded that if Demetrius had any private lawsuit, there were courts and magistrates for it; but public affairs must be handled in a lawful assembly, not a disorderly one, and not rashly stirred up at the impulse and whim of one man. Having also cast fear into them, he calmed them, since the proconsul had been given an opportunity to punish the city's wrongdoers. At Rome, Publius Servilius calmed the people with a flattering speech, and Menenius Agrippa did the same afterwards. Livy speaks of this in his book on the Catiline affair (?). To tell the truth as it is, it is desirable, as Euripides says in the Heraclidae, to fall in with an enemy who is wise and not stupid, since when he has become the stronger he is usually inclined to rage, but with a wise enemy a place is made for shame, justice and pardon. For nothing is great that is not made gentle. Hence Ovid, as cited above: The greater a man is, the more easily his anger is appeased, and a noble mind receives gentle impulses. And the old proverb rightly says: "Anger dies quickly in a good man." On the contrary, it is the mark of a small mind to loosen the reins of uncontrolled anger, to take it as a leader rather than a soldier, and to desire revenge. Undoubtedly David reasoned in silence with himself like this: "I know how sweet it is to take vengeance on enemies, especially those with whom you are justly angry.

units.la: Bonorum mentes sunt placabiles. vlcisci.Sed hoc quoq; scio præclarum & laudabile esse,illum impetum cohibere ac refrenare.Scio decere regem seueritatem:sed idé non ignoro, quàm non deceat eundé sæua & inexorabilis ira. Grauiter Nabal in me de liquit:comeruit pœnam non vulgare:Sed regis est talem se præbere ciuibus,qualem sibi Deum velit.Ego autem quàm sæpe,& quàm multò grauius in Deū peccó'cui, si quoties causa puniendi est,toties illi & voluntas esset,quę illi fulmina, quæ tormenta inferorum in meas vnius pœnas sufficerét.'Sic Alphonsus rex Hispanicus offensus alicuius,de quo benè meritus erat,ingratitudine,hac oratio ne se repressit: Quare ego isti succensèo,cū Deo multò plura dona mihi tribuerit & ego lögè ingratiorsim Deo,quà hic fuit erga me.'
units.tr: The minds of good men are easily appeased. But I also know that it is noble and praiseworthy to check and restrain that impulse. I know that severity becomes a king, yet I am not unaware how unbecoming it is for the same man to be savage and implacable in anger. Nabal has spoken grievously against me; he has deserved no ordinary punishment. But it is a king's part to show himself to his citizens as he would wish God to show himself to him. And yet how often, and how much more grievously, have I sinned against God! If God were willing to punish me each time there was cause, he would have fire and torments of hell enough for the punishment of me alone." So King Alphonso of Spain, offended by the ingratitude of someone to whom he had been greatly beneficial, restrained himself with these words: "Why should I be angry with him, when God has given me far more gifts, and I am far more ungrateful to God than this man has been to me?"

units.la: E diuerso verbū molestię, id est, respon-sum asperū & superbū irā vehemētius concitat hominemq; exasperat. Nabal sermone duro & contumelioso Dauide exasperat,vt iuret,se ipsum cū tota domo perditurū. Re-habeamus puerili animo atq; consilio cum stultis adolescentibus de regno constituen-do temerè deliberans,populum ita alienat, vt tribus ab eo decem ad Ieroboamū defice-rent: ipse tribus duas Iudæ & Beniaminis tantum retineret. Si prudens senū cōsilium sequu-
units.tr: On the other hand, a word of annoyance, that is, a harsh and proud answer, stirs anger more vehemently and exasperates a man. Nabal, by a hard and insulting speech, exasperated David so that he swore he would destroy him together with his whole household. Rehoboam, rashly deliberating on how to settle the kingdom with the counsel of foolish young men rather than of the prudent old, alienated the people so that ten tribes revolted from him to Jeroboam, and he kept only the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin. If he had followed the counsel of the wise old men and dealt gently with the people, and remitted something of the taxes, he would never have thought of creating a new king.

units.la: 1.Reg. 10. sequutus, placidè cum populo egisset, & aliquid de tributis remisisset, nunquam de novo Rege creando cogitasset. Saepe tyrannicae illae voces, (Nos sumus ius: viscera vestra nostra sunt) Resp. valde afflixerunt. Necessaria itaque est comitas & manuetudo. Incitare potentiorem vesania est: bonum malo penitare, scelus: Iratum potentiorem muneribus verbisque placare, sapientia. Vulgò enim dicitur, illum qui aues vult capere, non debere baculo eas petere: hoc est qui iratum placare vult, id non conuitijs sed benignitate efficiet.
units.tr: 1 Kings 10. Those tyrannical words, "We are the law; your entrails are our own," have often greatly harmed the commonwealth. It is therefore necessary to have courtesy and gentleness. To provoke a more powerful man is madness; to repay evil with good is a crime; to appease an angry and more powerful man with gifts and words is wisdom. It is commonly said that one who wants to catch birds should not go after them with a stick; that is, one who wants to calm an angry man will achieve it not by insults but by kindness.

units.la: Discimus etiam, exemplo Dauidis, qui ne mulierculam quidem admonentem contem fit, admonitiones quod ab obscuris & contemtis hominibus proficiscantur, non asper nandas, sed eo, quo fiant animo, gratatim accipiendas esse. Hoc enim sanctorum ingenium est, ut admoniti, non inuitè cedant: & agnoscant errorem suum, cum feriuntur verbo Dei. Postea quoque, cum à Nathane propheta grauissimè increparetur de teterrimo illo adulterio simul & homicidio, sicut scribitur 2. Samuelis 12. statim Peccaui in Iehouam, exclamat. Sed &, suae regiae Maiestatis & omnis priuatae existimationis omni huma no respectu posthabito, non modò sui illius sceleris historiam passus est scriptis tradi,sed etiam sempiternum ipsemet scripsit eius agnitionis testimonium,quo toti ecclesiæ satisfaceret.Nouerat enim vir sanctissimus,pudere nos peccati,nō refipifcentiæ,oportere: neq; eiusmodi publica quoq; confessione la bem inustam à peccato coràm ecclesia auge ri sed potius deleri:&c. Sic S.Thomas, cum videret Christum verè à mortuis refurrexif fe, repente ex obliuione & veterno ad seipsum rediens,dominus,præ admiratione, inquit, meus & Deus meus es. Nec dubiū est, quin pudore compulsus eruperit in hanc vocem, qua suam socordiam damnaret. Ita Petrus,cum à Paulo reprehenderetur,quod non recto pede incederet, vt veritati Euangelij congruebat (Nam antequam venissent quidam à Iacobo,vnà cum gentibus edebat: quum autem venissent,subduxit fe ac separa uit ab eis,metuens eos,qui erant ex circumcisione,eaq; re scandalum dederat fidelibus Ethnicis) nō respondit,fe melius scire,quid effet agendum,quàm illum:aut fe priore illo fuisse in isto munere, imo iam cum miraculà à fe edita, cum alter iste ecclesiâ Christi persequeretur,& Stephano lapidando, interefs set:sed statim dedit manus,& fassus est fe erraffe,&c.Impij verò nolunt erraffe: Etiamsi, intus accusati, à corde proprio conuincan- tur: tamé extra culpā se positos voluunt: Non nunquam eò impudentiæ deueniunt, vt er- rores etiam apertissimos manu velint defen- dere. Nempe putant, de sua autoritate nō pa- rum decedere, si vel leuissimū errore fatean- tur. Cum negare non possint, sed velint no- lint, fateri cogantur, se magnis in erroribus- versari: tamé sibi ipsis applaudunt, adeoq; in ipsis etiā vitijs placent ac palpant. Multi, quę iniquè & impiè faciunt, iurisiurandi religio- ne excusari putant: atq; ita veritatē (vt Pauli verbo vtamur) in mendacio detinentes, in- dies deteriores fiunt. Imò, quod nō satis de- mireris, dolet hominibus istis nonnunquā, quod oblata malè agendi occasione non sint vsi. Optarent sibi nō paucos annos decisos, dummodo plura possent flagitia committe- re. Tàm abest, vt Dauidis exemplo, Deo gra- tias agant, qui ab instituto, retractos, clemen- ter à scelere deliberato cohibuerit.
units.tr: We also learn, from David's example, that he did not despise even a humble woman who admonished him, so that admonitions coming from obscure and despised people are not to be received harshly, but gladly, in whatever spirit they are offered. For it is the nature of saints that, when admonished, they do not yield unwillingly, and they acknowledge their error when they are struck by the Word of God. Later also, when the prophet Nathan rebuked him most severely for that foul adultery and murder together, as is written in 2 Samuel 12, he at once exclaimed, "I have sinned against the LORD." Moreover, setting aside all human regard for his royal majesty and his private reputation, he allowed the story of that crime to be written down, and he himself wrote an everlasting testimony of his acknowledgement, by which he satisfied the whole Church. For that most holy man knew that we ought to be ashamed of sin, not of repentance, and that such a public confession does not increase the stain of sin before the Church, but rather wipes it away. So also St Thomas, when he saw that Christ had truly risen from the dead, suddenly came back to himself from forgetfulness and drowsiness, and exclaimed in admiration, "My Lord and my God." There is no doubt that, compelled by shame, he burst out into this word, by which he condemned his own dullness. So Peter, when Paul rebuked him because he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the gospel (for before certain men came from James he was eating with the Gentiles, but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing those of the circumcision, and by that act gave offence to the Gentile believers), did not answer that he knew better what should be done than Paul did, or that he had been in that office before him, or even that he had been present when this other man was persecuting the Church of Christ and stoning Stephen, with miracles performed by himself. Instead he at once gave in and confessed that he had erred, and so on. But the impious are unwilling to have erred. Even when they are accused within, and are convicted by their own heart, they still want to be placed outside guilt. Sometimes they come to such impudence that they wish to defend even the most open errors with their hands. Certainly they think that they would lose not a little of their authority if they admitted even the slightest error. Although they cannot deny it, yet, whether they like it or not, they are compelled to confess that they are caught in great errors, they still applaud themselves and so they fawn upon and flatter themselves even in their vices. Many think that what they do unjustly and impiously is excused by the sanctity of an oath; and so, to use Paul's words, holding the truth in unrighteousness, they become worse day by day. Indeed, as you may well marvel, these men sometimes grieve that they did not make use of the opportunity to do evil when it was offered. They would wish that not a few years had been cut off for them, provided they could commit more crimes. So far is it from them, following David's example, to give thanks to God, who turned them back from their undertaking and mercifully restrained them from a deliberate wickedness.

units.la: Adhęc videmus, in reprimēdis prauis scele- ratorū hominū conatib. nihil nō coniunctis operis, effici ac obtineri posse. Quid enim? sic la Abigael Dauidē furente exercitu stipatū, Ἀωεγισίν τ' ἀγανοῖσιν, ἐπεσί τε μειλιχίοισι, tanquā obice obiecto, coercet. Sed quid ho- die fit? Vbi malis est occurrendum, in alios
units.tr: Again we see that in checking the wicked attempts of depraved men, nothing can be achieved or secured unless efforts are joined together. For what did Abigail do? When David was surrounded by a raging army, she restrained him, as with a barrier set in his way, "with gentle words and soothing speeches" [ἀγανοῖσιν τ' ἐπέεσί τε μειλιχίοισι]. But what happens today? Where evils must be met, we turn them on others.

units.la: Studio iugi nihil arduū plærunq; prouinciam istam reijcimus.Quid foli (dicunt multi) effectum daremus.Ami cum aut socium habemus neminem,qui sua potentia & autoritate nos subleuet. Alij fe non eo dicunt genere natos,non ea ornatos eloquentia, quæ hostium potentiæ & conatibus reprimendis sufficiat. Pars Sisyphi saxum volui clamant.Rem explicari nullo modo posse. Verum enimuero,fi Vigilantij potius quam Dormitantij esse mallemus, nihil adeo arduum,adeo difficile effet, quod à nobis non posset studio acri & assiduo imperrari. Ac,quamuis negari non potsit, vsuras, ebrietatem,fcortationem,adulteria, aliaque scelera altissimas radices iecisse : tamen non dubium est,quin fi illi,qui alijs præsunt,in id sedulo incumberent,vt vitiorum fibras amputarent, breui ea radicitus extirparet. Sed quod illi ipsi,qui alijs exemplu virtutis præferre debebant, plærunq; fœdissimis vitijs laborent, hinc fit, vt omnia indies ruant in peius. Fœmina ista omnes illos iudicabit, qui in officio suo remissiores communem interitum à ceruicibus suorum pro virili nō depellunt,prauoq; exemplo inficiunt ac corrumpunt.
units.tr: We usually shrink from this task, however little it may demand constant effort. Many say, "What could we accomplish alone? We have no friend or ally who might support us with his power and authority." Others say they were not born to that station, nor endowed with the eloquence needed to restrain the power and attempts of enemies. Some cry out that they are doing the work of Sisyphus, rolling the stone, and that the matter cannot be accomplished in any way. Yet if we preferred to be the watchful rather than the drowsy, nothing so arduous or so difficult could fail to be achieved by keen and persistent effort. And although it cannot be denied that usury, drunkenness, fornication, adultery and other crimes have struck very deep roots, there is no doubt that if those who preside over others applied themselves diligently to cutting away the fibres of vice, these would soon be torn out root and branch. But because those very people who ought to set an example of virtue to others are often afflicted with the foulest vices, everything decays daily for the worse. That woman will judge all those who, remiss in their duty, do not as far as they can drive off the common ruin from the necks of their own people, and who infect and corrupt them with bad example.

units.la: Colligimus etiam,promissa,vota,ac iuramenta non omnia esse præstanda. Dauid, ira comcommotus, incogitans iurarat, se Nabalem & vniuersam domum eius deleturum esse: Ac,iam in procinctu erat.Et,quod Nabalem attinet, nemo recte negauerit, quin suppli- cium istud commeruerit.Dauidē enim,quē iam tum in Regem vnctum esse ignorare nō poterat,perfidiæ cum suis accusarat, cum il- le semper fidelissimus exstitisset & Saulo ip- si,& Reipublicæ. Arguerat etiam eum iniu- stitiæ,& tonsoribus postposuerat:qui tamen ipsius gregibus muro fuerat & propugnacu lo. Sed quid hæc vel ad Abigaelem vel ser- uitia? Primo in limine errarat Dauid, quod temere, bulliente adhuc ira, iurasset. Sed, cum à muliere admoneretur,iuramèto pru- denter & pie abiurato, Deo immortali gra- tias agit, quod in occursum ei hanc fœminā misisset, quæ ab instituto eum retraheret. Ad eundem modum,si non consilio, sed te- meritate ad iurandum lati fuerimus, idq; si- ne scelere magno præstare nos non posse, videamus, potius mutabimus sacramentum quàm adimplebimus. Nullum enim hic ali- ud periculum est,nisi ne videamur contem- nere Deum. At si quis non ex contemtu sed ex reuerentia erga verbum Dei, rescindat iusiurandum, aut votum, quod videat se id non posse exsoluere sine peccato, non pectasse dicendus est. Imo illi potius grauiter peccant, qui, quod stultè promiserunt, voluntetiam impiè persoluere.
units.tr: We also gather that promises, vows and oaths are not all to be performed. David, moved by anger, had thoughtlessly sworn that he would destroy Nabal and his whole household, and he was already ready for action. As for Nabal, no one could rightly deny that he deserved that punishment. For he had accused David, whom he could not fail to know had already been anointed king, of treachery together with his men, though David had always been most faithful both to Saul himself and to the commonwealth. He had also charged David with injustice and preferred shearers to him, yet David had been a wall and bulwark to Nabal's flocks. But what have these things to do with Abigail or with the servants? David had first erred at the very threshold, in swearing rashly while his anger was still boiling. But when a woman admonished him, he prudently and piously renounced the oath, and gives thanks to the immortal God that He had sent this woman to meet him and turn him back from his purpose. In the same way, if we have been carried into swearing not by deliberation but by rashness, and we see that we cannot perform it without great wickedness, we shall rather change the vow than fulfil it. For there is no other danger here, except that we seem to despise God. But if anyone annuls an oath or vow, not out of contempt but out of reverence for the word of God, because he sees he cannot discharge it without sin, he should be said not to have sinned. Indeed, rather those sin gravely who wish to discharge impiously what they foolishly promised.

units.la: Sed quia multa vltro citroq; de hac re di sputantur, prolixius aliquanto sententiam nostram explicabimus. Primo tenendū est; iuramentitaac promissa, non esse vnius gen-tis. Quædam enim licita sunt, eaq; omnino præstanda veniunt. Vt cum coniuges in sa-cro cœtu, præeunte Ecclesiæ ministro, mu-tuam sibi fidem pollicentur: Hanc enim vio-lare citra periurium non possumus. Quid e-nim? Si quis præsentibus tribus aut quatuor aliquid se facturum promittit, omnino id fa-cit, si sit vir bonus, & bona conscientia id fa-cere possit, quanto magis illa, quæ in con-spectu Dei & angelorum ipsius & tota Ec-clesia, coniuges sibi mutuo promittunt, præ-stare debent? Sic cum nos debitum dissolu-turos recipimus, omnino ad dictum diem fi-dem liberabimus. Ita, si quando diuturno morbo conslictati voueamus, nos postquam pristinæ valetudini, Dei beneficio, restituti fuerimus, diligentius deinceps sacras cõcio-nes audituros, alios ægrotos visitaturos, cre-pulam, ex qua multi morbi oriuntur, fugitu-ros, liberaliores erga pauperes futuros, &c. plane fidem exsoluemus. Sed & Magistratui fidè sacramento solennitèr datam, obedien-tia. tia debita cofirmabimus. Neq; est quod objj ciamus id citra iacturam nostram fieri non posse. Cogitandum potius est, nos sanctissimum Dei nomen interposuisse, qui vniuersè minatus est, quicunq; fe hoc scelere aftrinxe rit, non impunè laturum eoq; omnino promissis ftandū, idq; eò magis, quod illæsa con scientia id fieri possit. Non euitabimus iram Dei, vel nos ipsos excusabimus, etiamsi dicamus, Coacta iuramenta ipsi etiá Deo difpli- cere. Videndum enim omnino est, quid iure & hosti, adeoq; illi, qui à nostra religione diffidet, fidem seruabimus, fi iuramentum inter positum fuerit. Apud Ezechielem dominus contra Zedechiam vehementer fe iratū affir mat, quòd iusiurandū Nebucadnezari Babyloniorū Regi præstitū violarit. Pontificij ho die clamant, Hæreticis fidē nō esse seruandā, ac vulgo prouerbiū hoc in ore habent: Non esse regū & magistratuū, sed mercatorum sta re iuramentis. Cuius rei nō minus memora- bile quá luctuosum in Ladislao Pannonię re ge exemplū habemus, qui pacé cum Amura theTurcarū imp.solenni iureiurando inter- posito fecerat. Eugeni⁹PP. per Iulian. Cęsari núCard. cū benè gerēdę rei occasionē oblatā iactaret, fidē infidelib. seruandá nō esse Chri stiano regi psuadet, pliūq; acerrimū incēdit,
units.tr: But since much is argued back and forth on this matter, we shall explain our view at somewhat greater length. First, it must be held that oaths and promises are not all of one kind. Some are lawful, and these must indeed be performed. For example, when spouses in the sacred assembly, with the minister of the Church presiding, pledge mutual faith, we cannot violate this without perjury. For what? If someone promises in the presence of three or four that he will do something, he certainly does it, if he is a good man and can do it with a clear conscience; how much more must those things be performed which spouses promise each other in the sight of God, of his angels and of the whole Church? So too, when we accept a debt to be repaid, we shall surely keep faith on the appointed day. Likewise, if, afflicted by a long illness, we vow that once restored to former health by God's gift we will hear sacred sermons more diligently, visit other sick people, flee the chills from which many diseases arise, and be more generous to the poor, etc., we shall plainly fulfil our promise. And we shall also confirm the obedience owed to the magistrate, which we solemnly pledged by oath. Nor is there reason to object that this cannot be done without loss to ourselves. We should rather consider that we have interposed the most holy name of God, who has threatened universally that whoever binds himself by this wickedness will not go unpunished; so we must certainly stand by our promises, all the more because it can be done with a clear conscience. We shall not escape the wrath of God, nor excuse ourselves, even if we say that forced oaths displease God himself. For we must certainly consider what faith we keep in justice even with an enemy, and so with one who dissents from our religion, when an oath has been interposed. In Ezekiel the Lord declares himself vehemently angry with Zedekiah because he violated the oath he had sworn to Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians. Today the Papists cry out that faith is not to be kept with heretics, and commonly have on their lips the proverb that it is not for kings and magistrates but for merchants to stand by oaths. We have no less memorable, and no less lamentable, example of this in Ladislaus, king of Pannonia, who made peace with Amurath, emperor of the Turks, with a solemn oath interposed. Pope Eugenius, through Cardinal Julian Cesarini, when he boasted of an opportunity to act well, persuaded the Christian king that faith is not to be kept with unbelievers, and he kindled a most bitter war

units.la: in quo Amurathes cùm de fuga cogitaret, conspecta in hostilibus signis Christi imagine,impius Saracenus,ita fertur, exclamasse, crucifixe,crucifixe, vide gentem tuam perfidam,quæ à me non lacessita,contra iusiurandum violauit: Si Deus es aliquis,fac vt periurij pœnam luat. Itaq; instaurata pugna miserabilis illa clades ad Varnam,obtruncato Ladislao,item Iuliano perfidiæ ministro,morte non solùm misera, sed à Christianis ipsis probrosè execrata confumto, cæsis denique triginta Christianorum millibus sceleratæ perfidiæ funestissimum exemplum Romani Pontificis impietati consecrauit. Quanto rectius Tullius laudat non dico Regulũ:qui, vt hostibus fidem seruaret,ad supplicium redijt: sed Pomponium tribunum Manlij accusatorem, qui, cum terrore mortis coactus, iusiurandum dedisset Tito Manlij filio,se patris accusatio nem dimissurum,iurisiurandi religione motus,à caussa destiterit. Tantùm,ait,temporibus illis iusiurandum valebat. Atque hæc de licitis.
units.tr: in which Amurath, when he was thinking of flight and caught sight of the image of Christ on the enemy's standards, is said to have cried out, the impious Saracen: "Crucified one, crucified one, look at your faithless people, who, though I did not provoke them, have violated their oath. If you are any god at all, make them pay the penalty of perjury." And so, when the battle was renewed, came that wretched disaster at Varna: Ladislaus was cut down, and likewise Julian, minister of treachery, who perished in a death not only wretched but shamefully cursed even by Christians themselves; and finally, with thirty thousand Christians slain, that most deadly example of wicked treachery consecrated the impiety of the Roman Pontiff. How much more rightly does Cicero praise, I do not say Regulus, who returned to his punishment to keep faith with the enemy, but Pomponius, the tribune and accuser of Manlius, who, forced by terror of death, had sworn to Titus, the son of Manlius, that he would drop the prosecution of the father, and, moved by the sanctity of the oath, desisted from the case. "So much," he says, "did an oath count for in those times." So much for lawful oaths.

units.la: Quædam verò iuramenta sunt illicita:eaque omnino præstari non debent: Vt cum adulteræ perpetuam cum ea permanendi si dem pollicemur: cum iuramus,nos Euangelicas gelicas conciones non audituros, sacras lite ras non lecturos, Euangelium toto vitæ no- stræ tempore infestaturos: Multi, pecunia conducti, iurant, reclamante conscientia, se omnes eos, qui Lutheranæ aut Caluinianæ, quam vocant, sectæ adhæreant, ferro & igni excisuros: Multi monasteria ingrediun- tur, sperantes se vita monastica diuinam gra tiam assequuturos & peccata expiaturos: vo uent obedientiam, paupertatem spontaneã, & castitatem. Postea intelligunt, totum hoc vitæ genus, vt hodie in vsu est, diuinis literis ex diametro aduersari. Vident, dum obedi- entiam Abbati vel Priori præstant, se ã legiti ma obedientia sui Magistratus, nonnunquã etiam parentum, quibus eos Deus subiecit, subducere: vident paupertate meruim fucu esse: imò ad fugiendam paupertatem, ad cœ- nobia, tanquam ad asylâ, multos confugere. Quæ ratio fit castitatis, in seipsis experiun- tur, ac in aliis deprehendunt.
units.tr: Some oaths, however, are unlawful, and these must by no means be performed: for example, when we promise an adulteress perpetual faithfulness to remain with her; when we swear that we will not hear evangelical sermons, will not read the holy Scriptures, and will assail the Gospel throughout the whole of our lives. Many, hired for money, swear, though conscience protests, that they will put to the sword and fire all who adhere to the so-called Lutheran or Calvinist sect. Many enter monasteries, hoping by the monastic life to obtain divine grace and expiate their sins; they vow obedience, voluntary poverty and chastity. Afterwards they understand that this whole way of life, as it is practised today, is diametrically opposed to the divine letters. They see that while they render obedience to the abbot or prior, they withdraw themselves from the lawful obedience owed to their own magistrate, and sometimes even to their parents, to whom God has subjected them. They see that poverty is a pretence of merit; indeed many flee to the convents, as to sanctuaries, to escape poverty. As for what kind of chastity it is, they experience it in themselves and detect it in others.

units.la: Sed & in hisce & similibus casibus non te nemur. Nam & natura docet, iuramentũ nõ esse inuentum, vt fit iniquitatis & iniustitiæ vinculum. Item, satius esse, vnum scelus pa- trasse, quam peccata peccatis addere. Ex hoc fonte manauit, satius est recurrere, quàm mã se currere. Quo significatur, laudandos illos
units.tr: But in these and similar cases we are not bound. For nature itself teaches that an oath was not devised to be a bond of iniquity and injustice. Likewise, it is better to have committed one crime than to add sins to sins. From this source came the saying that it is better to turn back than to run badly. By this is signified that those men deserve praise

units.la: N esse, qui in rebus, quas male instituerunt, non pergunt, sed consilium mutant. Hinc est, quod sapientes gentilium etiam dicunt: promissam potius non faciendum, quam tetrum facinus admittendum esse. In vsitata iuris regula est, in stultis promissis rescinde fidem. Si in stultis, multo magis turpibus & impijs. In pontificijs legibus hac de causa multa disputantur, 22. Quaest. 4. in malis, &c. tandem expresse concluditur, Omnia iuramenta, quae cum verbo Dei & salute nostra pugnant, rescindenda esse. Herodes ab Ambrosio, Augustino, Cyrillo, Hesychio, Procopio Gazeo, aliisque fere patribus omnibus omnino male audit, quod non tantum leviter et inconsiderate iurarit, sed quod temere & incaute promisserat, ne videretur religionem verborum suorum violasse, impie & nefarie praestans, sanctum innocentissimi viri caput impudicissimi mę psaltrię tradiderit. D. Petrus apud Ioannem non vult dominum sibi pedes lavare: sed cum audiret, se ipsius non fore participem, nisi ipsum lavaret, Non solum, inquit, pedes, sed etiam manus atq; caput, &c. Ad eundem modum nos quoq;, vbi meliora fuerimus edocti, non relu&tabimur: sed diuino verbo obtemperabimus. Praestat enim verbis dun-taxat peccare, quam impia facta adiungere. Hæc non eo pertinent, vt homines leues aut socordes faciamus, & periurijs frenos laxemus: sed vt afflictas conscientias erigamus & errantes in viam reuocemus, ne magis magis a via salutis aberrent. Cæterà docemus, vera ac legitima iuramenta sanctè & religiosè etiá illis, qui à nostra religione disident, adeoq; etiam hostibus esse præstanda. Dolendum autem est, multos esse, qui iuramenta temerè ac leuiter suscepta, quæq; coràm Deo seruare non tenerentur, religiosissimè seruent: quæ verò omnino seruare oportebat, securè plærunq; negligant. Quod ad illos, qui iuramenta temerè concepta corrigunt, tàm abest, vt illis violatá fidem exprobemus: ac potius ipsis ex animo gratulari debeamus, quod in veram salutis viam reuerterunt. Atq; hæc ad priorē partē annotasse sufficiat.
units.tr: ...who do not persist in matters they have handled badly, but change their plan. Hence the wise men of the Gentiles also say that a promise ought rather not to be kept than a foul crime committed. There is a common rule of law: in foolish promises, break faith. If in foolish ones, much more in base and impious ones. In the Papists' laws, on this ground, many things are disputed (22 Quaest. 4, "In malis", etc.), and finally it is expressly concluded that all oaths which conflict with the word of God and our salvation must be rescinded. Herod is roundly condemned by Ambrose, Augustine, Cyril, Hesychius, Procopius of Gaza and almost all the other Fathers, not merely because he swore lightly and without consideration, but because, rashly and incautiously having made the promise, lest he should seem to have violated the sanctity of his word, he impiously and wickedly handed over the holy head of the most innocent man to the most shameless harlot of a dancer. Peter, in John, does not want the Lord to wash his feet; but when he hears that he will have no part with him unless he washes him, he says: "Not only my feet, but also my hands and head," etc. In the same way we too, when we have been taught better things, shall not hesitate, but shall obey the divine word. For it is better to sin in words only than to add impious deeds. We do not say these things to make men light or careless, and to loosen the reins on perjuries; but to raise up afflicted consciences and to call back those who wander into the way, lest they stray ever further from the path of salvation. Otherwise we teach that true and lawful oaths must be kept sacredly and faithfully, even by those who dissent from our religion, and therefore even to enemies. It is lamentable, however, that there are many who most scrupulously keep oaths taken rashly and lightly, which before God they were not bound to keep, while those which they ought altogether to keep they commonly neglect with complete unconcern. As for those who correct oaths rashly conceived, we are so far from reproaching them with broken faith that we ought rather to congratulate them heartily that they have returned to the true way of salvation. And let this suffice to have noted concerning the first part.

units.la: Quod ad secundam attinet, Dauid ab Abi gaele oblata sibi munera accepit: &, Ascende sanè domū cum bona pace, inquit, En, vocē tuá audiui, faciemq; tuá suscepi. Quibus verbis significat, se mariti culpā ipsi condonasse. Ita Christus, Remissa, inquit mulieri, sunt tibi peccata tua: vade in pace. Pax autem animi nulla sine fide constare potest. Dauid illam non violat: sed saluá & incolumē demittit, nec captam abducit, vt à Nabale homine ditissimo ἀντίλυτρον extorqueat: Nec statim ad vinum donatum prosilit, quemadmodū hodie non pauci,omisfsis rebus maximi momenti,ad vinum desidere solent:Nec militibus suis vt ef sent famelici, potestatem facit, vt in panem & carnes vulturum in morem,inuolent:sed illam cum bona pace dimittit,difciplinamq; obseruat militarem.
units.tr: As to the second, David received the gifts offered to him by Abigail; and he said: "Go up in peace to your house; behold, I have heard your voice and accepted your face." By these words he signifies that he has pardoned her husband's fault. So Christ says to the woman: "Your sins are forgiven you; go in peace." Now there can be no peace of mind without faith. David does not violate it, but lets her go safe and unharmed; nor does he carry her off captive, so as to extort a ransom from Nabal, the very rich man; nor does he dash off at once to the wine provided, as many today are wont to sit down over wine, neglecting matters of the greatest importance; nor does he give his soldiers leave to swoop upon bread and meat like vultures, that they might be starved no longer; but he dismisses her in peace and keeps military discipline.

units.la: Dauid munera accipit: Honoraria enim munera (vt & supra diximus)accipere non est illicitum,vt cum exhausti pecunijs,omni umq; rerū egeni cum fame collusiamur,obla-ta grato animo accipimus.Quin vt iratum potentiorem muneribus placare, sapientis est: ita munera accipere, animi iam placati est indicium.Quem enim oderunt homines cum solent reijcere cum muneribus.Corru ptoriorū,quæ vocant,munerum,vt quæ à li gantibus iudici dantur,vt peruertat iudiciū, ab adulteris vxoribus aut virginibus vt pu-dorem prostituant,&c.alia ratio est. Hæc e-nim nec offerenda nec accipienda. Dicunt nonnulli se munera quidem accipere,sed ni hilominus facere, quod rectum iustumq; vi deatur.At Deus, qui corda hominum explo rat,dicit,munera excæcare prudentes & mu-tare verba vel res iustorum. Si matrona ali-qua dona accipiat ab adulteris,quantumuis
units.tr: David accepts the gifts. For to accept honorary gifts (as we also said above) is not unlawful, just as when we are drained of money and in want of everything, and mock at famine, we accept with a grateful mind what is offered. Indeed, as it is wise to placate an angry superior with gifts, so to accept gifts is a sign of a mind now placated; for men are wont to reject with gifts those whom they hate. But the gifts of corruption, as they are called, which are given to a judge by litigants so as to pervert justice, or which adulterers offer to wives or virgins so that they may prostitute their modesty, are a different matter. For these are neither to be offered nor to be accepted. Some say they accept gifts, but nonetheless do what seems right and just. But God, who searches the hearts of men, says that gifts blind the wise and change the words or the cause of the just. If some matron should accept gifts from adulterers, however honourable she wishes to appear, her chastity will nonetheless be suspect.

units.la: honesta videri velit, tamen suspecta erit eius pudicitia. Homines, qui se muneribus corrumpi patiuntur, ligonem non amplius ligonem vocant, nec scapham scapham. Etsi vero non repente, tamen paulatim mali fiunt. Gentiles etiam intellexerunt, quanta munerum vis sit. Inter quos argute Menander: ὅσις, inquit, ὑπέχει ξένια τῷ χείρα, κ᾽ἂν μὴ φῇ, πονηρά βυλλόμενος. Ouidius:
units.tr: Men who allow themselves to be corrupted by gifts no longer call a spade a spade, nor a boat a boat. And even if it is not sudden, yet little by little they become evil. The Gentiles too understood how great is the power of gifts. Among them Menander shrewdly says: "Whoever offers hospitality with his hand, and does not say it, wishes it to be bad." Ovid:

units.la: Munera, crede mihi, placant homines et Deos:
units.tr: "Gifts, believe me, appease men and gods;

units.la: Placatur donis Iuppiter ipse datis. (det.
units.tr: Jupiter himself is appeased by gifts given."

units.la: Quid facit stultus? Sapiens quoque munere gaudet.
units.tr: "What does the fool do? The wise man too rejoices in a gift."

units.la: Ipse quoque accepto munere mitis erit.
units.tr: "Even the gentle man will be made mild by a gift received."

units.la: Recte ergo Phocion, cum Alexander ei multa dona per suos legatos misisset, eos interrogauit: Cur sibi soli ex tanto Atheniensium numero ea mitteret? Illi responderunt, Quia solum ipsum honestum & egregium virum iudicaret: Me igitur, dixit, talem porro esse sinat. Quid munera efficiant, etiam quotidiana exempla docent. Finge iudicem esse, qui ius dicat ex legibus, patriam, religionem & vitae honestatem colat: quamprimum, ardens auaritia, muneribus se corrumpi patitur, sententiam feret ex affectu, patriae libertatem prodet, religionem & honestatem amplius non curabit: breuiter, omnia habebit venalia. Multi ex doctis veritate agnoscunt: sed propter munera, more Bileami, eam non profitentur. Nec pauci, qui veritatem professi sunt, expugnati muneribus, ab ea turpiter resiliunt. Plurimi non illa, qua debebant, libertate docent, quo ad altiora posint ascendere, Vxores, virgines, si acceperint munera, statim pudoris obliuiscuntur. Quot propter munera innocentem sanguinem effundunt? In accipiendis igitur muneribus Graecorum prouerbium cogitandum est: οὔτε πάντων, οὔτε παρὰ πάντων, id est, nec omnia, nec passim, nec ab omnibus, Nam inhumanum à nemine accipere: sed passim vilissimum est: & omnia auarissimum, &c.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, when Alexander had sent him many gifts through his envoys, Phocion asked them why he alone of so great a number of Athenians was sent them. They replied that he judged him alone to be an honest and outstanding man. "Then let him allow me to remain such," he said. Everyday examples also teach what gifts bring about. Imagine a judge who pronounces law according to the statutes, who cherishes country, religion and integrity of life: as soon as, inflamed by greed, he allows himself to be corrupted by gifts, he will pronounce sentence from passion, betray the liberty of his country, care no more for religion and honesty; in short, he will have everything for sale. Many learned men acknowledge the truth, but on account of gifts, like Balaam, they do not profess it. Nor are few who, having professed the truth, when overcome by gifts shamefully recoil from it. Very many do not teach with the freedom they ought, so that they might rise to higher things. Wives and virgins, if they receive gifts, at once forget their modesty. How many shed innocent blood on account of gifts? In accepting gifts, therefore, the Greek proverb should be kept in mind: "Neither all things, nor from all, nor at random, nor from everyone": for not to accept from anyone is inhuman, but to accept at random is most base, and to accept everything is most greedy, etc.

units.la: Abigael hac ratione veniam sibi, marito, totique familiae impetrauit. Quemadmodum autem Nabal iste, etiamsi impius esset, tamen propter vxorem culpa illi condonatur: Ita hodie deus saepe viro impio propter vxorem piam, vxori propter maritum, propter parentes liberis parcit ne in grauiora periculaincidant. Quod nefarij homines permittuntur viuere, ac non statim perduntur, id debent iustis. Ita enim pollicitus est Deus, se velle parcere toti Sodomae, si vel decem tantum iusti in ea reperiantur.
units.tr: By this reasoning Abigail obtained pardon for herself, her husband and the whole household. And just as this Nabal, though impious, was pardoned his fault on account of his wife, so today God often spares an impious husband on account of a pious wife, a wife on account of her husband, and children on account of their parents, lest they fall into graver dangers. That wicked men are allowed to live and are not destroyed at once, this they owe to the righteous. For God promised thus, that he would spare all Sodom if only ten righteous men could be found in it.

units.la: Dauid, cum interueniret deprecatrix Abigael gael, consilium de vindicta prorsus abiecit, & Nabali, à quo grauissimè erat lesus, parcit: ita nos quoq; iniurias, quas accepimus, rogati æquo animo remittemus, easq;, qui nos aut nostros re aut oratione violarint, nõ inui tè cõdonabimus. Quod vt plane efficiamus, sæpe nos diuinæ literæ, vt iupra quoque dictum est, monent atq; hortantur: cum non beatos solùm eos dicant, qui ita prorsus faciunt, sed erratorum etiam veniam ijsdem à Deo datam affirmant. Qui verò hoc ipsum facere negligunt, aut omnino recusant, illam non consequuntur. Sed & nobilitatem quandam & perfectionem assequimur: quoniam condonandis iniurijs quodammodo Dei similes efficimur, qui solem suum oriri facit super bonos & malos, & pluit super iustos & iniustos. Præclarè ergo Augustinus: Malo, inquit, multas obliuisci iniurias, quàm imaginem & similitudinem cõditoris amittere. Est etiá naturę lege sancitũ, vt tales nos aliis prębeamus, quales eos in nos esse cupimus: verè vt impudentissimus ille sit, qui postulet à Deo, vt sui sceleris pœnam prætermittat, cum ipse in proximum animũ retineat arma tum, ac neminì se det ad lenitatem. An ne, ho mo, inquit Siracides, irá alat aduersus homi nẽ, & à domino salutẽ postulet? aut nũ peccata sua deprecetur, qui sui similis hominis miſereri dedignatur? Quod si homo mortalis iram fouet, & veniam petit a Deo, quis eius peccata expiet? &c. Amicitiæ debent esse immortales, inimicitiæ mortales. Et recte dicut Iurisconsulti. Fauores ampliandi sunt, odia restringenda.
units.tr: David, when the pleading Abigail intervened, altogether put aside the thought of vengeance, and spared Nabal, by whom he had been grievously wronged; so we too, when asked, shall with an even mind remit the injuries we have received, and shall not hesitate to pardon those who have harmed us or ours in deed or word. That we may fully achieve this, the divine letters often admonish and exhort us, as has been said above too, since they not only call blessed those who do exactly this, but also affirm that forgiveness of wrongs is given by God to those who err. Those who neglect or altogether refuse to do this do not obtain it. Yet we also attain a certain nobility and perfection, since by pardoning injuries we become in some measure like God, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the bad, and rains upon the just and the unjust. Augustine therefore says well: "I would rather forget many injuries than lose the image and likeness of the Creator." It is also sanctioned by the law of nature that we should show ourselves to others such as we wish them to be towards us; truly he is most shameless who asks of God that the punishment of his own wickedness be passed over, while he himself keeps his mind armed against his neighbour and yields himself to no gentleness. "Does a man," says Ben Sira, "nourish anger against a man, and seek healing from the Lord? Does he pray for his own sins who has no mercy on a man like himself? If a mortal man cherishes wrath and seeks forgiveness from God, who will atone for his sins?" etc. Friendships ought to be immortal, enmities mortal. And the jurists rightly say: favours are to be enlarged, hatreds to be restricted.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi. HOMILIA VI.
units.tr: THE LIFE AND DEATH OF NABAL THE DRUNKARD. HOMILY VI.

units.la: Nabal ab vxore de suo periculo, quod vix euaserat, edoctus, terrore concidit. Dauid de morte illius Deo gratias agit.
units.tr: When his wife informed Nabal of the danger from which he had barely escaped, he was struck with terror. David gives thanks to God for Nabal's death.

units.la: 36 Venit itaque Abigail ad Nabal, et erat ei conuiuium in domo sua, quasi conuiuium regium, & cor Nabal iucundum in eo, ipseque erat ebrius valde: ipsa autem non indicauit ei quidquam nec paruum nec magnum, vsque ad lucem matutinam.
units.tr: 36 So Abigail came to Nabal. He was holding a feast in his house, a feast fit for a king, and his heart was merry within him, and he was very drunk. She told him nothing, small or great, until the morning light.

units.la: 37 Postera autem die quum digessisset vinum Nabal, indicauit ei vxor eius verba ista, & emortuum est cor eius in medio eius, & fuit in lapidem.
units.tr: 37 But the next morning, when Nabal had slept off the wine, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him and became like stone.

units.la: 38 Quum autem transissent fere decem dies, percussit Iehova Nabal, & mortuus est.
units.tr: 38 About ten days later, Jehovah struck Nabal, and he died.

units.la: 39 Audiens autem Dauid, quod mortuus esset Nabal, dixit: Benedictus Iehoua, qui iudicauit iudicium opprobrij mei de manu Nabal, & seruum suum prohibuit a malo, & malum Nabal reuertifecit Iehoua in caput eius.
units.tr: 39 When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said: Blessed be Jehovah, who has judged the judgment of my reproach at the hand of Nabal, and has kept his servant from evil, and Jehovah has returned the evil of Nabal upon his own head.

units.la: SVpra diximus, quibus rationibus Abigael Dauidem a sanguine faciendo, & in iurijs per seipsum persequendis, cohibuerit. Porro videbimus, quid Nabal interim fecerit, quomodo Abigael illi postridie rem omnem narrarit: ex quo ille tanta animi defectione & corporis saxeo quodam stupore diriguit, ut paucos post dies a Deo ictus interierit: Qua re audita Dauid Deo ex animo gratias egerit.
units.tr: Above we said by what reasons Abigail restrained David from shedding blood and from pursuing his own rights by his own hand. Now we shall see what Nabal meanwhile did, and how Abigail told him the whole matter the following day. When he heard it, his spirit failed and his body stiffened into a kind of stony stupor, so that a few days later God struck him and he died. When David heard this, he gave heartfelt thanks to God.

units.la: 1. Abigael, vbi ad Nabalem venit, inuenit eum domi suæ securum in conuiuio, animoque lætum ac bene potum. Nihil ipsi negotij facescebat, quod Dauid ipsum fortunis omnibus euertere constituisset. Nihil enim horum sciebat. Hoc habent impij, ut, quando in maximo discrimine versantur, tunc ip si maximè sint securi. Cuius rei publica & priuata exempla habemus complura. Ita, qui proximè diluuium præcesserunt, comedebant, bibebant, ducebant vxores, nubebant,vfq; ad eum die, quo ingresso in arcam Noeo,diluuio præter spem sunt absorpti.Lota,temporibus Lothi,comedebant,bibebát, emebant,vendebant,plantabant,ædificabát, donec Lotho Sodomá egresso, Deus illos igne & sulphure funditus omnes cósumeret. Securos fuisse vel inde apparet, quod illos nupsisse,ædificasse dicit Dominus.Enimuerò cum vel pestis,vel annonę ,vel belli periculum est,animú nó facilè vel ad nuptias vel ad ędiú substructiones applicamus.Econtra vbi nullus metus est,nupturimus, & insana ædificandi libidine titillamur.Daniel.5.Balthasar Babyloniorum rex, mille suis proceribus cóuiuium lautum habet,& apud eos vino potus,iubet inter pocula proferri, aurea argenteaq; vasa , quæ auus eius Hierosolymis è templo rapta deportarat, & exijs ad mensuram cum aulicis suis & concubinis potat,impossibile ratus,Persas &Medos Babylone suá potituros : Sed illa ipsa nocte,in conuiuio illo suo (quod proculdubio ad aliquot dies durarat) à Cyro confoditur. Christus apud Lucam diuitem quendam in ducit,qui cum eius fundus abunde extulisset,sic secum ipse cogitarit:Quid agam, cum non habeam , quò fruges meas congeram? Tandem,Hoc agam, inquit, horrea mea diruam.
units.tr: 1. When Abigail came to Nabal, she found him at home, at ease at his feast, cheerful in spirit and well in his cups. He had no worry at all, for he did not know that David had resolved to overturn all his fortunes. For he knew nothing of these things. This is the way of the wicked: when they are in the greatest danger, then they are most secure. We have many examples of this, both public and private. So those who lived just before the Flood ate and drank, took wives and were given in marriage, right up to the day when Noah entered the ark and the Flood swept them away, against all expectation. In the days of Lot, they ate, drank, bought, sold, planted and built, until Lot went out of Sodom and God destroyed them all utterly with fire and brimstone. That they were secure is clear from the Lord's own words, that they were marrying and building. Indeed, when there is danger from plague, famine or war, we do not readily turn our minds to weddings or to building houses. On the contrary, where there is no fear, we marry and are tickled by a mad desire to build. Daniel 5. Belshazzar, king of the Babylonians, gave a lavish feast for a thousand of his nobles, and drinking wine in their company, he ordered the golden and silver vessels that his grandfather had carried off from the temple in Jerusalem to be brought in among the cups. He drank from them with his courtiers and concubines, thinking it impossible that the Persians and Medes would take Babylon. But that very night, at that same feast (which had doubtless lasted for some days), he was slain by Cyrus. Christ, in Luke, introduces a certain rich man whose land had yielded abundantly, and who thought to himself: What shall I do, since I have no place to store my crops? At last he said: This I will do, I will pull down my barns.

units.la: Balthasar inter scorta & pocula confoditur.
units.tr: Belshazzar is slain amid his harlots and his cups.

units.la: Luc.12. ruam, & maiora construam, eoque omnes meos prouentus & bona congeram, atq; ita animæ meæ dicam: Anima habes multa bona in multos annos, condita: Requiesce, ede, bibe, indulge voluptati. Sed quid ad hæc Deus? O demens, inquit, hac nocte reposcetur à te anima tua: Ista autem, quæ paraifi, cuius erunt? Stultus iste multos adhuc annos, quibus se in omnes voluptates ingurgitaret, pollicebatur: Sed illa ipsa nocte, qua nihil minus expectabat, insperato decedit. D. Bernardus prudenter addit: Tu ipse, qui ea parasti, cuius eris? Ita Arius, cum iussu Imperatoris restituendus esset Ecclesiæ & iam animo secuto esset, mortuus est in itinere. Ita Iulianus Apostata, cum certus esset de victoria contra Persas, Christianiq; nominis cuerfionem animo cogitaret, sagitta, ab incerto auctore vibrata, ictus, è veltigio est interfectus. Ita Iulius Cæsar, cum pridie vesperi ociosè & secure disputasset de optimo genere mortis, postridie in Senatu est confossus. Recte ergo D. Paulus, cum de aduetu Christi dissereret, nos in omne momentum paratos esse iubet. Cū enim dicet homines, ait, Pax & tuta oia, tū repente, vt dolor vterū fereti, sic eis instabit interit, quē non effugient. Quę verò ille de nouiss. die dicit. ea ad ipsorum diem nouissimum, vel mortis articulum transferri possunt.
units.tr: ...pull them down, and build greater ones, and there gather all my produce and goods; and so I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, indulge in pleasure. But what did God say to this? O fool, he said, this night your soul will be required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? That fool promised himself many years in which to gorge himself on every pleasure, but that very night, when he expected it least, he died unexpectedly. Saint Bernard wisely adds: You yourself, who have prepared these things, whose will you be? So Arius, when by the Emperor's command he was to be restored to the Church, and already his heart was set on it, died on the way. So Julian the Apostate, when he was certain of victory over the Persians and was planning the overthrow of the Christian name, was struck by an arrow shot by an unknown hand and killed on the spot. So Julius Caesar, having discussed at leisure and without care, the evening before, the best kind of death, was stabbed in the Senate the next day. Rightly, then, Saint Paul, when he spoke of the coming of Christ, bids us to be ready at every moment. For when men say, "Peace and all is safe," then suddenly destruction will come upon them, as labour pains come upon a woman with child, and they will not escape. What he says of the last day may be applied to their last day, or to the moment of death.

units.la: Quæratautem aliquis, vnde ista securitas hominibus carnalibus nascatur? Nempe ex eo, quod Deum contemnant, & certo sibi persuadeant, eum nunquam poenas de peccatis sumturum. Clementem enim esse, non vindictæ cupidum, qualem illum iustitiarij faciant. Sed & peccata non tanta iudicant, & iram Domini contra peccatum, vt res digna sit aliqua correctione, aut cura grauiore. Altera autem est spiritualis securitas, εὐθυμίαν Græci vocant, quæ ex vera fide orta, iustissimæ Dei voluntati, rebus etiam aduersissimis aquiescit, ijsq; gloriatur: vt quæ norit (quemadmodum præclarè Paulus) quòd afflictiones patientiæ nos assuefaciant, patientia verò bonitatem Dei nobis reddat exploratam: ista deniq; experientia spem non stram alat, quæ quidem nunquam nos frustratur. Cæterà, vt verè Augustinus, Vbi securitas inquit: Hic nusquam: in ista vita nusquam, nisi in sola spe promissionum Dei. Vbi autem illuc peruenerimus, perfecta securitas, cum claudentur portæ. Et in sententijs illius refertur: Nunquam secura esse debet felicitas: quia sunt periculosiora animo securæ, quàm corpori aduersa. Et lib. 10. Confess. fess.cap.32. Nemo in hac vita securus esse de ber,quæ tota tentatio nominatur. Et Hieronym.cap.9.Danie l. Securitas, inquit,negligentiam parit,&c.
units.tr: But someone may ask, whence does this security arise in carnal men? Surely from this, that they despise God and firmly persuade themselves that he will never take vengeance for sins. For they think him merciful, not eager for vengeance, as those who make him a dispenser of justice would have him. They also judge their sins not to be so great, and God's wrath against sin not such that it deserves any correction or serious care. There is, however, another, spiritual security, which the Greeks call euthymia, which arises from true faith and acquiesces in the most just will of God, even in the most adverse circumstances, and glories in them. It knows (as Paul excellently says) that afflictions work patience in us, and patience makes God's goodness proven to us, and this proven hope nourishes our hope, which never disappoints us. Otherwise, as Augustine truly says: "Where there is security, here it is nowhere; in this life nowhere, except in the sole hope of God's promises. But when we shall have come there, perfect security will be ours, when the gates are shut." And in his sayings it is recorded: "Happiness should never be secure, for adversity to the body is less dangerous than security to the mind." And in book 10 of the Confessions, chapter 32: "No one in this life ought to be secure, for this whole life is called a temptation." And Jerome on Daniel, chapter 9: "Security," he says, "begets negligence," and so on.

units.la: Quod verò Nabal suis conuiuium lautú parat,per se culpari non potest.Nam, quod & supra diximus,laboribus aliorum non est abutendum,siue illi serui,siue mercenarij,si ue artifices sedentarij sint. Qui multum laborant,cibo vberiore indigent.Sunt,qui ad laborandum quidem suos vrgent, sed non suppeditant eis tantum cibi, vt vel latrantŏ stomachum placare possint.Alij cibum non rectè parant,nec in tempore esculenta proferunt,sed malunt illa perire.Sunt,qui cibos quidem apponant,sed indignè ferunt,si serui ad saturitatem comedant. Sed quid fit? Serui & ancillæ, si videant eos tam parcos & tenaces, clam multa abliguriunt: Sed & segnius & remissius officium agunt.
units.tr: That Nabal prepared a lavish feast for his fellows cannot in itself be blamed. For, as we said above, the labours of others must not be abused, whether they are servants, hired workers, or sedentary craftsmen. Those who labour hard need more abundant food. There are some who drive their people to work but do not give them enough food to quiet their barking stomachs. Others do not prepare food properly, nor bring out victuals in good time, but prefer that they spoil. There are some who indeed set out food, but take it badly if the servants eat to their fill. But what happens? Servants and maids, when they see their masters so sparing and tight-fisted, secretly snatch a great deal, and they also perform their duties more sluggishly and carelessly.

units.la: Nec hoc nomine reprehendi iure potuis set Nabal, quod amicos, vicinos aliosq; ad conuiuium inuitasset,frontemq;, quod dici tur,exporrexisset. Nec enim damnantur à sacris literis hospitalitatis officia, quæ amicis,fratribus,cognatis aut vicinis,etiam opu lentioribus, & in aliqua dignitate constitutis exhibentur.Sed & naturæ lex est, vt bonam gratiâ quibuscunq; referamus, & amó-rem inter nos mutuis officijs foveamus.
units.tr: Nor could Nabal rightly be reproved on this ground, that he invited friends, neighbours and others to his feast, and, as they say, showed a bold face. For the sacred writings do not condemn the duties of hospitality, which are shown to friends, brothers, kinsmen or neighbours, even to those wealthier and placed in some dignity. Indeed, it is a law of nature that we repay good turns to all, and foster love among ourselves by mutual kindnesses.

units.la: Quod si hominis ingenium spectemus, nos ad societatem & amicitiam natura propen-sos esse constat, & inde factum esse, vt olim in ciuitates coirent, qui prius dispersi vagaban-tur. Ad societatem verò vel ineundam vel confirmandam, conuiuia honesta & amica plurimum conferre nemo negauerit, qui vel mediocrem habet rerum humanarum vsum.
units.tr: If we consider the disposition of man, it is plain that we are inclined by nature to fellowship and friendship, and that this is why, of old, those who wandered dispersed came together into cities. Now, that honourable and friendly feasts contribute greatly both to entering into and to strengthening such fellowship, no one will deny who has even a moderate experience of human affairs.

units.la: Et ipsa conuiuij vox communione vitæ signifi-cat, qua nihil iucundius, nihil vtilius, nihil de-niq; magis necessarium est, cum sine illa seneque priuatæ amicitiæ, neq; ciuitatum con-cordia: imò nec, quæ in Christi ecclesia habetur salutis æternæ communio, siue socie-tas consistere potest. Quapropter honora-ria conuiuia sanctissimis quoq; Patribus se-per in vsu fuisse legimus, quemadmodum a-liquot exemplis ad 1.caput Iobis docui. Sed & Deus nobis gaudia honesta concedit. Ve-rum, quod modum excedimus omnem, id demum repræhensionem meretur. Cogitan-dum cuiq; venit, quid statum suum deceat, minusue. Ciuis, vel rusticus etiam ditissimus non debet certare cum Barone aut Comite, ne dū Principe. Inprimis verò culpandū est quod & se, & qui fœdus istorū hominū mos est, hospites suos vino onerat & ingurgitat.
units.tr: And the very word convivium means a sharing of life, and nothing is more pleasant, more useful, or indeed more necessary than this. Without it, neither private friendship nor concord in cities can stand; nor even that communion of eternal salvation which is found in the Church of Christ. For this reason we read that honourable feasts were always in use among the most holy Fathers, as I have shown by several examples on the first chapter of Job. God also grants us honest joys. But when we exceed every measure, that alone deserves reproof. Each person ought to consider what befits his station, and what does not. A citizen, or even a very wealthy countryman, ought not to vie with a baron or a count, let alone a prince. Above all, it is to be blamed that, as is the custom of these men, they load and gorge both themselves and their guests with wine.

units.la: Modus in conuiuijs feruandus.
units.tr: Moderation to be observed at feasts

units.la: vt neq; manus neq; pes neq; lingua officium faciat. Neq; enim vinū ebriosis sapit, nisi aliōs quoq; eò sepultos videant vt incedere am plius non possint, quos non aliter inclamat & impellunt ac aurigæ suos cum in palude subsistunt, equos. Sed & pauperum in conui uijs ratio est habenda, quanuis nulla retribu tionis spes affulgeat. Id quod Nabal noster parum obseruauit. Nā vt in cōbibones suos esset liberalissimus, in solos famelicos parcis simus erat, imò de re familiari sua iam actum esse putasset, si vel micam famelico alicui de disset. Hodie quoq; multi diuites eo sunt in-genio, vt cum in mensas plus quàm Sybariti cas, res item nihili & inhonestas, mira prodi galitate opes ingentes profundant, & nimij sint erga homines leues ac futiles, vel eos e-tiam, qui seipsos alere poterant, erga solos pauperes pumice aridiores sint, imò hoc so lum perditū aut saltem male collocatū arbi-trentur, quod in illos cōfertur. Quidam etiā erga cōiuges & liberos duri sunt, ac de victu familiæ subministrando, appellati, animo æ-stuant. Ac quàto satius erat cogitare, se plus vini superfluè quàm ad necessitatem vti:tur piter oblitis fidelis illius Christi admonitio nis: Cauete vobis, ne quando grauentur cor da vestra crapula & ebrietate: & curis huius vitæ, &c.
units.tr: Moderation must be kept so that neither hand, nor foot, nor tongue performs its office. For wine does not taste good to drunkards unless they see others buried there too, so that they can no longer walk, and they shout at and push these men no differently than charioteers do their horses when the horses stick fast in a marsh. But care must also be taken for the poor at feasts, even though no hope of repayment shines forth. Our Nabal observed this poorly. For while he was most generous to his drinking companions, he was most stingy toward the hungry alone. He would indeed have thought his household property already ruined if he had given even a crumb to some hungry man. Today too many rich people are of such a disposition that, while they squander great wealth with astonishing prodigality on Sybaritic tables and on trifling and disgraceful things, they are lavish toward frivolous and shallow people, or even toward those who could feed themselves, yet are drier than pumice toward the poor alone. Indeed they think the only thing lost, or at least badly spent, is what is conferred on those people. Some are also harsh toward wives and children, and when they are asked to provide food for the household, they seethe with anger. How much better it would be to consider that they use more wine than necessity requires, and in doing so forget, at the same time, the faithful admonition of Christ: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness, and with the cares of this life," etc.

units.la: 2 Abigael cum virum videret ita affectu, nihil ei prorsus ante posterum diem retulit. Quippe norat, se cum absente acturam, Expectat ergo vt animum colligat & ad se redeat. Mane, vbi crapula exhalata, vinum edormisset, rem isti omnem indicauit. Vulgo fertur, Eum, qui ebrio loquatur, mortuo, vel, quod in idem recidit, absenti verba face re: Item: Ebrio & plaustro oriusto, de via cedendum. Cleoftratus (vt est apud Stobaeu) de ebrietate accusatus, ac rogatus, num ipsum tam foedi vitij puderet: Anno te, inquit, pudet, qui ebrium vel moneas, vel cum illo verbum commutes. Etiamsi Abigael cum illo loqui voluisset inter vinum, tamen illam non audiuisset, vel non intellexisset: vel intelectam contumelijs affecisset. Adhaec noluit set se, praesentibus alijs, ijsq;, vt credibile est, bene potis castigari. Recte ergo rem in aliud tempus differt. Ita Dominus in Euangelio docet: Margaritas non esse proijciendas ante porcos. Non fuisset operae precium, foeminam illam graui aliqua oratione coram porcis istis incassum vti.
units.tr: 2 When Abigail saw her husband so affected, she told him nothing at all until the next day. Indeed she knew she would be dealing with him while he was absent from his senses. So she waited for him to collect his mind and come back to himself. In the morning, when the drunkenness had evaporated and he had slept off the wine, she disclosed the whole matter to him. It is commonly said that one should speak to a drunk man either when he is dead, or, which comes to the same thing, when he is absent. Likewise: one should give way to a drunk man and to a loaded wagon. Cleophratus (as it is in Stobaeus), accused of drunkenness and asked whether he was not ashamed of so foul a vice, replied: "Are you not ashamed, you who would either admonish a drunk man or exchange a word with him?" Even if Abigail had wished to speak with Nabal while he was drinking, he would either not have heard her or not understood her, or, having understood, would have treated her with insults. Moreover she did not want him to be rebuked while others were present, who were, as is likely, well drunk. So rightly she put the matter off to another time. Thus the Lord teaches in the Gospel that pearls are not to be cast before swine. It would not have been worth the trouble for that woman to use some weighty speech in vain before those swine.

units.la: Vxor non solum potest, verum etiam debet, maritum castigare, &c, vt sibi caveat, admonere. Enimuero, vt multis Chrysostomus, Grande momentum est mulier ad virum re-
units.tr: A wife not only can but also ought to rebuke her husband, etc., so that he takes care of himself, and to warn him. Indeed, as Chrysostom says in many places, a wife has great weight with her husband.

units.la: Stob. Ser. 34. de tem pest. oratio ne.
units.tr: Stob. Ser. 34. On the tempest of the mind, an oration.

units.la: In Ioan. Euangel. Vxoria ad monitio qualis esse debeat. tum recte admonendum, & si qua inuaserit animum illius tempestas, sedandum. Neque enim maritus vel patri æquè vel magistro aut icultabit, ac coniugi probæ. Habet voluptatem nescio quam, haud sane exiguam, admonitio vxoria, quandoquidem ex ingenti beneuolentia videtur nasci. Amat enim mulier hunc, cui consulit: nec aliter prospectum ei cuperet, quàm sibi ipsi. Sed reuera momenti ad hanc rem habet plurimum, si personæ, loci, temporis & aliarum συνεσήσεων diligentè habeat rationem. Maritus enim non vult, vxore audientibus aliis, de curis suis & cogitatibus omnibus referre: Sed nec omnia tempora sunt consentanea. Irato marito, vel ebrio, vxor plus dabit incomodi, quàm commodi. Quemadmodum enim externi ebriorum oculi ita offuscantur, vt simplicia illis dupla videantur, & recta incurua: ita animus excæcatur, vt bonum malum esse arbitretur, & malum bonum. Sigillum molli cera imprimes, & monita molli animo: scilicet cum pectus illius nulla perturbatione agitur, seorsim & semotis arbitris. Adhæc singularis debet ab vxoribus modestia adhiberi. Nihil hic audimus acerbæ reprehensionis: non rixatur, nec euertit mensas, non verberat ebriū: Satis put tauit esse, vt rem illi simpliciter proponeret. quid nempe expectandum fuisset: quantam Deus pro illo curam egerit: quàm parum omnes ab internecione abfuerint, &c.
units.tr: (In John's Gospel. What a wife's admonition ought to be like.) Then she should rightly admonish him, and if some storm has invaded his mind, she should calm it. For a husband yields no less willingly to a father or to a master than to a virtuous wife. A wife's admonition has a pleasure of some kind, and by no means a small one, since it seems to arise from great goodwill. For a woman loves the one whom she advises, and she would wish provision for him no differently than for herself. But in truth a great deal depends on this matter, if she carefully takes account of the person, the place, the time and the other circumstances [συνεσέων]. For a husband does not wish, with others listening, to report to his wife all his cares and all his thoughts. Nor are all times suitable. With a husband who is angry or drunk, a wife will cause more trouble than benefit. For just as the eyes of drunkards are so clouded that single things seem double to them and straight things crooked, so the mind is blinded so that it thinks good to be evil and evil to be good. You press a seal into soft wax, and admonitions into a soft mind: namely, when his breast is stirred by no agitation, and when they are apart and the witnesses removed. Moreover, singular moderation must be shown by wives. Here we hear nothing of bitter rebuke: she does not quarrel, nor overturn the tables, nor beat the drunkard. She thought it enough to set the matter simply before him: what, namely, was to be expected; how great a care God had for him; how little all of them had been from destruction, etc.

units.la: Quod de vxoribus dicitur, in genere ad omnes transferri potest. Officium enim extra tempus molestia est. Recte Poeta ille:
units.tr: What is said of wives can in general be applied to everyone. For a duty performed out of season is an annoyance. Rightly that poet says:

units.la: Intempestiue qui monet, ille nocet.
units.tr: He who admonishes at the wrong time does harm.

units.la: Omnino igitur occasiones captandę, si quid aliquè monere velis: vt medici solent, si quid volunt ægroto propinare. Neq; id iniuria. Nam, vt scitè ille,
units.tr: Altogether, therefore, opportunities should be seized if you wish at any time to admonish someone, as physicians do when they wish to give something to a sick man. Nor is this without reason. For, as that wise man says:

units.la: Tèporibus medicina valet, data tempore prosunt:
units.tr: Medicine works by timing; given at the right time, they help.

units.la: Et data non apto tempore vina nocent, &c.
units.tr: And wines given at an unsuitable time do harm, etc.

units.la: 3 Nabal, vxori de Dauidis iracundia iusta, & de suo periculo, quod vix euaserat, vt ba facienti, quod hactenus ipsi nullis vnquam mendacijs illusisset, fidem habet amplissimam. Sed quid fit? Cor ipsius ita statim emoritur in illo, vt destiterit facere officium suum, & corpus calefacere. Grauiter enim commouentur spiritus vehementibus & repentinis affectibus. Insperata enim opinio de ingenti aliquo bono, aut malo, ita verberat & affligit cor, vt legamus quosdam timore, dolore, adeoq; etiam gaudio fuisse mortuos. Hinc Nabal noster in lapidem dirigu̇t. Intra decem circiter dies à Domino percussus, interijt. 2. Paralip. 13. de Ieroboamo rege authore & capite idololatriæ & rebellionis etiam dicitur, quòd Dominus illum percussērit, & mortuus sit. Quo morbi genere sublatus sit, non exprimitur: sed videtur his verbis significari, illum nō vulgari morte perijsse. Tyranni enim plerunq; tragicos habent exitus. Vereq; omnino dixit ille: Ad generū Cererūs sine cæde & sanguine pauci Descendunt reges & sicca morte tyranni. Tametsi verò Nabal nostèr & Ieroboamus placida morte obijssent, certum tamen est, quòd, nisi pœnitentiam egissent, ac firma spe in futurum Mesiam toti recubuissent, æternum fuissent condemnati. Aperte enim Christus: Qui in filium Dei credit, non condemnatur: Qui verò non credit, iam condemnatus est, quod in vnigeniti Dei Filij nomé non crediderit. Et: Qui in filium credit, vitā consequuturus est sempiternā: Qui autē Filio nō credit vel paret, in Græco est ἀπειθῶν quod vtrunq; significat, is vitam non videbit: Sed ira Dei manet super ipsum, vers. 36.
units.tr: 3 Nabal gives the fullest credence to his wife, who tells him of David's just anger and of his own danger, which he had barely escaped, since she had never hitherto deceived him with any lies. But what happens? His heart at once dies within him, so that it ceases to perform its office and to warm the body. For the spirits are gravely stirred by vehement and sudden emotions. An unexpected report of some great good or evil so strikes and afflicts the heart that we read of some having died of fear, of grief, and even of joy. Hence our Nabal is turned to stone. Struck by the Lord about ten days later, he died. Of Jeroboam the king, the author and head of idolatry and rebellion, it is also said in 2 Paralip. 13 that the Lord struck him and he died. The kind of disease by which he was carried off is not stated, but it seems to be signified by these words that he did not perish by an ordinary death. For tyrants usually have tragic ends. And truly that poet said: Few kings and tyrants go down to the house of Ceres without slaughter and blood, by a dry death. Although our Nabal and Jeroboam died a peaceful death, it is nevertheless certain that, unless they had repented, and had rested wholly on a firm hope in the Messiah to come, they would have been condemned eternally. Christ says plainly: "He who believes in the Son of God is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God." And: "He who believes in the Son shall have eternal life; but he who does not believe or obey the Son [ἀπειθῶν, which in Greek means both] shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides on him," ver. 36.

units.la: Nabal, audita coniugis relatione, obstupuit, steterunq; comæ & vox faucibus hęsit, menteq;, qua prius magna parte carebat, in totum priuatur. Impij rebus ad voluntatem fluentibus, securi sunt, verique Vcalegones de periculis admoniti, ridēt, suasque res
units.tr: Nabal, having heard his wife's report, was stunned; his hair stood on end, his voice stuck in his throat, and he was wholly deprived of his mind, which he had already largely lacked. The wicked, while things flow to their liking, are secure; and when warned of dangers, they laugh like true Ucalegons and think all their affairs are in harbour.

units.la: omnes in portu esse putant: Rebus arctis, nihil superesset, nisi ut desperent. Cuius rei memorabile in Balthasare Babyloniorum rege ultimo habemus exemplum. Quis enim illo inter scyphos confidentior? quis audacior? Deo vero contempto & irriso, deos suos aureos, argenteos, aereos, ferreos, ligneos, lapideosque collaudat, & sibi tuta omnia pollicetur. Verum, ubi primum quanda quasi manu literas in parietis tectorio e regione candelabri ignotas pingentē videt, expallet, adeoque mente perturbatur, ut eneruatis lateribus, genua eius inuicē cōfligeret. Ad eundem modū omnes impij, dum res in tuto sunt, fe rociunt: periculis instantibus, nulli sunt, toti occidunt, cor metu moritur, membra miseris tremunt, nesciunt unde auxilij, praesidij perfugij sibi, aut opum copiam comparent aut expetant.
units.tr: When things are straitened, nothing is left to them but to despair. Of this we have a memorable example in Belshazzar, the last king of the Babylonians. For who was more confident than he among the cups? Who more audacious? God being despised and mocked, he praises his gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone, and promises himself that all things are safe. But as soon as he sees letters, unknown, painted as if by a hand on the plaster of the wall opposite the candlestick, he turns pale, and is so troubled in mind that, with his loins weakened, his knees knock together. In the same way all the wicked, while things are safe, grow fierce; when dangers press, they are nothing and utterly perish. The heart dies of fear, the wretched limbs tremble; they do not know whence to obtain help, protection or refuge, nor do they seek or procure any store of resources.

units.la: Hoc loco videmus, impijs quoq;, & non nunquam opinione citius moriendum, ut vi deantur in pios perpetuo grassaturi. Imprimis vero docemur, conuersionem ad Deum non differendā. Paulatim enim vitiis assuescimus, ut postea ab illis cauere non possimus, imo vitia virtutum loco habeamus. Quàm multi subitis casibus oppressi in peccatis suis pereunt? Ne igitur abutamur bonitate Dei ad confirmandâ securitatê, sed Deo gratias agamus, concedenti nobis spaciū ad pœnitentiā, quâ Nabalê egisse non apparet. Diriguit enim illico in lapidê, omnēq; sensum amisit. Quanuis post 10. demū dies decesserit: forte ne quis suspicaretur, eū aut ve neficio, aut suasu Dauidis, aut à familia iussu Abigaelis fuisse sublatum. Bene operemur, dum occasio à Deo nobis conceditur; nesci mus, quid ferus vesper vehat.
units.tr: Here we see that the wicked too sometimes die sooner than anyone expects, though they seem set to rage against the godly forever. Above all we are taught that conversion to God must not be put off. For we gradually grow accustomed to vices, so that afterwards we cannot guard against them, and indeed we come to regard vices as virtues. How many, overtaken by sudden misfortunes, perish in their sins? So let us not abuse the goodness of God to confirm our security, but let us thank God, who grants us time for repentance, which Nabal does not appear to have used. For he at once turned to stone and lost all feeling. Although he died only after ten days, perhaps this was so that no one would suspect he had been removed by poison, or at David's persuasion, or by the household at Abigail's command. Let us do good while God grants us the opportunity; we do not know what the wild evening will bring.

units.la: Fit etiam, vt pij quoq; aliquando apoplexia tacti, loquendi facultatem omnino amittant, & sine sensu iaceat ad aliquot dies. Sed quod animo longè aliter affecti sint, quâ impij, (Sani enim mane, vesperi, &c. precibus se Deo commendant, & cum se mortales & in hoc mundo peregrinos esse norint, nunquâ non vigilant, adeoq; cupiut dissolui, vt cum Christo in cœlis viuere possint) benè de ipsis est sperandum, etiamsi nō redeant ad sensus. Alia ratio impiorum est, qui, cum Deum sani non curarint, imò ventrem Deū habuerint, in eiusmodi casibus, nihil habent, quo se recipiant. Neq; enim Deū inuocat, neq; peccatum agnoscūt, neq; pœnitentia ducuntur. Qui plura hac de re cupit cognoscere, legat librum consolatorium Ambrosii Blaureri.
units.tr: It also happens that the godly, when struck by apoplexy, sometimes lose the power of speech altogether and lie without sense for some days. But since they are affected in a quite different way in their minds from the wicked (for morning and evening, and at other times, they commend themselves to God in prayer, and since they know they are mortals and strangers in this world, they are never not watchful, and so they desire to be dissolved that they may live with Christ in heaven), good hope may be had for them, even if they do not return to their senses. The wicked are in another situation: since they did not care for God while healthy, but rather made their belly their god, in such cases they have nothing to which they can turn. For they neither call upon God, nor acknowledge sin, nor are led to repentance. Whoever wishes to learn more on this matter, let him read the consolatory book of Ambrosius Blaurer.

units.la: Qualem omnem vitam egerat, tali defun{a}ctus est morte. Truncus vixerat; ita nunc in truncū mutatur; imò plane in lapide dureccit: sensu omni amisso, ἀναίσθητος perit: Breuiter, sicut vixit, ita morixit, vt ioculari dicitur prouerbio. Quid illi iam ingēs opū acer uus, quid auctoritas, quid pompa, aliaq; q̄ in sanus mundo deperit, magniq; facit, pdest.
units.tr: As was the life he led, so was the death he suffered. He had lived like a stump; now he is turned into a stump; indeed he has hardened altogether into stone, and having lost all feeling he dies insensible [ἀναίσθητος]. In short, as he lived, so he died, as the proverb says in jest. What now is the use to him of his huge heap of wealth, his authority, his pomp, and the other things the world loves and esteems?

units.la: Mirum autem, quantum tragicus ste tru culenti istius hominis exitus ad consolatio- nem piorum faciat. Ita enim ratiocinantur; Qui effrenem impotentis huius hominis au daciam, sublimemq; insolentia subito fregit: ille hodie etiam hostes suos potest compes- cere, ne suos diutius vexent. E contra tyran nis est horrori. Hinc enim colligunt, vitam suam angustis spaciis à Deo circumscriptā, qui illos plerunq; nihil tale expectantes, im proviso tollit.
