In Actis de Herode Agrippa Aristobuli quarti filio legitur, quod cum sta tuta die induitus veste regia, & sedens pro tribunali, concionaretur ad eos: populus au tem acclamaret, Dei vox, & nō hominis, per cusserit eū angelus Domini morbo lethali, eo quod non dedisset gloriam Deo, intestina eius putrefacta cum vermes roderent, die 5. post moritur, ingenti & membrorū & con- scientiæ cruciatu, coquerens & lamentans, nullum vspiā in terris hominē se miseriorem viuere.
units.tr: It is remarkable how much the tragic and grim end of this man yields for the consolation of the godly. For they reason thus: he who suddenly broke the unbridled audacity of this powerless man and his lofty insolence can today also restrain his enemies, so that they no longer harass his people for long. On the contrary, it is a horror to tyrants. For from this they conclude that God, who often takes away unexpectedly those who look for nothing of the kind, has circumscribed their life within narrow limits. In Acts we read of Herod Agrippa, son of Aristobulus the fourth, that on a set day, clothed in his royal robe and sitting on the tribunal, he harangued them, and the people shouted, "The voice of God, and not of man!" An angel of the Lord struck him with a deadly disease, because he had not given glory to God. His intestines rotted while worms gnawed at them, and on the fifth day after he died, in great torment both of body and conscience, complaining and lamenting that no man on earth lived more wretchedly than he.

units.la: In primis vero tanquam in speculo cernimus, quis ex ebrietate fructus redeat Nabali ea demum voluptas erat, si & se & alios vi no adobrueret. Quare subito animam tremulentam euomit. Forte per aetatem, pro conditione corporis, diutius viuere potuisset. Quod si dicas metum, non ebrietatem, causam mortis fuisse: respondeo, horrorem istum inde prouenisse, quod secum cogitaret, quàm parum, ebrietatis suae culpa, abfuisset ab extremo exitio. Omnes medici in eo consentiunt, multos magnos & difficiles morbos ex ebrietate, tanquam ex fonte promanare, quorum doloribus ebriosi illi superati aduersus Deum quoque porcorum instar grunniunt, & saepe apertas proferunt blasphemias.
units.tr: Above all, we see as in a mirror what fruit drunkenness brought to Nabal. That was at last his pleasure, to drown both himself and others in wine. Therefore he suddenly gave up his trembling soul. Perhaps, by his age and the condition of his body, he could have lived longer. But if you say that fear, not drunkenness, was the cause of death, I answer that this horror arose from his reflecting how little, through the fault of his drunkenness, he had been kept from utter ruin. All physicians agree that many great and difficult diseases flow from drunkenness as from a fountain, and under the pains of which those drunkards, overcome, grunt like pigs even against God, and often utter open blasphemies.

units.la: Quid enim aliud facerent, qui opera Dei nunquam contemplati sunt, & vitâ absque omni religione transegerunt? Accedit frequenter mors improuisa, dum vino madidi vel ex casu aliquo miserè pereunt, vel ab ipsis sociis inter pocula confodiuntur, vel in aquas plapsi, elemento sibi maximè inuiso, suffocantur, vel aliis casibus praesenti infelicè animâ, absque omni peccatorum suorum agnitione, absque precibus & diuinae misericordiae invocatione exhalant. Quid vero de talibus aliud dici potest, quàm eos in peccatis suis mori?
units.tr: For what else would they do, who never contemplated the works of God and spent their lives without any religion? Frequently an unforeseen death comes too, when men soaked in wine either perish wretchedly by some accident, or are stabbed by their own companions among the cups, or drown in water, the element most hateful to them, or else breathe out their unhappy souls by other mishaps, without any acknowledgment of their sins, without prayers and without invoking the divine mercy. But what else can be said of such men than that they die in their sins?

units.la: Quod Apostolus obseruauit, quando illos in eorum catalogo non postremos numerat quos regnum Dei vnquam possessuros aperte negat. Hæc cum ita sint, ebrietatem su giamus, sobrietatem, suauissimam piarum cogitationum nutriculam, sectemur. Vide Prouerb. 23.
units.tr: The Apostle observed this when he counts them, and not among the last, in the catalogue of those whom he plainly says will never possess the kingdom of God. Since these things are so, let us flee drunkenness and pursue sobriety, the sweetest nurse of godly thoughts. See Proverbs 23.

units.la: Quale funus Nabal iste habuerit, non indicatur. Credibile tamen est, illud magnificè & non sine pompa ductum fuisse. Plerunque enim, iuxta veteres rythmos:
units.tr: What funeral Nabal had is not recorded. Yet it is credible that it was conducted magnificently and not without pomp. For generally, according to the old verses:

units.la: Cum moritur dives, concurrunt undiq; eius coq; magis, si bonus, vt vocant, socius fuerit. Sed quidquid de illis agatur, tamen certo certius est, sepulturas, quantumuis magnificas, animarum saluti nihil conferre. Itaque, dum lucis istius vsura frui datur, ad poenitentiam conuertamur. Hic, vt præclarè Cyprianus, vita acquiritur, hic amittitur. Sæpe turbamur florenti impiorum statu, nobisq; persuademus, illos perpetuo prospero rerum successu vsuros. Sed quot florenti ætate tolluntur? Ac, vt Deus illos non illico percutiat, tamen sixum ab illo termino non prærergradientur. Quæ cum ita sint, persequutiones eleganter feramus, memores, restare tempus, quo præmijs boni, mali supplicijs sint afficiendi.
units.tr: When a rich man dies, his cooks gather from every side, all the more if he was a good (as they say) companion. But whatever becomes of those men, it is surer than sure that tombs, however magnificent, contribute nothing to the salvation of souls. Therefore, while the enjoyment of this light's usury is granted to us, let us turn to repentance. Here, as Cyprian admirably says, life is gained; here it is lost. We are often disturbed by the flourishing state of the wicked, and persuade ourselves that they will enjoy perpetual prosperous success. But how many are taken away in the flower of their age? And even if God does not strike them at once, yet they will not pass beyond the fixed term set by him. These things being so, let us bear persecutions gracefully, mindful that there remains a time when good men are to be rewarded and bad men punished.

units.la: 4. Dauid,audita Nabalis morte, Iehouæ gratias agit, qui suam contumeliam in Naba lem animaduertisset,seq; à scelere,id est, cæde iam deliberata,prohibuisset.
units.tr: 4. David, on hearing of Nabal's death, gives thanks to Jehovah, who had avenged his insult upon Nabal and had restrained him from crime, that is, from the murder already resolved upon.

units.la: Pij, Deo gratias agunt, illum pro sua immensa bonitate,non tantùm mala pœnæ,sed etiam mala culpæ à se benignè auertere, ex eoq; plus veræ voluptatis capiunt, quàm si opes infinitæ contigisset. Impij autem, si prohibeantur à peccato, æstuant animo, Deumq; mala consilia impedientem, & vehementes ipsorum impetus frenantem, impatienter ferût:Quin & illos omnes diris devouent,qui ipsos à malo retrahunt,prauisq; ipsorum conatibus obsistunt. Sublatos cuperent omnes illos, qui ipsos de scortatione,adulterijs,vsuris,militia mercenaria, &c. ex Dei verbo reprehendunt.Neque hæc po strema acerbissimi,quo multi erga Euangelium laborant,odij causa censenda est,quod ab illo à vitijs ad recte & honestè facta inuitentur.Et tamen Euangelij nuncium eo nomine inuisum & exosum reddere apud vulgus non erubescunt, quòd omne benè & honestè viuendi studium exstinguat,omni scelerum generi viam sternat:cum tamen diuersum sit.
units.tr: The godly give thanks to God that, in his immense goodness, he kindly turns away from them not only the evils of punishment but also the evils of guilt, and from this they take more true joy than if infinite riches had fallen to them. But the wicked, if they are prevented from sin, seethe in mind, and impatiently bear God who thwarts their evil plans and restrains their violent impulses. Indeed they curse all those who call them back from evil and resist their depraved attempts. They would wish all those dead who rebuke them from God's Word for fornication, adulteries, usury, mercenary soldiering, and so on. Nor should this extreme bitterness, with which many labour against the Gospel, be reckoned a cause of hatred, merely because the Gospel invites them from vices to what is right and honourable. And yet they are not ashamed to make the message of the Gospel hated and detested among the common people on this ground, that it extinguishes all zeal for living well and honestly and paves the way for every kind of crime, when in fact the reverse is true.

units.la: Addit Dauid,Deum,malum capiti Nabal lis retaliasse, quo significare vult, deū qua est iustitia, Nabalis scel9 in ipsi9 caput retorsisse.
units.tr: David adds that God has repaid Nabal's evil upon his own head, by which he wishes to signify that God, who is justice itself, turned Nabal's wickedness back upon his own head.

units.la: In summa, Dauid triumphau t Deum hostem suū sustulisse, supplicioq; affecisse. Qu�ح rat tamen aliquis, quomodo hoc charitati consentiat? An non dicit Solomon: Quū cecideritinimicus tuus, ne læteris: & quum impegerit, ne exultet cor tuum: ne forte videat Iehoua, & displiceat ei, & auertat ab eo iram suam ac in te retorqueat. Sed & Christus: Di ligite, ait, inimicos vestros, benedicite ijs, qui deuouent vos, benefacite ijs, qui oderunt vos, & precamini pro eis, qui vos infestant & persequuntur vos, vt sitis filij Patris vestri, qui est in cœlis: Facit enim, vt Sol ipsius exoriatur super bonos ac malos, & pluat super iustos & iniustos: Nam si dilexeritis eos, qui diligunt vos, quàm mercedē habebitis? Non ne & publicani idem faciunt? Et si complexi fueritis fratres vestros solū, quid amplius facitis? nonne & publicani ita faciunt? Estote igitur vos perfecti, vt Pater vester, qui est in cœlis, perfectus est. E cōtra Psaltes impijs pœnam denunciat, elegantibus comparationibus ostendens, potentia eorum durabile non esse. Postea subijcit: Lętabitur iustus, cū viderit vindicta, pedes suos in sanguine impij lauabit. Sed & Salomon ciuitatem bene ininstítutam exultare dicit, si impij intereant. Adhæc legimus, Hebræos, Pharaone & omni bus eius copijs in medijs sinus Arabici gurgitibus submersis, ita Mosi diuinitus sibi dictata præfanti, hinc quidem succinentes viro rum choro, inde vero præeuntem Mosis sororem Mariam prophetissam, insecutis & amœbeü carmé repetetibus fœminis, pompa cerce longe celeberrima ἐπινίκιον decantasse, quod in sacras postea tabulas relatū: Quin etiá in Apocalypsi angelus omnes sanctos in cœlis hortatur, vt ob delētā Babylone exul-tent. Quid igitur ad locos illos in speciem re-pugnantes dicemus? Sunt, qui ita respondeant: Inimico nostro aliqua calamitate presso, non licere nobis gaudere, quod de voluntate Dei nondum nobis constet. Quando verò videamus Dei consilium, hoste nostro attrito & cōfecto, licere gaudere. Sed simplicius exi-stimo respondere posse, nos diuersa ratione gaudere. Lætamur enim de hostium calami-tatibus ex prauo affectu, ira, odio, cupiditate vindictæ, & tunc non possumus excusari à peccato. Lætamur deinde ex bono zelo propter gloriā dei, ꝙ oppressis impijs, verbū veritatis possit propagari & amplificari no-men dei. Lætamur propter afflictos, quod à tyrannide afferantur. Lætamur item propter ipsos impios, quòd casus ad eorū commoditatem spiritualem faciant, & peccata eorum impediantur: Et sic non peccamus. Ipsis enim florentibus, non desinunt peccare, sed flagellis correpti interdum resipiscunt, & in viam redeunt.
units.tr: In sum, David exults that God had removed his enemy and visited him with punishment. Yet someone may ask how this agrees with charity. Does not Solomon say: "When your enemy falls, do not rejoice; and when he stumbles, let your heart not exult; lest the LORD see it and it displease him, and he turn his anger away from him and direct it against you" (Prov. 24)? And Christ says: "Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven; for he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the just and the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you embrace only your brothers, what more do you do? Do not even the tax collectors do so? Therefore be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect" (Matth. 5). On the other hand, the Psalmist announces punishment to the wicked, showing by elegant comparisons that their power is not lasting. Afterwards he adds: "The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his feet in the blood of the wicked." Solomon too says that a well-ordered city exults when the wicked perish. Besides, we read that the Hebrews, when Pharaoh and all his forces had been submerged in the waves of the Arabian gulf, as Moses, who was foretelling it by divine dictation, had said, sang on one side with the chorus of men answering, and on the other side Moses' sister Miriam the prophetess went before, with the women following and repeating the alternating song, a victory song [ἐπινίκιον], most famous for its solemn procession, which was afterwards recorded on the sacred tablets. Indeed in the Apocalypse too an angel exhorts all the saints in heaven to exult because Babylon has been destroyed. What then shall we say to these passages, which seem to contradict one another? Some answer thus: when our enemy is pressed by some calamity, it is not lawful for us to rejoice, because the will of God is not yet clear to us; but when we see the counsel of God, our enemy having been worn down and destroyed, it is lawful to rejoice. But I think it is simpler to answer that we rejoice for different reasons. For we rejoice at our enemies' calamities out of a depraved disposition, anger, hatred, desire for vengeance, and then we cannot be excused from sin. Then we rejoice out of good zeal, for the glory of God, that with the wicked oppressed, the word of truth may be propagated and the name of God magnified. We rejoice for the afflicted, that they are rescued from tyranny. We likewise rejoice for the wicked themselves, that their fall works for their spiritual advantage and their sins are checked; and so we do not sin. For while they flourish they do not cease to sin, but when they are struck by scourges they sometimes repent and return to the way.

units.la: At cauendum, ne zelum iustitiæ prætexentes, nostra quæramus, & impulsu odij de aliorum afflictionibus gaudeamus. Gauden dum est de pœna proximi, non in quantum est pœna, sed in quantum est medicina. Recte Chrysostomus, Si Deus illos, ait, qui ob inimicorum commoda lætantur, non sinet esse impunitos: multò maioribus profecto eos, à quibus innocentes per inuidiam exagitantur, supplicijs tradet. Vide quæ ad 18. versic. 24. Prou. annotauimus.
units.tr: But we must take care that, while pretending zeal for justice, we do not seek our own ends, and that we do not rejoice in the afflictions of others out of hatred. We may rejoice at a neighbour's punishment, not insofar as it is punishment, but insofar as it is a remedy. Chrysostom rightly says: "If God will not let those who rejoice at their enemies' misfortunes go unpunished, he will surely hand over to far greater punishments those by whom the innocent are harassed out of envy." See what we have noted on Proverbs 18, verse 24.

units.la: Videmus etiam hoc loco, quid illos maneat, qui vel fideles persequuntur, vel crapulæ, ebrietati, auaritiæ, alijsque vitijs sunt diditi, & alligati. Non dicitur simpliciter, Nabalem mortuum esse, sed ab ipso Deo percussum, animam temulentam euomuisse. Consentaneum est, illum per ætatem diutius viuere potuisse: sed, Homines fundendi sanguinis auidi & perfidiosi, Dauide dicente, ne dimidium quidem dierum suorum asequuntur. versu 24. Id quod non tantum ex sententia impiorum debet intelligi, qui, cum sibi
units.tr: We also see in this passage what awaits those who either persecute the faithful or are given over and bound to drunkenness, gluttony, greed and other vices. It is not simply said that Nabal died, but that he was struck down by God himself and breathed out his drunken soul. It is likely that, by his age, he could have lived longer. But men greedy and treacherous for shedding blood, as David says, do not reach even half their days (verse 24). This must be understood not only of the opinion of the wicked, who, while promising themselves many more years in which to carry out their schemes, at last see themselves wretchedly disappointed in their hope, but also of their bringing their own lives to an end and drawing death on themselves before its time.

units.la: Psal. 55. sibi ipsis multos adhuc annos polliceantur, quibus hæc vel ista sint patraturi, tandem se miserè spe sua frustratos vident: Sed quòd sibi ipsis vitam decidant, mortemque immaturâ attrahant. Quot mœchi & scortatores, philtris malè à scortis præparatis, lenta tabe consumti, deceßerunt? Quot scabiè Gallica, pustulis, bubonibus, aliisue fœdis morbis sunt depasti? Quot à maritis, affinibus & cognatis ἐν αὐτοφώρῳ deprehensi in sperato sunt occisi? Aliquando in alia scelera prolapsi (ut nullum peccatum solum est) quorum causa illis per Magistratum supplicium est illatum. Quot in militiam vilis lucelli gratia profecti, ferro, fame, frigore perierunt, qui, si domi manßissent, in multos adhuc annos superesse potuissent? Quot contentiosi homines vita sua contentiones finierunt? Quot magi à sathana homicida & mendaces subitanea eaq; fœda morte sunt exstincti? Sed & auari, vitam suam, alioquin multis ærumnis obnoxiam fugacemq;, sibi amariorem reddunt ac decurtant. Noctes insomnes ducunt, cogitantes, quomodo opes suas, etiam cum proximi sui iniuria, velint augere. Atq; ita se priuant beneficio somni, quo Deus homines recreat atque reficit, ut perferendis laboribus sint idonei. Inuidi quoque seipsos conficiunt. Est enim inuidia lentum quoddam venenum, quod tandem cor enecat. Vtà tineis vestis corrumpitur: ita inuidia illos, qui ab ea occupati sunt, paulatim consumit. Idem de aliis quoque scelestis dici potest. Multi ex medio vitae cursu quasi repentino turbine, à Deo abripiuntur, ne ultra negotium pijs facessant, ijsque iniuriam inferant. Quae cum ita sint, Deo vindicatam commendabimus, cui, cum probetur iustitia, fieri non poterit, vt sinceros suos cultores deserat, fraudetque sua ope & consilio. Psal. 37. verf. 39. & 40.
units.tr: Psal. 55. How many adulterers and whoremongers have died, wasted by a slow decay, after being poisoned by love-potions badly prepared by harlots? How many have been eaten away by the French pox, pustules, buboes and other foul diseases? How many have been killed by husbands, relatives and kinsmen when caught in the very act [ἐν αὐτοφώρῳ], as they had hoped to escape? Sometimes they have fallen into other crimes (since no sin is ever alone), for which they have been punished by the magistrate. How many who went off to war for the sake of paltry gain perished by the sword, famine and cold, when, had they stayed at home, they might still be alive for many years? How many quarrelsome men have ended their lives in quarrels? How many sorcerers, murderers and liars, under the influence of Satan, have been snuffed out by sudden and disgraceful deaths? But misers also make their lives, otherwise burdened with many troubles and fleeting, more bitter for themselves and cut them short. They spend sleepless nights thinking how they may increase their wealth, even at their neighbour's expense. So they deprive themselves of the benefit of sleep, by which God refreshes and restores people so that they are fit to endure their labours. Envious people also consume themselves. For envy is a slow poison, which at last kills the heart. As moths corrupt clothing, so envy gradually wastes away those who are seized by it. The same can be said of other wicked people. Many are snatched away by God from the middle of their course, as by a sudden whirlwind, so that they no longer harass the godly or do them wrong. Since these things are so, we shall commit the avenging to God, who, since he is tested in justice, cannot abandon his sincere worshippers or fail them in his help and counsel. Psal. 37, verses 39 and 40.

units.la: DE VITA ET OBITV Nabalis ebriosi. HOMILIA X.
units.tr: On the Life and Death of Nabal the Drunkard. Homily X.

units.la: 40 Misit insuper Dauid et loquutus est ad Abigail, vt acciperet eam sibi vxorem.
units.tr: 40 Moreover David sent and spoke to Abigail, that she should take her to be his wife.

units.la: 41 Venerunt itaque serui Dauidis ad Abigail in Charmel, loquutique sunt cum ea, dicendo: Dauid misit nos ad te, vt acciperet te sibi in vxorem.
units.tr: 41 So the servants of David came to Abigail at Carmel and spoke with her, saying: David has sent us to you, that he may take you to be his wife.

units.la: 42 Quae surgens incuruauit se in faciem in terram, & dixit: Ecce ancilla tua in ancillam ad lauandam pedes seruorum domini mei.
units.tr: 42 And she rose up, bowed herself to the earth on her face, and said: Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of my lord's servants.

units.la: 43 Festinans ergo surrexit Abigail, & insedit Asino, & quinque puellae eius, quae ambulabant ad pedes eius, atq; abijt post nuntios Dauid, & fuit ei vxor.
units.tr: 43 Abigail therefore hastened and rose up, and sat upon an ass, and her five maidens who walked at her feet went with her, and she went after the messengers of David, and became his wife.

units.la: 44 Sed & Ahinoam accepit Dauid de Izreel, fueruntque etiam ambae vxores.
units.tr: 44 But David had also taken Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them were his wives.

units.la: 45 Saul autem dedit Michal filiam suam vxorem Dauidis ipsi Palti filio Lais, qui erat de Gallim.
units.tr: 45 But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.

units.la: QVod superest ex hoc capite, distribui potest in duas partes: quarum prima habet petitionem Dauidis: altera consensum Abigaelis ad coeundum matrimonium.
units.tr: What remains of this chapter can be divided into two parts. The first contains David's request; the second, Abigail's consent to enter into marriage.

units.la: Quod ad primam attinet, dicitur Dauid legatos suos ad Abigaelem misisse, qui illius voluntatem explorarent. Quo tempore autem hoc factum sit, statim ne a morte Nabalis, vel interposito aliquanto tempore, hoc tamen loco ob historiam insertum, non appareret ex textu. Consentaneum tamen est, interiectum fuisse aliquod temporis spatium, amorte Nabalis, & Dauidem consulere voluisse & suo pudori ac mulieris. Ignominiosum fuisset Dauidi, si illam ante ambiuisset, quae prior, quod prouerbio dicunt, maritus refrixisset. Sed & Abigaeli probro cessisset, si de nouis nuptijs euéstigio cogitasset. Qui paulò sunt honestiores, hodie quoque non magni faciunt fœminas eas, quæ ilico à mariti funere aut post paulum, animum ad secundas nuptias adijciunt: imò vix ac ne vix quidem maritum priorem terræ mandari expectare possunt. Qua tamen impudentia nihil hodie vulgarius. Quædam à priori grauidæ, iam ad secundas nuptias conuolarunt. At partus tempus, vel suspicionis fugiendæ caussa, expectare illas decebat.
units.tr: As for the first part, it is said that David sent his messengers to Abigail, to learn her wishes. The text does not show at what time this happened, whether immediately after Nabal's death or after some interval; it has been inserted here for the sake of the story. It is nonetheless fitting that some time passed between Nabal's death and David's wish to consult her, both for his own modesty and for hers. It would have been disgraceful for David to court her at once, since, as the proverb says, the husband would have cooled toward the first wife. And it would have been a reproach to Abigail too, if she had thought of a new marriage straight away. Even today, the more respectable women do not think much of those who, immediately after their husband's funeral or soon after, turn their minds to a second marriage; indeed they can hardly wait even until the former husband has been laid in the earth. Yet nothing is more common today than this shamelessness. Some women who were already pregnant by the first husband have hurried into a second marriage. Such women ought to have waited for the time of childbirth, or at least for the sake of avoiding suspicion.

units.la: {a}Cæterùm, scripturæ nullum certum spatium ad nubendum præscribunt, quin legitimæ sint nuptiæ, quocunq; tempore inean-tur. Nec Paulus aliam legem de viduis vllá tulit, quod ad hanc rem attinet, nisi, vt nubant in domino. Numa tamen Pompilius vi duas Romanas ad 10. menses continuare luctum voluit: nec prius ad nouas transire nuptias, ne soboles dubia & incerta redderentur. Qua de re Alexander ab Alexandria 3. genial. dier. 7. In Codice autem de secundis nuptijs decernitur, si qua vidua nubat inter spacium vnius anni à morte prioris mariti, infamem fore. Quæ tamen seueritas postea sublata est per Canones, Extra de diuortijs, l. vlt. & penult.
units.tr: Moreover, the Scriptures set no fixed period for remarriage, so that marriages are lawful whenever they are entered into. Nor did Paul make any other law concerning widows in this matter, except that they marry in the Lord. Yet Numa Pompilius wished the two Roman widows to continue mourning for ten months, and not to pass to new marriages before then, lest the offspring be doubtful and uncertain. Alexander ab Alexandro discusses this matter in Genial. dier. 3, c. 7. In the Code, however, it is decreed that if any widow marries within a year of her former husband's death, she shall be infamous. Yet this severity was later removed by the canons, Extra, De divortiis, last and penultimate law.

units.la: Valerius Maximus antiqua referens insti tuta, Quæ vno,inquit, contentæ matrimo- nio fuerunt, corona pudicitiæ honoraban- tur : Existimabant enim eum præcipuè ma- tronæ sincera fide incorruptum esse animū, qui post depositæ virginitatis cubile, in pu- blicum egredi nesciret: multorum matrimo niorum experientiam,quasi legitimæ cuiuf- dam intemperantiæ signum credentes. Sed & Germanas fœminas tantum virgines nu- pfiffe scribit Cornelius Tacitus: & cum aliæ maritis in prima iuuenta orbatæ, tùm infi- gnes maximè,Valeria Meflalorum soror, & Portia minor Catonis filia : Apud quam e- tiam,cum fœmina laudaretur optimis præ- dita moribus, quæ fecundum haberet ma- ritum, Portia respondit, Fœlicem & pudi- cam matronam nunquam bis nubere. Cor- nelia Gracchorum mater, Ptolomæi Ægy- ptij regis nuptias,ad quas poftGracchi mor tem ingentibus alliciebatur promissis, recu fauit,maluitq; Cornelia Gracchi esse quàm diuitis Ægypti regina.Iam & in scena & thea tris fecunda matrimonia exagitantur etiam Mimorum carminibus. Habent (inquit)ma ledicti locum crebræ nuptiæ: & mulier quæ multis nubit,multis non placet.Sed & non- aulli Patrum, atque inter eos cumprimis
units.tr: Valerius Maximus, recounting the ancient customs, says: Women who were content with one marriage were honoured with the crown of chastity. For they thought that the mind of a matron was most of all sincere and uncorrupted when it did not know how to go out in public after the bed of its lost virginity, regarding the experience of many marriages as a sign of a certain lawful intemperance. Cornelius Tacitus also writes that the German women married only once, as virgins. And of the Romans, though many were bereft of their husbands in early youth, the most notable were Valeria, sister of the Messalae, and Portia, the younger daughter of Cato. When a woman of excellent character was praised, and it was said that she had a second husband, Portia replied that a happy and chaste matron never marries twice. Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, refused the marriage of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, to which she was enticed by great promises after the death of Gracchus. She preferred to be Cornelia, the daughter of Gracchus, than the queen of wealthy Egypt. Even on the stage and in the theatre second marriages are mocked in the songs of the mimes: "Frequent marriages," they say, "have a place among the curses; and the woman who marries many, pleases none."

units.la: P Tertullianus, & Hieronymus, fecundas nu-ptias aperte improbarunt, argumentis ad hanc rem vsi in speciem probabilibus, reue-ra autem omnino infirmis. Scriptura certè longè diuersum sentit. Paulus enim Corin-thijs scribens, Celibus, inquit, & viduis di-co, Bonum eis est, si manserint vt ego. Quod si se non continent, continere se nó possunt, aut alia ratione sibi non expedire iudicant, vt coniugij expertes maneant, age matrimó-nium contrahant: Præstat enim matrimoni-um contrahere, quàm libidine ita stuare: vt aut voluntas succumbat tentationi, aut cer-tè Deum pacata conscientia non possis in-uocare. Id enim vrendi vocabulo Apostolus intelligit. Ad Timotheum vero: Iuniores, ait, velim nubere, liberos gignere, domum admi-nistrare, nullam occasionem dare aduersario ad maledicendum. Iam enim nonnullæ de-flexerunt, sequutæ satanam. Eodem pacto mandat ad Titum cap. 2. Castitatem enim ab illis requirit, vt sint ἁγναί: Quod si non pos-sint, vult esse ὑποταγὰς: hoc est, in honesto matrimonio viris legitimis subditas. Nemo ergo vitio verterit Abigaeli, secundas nupti-as: sed Dei bonitatem agnoscat, qui, cum fœ-minam istam leétissimam, pertulisse nosset, diuturnam crucem sub Nabale viro et stulto & duro & importuno: cui tamè illa nunquà
units.tr: Nor have some of the Fathers, and among them above all Tertullian and Jerome, failed to openly disapprove of second marriages. They used arguments that seem plausible in appearance but are in fact entirely weak. Scripture certainly thinks quite differently. For Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: "I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, or judge that it is not expedient for them to remain without marriage, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn with lust, so that either the will yields to temptation, or at least you cannot call upon God with a quiet conscience." By the word "burn" the Apostle means exactly that. But to Timothy he writes: "I would have the younger women marry, bear children, manage the house, and give the adversary no occasion to speak evil; for some have already turned aside, following Satan." In the same way he commands Titus, in chapter 2, to require chastity of them, that they be hagnai [ἁγναί]; but if they cannot be so, he wishes them to be hypotagas [ὑποταγάς], that is, subject in honourable marriage to their lawful husbands. Therefore no one should find fault with Abigail for a second marriage. Rather let him acknowledge the goodness of God, who, knowing that this most excellent woman had endured a long cross under Nabal, a husband foolish, harsh and unbearable, yet to whom she had never failed in the duty of a good wife, Tit. 2. also bestowed a remarkable benefit on her: the Christ of the Lord, David. Therefore he did not wish her to depart without reward, but joined her to David in marriage. It was a fitting pair indeed: both had lived under the cross, and David was still living under the cross; both had piously and rightly sustained themselves by calling upon God. And so God provides for both of them a suitable marriage. For we must first seek the kingdom of God; all other things will be added abundantly. Formerly many things were regarded as sins which God had never forbidden, and many things were brought in as rightly and honourably done which were quite contrary to the divine Word.

units.la: Tit. 2. negauerat officium vxoris probæ: contulisse etiam insigne beneficiû in Dauidem Christum domini: Ideo noluit eam discedere nõ remuneratam: sed Dauidi in matrimonium collocauit. Pulchrum sanè par: vterq; in cruce vixerat: imò Dauid etiam tum versabatur in cruce: vterq; invocatione-sua sese piè et re{a}ẽ gesserat. Ideoq; deus vtriq; prospicit de cõmodo matrimonio. Primũ enim quærendum est regnũ dei: post alia omnia cumulatè adijcientur. Olim multa peccatorũ loco habita sunt, quæ à deo nunq; interdicta fuere: multa è contra in locũ recte et honestè facto rum venerunt, quæ ex diametro diuino verbo repugnarunt. Quod autè Dauid nõ per seipsum petat matrimoniũ, fortè ideò factũ est, vt eò certius exploraret, quo erga ipsum animo esset affecta: an ità in nuptias consentire vellet, vel secus. In quo non parũ situm est. Nuptiæ enim ad quas inuiti impellimur, raro felicem habent exitũ. Id verò longè re-ctius per legatos explorare potuit. Etenim si ipse ad eam adijsset, fortè præ metu & pudore illi denegare nihil potuisset. Omnino liberius cum legatis differere poterat, &, quid animi haberet, aperire: Legatis Principum multa sæpe negantur, quæ, si Princeps ipse peteret, negari non possent. Fortasis ea etiam de caufla ire noluit,ne,fi repulsam tu-liffet,pudore suffunderetur.
units.tr: That David did not seek the marriage in person was perhaps done so that he might more surely learn with what disposition of mind she was toward him, whether she wished to consent to marriage or not. This matters greatly. For marriages into which we are driven against our will seldom have a happy outcome. He could certainly learn this far more correctly through messengers. For if he had gone to her himself, perhaps she could have denied him nothing for fear and shame. But with the messengers he could speak more freely and reveal what he himself felt. Princes' envoys are often refused many things which could not be refused if the prince himself asked. Perhaps he also did not wish to go for this reason: lest, if he had received a rebuff, he should be overwhelmed with shame.

units.la: Hoc loco discimus,quomodo coniugium fit contrahendum: Nempe, fi alicuius con-nubium expetamus,eam per viros honestos ambiamus. Dauid non à congressu incipit: sed illam prius per legatos, viros honestos petit.Idem nos quoq; faciemus. Incredibile dictu, quot & quanta incommoda inde fe-quantur,cum nuptias non à precibus in coe tu sacro habitis, sed à concubitu ordimur. Aliquando enim deprehenditur, matrimo-nium vel in prohibitis gradibus contracţu, vel etiá alijs promissum. Inuenias, qui,quod rem, semotis testibus, transegerint, sedulò negando velint euadere. Quibus omnibus occurri posset facilè,fi post legitimè contra-ctum & approbatu coniugium,non ante iu-re maritali vteremur.
units.tr: From this place we learn how marriage ought to be contracted. Namely, if we desire the marriage of anyone, we should seek her through honourable men. David does not begin with intercourse but first seeks her through honourable men, his envoys. We too shall do the same. It is incredible to say how many and how great the inconveniences follow when we begin marriages not with prayers, held in the holy assembly, but with carnal union. For sometimes it is discovered that a marriage has been contracted within forbidden degrees, or even promised to another. You will find people who, having done the deed with witnesses removed, stubbornly deny it in order to escape. All these problems could easily be met if we used the rights of marriage only after a lawful and approved marriage has been contracted, and not before.

units.la: In primis vero caueant iuniores, ne citra consensum parentum,propinquorum, & tu-torum matrimonia temere ineant.Enimue-ro,cum dicit dominus,Honora patre & ma-trem tuam,vt,&c. eadem opera præcipit, ne prauos suos affectus hac in re sequantur li-beri,sed parentum consilio vtantur. Certè, quidquid illis porrò accidit, pleniori spe ad illos accedunt. Cætera, subinde Terentij il-lud lud audire coguntur: Tute hoc in tristi, tibi omne exedendum est. Sed & mariti aliquan do vxores suas eo nomine tractant ignomi‑niofius, quod sibi, inconsultis parentibus, nupserint.Si mores meos indignius fers,eas inquiunt,licet,ad parentes,ac de iniuria con queraris.
units.tr: Above all, young people should take care not to enter marriages rashly without the consent of their parents, relatives and guardians. When the Lord says, "Honour your father and your mother," etc., he at the same time commands that children not follow their own depraved desires in this matter, but make use of their parents' counsel. Certainly, whatever happens to them afterwards, they approach it with a fuller hope. Otherwise they are constantly forced to hear that line of Terence: "You brought this on yourself in your misery, so you must eat it all up." Husbands, too, sometimes treat their wives more shamefully on this very ground, that they married without their parents' consultation. "If you bear my ways with less than good grace," they say, "you may go to your parents and complain of the wrong done to you."

units.la: Habemus etiam hoc loco illustre exem-plum,quo docemur,Deum aliquando suos, etiam in hac vita, diuturnis ærumnis ac ca‑lamitatibus ereptos, fplendidiore fortuna ornare ac quodammodo beare. Abigail ista in tormento erat maximo. Maritus enim e‑ius & ipsa ingenio erant plane dissimili. Ille enim homo erat impius, stultus, asper, im-portunus, ebrius: adhæc leonino, quod a‑iunt,vino inebriabatur: Enimuero vbi me‑ro,aliquanto liberalius hausto,incaluisset,su riofi hominis instar,in quosuis grassatus,ne-minem non volebat occisum, saltem lingua. Et vt maximè voluisset, ille aliam mentem inijcere, tamen non poterat. Sed quod rem Deo committeret,maritiqué iniurias & ftul titiam patienter ferret perpetua modestia, officioque suo probè fungeretur, præter spem & expectationem, Deo bene iuuante, ad luculentifsimum matrimonium expeti‑ta,fit regina Israelis.
units.tr: Here we also have a notable example, from which we learn that God sometimes adorns with a more splendid fortune those whom he has rescued from long-lasting distress and calamity, even in this life, and in a way makes them blessed. Abigail was in the greatest torment. Her husband and she were utterly unlike in temperament. He was an impious, foolish, harsh, troublesome man, a drunkard; he was inflamed, as they say, with lion-like wine. Indeed, when he had grown hot after drinking rather freely of undiluted wine, he raged against whomever he met like a madman, and would have had everyone killed, at least with his tongue. And though she wished most earnestly to bring him to a different mind, she could not. But because she committed the matter to God, bore her husband's wrongs and folly patiently with constant gentleness, and performed her duty faithfully, then, with God helping her, beyond all hope and expectation, she was raised to a most splendid marriage and became queen of Israel.

units.la: Plenus est hodie orbis terrarum huiufmo di Nabalibus, qui, vbi vino nimio fe ingurgi- tarunt, temulenti, in quosuis feruntur, om- nes trucidatos volunt: nonnunquam vxo- res & liberos ftri&tis gladijs insequuntur. Nabales isti nonnunquam vxores in matri- monio habent, quæ, etiamsi videant, fe ab il- lis nec ope nec consilio iuuari, tamen, quod porrò meliora sibi de illis polliceantur, ni- hilominus, quæ ex officio decet, satagere non cessant. Has etiam Deus suo tempore proculdubio assertas, in libertatem vindica- bit. Interim omnino vxorum est, opem Dei patienter expectare: maritorumque importunitatem eleganter ferre. Non dubium est, quin matronis honestis & sedulis ex- nimo doleat, quod sibi ac dulcissimis liberis efuriales (quas vocat Plautus) ferias à ma- ritis, erapulam nunquam edormientibus in dici, ac, præter meritum, indignius fe haberi ac tantum non pedibus conculcari videant: Sed num ea re ab officio discedent suo? Ni- hil minus. Quin cogitabunt, hanc suam cru- cem esse, quam, animo eleganti, ferre de- ceat: Quemque sua afflictione exerceri. Quot veræ religionis nomine, in carcerem coniecti, suauissimo Solis & Lunæ afpe- ctu priuantur? Quot ad trimemes damnantur? Ad eundem modum Deus matronarum multas maritis dissolutis, tanquam carcere alligatas habet, quas, suo tempore, quin velit & posit, liberare, non est, quod dubitent. Etiamsi diuortium facere possent: tamen id non semper tutum est consultumque, praesertim vbi liberi sunt. Ferant igitur, non culpent, quod vitari non potest: nec apud se dicant: Cum videam omnia pessum ire, maritumque dilapidare omnia, dabo & ego operam, ne mihi defuisse, genioque minus indulsisse, recte dicat. Quin cogitent: Cum marito ignauiam male cedere, eumque adulterij, aliorumque vitiorum nomine pesimè apud omnes audire norim, tamen ego, saltem Dei praecepto adducta, Spartam, quam nacta sum, exornare sedulò pergam, nullumq; probe ac frugi vxoris officium praetermittam. Nec dubium, quin deus me quoq; tempore cum primis opportuno sit liberaturus, ac vel mortis interuentu exmiserijs hisce ad beatiorem vitam euocaturus, vel etiá à mariti obitu de commodiore matrimonio prospecturus. Etiáfi nō omnes regibus in matrimonio collocentur, tamen potest deus illas, etiam in hoc praesenti secul o reficere ac recreare. Sed &, vt scitè Mimus Casta ad virum matrona parendo imperat. Pudica enim vxor hoc impetrat obsequio suo, vt quicquid velit ipsa, faciat maritus: & magis impetrat cum obsequitur, quàm cum exigit.
units.tr: Today the whole world is full of Nabals of this kind, who, once they have gorged themselves on too much wine, become drunk and rush upon whomever they meet, wanting everyone slaughtered; sometimes they pursue their wives and children with drawn swords. Such Nabals sometimes have wives in marriage who, although they see that they receive neither help nor counsel from their husbands, nevertheless do not cease to do what befits their duty, because they hope for better things from them. God will undoubtedly also in his own time vindicate these women and set them free. Meanwhile it is altogether the wife's part to wait patiently for the help of God, and to bear her husband's unruliness gracefully. There is no doubt that honourable and diligent matrons, when they see that their own sweet children and themselves are denied (as Plautus calls them) the holidays of feasting by husbands who never sleep off their drunkenness by day, and are treated more shamefully than they deserve, almost trampled underfoot, grieve in their hearts. But will they therefore depart from their duty? Not at all. Rather they will think that this is their cross, which they ought to bear with a noble mind, and that each is exercised by her own affliction. How many, imprisoned in the name of true religion, are deprived of the sweetest sight of the sun and moon? How many are condemned for three years? In the same way God holds many wives bound, as if in prison, to dissolute husbands, and they have no reason to doubt that he will, in his own time, free them, whether he wills and is able to do so. Even if they could obtain a divorce, that is not always safe or advisable, especially where there are children. Let them therefore endure, not complain about, what cannot be avoided; and let them not say to themselves: "Since I see everything going to ruin and my husband squandering everything, I too will take care not to be found wanting, nor to have indulged my own inclination less than is right." Rather let them think: "Since I know that idleness goes badly with a husband, and that he is shamefully spoken of by everyone for adultery and other vices, yet I, at least moved by God's command, shall persist diligently in adorning the Sparta I have obtained, and I shall omit no duty of a upright and thrifty wife." Nor is there any doubt that God will also free me at a most suitable time, and either by the intervention of death call me to a happier life out of these miseries, or provide for me, after my husband's death, a more agreeable marriage. Even if not all are placed in marriage with kings, God can nevertheless restore and refresh them even in this present age. But also, as the mime shrewdly puts it, a chaste matron commands her husband by obeying him. For a modest wife obtains by her obedience that her husband does whatever she herself wishes, and she obtains more by yielding than by demanding.

units.la: E contra, multi quoq; honesti viri in foeminas incidunt, non tantum non οἰκουρὰς, sed fide turpiter fracta, turpius se aliis prostituentes. Quod etsi ipsos non lateat, tamen quod secundum iuris regulas, liquido probare non possint, patienter crucem ferant: perfuasissimum habentes, Deum, qui Nabalem nihil minus expectantem percussit, in impudicas istas perfidasque foeminas suo etiam tempore animaduersurum, animaq; vel animo sublatis, ipsos Abigaelis exemplo, clementissimè liberaturum.
units.tr: On the other hand, many honourable men also fall in with women who are not at all stay-at-home wives [οἰκουρὰς], but who, having shamefully broken faith, prostitute themselves disgracefully to others. Although this is not hidden from the men themselves, yet, because they cannot clearly prove it according to the rules of law, let them bear the cross patiently, being fully persuaded that God, who struck Nabal when he least expected it, will in his own time also take vengeance on these shameless and faithless women, and that he will most mercifully deliver them, as he did Abigail, when their spirits are lifted up or their courage restored.

units.la: Sed vt ad secundam partem veniamus, ec quid, quaesfo, matrona ista lectissima responsi legatis Dauidis dedit? Primò, surgens se in faciem ad terram incuruauit, atque ita Dauidi hero suo honorem debitum demisse praebuit. Deinde, Ecce, inquit, ancilla tua in ancillam, ad lauandum pedes seruorum domini mei. Quibus verbis ostendit, se non digna ad quam legatos mittat: ac pollicetur se illi non vxorem fore, sed paratissimam, vel seruorum eius lauare pedes. Qua phrasi vilissimum mum obsequij genus significare voluit. Tale enim illud est,vt ne à famulitio,saluo pudore,confidenter petere audeamus.D. Pau lus de viduis, quarum opera ad pauperum præsertim ægrotorum curam vtebantur,dis ferens,Vidua, inquit,cooptetur(scilicet ad ministrandum ) ei ἀγίων ποδας ἐνιψεν, id est,si sanctorum pedes lauit. Hac autem vna specie officij,quod tum in illis regionibus vsurpari solebat, cum peregrè aduenientes viatores exciperentur, reliqua etiam obsequia significauit apostolus.Nec temerè etiam hoc tanquam abiectissimum ministerij genus delegit. Etenim cum vilissima & sordidissima hominis pars ferè sint pedes, quos, quæcunq; ita contrectare & curare non dedignatur , certè nec vilia quælibet alia munera & ministeria , quæ pauperibus ægrotantibus impendi necesse est,obire eadem nunquam recusabit. De Christo ipso dicitur,quòd,facta cœna, discipulorum pe- des lauare instiserit,& linteo , quo præcin- ctus erat,abstergere. Postquam rursus accu buit, Exemplum, inquit,præbui vobis,vt quemadmodum ego vobis feci,vos quoque faciatis.Non quod anniuersarium ritū com- mendet,comicamue aliquam pompam insti tuat, qualem Papistis in vsu esse videmus, qui postquam duodecim hominibus lauerunt pedes, inani nudaq; ceremonia sepulchrè defunctos esse putant: defuncti, sibi per mittunt fratres contemnere, &c. Sed nos to ta vita paratos esse iubet ad lauandos fratrum pedes; docetq;, nimium sibi homines arroga re, qui non cogitant ea lege se inter infirmos fratres versari, vt officijs etiam in speciem sordidis, benignè & comiter sese subijciant. Quod vt ab omnibus, ita in primis à ministris verbi diuini requiritur. Incredibile enim dictu est, quot & quanta mala inde oriantur, vbi ministri gloriam suam diuinæ, commodum priuatum saluti publicæ ambitiosè antéponunt. Exempla huius generis, & quidé atrocissima, passim in sacris & profanis historijs occurrunt. Et vtinam non hodie magno nostro malo experiremur, ambitiosis ministrorum ecclesiæ contentionibus ecclesias passim turbari, & euangelij cursum impediri: multos item simpliciores offendi, vt à fide deficiant, in qua progressus magnos facturi videbantur. Quantus illorum numerus est, qui, etsi veritatem habeant perspectis simam, tamen, ne fauorem ac gratiam, quam apud viros principes assequuti sunt, amittant, salarioq; excidant, errores pertinaciter defendefendunt,replicas,triplicas scribunt, nihil inausum,nihil intentatum relinquunt. At quanto satius erat cogitare, quid Christus, qui longè super omnes eminet, in nostri gratiam fecisset : Momentanea nostra essé omnia : mendacia non diu fallere : nostem tam diu esse, quàm diu illuscescat dies : clarificato autem die & Sole oborto, luci tenebras & caliginem cederet; rationem iusto iudici celerius opinione reddendam?&c.Sed ad propositum.
units.tr: But to come to the second part: what, I ask, did that most select matron give as her answer to David's messengers? First, rising, she bowed herself to the earth on her face, and thus humbly paid the honour due to David her lord. Then she said, "Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." By these words she showed that she was not worthy to be sent for by him, and she promised that she would be not his wife but most ready to wash the feet of his servants. By this phrase she wished to signify the most lowly kind of service. For it is such that we dare not confidently ask for it from a servant without loss of modesty. St. Paul, speaking of widows, whose work they used especially for the care of the poor and sick, says: "Let a widow be enrolled" (namely for ministering) "if she has washed the feet of the saints" [ἐνιψεν ἁγίων ποδας], that is, if she has washed the feet of the saints (1 Tim. 5). Yet by this one kind of service, which was then customarily employed in those regions when travellers arriving from abroad were received, the apostle signified the other services as well. Nor did he choose this kind of ministry, the most abject of all, at random. For since the feet are almost the most vile and filthy part of a person, whoever does not disdain to handle and tend these will certainly never refuse to perform any other lowly offices and ministries that must be rendered to the sick poor. Of Christ himself it is said that, when supper was made, he began to wash the feet of his disciples and to wipe them with the linen cloth with which he was girded. When he had reclined again, he said, "I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, you also should do." He did not thereby commend an annual ritual or institute some theatrical pomp of the kind we see in use among the Papists, who, after washing the feet of twelve men, think they have performed an empty and bare ceremony at a tomb, and who send their brothers to despise, etc. Rather he commands us to be ready all our life to wash the feet of our brothers, and he teaches that men arrogate too much to themselves, who do not consider that by that law they live among weak brothers so that they may submit themselves kindly and courteously even to offices that appear sordid. This is required of all, and in the first place of the ministers of the divine Word. For it is incredible to say how many and how great evils arise from this, when ministers ambitiously place their own glory above the divine, and private advantage above the public welfare. Examples of this kind, and indeed most atrocious ones, occur everywhere in sacred and profane histories. And would that we did not today experience to our great harm that the churches are everywhere disturbed by the ambitious contentions of the ministers of the Church, and the course of the gospel is impeded; and that many simpler people are offended, so that they fall away from the faith in which they seemed about to make great progress. How great is the number of those who, although they hold the truth most clearly perceived, nevertheless, lest they lose the favour and grace they have obtained with princes and lose their salary, obstinately defend errors, write replies and triplies, and leave nothing unattempted or unventured. But how much more fitting it would have been to consider what Christ, who stands far above all, has done for our sake: that all our things are momentary, that lies do not deceive for long, that night lasts only as long as the day has not dawned, and that when the day has been made clear and the sun has risen, it will yield darkness and gloom to the light, and that an account must be rendered to the just Judge sooner than we think. But to the matter at hand.

units.la: Hæc,ubi dixisset Abigael,protinus proficiscitur,& asino insidés, comitantibus quinque pedisequis, nuncios Dauidis subsequitur, illiqué nubit. Non diu suspensum tenet Dauidem, sed quid secum constituerit, maturè significat. Non considerat tempus aut conditionem Dauidis: aut potentiam & furorem Saulis : Sed tantum ptomisionem Dei, à quo non dubitabat, Dauidem non esse deserendum. Sciebat illum in exilio suo, subuentione cum primis egere. Quod de muneribus dicitur:Bis dare illum, qui citò dat, non inepte ad responsa in tempore data transtuleris. Quare maturè respondet, & occasionem istam oblatam utraque quod aiunt,manu amplectitur, Dauidisque nuncios subs sequuta,ipsi nubit. Peractis enim sponsali- bus non vtile est nuptias diu differri. Sata-nas enim interea zizania potest serere , & concordes discordes facere. Recte quoque & prudenter à veteribus constitutum est, vt noui coniuges publicè in sacris cœtibus à ministro ecclesiæ copulentur. Nam hac re testamur, Coniugium rem sanctam, non opus tenebrarum esse, cuius nos pudere debeat. Accedunt etiam aliæ vtilitates. Videmus enim, quinà legitimi sint coniuges, qui non. Hoc etiam incitat coniuges ad coniugalem fidem mutuò seruandam, quod in sacro cœtu, præeunte ecclesiæ ministro, id verbis & data manu promiserunt. Adhæc to ta ecclesia apud Deum intercedit ac precatur, vt coniugium felix sit & saustum: de quo nos cum plura ad 4. cap. Ruth. homil. 23. & 24. dederimus, hoc loco breuiores sumus.
units.tr: When Abigail had said these things, she immediately set out. Mounted on her donkey and accompanied by five maidservants, she followed David's messengers, and she became his wife. She does not keep David waiting long, but promptly makes known what she has decided. She does not weigh the time or David's circumstances, nor the power and fury of Saul. She considers only God's promise, that David would not be forsaken, and she does not doubt it. She knew that he, in his exile, would be in great need of help. What is said of gifts, that he gives twice who gives quickly, may fitly be applied to answers given in due time. So she replies promptly, and seizing the opportunity offered, as they say, with both hands, she follows David's messengers and marries him. Once the betrothal is concluded, it is not useful for the wedding to be long delayed, for Satan may meanwhile sow tares and turn the agreeing into the disagreeing. The ancients also rightly and wisely ordained that new spouses be joined publicly in the sacred assembly by a minister of the Church. For by this we bear witness that marriage is a holy thing, not a work of darkness, of which we ought to be ashamed. There are other advantages as well. For we see who are lawfully married and who are not. This also urges spouses to keep faithfulness to one another, since in the sacred assembly, with the minister of the Church leading, they have promised this in words and by the giving of hands. Besides, the whole Church intercedes and prays before God that the marriage may be happy and prosperous. Since we have treated this at greater length on Ruth 4, Homilies 23 and 24, we are briefer here.

units.la: Obseruandum quoq; est, Abigaelem no- stram quinque pedísequas secum assumsisse. Honestæ enim fœminæ non debent facile solæ in publicum prodire, vel longo itineri se dare, nisi comites se inferant honestæ. Nihil enim est fama & existimatione fœminarum tenerius, aut magis iniuriæ obnoxiû, vt non immeritò de filo araneæ pendere videri possit. Porrò, maledicto (vt Cicero ait) nihil est magis volucre, nihil facilius emittitur, nihil citius excipitur,nihil lati9 dissipatur. Quod si semel hæsit in fœmina ex hominum existi mationibus nota aliqua,sempiterna ferè per durat:nec eluitur,nisi maximis pudicitiæ & sapientiæ ostensis argumentis. Hinc Sufan- na non minus sanctitate, quàm forma exi- mia prædita,cum in pomario domus suæ la uare cuperet,duas pedisequas assumit. Sed & Homerus Penelopem suam in consessum procorum descendisse canit:sed non solam, verum duabus comitatam probis ancillis, cum tamen domæ suæ esset & Telemachus filius inter procos sederet, iam tum ado- lescens.
units.tr: It should also be noted that Abigail took five maidservants with her. For honourable women ought not to go out in public alone, or undertake a long journey, unless honourable attendants go with them. Nothing is more delicate than a woman's reputation and good name, or more open to injury, so that it may not undeservedly seem to hang by a spider's thread. Moreover, as Cicero says, nothing is more winged than slander, nothing is more easily sent forth, nothing more quickly received, nothing more widely spread. If any stain from men's opinions once sticks to a woman, it lasts almost forever, and it is not washed away unless the greatest proofs of chastity and wisdom are shown. Hence Susanna, endowed no less with holiness than with exceptional beauty, when she wished to wash in the orchard of her house, took two maidservants with her. And Homer sings that his Penelope came down to the assembly of suitors, but not alone; she was accompanied by two worthy maids, although she was in her own house and her son Telemachus sat among the suitors, already grown up at that time.

units.la: In genere ex hoc exemplo discere debent nostræ mulieres,animi submissionem & erga maritos obseruantiam,vt contra ex histo ria Vasthi reginæ fugere superbiam & inso- lentiam.Inuenias,quæ maritos propter for- mam,diuitias,genus despiciant. Non ita A- bigael:quæ,vt forma & animi & corporis in signi esset,Nabalem tamen,hominem moro sum & difficilem,amat,nullumq; obsequen- tis coniugis officium prætermittit. Dauid em itidem obseruat, & se ad infima etiam officia offert,videlicet ad lauandos pedes fa mulorum ipsius.Multæ nec seruitia,quibus in administranda re familiari carere facilè non possumus, sustinere possunt.
units.tr: From this example, our women ought to learn in general a submissive spirit and obedience toward their husbands, and, on the other hand, from the history of Queen Vashti, to flee pride and insolence. You will find women who despise their husbands for their looks, riches, or birth. Not so Abigail, who, though outstanding in both the beauty of her mind and of her body, nevertheless loved Nabal, a man who was foolish and difficult, and omitted no duty of an obedient wife. David likewise showed respect, and offered himself even for the lowliest services, namely washing the feet of his servants. Many women also can endure those household tasks without which we cannot easily manage our domestic affairs.

units.la: Nec dubium est, quin, quae verbis iniuerit, ea re ipsa praestiterit. Vxores, quęrem do mesticam administrare nec possunt nec volunt, interim maritos conuitijs iurgijsq; continuis obruunt, in causa nonnunquam sunt, vt mariti domo pulsi tempestate illa, se in publicum diuersorium, tanquam tutissimum portum, ad bonos socios recipiant, quorum familiaritate corrupti, otio, puluinari satanę assuescunt, nonnunquam ad extremam paupertatem redigunturi
units.tr: Nor is there any doubt that she carried out in deed what she had promised in words. Wives who neither can nor will manage the household, meanwhile overwhelm their husbands with insults and constant quarrels, and are sometimes the cause that husbands, driven from home by that storm, take refuge in a public inn, as in the safest harbour, among good companions. Corrupted by their company, they grow accustomed to idleness and to Satan's pillow, and sometimes they are reduced to extreme poverty.

units.la: Interim mariti, vxorum promptitudine, parendiq; alacritate non abutentur: easq; ad sordidissima quæq; officia detrudant, sed liberaliter & honorifice eas tractent. Quain re meminisse oportet, Euam ab Adamo sociam appellatam esse, cum inquit: Mulier, quam dedisti mihi sociam. Cuius rei causa aliqui Patres, atq; inter hos Chrysostomus, factum esse docuerunt, vt ea non ex pedibus sed ex latere viri formaretur: quemadmodum etiam ex capite condita non est, vt se viri dominam non esse intelligeret, sed viro potius subiectam. Paulus Ephesijs scribens, vult, maritos diligere vxores suas, sicut & Christus dilexit ecclesiam, & semetipsum expósuit pro ea. Paulo infra vt sua ipsorum cor
units.tr: Meanwhile, husbands should not take advantage of their wives' readiness and eagerness to obey, and thrust them down into the most menial tasks, but should treat them generously and honourably. In this matter we ought to remember that Eve was called Adam's companion, when he said: "The woman whom you gave me as a companion." For this reason some of the Fathers, and among them Chrysostom, taught that she was not formed from the feet but from the side of the man, just as she was not made from the head, so that she might understand she was not the mistress of her husband but rather subject to him. Paul, writing to the Ephesians, wishes husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her. A little further on, Paul says that they should love their own bodies.

units.la: Officium maritorum. Gen. 3. Homi. 20. in epist. ad Ephes. Ephes. 5. Verf. 25. Verf. 28. corpora: additq;: Qui diligat vxorem suam, seipsum diligere. Petrus vero, qui haud dubie fuit blandus pater & concors maritus requirit in marito ἐπιεικίαν & iustitiam distributuam: Viri, inquit, vnà versentur κατὰ γνῶσιν id est, vt scientes decet, vasi mulieri bri, vt infirmiori, tribuentes honotem, vtpote te quum vnà etiam haeredes gratiæ vitæ sint, ne interrumpantur preces vestræ. Meminerint etiam mariti Christiani grauissimum Pythagoræ dictum, quod citat Aristoteles in Oeconomicis: Maritus debet vxori bene ficentiam & clementiam: Quia sponsa ei ad aram, vt supplex, commendatur. Iam vero non summo iure cum supplicibus, qui se totos in nostram potestatem dedunt, agendum est: sed benignè ac liberaliter habendi. Sunt enim:
units.tr: The duty of husbands. Gen. 3. Homily 20 on the Epistle to the Ephesians. Eph. 5, verse 25; verse 28: "Those who love their wives love themselves," and so on. Peter, who was doubtless a kindly father and an agreeable husband, requires in the husband ἐπιείκεια [epieikeia] and distributive justice. "Husbands," he says, "live with your wives according to knowledge [κατὰ γνῶσιν], as is fitting for those who know, giving honour to the female vessel as to the weaker, since they are also heirs together with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers are not hindered" (1 Pet. 3). Let Christian husbands also remember the very weighty saying of Pythagoras, which Aristotle cites in his Oeconomica: "A husband ought to show goodwill and mercy to his wife, because she is commended to him as a suppliant at the altar." Indeed, one should not deal with suppliants by the full rigour of the law, especially those who have given themselves wholly into our power, but treat them kindly and generously.

units.la: ἱερὸς τε καὶ ἄγγελος.
units.tr: Sacred and a messenger [ἱερὸς τε καὶ ἄγγελος].

units.la: Phrasis, quia hoc loco spiritus sanctus, An illas Abigaelis ad pedes eius ambulasse dicit, de famulis quoque Dauidis extat: Sensus est: illos summa animi alacritate & promptitudine officio suo functos esse. Quod sit seruorum munus, scriptura pasim indicat. Paulus ad Ephesios scribens: Serui, inquit, parete vel auscultate ijs, qui vestri domini sunt secundum carnem, id est, quod ad corpus & res externas attinet (Nam conscientia vnius Dei est) cum timore ac tremore, id est, cum solita reuerentia, cum simplicitate cordis vestri, vt Christo, non ad oculum seruientes, id est, vt facere solent, qui praesentibus tantum dominis obsequuntur, absentes aspernantur, aut etiam ludibrio habent, vt qui hominibus placere student: sed vt serui Christi, facientes ex animo voluntatem Dei: cum beneuolentia seruientes, vt Domino, id est, Dei voluntate & reuerentia comoti, & quasi Deo, non autem in ipsorum se hominum gratiam, &c. Eandem sententiam Col. 3. repetit, verf. 22. Ad Titum: Seruos ait, hortare, vt suis dominis subijciant se, vt in omnibus (quae sine Dei offensione praestari possunt) sint eis accepti, id est, ita se gerant, vt dominis placeant, illorum obsequia: non responsatores: nihil interuertentes, sed omnem bonam fidem ostendentes, id est, fideliter & absque vlla fraude res domini sui tractantes, &c. Petrus Famuli, inquit, subditi estote cum omni timore dominis non solum bonis & aequis, sed etiam <bl>οἰκέταις</bl>, id est, asperis & saeuis. Hoc non cedit gratiae, si quis propter conscientiam Dei, id est, quod ei sit religio Deum offendere, cuius voluntate intelligit
units.tr: The phrase is used here because the Holy Spirit says that Abigail's servants walked at her feet; the same is found of David's servants as well. The meaning is that they performed their duty with the greatest eagerness and readiness of mind. Scripture everywhere shows what the task of servants is. Paul, writing to the Ephesians: "Servants," he says, "obey those who are your masters according to the flesh," that is, in matters that concern the body and external things (for the conscience belongs to the one God), "with fear and trembling," that is, with the customary reverence and with simplicity of your heart, "as to Christ, not serving with eye-service," that is, as those do who obey their masters only when they are present and despise them when absent, or even mock them, being men-pleasers; "but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with goodwill as to the Lord," that is, moved by the will and reverence of God, "and as to God, and not to men for their favour," etc. (Eph. 6). He repeats the same sentiment in Col. 3, verse 22. To Titus: "Exhort servants," he says, "to submit themselves to their masters, to be well pleasing to them in all things (which can be done without offence to God)," that is, to behave so that they please their masters in their service; "not answering back, not pilfering, but showing all good faith," that is, faithfully and without any fraud handling their master's property, etc. (Titus 2, verse 9). Peter: "Servants," he says, "be subject with all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh and cruel [οἰκέταις]" (1 Pet. 2). This does not count as grace, if someone, for the sake of conscience toward God, that is, because it is his religious duty not to offend God, whose will he understands,

units.la: Tit. 2. verf. 9.
units.tr: Titus 2, vers. 9.

units.la: 1. Pet. 2. verf. 18. ligit hoc onus sibi impositum, suffert molestias iniustè afflictu.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 2, vers. 18. [He] understands this burden to be laid upon himself, and bears the troubles of being unjustly afflicted.

units.la: Quærat autem aliquis, cur Dauid, cum haberet antea in matrimonio Micholem & Achinoem, plures uxores, & ut in Samuele dicitur, concubinas duxerit? An verò nescie bat, se à Deo in regem vnctum, qui Deuteronom. 17. cap. disertè præcepit, ne rex plures uxores ducat? Hic respondent nonnulli Deum vetuisse, ne rex haberet magnum numerum uxorum, quod de Solomone tradunt historiæ: non autem, ne liceret habere duas, aut tres aut omnino villas. Nam in eadem lege edici, ne plures equos alat: aurique & argenti multum habeat: nec tamen inde sequi, illum nec equos complures possidere posse nec summam aliquam auri & argenti: sed in hisce rebus tenendum esse modum. Addi enim in contextu, Quæ auertant animum eius à cultu Dei. Sed simplex sensusest: Illum vna vxore debere contentum esse. Neq; id iniuria. Populus enim ingenti sumtu grauatus fuisset: quia, vt fert mulierum ambitio, regaliter omnes tractari voluissent: & certassent etiam lautitiis. Quid quod reges nimia ista vxorum copia, à negotijs regni cognoscendis auocati essent? Cum debuissent subditorum causas cognoscere, aures vxoribus dare coacti fuissent, &c. Hinc videre est, Dauidem peccasse plures vxores ducendo, nisi a Deo priuilegium singulare habuerit. Quod a vero non visq; adeo est alienum. Nathan enim, qui in reliqua illius vitia acerrime est inuectus, ei non vitio dat, quod plures vxores haberet: sed dicit, Deum illas ipsi tradidisse. Quanuis, vt quod sentio, dicam liberè, hoc argumentum non videatur satis firmum. Nam de Absolone quoque dicitur, quod Deus traditurus sit ei vxores Dauidis, qui propterea non excusatur a peccato.
units.tr: But someone may ask why David, although he had previously in marriage Michal and Ahinoam, took several wives and, as it is said in Samuel, concubines. Did he not know that he had been anointed king by God, who in Deuteronomy 17 expressly commanded that a king should not take many wives? Some answer here that God forbade a king to have a great number of wives, as the histories tell of Solomon, but not that he might not have two, or three, or indeed any at all. For in the same law it is commanded that he should not keep many horses, nor have much gold and silver; yet it does not follow from this that he may not possess several horses or some considerable sum of gold and silver, but that moderation must be kept in these things. For it is added in the context: "which would turn his heart from the worship of God." But the plain sense is: he ought to be content with one wife. Nor is this without reason. For the people would have been burdened with immense expense, since, as women's ambition brings, they would all have wanted to be treated like royalty, and would have vied with one another in luxury. And what of the fact that kings, distracted by so great a number of wives, would have been kept from attending to the affairs of the kingdom? Whereas they ought to have heard the causes of their subjects, they would have been compelled to give their ears to their wives, and so on. From this one may see that David sinned in taking several wives, unless he had a singular privilege from God. Which is not so very far from the truth. For Nathan, who inveighed most sharply against his other faults, does not charge him with fault for having several wives, but says that God had given them to him. Although, to speak freely as I think, this argument does not seem strong enough. For concerning Absalom too it is said that God would give him David's wives, and yet he is not excused from sin on that account.

units.la: Vxor eius prima, Michal nomine, id temporis illi non cohabitabat. Saulus enim ipsius pater, eam, cuidam alteri, Phalti nomine, filio Lais, Gallinensi locauerat. Dederat eam antea Dauidi non animo bono: Sed vt ille ea, tanquam laqueo, caperetur. Sperabat enim filiam suam, sibi ad hanc rem, quam parabat, operam omnem collaturam. Verum illa animo in maritum erat fideli, quō immissis speculatoribus regijs, fune per fenestram noctu dimisso, ingenio muliebri milites elusit. Sed cum videret conatus suos non succedere, filiam suam alteri collocauit: idq; duplici de causa. Primò vt Dauidi egre faceret, cumq; illum, quod maximè cupiebat, lædere non posset, læderet tamen in vxore. Dein de,cum sciret, se hoc nomine male audire, quod generum suum persequeretur, filiam suam, ex qua nullos liberos suffulerat Dauid,eripuit,vt nouis istis nuptijs,omnem illam veterem affinitatem extinguere. Sed in istis Saulus iniuftifsime sese gerit,& quantum potest,pugnat cotra Deum. Erat enim ea Dauidis,non solum iure matrimonij, sed etiam iure emtionis. Redemerat enim eam ducentis praeputijs Palaeftinorum :Deinde etiam iure promissionis. Promiserat enim eam Saulus illi, quicunque Goliadum Gethaeum, viribus & vastitate corporis confidentem interfecisset. Bis ergo nunc peccat Saulus, & quod eam eripit marito suo, & eam tradit alteri, qui eius maritus esse non potuit. Quos Deus coiunxerat, Saulus non debebat distraxisse,&c.
units.tr: Michal, his first wife, was not living with him at that time. Saul, her father, had given her to another man, Phalti, son of Laish, of Gallim. He had earlier given her to David, but not in good faith: he meant her to be a snare to catch him. For he hoped his daughter would devote all her effort to the plan he was preparing. But she was faithful to her husband in her heart. When the royal scouts were sent, she let David down through a window at night with a rope and, with womanly cleverness, eluded the soldiers. When Saul saw that his attempts were failing, he married his daughter to another man, and he did so for two reasons. First, to vex David: since he could not harm him, which he most wanted, he harmed him through his wife. Second, since he knew he was ill spoken of for persecuting his son-in-law, he took away his daughter, from whom David had had no children, so that by these new marriage ties he might wipe out that old kinship. But in this Saul acts most unjustly and, as far as he can, fights against God. For she belonged to David not only by right of marriage but also by right of purchase, since he had redeemed her with two hundred foreskins of the Philistines. She belonged to him also by right of promise, for Saul had promised her to whoever killed Goliath the Gittite, the man who trusted in his strength and bodily bulk. So Saul now sins twice: he snatches her from her husband, and he gives her to another man who could not be her husband. Saul ought not to have separated those whom God had joined together, etc.

units.la: Quanuis autem Sauli peccatum sit grauisimum, Phalti tamen etiam & Michal non leuiter peccarunt. Nam cum essetres ea pesimi exempli, non debebant vllo modo assentiri. Neque enim excusari possunt tituio bonae intentionis. Quomodo enim potuit illa habere virum non suu,& ille vicisim vxore non suam? Si Dauid ipsi nunc ium repudij remisisset, illam secundu legē repetere non potuisset. Quod si dicas:Miti-
units.tr: Although Saul's sin is most grievous, Phalti and Michal did not sin lightly either. Since the example was most pernicious, they ought in no way to have assented to it. Nor can they be excused by the plea of good intention. For how could she have a husband who was not hers, and he in turn a wife who was not his? Even if David had afterwards sent her away with a bill of divorce, he could not have taken her back according to the law. But if you say: their deed was softened

units.la: Q. 2 gari illorum factum propter tyrannidem atque impotentem Sauli ferociam: nihil dixeris. Nullo enim periculo etiam praesentisimo, adduci debemus, vt ea quae in diuino verbo honestatique aduersantur, committamus. Causis matrimoniorum non est ludendum, vt astragalis. Etsi mundo sint excusati: tamen non Deo, cui potius parendum est quam hominibus. Qui amat patrem, inquit Christus, aut matrem supra vel praeme, non est me dignus: & qui amat filium aut filiam supra me, non est me dignus, id est, mihi non est idoneus, seu conueniens. Nam alioqui nemo sane ne angelis quidem exceptis, dignus est, quem Christus pro discipulo adscisçat, vel etiam adscitum agnoscat. Apud Lucam rem amplius illustrat. Si quis venit ad me, ait, & non odit patrem suum & matrem, id est, amat supra me, & vxorem & liberos & fratres & sorores, atque adeo etiam animam suam, id est, seipsum, siue suam ipsius vitam, vt loquitur Matthaei 16. Cap. ver. 21. non poterit meus esse discipulus. Quid nostri sit officij, cum ea nobis imperantur, quae cum verbo Dei repugnant, exemplo obstetricum Aegypti, sociorum Danielis, Apostolorum, &c. docemur. Omnino eam oportuit Dauidem etiam in exsilium sequi,&c. 2.libro Samuelis tertio capite Dauid restitutus eam ab Isbosetho affine petit quod non potuisset, si fuisset repudiata. Sanc-itur enim in Deuteronomio, Si quis repudiauerit vxorem suam, eam illi postea profanam & immundam fore. Rabbini arbitrantur, istum Phalti, cum esset vir bonus & timens Dei, non attigisse Michalem: idq; ex eo maxime liquere, quod Dauid eam postea repetijt: Sed, quidquid id est, nihil de eo constare certò potest è scripturis.
units.tr: because of the tyranny and unbridled ferocity of Saul, you would be saying nothing. For no danger, however immediate, should lead us to commit what is opposed to the divine word and to honesty. Matters of marriage are not to be played with like dice. Even if we are excused before the world, we are not excused before God, to whom we must obey rather than men. "He who loves father or mother more than me," says Christ, "is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me," that is, is not fit for me, or suitable. For otherwise, to be sure, no one, not even the angels excepted, is worthy that Christ should take him as a disciple, or even acknowledge him once taken. Luke illustrates the matter more fully: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother," that is, loves them more than me, "and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own soul," that is, himself, or his own life, as it is put in Matthew 16, verse 21, "cannot be my disciple." What our duty is, when we are commanded things that conflict with the word of God, we are taught by the example of the midwives of Egypt, the companions of Daniel, the Apostles, etc. She ought altogether to have followed David even into exile, etc. In 2 Samuel, chapter 3, David, once restored, asks for her from Ishbosheth, her kinsman. He could not have done this if she had been repudiated. For it is laid down in Deuteronomy: if a man has put away his wife, she shall afterwards be profane and unclean to him. The rabbis think that Phalti, since he was a good man and feared God, did not touch Michal, and this is especially clear from the fact that David afterwards took her back. But whatever the truth is, nothing certain can be established about it from the Scriptures.

units.la: Quod ad polygamiam in genere attinet, varie & ambigue iam olim à multis disputarum est, an liceat, vno eodemque tempore, duas pluresue vxores in matrimonio habere. Verum enimuero certo certius est, polygamiam à matrimonij natura primaque institutione prorsus alienam esse. Deus enim, qui primus matrimonij author est, primosque coniuges, Adamum nempe & Euam parentes nostros coniunxit, Adami ipsius ore hanc legem coniugalem pronuncia-uit: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis. Propter hoc relinquet homo, patrem & matrem, & adhærebit vxori suæ, & erunt duo in carne vnam, hoc est, ita coalescent, vt sint vna caro. Adamo vnam tantum vxorem, non plures locauit. Secundum istā legem primi patres,Sethus,Enos,& alij matrimonia contra xerunt. Quisque vxorem legitimam in matrimonio habuit, ex qua liberos sustulit. Primus, qui duorum animorum coniunctione, quam inter virum atq; fœminam Deus constituerat, in plures amores diuulgauit, vnoque tempore, contra decretum diuinum, duas vxores petulanter duxit, Lamechus fuit homicida, qui à Caino fratricida ortum traxit. Post diluuium Sara annis & sterilitate emortua, propter spem promissionis Abrahamo iancillam despondet, prolis causa: Deus enim illi inter multas exsuliorum ærumnas, aliquoties hanc promissionem repetierat, de ipsius videlicet femine eum pro diturum, in quo sint benedicendi omnes populi terrarum. Sed & Iacobus duas vxores eodem tempore in matrimonio habuisse legitur, non libidinis explendæ causa: sed quod ab auunculo suo, qui eum propter fidem & diligentiam generum legerat, non tam in mercede numeranda, quam collocanda filia fraudauerat. Atque hæc ante legem à Mose latam accidere. Exinde de Helcana quoque obseruatore legis Dei diligenti, proditum est memoriæ, cum Peninam & Hannam eodem tempore vxores habuisse.
