Ac tam abest, vt hæc coniugia culparit Deus, vt etiam forfortunauerit.Hucadde,quodDeus,cumin Deut.cauéret nominatim,de boue cornupe ta,de excusso dente.deq; omnibus rebus leuisimis,nihil vnquá cauit de polygamia: Imò contra ex ἐπιθέσει videri potest polygamiá permittere.Nā ca.21.Deut.ita statuit: Si quis habeat duas vxores,alterá dilectam, alteram odiosam,ne filium dilectæ præferat odiosæ. Quanquam hic locus non multum probat.Poterat enim altera vxor esse repudiata.Ac quod ad Patrū exempla attinet,nō sequitur:Si hæc patribus licuere,licent etiá nobis. Multa enim de patribus habentur in sacris literis, quæ non sunt à nobis in exemplum trahenda. Deus illis certis de causis multa concessit, quæ nobis sunt interdicta. Si quid collapsum videamus in matrimonio id reuocandum est ad primum ἀρχέτυπον. Alia tempora alios mores postulant.Patriarchæ non libidinis saturandæ causa, sed necessitate polygamiam sectati sunt.D.Augustinus quodam in loco dicit, illos ideo plures simul vxores duxisse, vt propagando mundo sufficerent.De Iudæis dicitur,quod cum ex Babylonica captiuitate in patriam redijssent, nonnulli etiam ex sacerdotibus & Leuitis,repudiatis vxoribus iam vetulis, iuuenculas forma præstantes induxerint.
units.tr: As for polygamy in general, it has long been disputed by many in various and ambiguous ways whether it is lawful to have two or more wives in marriage at one and the same time. Yet it is more certain than certain that polygamy is wholly alien to the nature and first institution of marriage. For God, who is the first author of marriage, joined the first spouses, Adam and Eve, our parents, and through Adam's own mouth he pronounced this marriage law: "This now is bone of my bones. For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh," that is, they shall so cleave together that they are one flesh. He gave Adam one wife only, not several. According to this law the first fathers, Seth, Enos and the others, contracted marriages. Each had one lawful wife in marriage, by whom he had children. The first man who, departing from the union of two souls which God had established between man and woman, spread himself among several loves, and at one time, against the divine decree, wantonly took two wives, was Lamech, a murderer, who traced his descent from Cain the fratricide. After the Flood, Sarah, worn out by age and barrenness, betrothed her maidservant to Abraham for the sake of offspring, because of the hope of the promise. For God, amid the many hardships of his exile, had several times repeated this promise to him: that he would bring forth from his own seed the one in whom all the peoples of the earth would be blessed. But it is also read that Jacob had two wives in marriage at the same time, not for the sake of satisfying lust, but because his uncle, who had chosen him as a son-in-law for his faith and diligence, had cheated him, not so much over the wages to be counted out as over the giving of his daughter. And these things happened before the law was given by Moses. Afterwards, it is also recorded in memory that Elkanah, a diligent keeper of God's law, had Peninnah and Hannah as wives at the same time. And God is so far from condemning these marriages that he even blessed them with fruitfulness. Add to this that God, when in Deuteronomy he cautioned by name about the goring ox, the knocked-out tooth, and all the very slight matters, never gave any caution about polygamy. On the contrary, from the context it can seem that he permits polygamy. For in Deuteronomy chapter 21 he lays down: "If a man has two wives, one loved and the other hated, he shall not prefer the son of the loved wife to the son of the hated." Yet this passage proves little, for the other wife could have been put away. As for the examples of the fathers, it does not follow that if these things were permitted to the fathers, they are permitted to us also. For many things are recorded of the fathers in the sacred writings which are not to be taken by us as examples. God for certain reasons granted them many things that are forbidden to us. If we see anything fallen in marriage, it must be brought back to the first archetype. Other times demand other customs. The patriarchs followed polygamy not for the sake of sating lust but out of necessity. Saint Augustine says in a certain place that they took several wives at once so that they might suffice for populating the world. It is said of the Jews that when they returned to their homeland from the Babylonian captivity, some of the priests and Levites also, having put away their wives who were now old, took in young women outstanding in beauty.

units.la: Quo nomine cum eos Maleachus propheta rum vltimus, acriter obiurgaret. Annon, inquiunt,vnus fecit?hoc est:Annon Abraha mus,qui est vnus ille pater generis,dedit no bis exemplū? Quod ipsi tanto spiritu prædi to,licuit,nobis non liceret? Sed quid Pro-pheta? Quid vnus?inquit,quæpeнs semen Dei?Sensus est:Longè aliud fuit propositū sanƈto isti viro,quàm vt libidini suæ indulge ret.Quærebat enim semen illud sanƈtū, cui-spes propter sterilitate vxoris,proueƈtamq; ætate erat ablata. Potuit igitur error Abra-hami excusari, cum finis eius reƈtus fuerit.
units.tr: For this reason Malachi, the last of the prophets, sharply rebuked them. "Did not one," they say, "do this?" That is: did not Abraham, who is that one father of the race, give us an example? If he, endowed with such a great spirit, was permitted, why should it not be permitted to us? But what does the Prophet say? "What of the one? Why, he sought a godly seed." The sense is: that holy man had a purpose far different from indulging his lust. For he sought that holy seed, whose hope had been taken away by his wife's barrenness and her advanced age. Therefore the error of Abraham could be excused, since his end was right.

units.la: Sed quid opus est, longiorem hac de re di-sputationem instituere, cum Christus ipse totam hanc causam decidat.Enimuerò,cum Pharifæi illū,tentandi gratia,interrogarent, Liceat ne homini dimittere vxorem quauis ex causa?Non legistis,inquit, opificem abi-nitio fecisse masculum & fœminam ? Et di-xisse, Propterea relinquet homo patrem& matrem,& agglutinabitur vxori suæ, & qui duo,erunt caro vna,&c. Ac deinde subiun-git : Itaq; non amplius sunt duo sed vna ca-ro.Quibus verbis planū fecit,matrimonium itaà Deo institutum esse,vt duorū tantū,nō pluriū coiunƈtione,definiretur.Quid enim? Non plu-
units.tr: But why should we go on at length about this matter, when Christ himself settles the whole question? When the Pharisees, to test him, asked whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause, he answered: "Have you not read that the Maker, from the beginning, made them male and female, and said, 'For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,' etc.? And he adds: 'So they are no longer two but one flesh.'" By these words he made it plain that marriage was so instituted by God as to be defined by the union of two only, not of many. For what? Not more-

units.la: Note: the margin notes read "Malach.2.", "Expónitur locu Matthei 19.", "Genef.1. verf.14.", "Genef.2. verf.24."
units.tr: Notes in the margin: "Malach. 2.", "The passage of Matthew 19 is explained.", "Gen. 1, verse 14.", "Gen. 2, verse 24."

units.la: Non plures, inquit Christus, fœminas fecit, quas Adamus pro suo arbitrio permutaret: nec etiam ad vnius mulieris libidinem exsaturandam plures viros creauit: sed Adamo, qui vnus & solus erat, Euam quoque vnicam, ex costa ipsius formatam, coniunxit: & duos hosce mutuo & indiuulfo amore sibi inuicem adhærere iussit. Et quia coniugium ita instituit Deus, tanta illius seruandi religio esse debet, vt homo, parentibus quoque relictis, vxori suæ agglutinari debeat, adeo, vt qui prius duo homines erant, nunc in vnam quodammodo carnem, id est, in vnam personam vel vnum corpus coalescant, cuius vna & eadem voluntas, idem vtrinque amor, & idem sit erga suum comparem gratificandi studium. Sed & Paulus, propter fornicationes, ait, suam quisque vxorem habeto (non vxores plures) & propriam quaeque virum habeto. Dialectici autem optime id definierunt esse proprium, quod vni, sem per & soli conuenit. Iam & hoc constat, Coniugium mysterium esse fœderis inter Christum & Ecclesiam: Diligit autem Christus vnam Ecclesiam & solam, omnibus aliis sectis & populis impijs exclusis: Ergo etiam Maritus vnam vxorem, eamq; solam, diligere & complecti debet. Præterea Impp. legi bus Polygami infamia notantur. C. de incestis & inutilibus nuptijs l.2. Neminem,qui, &c.Adhæc Concilio Eliberino, quod etiam citatur 31.9. ca. de ijs, decernitur,ne Clerici huiusmodi nuptijs benedicant. Idem habetur Extra de secundis nuptijs,lege 1.Postremò naturalis ratio & experientia ostendit, non modò pacem domesticam in Polygamia conseruari non posse, verum etiam alia infinita incommoda sequi: Quæ insigni & planè rhetoricè ornata sententia describit Euripides in Andromacha. Versus inter alios hi sunt:
units.tr: Christ says that God did not make many women for Adam to exchange at his pleasure, nor did he create many men to satisfy the lust of one woman. Rather, he joined to Adam, who was one and alone, one Eve also, formed from his rib, and he commanded these two to cleave to each other in mutual and undivided love. Since God so instituted marriage, its preservation must be held in such reverence that a man, leaving even his parents, should cleave to his wife, so that those who were before two men now coalesce, in a sense, into one flesh, that is, one person or one body, having one and the same will, the same love on both sides, and the same eagerness to please their partner. Paul too says, "Because of fornications, let each man have his own wife (not wives in the plural), and let each woman have her own husband." The logicians have defined a property, quite rightly, as that which belongs to one alone and always and to no other. Again it is agreed that marriage is a mystery of the covenant between Christ and the Church. Christ loves one Church and only one, all other sects and impious peoples being excluded; therefore a husband too should love and embrace one wife, and her only. Moreover, the imperial laws brand polygamy with infamy (C. on incestuous and invalid marriages, law 2, "No one who..."). In addition, the Council of Elvira, which is also cited at Decretum 31, distinction 9, chapter "On those", decrees that clergy must not bless such marriages. The same is found in Extra, On second marriages, law 1. Lastly, natural reason and experience show that polygamy not only cannot preserve domestic peace but also brings in its train countless other troubles. Euripides, in Andromache, describes these with a striking and thoroughly rhetorical sentiment. Among other lines are these:

units.la: — ὦ δὴ ϗ̣ὸ καλὸν, inquit,ἄνδρα γυναῖκα ... ἀλλ' εἰς μίαν βλέπουσα συμφορὰν ... ἐργάτιν, ὅς τις μὴ κακῶς οἰκεῖν θέλει.
units.tr: "Oh, what a fine thing," he says, "a husband and a wife ... but looking upon one misfortune ... a worker, whoever does not wish to live badly." [ὦ δὴ τὸ καλὸν, ἄνδρα γυναῖκα ... ἀλλ' εἰς μίαν βλέπουσα συμφορὰν ... ἐργάτιν, ὅς τις μὴ κακῶς οἰκεῖν θέλει.]

units.la: In Phormione senex Chremes cum uxorem haberet Athenis diuitem & aliam ducere vellet in Lemno, cogebatur mutare nomen, & se Stilphonem appellare. Nisi enim ita fecisset, fortasse secunda illa Lemnienfis illi non nupsisset. Imò Chremes à parasito Phormione accusatur de Polygamia, quasi de graui crimine. Ex quibus omnibus constare arbitror, simpliciter non licere Polygamiam. Qui plura hac de re cupit, legat P. Martyrem ad hunc locum:Et est copiose de toto hoc argumento disputatum tota 32. quæst.4.Item ab Augustino lib.1.de nuptijs, cap.13.14.&c.
units.tr: In Terence's Phormio, the old man Chremes, who had a rich wife at Athens and wished to take another at Lemnos, was forced to change his name and call himself Stilpho. For unless he had done so, perhaps the Lemnian second wife would not have married him. Indeed, Chremes is accused of polygamy by the parasite Phormio as though of a grave crime. From all these things I think it is established that polygamy is simply not lawful. Whoever desires more on this matter should read Peter Martyr on this passage; the whole argument is also disputed at length in Decretum, cause 32, question 4; likewise in Augustine, On Marriage, book 1, chapters 13, 14, etc.

units.la: Etsi vero Deus certis de caussis viris indulsit, plures vt vno tempore vxores haberent: vxor tamé plures maritos habere non poterat; nec est vnquam factitatum, ac ne inter Ethnicos ipsos, vti docet Augustinus de bono coniugij cap.17.Forte,ne proles dubia redderetur.Sed & hæreditates dissipatę fuissent & confusæ: multæque aliæ infequutæ absurditates,&c.
units.tr: Although God, for certain reasons, indulged men so that they might have several wives at one time, a wife could not have several husbands. Nor has this ever been done, not even among the heathen themselves, as Augustine teaches in On the Good of Marriage, chapter 17. Perhaps this was so that offspring should not be rendered doubtful. But also inheritances would have been squandered and confused, and many other absurdities would have followed.

units.la: Nonnulli historiā istam de Dauide & Nabale ἀλληγορικῶς exponunt. Dauid eiusq; milites in exilium pulsi cum fame colluctantur: Sic, qui Christo vera fide adhærescunt, hodie quoque auitus sedibus expulsi, omni afflictionum genere exercentur. Dauid per legatos à Nabale cibaria petit,qui, ipsi, heri fui nomine fausta precatur:omnia: Christus legatos suos ad mundum,Nabalis more desipientem mittit, studiumq; ipsi deferens veniuersum,ab illo nihil præter fructum pœnitentia dignum exigit.Nabal tenax, crudelis & sordidus, legatis Dauidis non solum commeatum negat, verum etiam contumeliam verborum addit, & Dauidem tribulé suum, tamq; fugitiuum & perduellem vituperat: Mundus legatis Christi tàm abest,vt aliquid largiatur, vt illis sua quoq; per vim auferat: Adhæc schismaticos,hæreticos, rebelles, sacrilegos ad rauim vociferatur. Dauid, etsi coftituiffet, Nabalem totamq; eius domum ferro euertere,& videbatur iustam iræ causam habere, tùm quod rex effet, tùm quod greges Nabalis defendisset:tamen cum inter ueniret deprecatrix Abigael, abiecto profusus de vindicta consilio Nabali parcit. Ita Deus,cum Ecclesia (quam sanctorum communionem definit symbolum) fit deprecatrix, mundo parcit: ac mauult vt innumerabiles impij viuant, quàm vt vel vnus pius vnà cum illis pereat. Maior est Dei in vnum pium amor, quàm in omnes impios odium, quem quidem eius amorem debent imitari pij. Tandem, Nabale nihil minus expectante,percusso: Abigael seruata, Dauidi in matrimonium collocatur : Ita Ecclesia Christi calamitatibus hisce mundanis erepta, Christo vero animarum sponso adducitur. Verùm, vt Deus Nabalem non externis armis, sed spiritu suo configit : Ita eos omnes, qui Dauidem,id est,Iesum Christum ftoccipendunt,spiritu oris fui,nec inopinantes, confectos,è medio tollet.
units.tr: Some expound this story of David and Nabal allegorically. David and his men, driven into exile, struggle with hunger; so those who cling to Christ with true faith, today too, driven from their ancestral seats, are exercised by every kind of affliction. David sends envoys to Nabal to ask for provisions, and Nabal, in the manner of a fool, answers them. Christ sends his envoys into the world, to men who are foolish like Nabal, bringing them his whole goodwill, and from them he demands nothing but fruit worthy of repentance. Nabal, stingy, cruel and sordid, not only refuses the envoys of David their supplies but adds insulting words and reviles David as a runaway, a rebel and a traitor. The world is so far from giving anything to the envoys of Christ that it even seizes their goods by force; moreover, it bawls out that they are schismatics, heretics, rebels and sacrilegious. David, though he had resolved to overthrow Nabal and his whole house with the sword, and seemed to have a just cause for anger, both because he was king and because he had defended Nabal's flocks, nevertheless, when Abigail came between as an intercessor, he abandoned his plan of vengeance and spared Nabal. So God, when the Church (which the creed defines as the communion of saints) intercedes, spares the world; and he prefers that countless wicked men should live rather than that one godly man should perish along with them. God's love for one godly man is greater than his hatred of all the wicked, and the godly ought to imitate this love. At last, Nabal being struck down when he least expected it, Abigail was saved and was given in marriage to David. So the Church of Christ, snatched from these worldly calamities, is brought to Christ, the spouse of souls. But just as God struck down Nabal not with external arms but with his own Spirit, so he will take out of the way, by the breath of his mouth and unexpectedly, all those who despise David, that is, Jesus Christ.

units.la: Quamuis autem allegoriæ nonnunquam locum suum habeant. (Multas enim historias allegoricè quoque exponendas esse ex Christi & Apostolorum verbis colligitur, Ioan.3. & 6.1.Cor.10.1. Petri 3.) tamen non prius ad illas descendemus, quàm excussa fuerint, primum quæ ad sensum grammaticum, deinde quæ ad moralem, siue (vt Apostolus loquitur) {ωεῖς παιδείαν} spectant. Quamuis nec semper nec temerè: sed tunc tantùm, cum vel cogit aliqua orationis necessitas, vel suadet singularis auditorum vtilitas. Vtrunq; quomodo contingat, elegantér in Theologo suo Hyperius ostendit, qui inter cætera scitè, Improbandum quidem est, inquit, nolle vsquam vltra sensum grammaticum progredi: at multò improbandum vehementius, velle vbique & quauis occasione ad allegoricas interpretationes convolare.
units.tr: Although allegories sometimes have their place (for it is gathered from the words of Christ and the Apostles that many histories are also to be expounded allegorically: John 3 and 6, 1 Cor. 10, 1 Peter 3), nevertheless we shall not descend to them before the matters which pertain first to the grammatical sense and then to the moral sense, or, as the Apostle puts it, [ὠφέλιμος πρὸς παιδείαν] "profitable for instruction", have been thoroughly examined. Nor should this be done always or rashly, but only when some necessity of the discourse compels it or the particular usefulness of the hearers recommends it. How both may happen, Hyperius elegantly shows in his Theology, where among other wise remarks he says: "It is certainly to be disapproved to refuse ever to go beyond the grammatical sense; but much more strongly to be disapproved is the wish to rush into allegorical interpretations everywhere and on any occasion."
